course_name: Advanced Placement English Literature and Composition
description:
The primary goal of this class is to help students become independent thinkers, readers, and writers through college-level material and assignments. The course requirements are aligned with the curricular requirements described in the AP English Literature Course Description. Any students who are willing to put forth the time and effort to meet these requirements may enroll in the class. However, they must rise to meet the requirements of the course.

Students engage in close, active reading of a variety of works, ranging in era and genre. All reading assignments include annotating, journalizing, or note-taking. Students are frequently required to participate in and/or lead both small group and whole-class discussions on topics related to their readings. The topics include but are not limited to the way in which literary elements such as diction, detail, imagery, figurative language, syntax, etc., help convey tone which aids in unveiling the work's meaning as a whole. In facilitating the search for the meaning of a work, students are required to acknowledge and discuss the time period in which the work was written and the background of the author.

Writing is a major part of the class. The focus is on analytic responses to literature, emphasizing how the author's choices of literary and rhetorical devices (parallel structure, imagery, repetition, allusion, apostrophe, symbolism, figurative language, etc.) convey the work's meaning. However, students also write critical essays in which they support their judgments about a work's social and cultural value. In addition, students write fiction; poetry, both original and imitative; and character pieces in which students assume the voice and point of view of a character from a work of literature. Though the AP Exam is optional, some class time is devoted to exam practice and strategies.
notes: Requirements: Summer reading of four assigned literary works and an essay for each are due the first day of class in the fall. Description continues on p.13.

description: Creative Writing introduces students to the four genres of creative writing: creative nonfiction, fiction, poetry, and playwriting. Through reading examples of and writing in these four genres, students will discover that each genre differs greatly in purpose, form, audience, and presentation. They will also see that all four genres share properties endemic to any creative expression. Therefore, a writer should never say they are solely a poet, a novelist, essayist, memoir writer, or playwright.
This course is a continuation of Creative Writing, and involves a more in-depth exploration of writing as creative expression.

description: Explore the power of storytelling across mediums in this engaging course that pairs classic literature with its most compelling film adaptations. Students will examine how themes, characters, and conflicts translate from page to screen, analyzing what changes, what stays the same, and why these stories continue to resonate. Through discussion, comparison, and critical analysis, students will deepen their understanding of both literature and film as art forms.

Have you ever had a great idea for a product, brand, or business, but didn’t know how to get started? In this class, you’ll learn how to turn your ideas into action through the power of writing and communication, combining entrepreneurial thinking with practical writing skills. You'll build a brand, pitch your vision, and communicate effectively like a professional.

Throughout the semester, you’ll develop a business idea, craft compelling written content, and create your website using Google Sites. You’ll write resumes, product descriptions, social media posts, pitch emails, personal bios, and more—all while learning how to tell a story that gets people to listen, click, and invest. The course will also introduce the basics of branding, audience analysis, persuasive techniques, and digital storytelling.

Whether you want to start a business, build a personal brand, or just become a sharper, more confident communicator, this course will help you write your way into the real world.

course_name: Senior English Project: Voice, Choice, and Reflection
description:
This English course is designed to give students the freedom to explore, create, and express their voice as they prepare for life beyond high school. In Senior Seminar, students choose what matters to them. Through independent projects, self-directed reading, and real-world writing tasks, students will shape their learning journey while developing the communication, critical thinking, and storytelling skills necessary for success in the world ahead.

Students will:
• ● Design and complete independent inquiry projects on topics they care about
• ● Choose readings that inspire or challenge them
• ● Write in a variety of genres—college essays, persuasive letters, blog posts, spoken word, op-eds, or podcasts
• ● Collaborate with peers to share feedback and build a supportive, creative community
• ● Create a final portfolio that reflects student identity, interests, and growth as writers and thinkers

Whether students are preparing for college, career, or creative life, this course will help them take ownership of their ideas and tell their story with power and authenticity.

Final Project: A passion-driven, research-informed, or creative capstone project, along with a curated writing portfolio.

4. Statistical inference: confirming models.

The course focuses on the relationships and interactions among the organ systems that maintain balance (homeostasis) by responding to internal and external stimuli. Dissections, labs, and case studies are integral to this course. This course is ideal for students interested in human medicine, veterinary science, allied health, and the biological sciences.

description: AP Biology provides a rigorous, college-level exploration of the natural world, specifically designed to mirror the introductory curriculum for university biology majors. Moving beyond simple memorization, students cultivate a deep conceptual understanding of life’s governing processes through four "Big Ideas": Evolution, Energetics, Information Storage and Transmission, and Systems Interactions. Through a combination of multimedia resources and an inquiry-based laboratory program that meets College Board requirements, students will investigate key topics including biochemistry, cell structure and communication, genetics, and ecology. This course challenges students to think critically and master advanced lab techniques, effectively preparing them for the AP Exam, offering the chance to earn college credit while exploring how biological systems interact. This course is ideal for students interested in future study in the STEM, biological sciences, and allied health careers.

description: This full-year elective course explores the wonder of matter and energy. Students will engage in investigations of the microscopic world of atoms and molecules and the macroscopic properties of chemical systems. Chemistry expands students’ current science knowledge and methods learned in their physical and biological sciences. Emphasis is placed on the strategies needed for critical scientific thinking. Topics include gasses, atomic and nuclear structure, periodic properties, chemical reactions, chemical bonding, molecular structure, intermolecular forces, acids and bases, and electrochemistry. Two separate lab periods a week are part of this course.

Algebraic skill and an understanding of basic trigonometry are important for success, but principles will be represented in non-mathematical models as well. Lab experiments and projects are an integral part of the course as they illustrate the process of scientific discovery. Topics include kinematics, Newtonian motion, light, sound, electricity, and astronomy.

description: Food Science explores the fascinating intersection of chemistry, biology, and nutrition through the everyday lens of what we eat. Students investigate how ingredients interact, how cooking transforms food on a molecular level, and how science drives the development of safe, nutritious, and appealing products. Through hands-on labs, sensory evaluations, and small research projects, learners gain practical skills in experimentation, critical thinking, and food preparation. This course is ideal for students curious about culinary arts, health, or STEM fields, and offers a deeper understanding of the science behind the foods we enjoy.
prerequisites: 9th grade science and a willingness to prepare and consume a variety of foods.

description: Materials in Motion invites students to explore how the physical world shapes creative expression. Blending materials science with art studio creations, this course examines how the structure, properties, and behavior of materials influence the way artists design, build, and innovate. Students investigate metals, polymers, ceramics, composites, and emerging smart materials through hands‑on labs and creative projects, learning how factors like strength, flexibility, conductivity, and optical properties open new artistic possibilities.
prerequisites: 9th grade science and a willingness to create and engineer ceramic, glass, and metal designs.

description: Forensic Science explores the fascinating intersection of biology, chemistry, and law through the investigative lens of the modern crime lab. Students investigate how scientists process a crime scene, how physical evidence like DNA can identify a suspect, and how technical data drives the pursuit of justice. Through hands-on labs in blood spatter analysis, toxicology, and mock crime scene investigations, learners gain practical skills in evidence collection and microscopic analysis. As a Flexible Pathway course, students develop key transferable skills in inquiry and communication. A cornerstone of this experience is Professional Field Engagement, where students meet with and interview experts in law enforcement, the legal system, or medical forensics. These interactions allow students to bridge the gap between classroom simulations and the high-stakes reality of criminal justice. This course is ideal for students curious about medical science or law, offering a personalized roadmap for exploring careers in the forensic field.
prerequisites: Biology (completed or taken concurrently)
notes: This course explores mature and sensitive topics, including violent crime, forensic pathology, and crime scene evidence. Students will engage with graphic visual materials and participate in labs involving simulated biological evidence. Described as a Flexible Pathway course.

description: One Health: Animals, Habitats, and Medicine explores the vital connection between animal healthcare, wildlife management, and global biodiversity. Students investigate the biological needs and welfare of a diverse range of species, from companion pets and equine athletes to livestock and exotic wildlife. Through "medical detective" case studies, learners develop practical skills in physical exams, diagnostic imaging, and health assessments while shifting focus toward holistic animal well-being and ethical care. This Flexible Pathway course prioritizes student agency, allowing individuals to customize their experience through self-directed research or community-based projects—whether they are mastering patient care protocols for veterinary assisting, exploring equine stable management, or collaborating with conservationists on local habitat initiatives. By merging clinical science with advocacy, students build a personalized roadmap toward careers as veterinarians, vet techs, game wardens, or professional animal caretakers.
prerequisites: Biology (completed or taken concurrently).

description: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the foundational principles, structures, and processes of American government and political life, focusing on the rights and responsibilities of informed citizenship. Through the exploration of the U.S. Constitution, the Bill of Rights, and key Supreme Court decisions, students will analyze the framework of federalism and the functions of the legislative, executive, and judicial branches. We will examine historical and contemporary political issues, engage in civil discourse, and develop critical thinking skills necessary to evaluate media, participate in the democratic process, and effectively advocate for their beliefs as engaged members of their community and society.

description: This course is designed to provide students with an in-depth look at American history during the twentieth century. Students will study the factors that transformed the United States into a modern nation including economic development, military action, social change, and political ideals. This thematic approach will give students the opportunity to discover the evolution of these factors that have created the country they live in today. Students will read and analyze the text and a variety of primary documents. The course will also emphasize critical thinking, class discussion, and analytical writing.
fulfills_text: A U.S. History course is required for all AMHS students.
notes: Catalog heading includes '(Standard & Honors)': one record covers both levels.

description: This course examines the pivotal events, transformative movements, and profound connections that shaped global society during the 20th century. Beginning with the causes and consequences of World War I, students will trace the rise and fall of totalitarian regimes, the devastating impact of World War II, and the subsequent ideological conflict of the Cold War. The curriculum will also cover critical topics such as decolonization, independence movements in Asia and Africa, the development of modern technology, globalization, and the ongoing struggles for human rights, encouraging students to analyze historical evidence and consider diverse perspectives.

This course will focus on using critical thinking as we look at major, controversial moments in United States History. Prior to the history we will be discussing, we will be taking a deep, analytical look at defining the term “conspiracy theories”, discussing why Americans have become so interested in the concept, and the issues and dangers surrounding belief in these theories. Through reading, writing, watching, and discussing the class will take an analytical look at moments that have changed the United States. Topics will include: the use of spies throughout US History, Aaron Burr’s attempted coup, Confederados, numerous assassinations (MLK/Malcolm X/JFK), Project MK Ultra, Project Paperclip and the use of Nazi and Japanese science after the Second World War, among numerous other issues and complicated events through United States History.

The course will provide the students with the historical background of the field of philosophy. Content will include the major historical philosophers and the evolution of philosophical ideas. Students will be engaged in class discussions to evaluate the proposals of past philosophers and to also defend their own views on the major topics. Students will use an online college-level text in order to get the necessary content for the course.

This course was designed to make students think deeply about a wide array of issues in the field of psychology. The class will focus mainly on the the many ways that the field of psychology impacts the individual student. Students will use an online college-level text in order to get the necessary content for the course.

This course will focus on aspects of the law and government in the United States. It will focus on the foundations of law throughout history, including the philosophical foundations and laws within ancient civilizations. Students will then interact with Constitutional, Criminal, and Civil Law in the United States and the impact it has on individuals and groups. Students will interact with secondary and primary sources, movies and documentaries, and a number of projects revolving around the different topics.

This course will look at the history of the United States through the 1960s. We’ll be looking at major political, social, military, and cultural aspects of the time period. Students will be required to read, write, analyze, and discuss numerous aspects of the 1960s through primary sources, secondary sources, and film.

This course will study the concept of “exploration” and how it was interpreted by cultures of the past. There will be a focus on cultures throughout human history that have endeavored to explore the world around them. As a class, we will conduct research on these explorative peoples and seek to find the motivations and goals of exploration.

This course will look to instill in students a desire to gain a better understanding of the world around them. Students will study the geography of the world, the US, Vermont, and Arlington. Students will learn the basic principles of features of physical geography. Students will then take their knowledge and understanding of geography to examine the effects of geography on the people and cultures that inhabit the different parts of the world.

This course will look at the history of the United States from the 1900s to modern day with a focus on major eras (Great Depression, Civil Rights Movement, or the War on Terror). The class will require analysis, synthesis, and critical thinking, with approximately 8-10 total films being watched and a 3-5 page paper due for each film. In addition, students may have to watch movies on their own time. The expectation will be that students will understand the context of the films, analyze them for numerous aspects (culture, accuracy, symbolism, etc.), and take part in discussions.

description: This course is designed in order to help students understand and gain additional knowledge about the “Crime with no Name.” This course focuses on understanding the concept and legal definition of Genocide and then researching, discussing, and writing about numerous genocides throughout world history, starting with the Age of Imperialism and moving up through the current day. During each genocide, students will research and discuss the historical context, underlying causes, the history of the event itself, and potential consequences for both the victims and the perpetrators.

description: The American Military History course will analyze the evolution and development of the American military throughout history. Students will develop skills in analysis, reading, and writing throughout the course.

description: Students are introduced to basic written and conversational Mandarin. Students are encouraged to speak Chinese and engage in performing dialogues and skits in the target language. By the end of the course, students will converse on personal matters, meeting and introducing people, ethnicity and nationality, eating, working, numbers, time expressions and shopping. Students will also be familiar with the foundations of the Chinese writing system including both pinyin Romanization and simplified characters. Through projects, students will learn about Chinese culture, festivals, food and geography. Students will also watch Chinese movies and listen to both traditional and popular Chinese music.

Chinese II is sequential to Chinese I. In this course, students further develop their language skills and cultural understanding. Students will learn how to talk about daily schedules, expressing emotions, currency, describing people and places, occupations, colors, and clothing. Students will research and discuss Chinese painting, opera, and forms of traditional Chinese literature and poetry. In addition to the textbook, we will continue to use films and music as a way of furthering our understanding of Chinese culture. Calligraphy is introduced to help students understand character formation and establish a strong foundation in the Chinese writing system. Students will be taught how to type in Chinese and assigned projects involving computers. Students will keep a journal in Chinese which they will use weekly to help build composition skills.
prerequisites: Chinese I

description: Chinese III is sequential to Chinese II. This course will help students develop deeper comprehension and the ability to express oneself effectively and appropriately in Chinese. Students will make the transition from sentence level discourse to longer, more nuanced modes of self-expression. Students in Chinese III will use Chinese as their major mode of communication during class. Topics include: making apologies, accepting gifts, discussing a trip, making offerings, talking about classes, and traveling on public transportation. Students in Chinese III will use authentic materials to improve their understanding of the language, and also begin reading short stories and poetry in Chinese in order to build up their character recognition and reading comprehension. Students will keep a journal in Chinese which they will use weekly to help build composition skills. Projects will include learning how to compose letters and cards in Chinese, researching and presenting on festivals, literature, and various other areas of student interest. Students are expected to be able to type short essays in Chinese and present in Chinese to the class on projects and research.
prerequisites: Chinese II
notes: Description continues on p.26.

description: Chinese IV is sequential to Chinese III. Students in Chinese IV will use Chinese as their major mode of communication during class. Students will watch a movie with a complete film script and be asked to read authentic Chinese stories, poems, newspapers, and other social and cultural forms of the written language. Students will continue to keep a journal and be required to compose essays each week on varying subjects. In preparation for future study of Chinese at the college level, Chinese IV begins to introduce higher-level discourse that students will need to continue to mature in their language abilities. Students will learn to travel, chat with native speakers of Chinese, express opinions, and learn how to express emotions. A heavy emphasis will be placed on practical, colloquial Chinese and more formal professional Chinese writing.

Writing, another integral part of the course, will focus on critical analysis, including expository, analytical, and argumentative essays, but creative writing opportunities will also be provided. description: In this course, students will be challenged to consider what responsibility they have – within their political, social and local spheres – to participate as active global citizens. Topics will include civic engagement, media literacy, race, gender, sexuality, class, and popular culture among others. A major component of the course is the development of critical thinking skills, bias identification and collecting reliable evidence to support opinions in regards to controversial topics as well as discussing and debating these topics intelligently while respecting other points of view.

description: ¡Bienvenidos al mundo de español! Welcome to the world of Spanish! In Spanish I will introduce the student to the Spanish-speaking world: the people, their culture and customs. Students will learn the pronunciation and basic grammatical structures of Spanish while also building vocabulary, and the comprehension of conversational Spanish by using storytelling. The stories are an essential part of our class, and they are both students produced as a class, but also introduced throughout each unit. These stories do not isolate grammatical topics, and are used to build grammatical and vocabulary foundations and overall confidence for students. Students will increase their understanding of the language and their ability to communicate through a variety of learning activities and materials, including videos, music and songs, role-plays, current events and news, computer programs and the Internet, and artistic expression.
notes: Level 3

description: ¡Tú hablas español! You speak Spanish! In Spanish II emphasis will be placed on continued development of the basic conversational skills, as well as expanding appreciation of the Hispanic culture. Students will continue to improve their Spanish primarily through the use of storytelling. Once again, as in Spanish One, these stories do not isolate grammatical topics, and are used to build grammatical and vocabulary foundations and overall confidence for students.Students will continue to work with higher level grammatical structures and vocabulary through the various learning activities and materials used in Spanish I.
prerequisites: Teacher recommendation, proficiency in Spanish I language skills.
notes: Level 3

description: ¡Trabajamos más en español! Let’s work more in Spanish! Intermediate Spanish III marks the first steps in intermediate language study. Students will have mastered basic communication skills and grammatical structures and are ready to move into more complex areas of the language. Students will continue to improve their Spanish primarily through the use of storytelling. Once again, as in Spanish One & Two, these stories do not isolate grammatical topics, and are used to build grammatical and vocabulary foundations and overall confidence for students. Confidence in speaking will be supported through student-led discussions and role plays. Reading and writing will become more of a focus, along with continued emphasis on speaking and listening. Projects and presentations will offer the students interesting avenues for expression, as well as opportunities for doing research.
prerequisites: Teacher recommendation and proficiency in language skills appropriate for this level.
notes: Level 4

description: This course is designed for freshmen. Earth Science is the study of the earth's origins, structure, and processes. It draws upon each of the three main branches of science: Physics, Chemistry, and Biology. Earth Science includes, but is not limited to: hydrology, geography, meteorology, geology, and astronomy. The course will give an introduction to the methods of science and an overview of basic physical science concepts. Topics covered include but are not limited to plate tectonics, watershed science, global climate, and the sun-earth-moon system. Students will understand and analyze the origins, interactions and relationships between and among the Earth, our solar system, and the universe as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (ESS1). Students will also understand and analyze Earth’s systems and the relationship between human activity and the earth as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (ESS2 & ESS3). The foundation level course will cover the same basic materials as the level 3 version, however it will allow for additional time on material, more hands-on instruction, and additional support throughout the class. It will also spend additional time building up the science basics before diving into specific material. Students should successfully complete Earth Science/Honors Earth Science before taking other science classes.

description: This course is designed for sophomores. Emphasis is placed on basic biology subject matter including ecology, the cell, evolution, genetics, energy, and ecology. The foundation level course will cover the same basic materials as the level 3 version, however it will allow for additional time on material, more hands-on instruction, and additional support throughout the class. It will also spend additional time building up the science basics before diving into specific material. Students that successfully complete this course will demonstrate proficiencies in the following areas: 1. Understand and analyze molecular, structural, and chemical biology as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS 1); 2. Understand and analyze the characteristics, functions, and behavioral interactions within an ecosystem as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS 2); and, 3. Understand and analyze genetics, adaptation, and biodiversity as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS 3 + LS 4).

It is a fast-paced, active, hands-on class with high expectations for students. Completion of this class with a B or better will prepare for upper level electives and for the college experience. Students that successfully complete this course will demonstrate proficiencies in the following areas: 1. Understand and analyze molecular, structural, and chemical biology as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS 1); 2. Understand and analyze the characteristics, functions, and behavioral interactions within an ecosystem as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS 2); and, 3. description: This course is designed for high-achieving, college-bound students who may intend to pursue further studies in the life science and related fields and who would like a substantial amount of laboratory experience for college entrance. Emphasis is placed on an extension of basic subject matter (including the cell, genetics, evolution, human physiology, and basic ecology) to include inductive reasoning skills and open-ended lab investigations. Students should have strong written and oral communication skills and strong math skills. Written lab reports, daily homework assignments, frequent tests and quizzes, research papers and other projects will be required. This course is generally taken after Honors Earth Science. Students that successfully complete this course will demonstrate proficiencies in the following areas: 1. Understand and analyze molecular, structural, and chemical biology as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS1); 2. Understand and analyze the characteristics, functions, and behavioral interactions within an ecosystem as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS2); and, 3. Understand and analyze genetics, adaptation, and biodiversity as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (LS3 & LS4). Students in the honors level course are expected to exceed the standard level of proficiency for the indicators of this course.
prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science.
notes: Level 4

description: This course presents a challenging introduction to chemistry. Lectures, readings, laboratory investigations and problem solving provide insight into the chemical properties of matter and the causes and effects of chemical interactions. Topics include: atomic structure, chemical reactivity, energy and entropy, equilibrium, kinetics, acid-base, oxidation-reduction and electrochemistry. Problem solving and critical thinking skills will be developed and applied. High expectations for student effort and performance make this course appropriate for college or career oriented students. Students that successfully complete this course will demonstrate proficiencies in the following areas. Students will be able to understand and analyze matter, reactions and physical systems as demonstrated through the integration of scientific and engineering practices and cross-cutting concepts (PS 1 & PS 2). Students will use the periodic table as a model to predict the relative properties of elements based on the patterns of electrons in the outermost energy level of atoms. (HS-PS1-1), construct and revise an explanation for the outcome of a simple chemical reaction based on the outermost electron state of atoms, trends in the periodic table, and knowledge of the patterns of chemical properties. (HS-PS1-2), plan and conduct an investigation to gather evidence to compare the structure of substances at the bulk scale to infer the strength of electrical forces between particles. (HS-PS1-3), and develop a model to illustrate that the release or absorption of energy from a chemical reaction system depends upon the changes in total bond energy. (HS-PS1-4).
prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology, and Algebra I (or be concurrently enrolled in Algebra I or higher.)
notes: Level 3

A major goal is to develop a new way of looking at things, problem solving and critical thinking skills. The course is meant to be challenging and teacher expectations of the student are high. Laboratory work is used to discover the nature of matter and develop chemical laboratory skills. The students will discover that algebra is part of the language of chemistry. Topical content is similar to that of General Chemistry. However, there is a greater emphasis on quantitative problem solving and application of chemical principles. This course is designed for college-bound students with a good background in mathematics, who intend to pursue a scientific or health-care focused course of study. (HS-PS1-3), and develop a model to illustrate that the release or absorption of energy from a chemical reaction system depends upon the changes in total bond energy. (HS-PS1-4). Students in the honors level course are expected to exceed the standard level of proficiency for the indicators of this course.

(MS-PS2-5).

description: Forensic Science is the application of science to those criminal and civil laws that are enforced by police agencies in a criminal justice system. It has become a comprehensive subject incorporating Biology, Chemistry, Physics, Entomology, Earth Science, Anatomy and Physiology as well as other aspects of Science. Major topics include processing a crime scene, collecting and preserving evidence, identifying types of physical evidence, organic and inorganic analysis of evidence, hair, fibers, and paint, toxicology, arson and explosion investigations, serology, DNA, fingerprints, firearms, and document analysis . The main focus of this course will be to emphasize the evidential value of crime scene and related evidence and the services of what has become known as the crime laboratory. This course combines basic theory and real laboratory experiments, using a case-study based situation for the better understanding of the students. The experiments used reinforce previously learned scientific principles rooted in Biology, Chemistry and Physics. (LS1-4, PS1-4)
prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology
notes: Level 4

description: This 1 credit course is designed for juniors and seniors who have a special interest in ocean science and marine biology. This class will only be available in the fall semester. We will investigate ocean systems and compare a variety of saltwater ecosystems to our local freshwater ecosystems (HS-LS2-4+LS2-5). Students will conduct water quality tests and learn how organisms in both habitats are specifically adapted to their environment. (HS-ESS2-4+Ess2-5) Students will grow to appreciate the biodiversity of aquatic species found in oceanic and freshwater ecosystems, and will learn that to preserve healthy aquatic ecosystems is to sustain a healthy quality of life for all. We may have a field trip opportunity to the University of New Hampshire Floating Lab program. If possible, students will board a whale watching boat equipped with scientific equipment and conduct laboratory testing of the Gulf of Maine. https://seagrant.unh.edu/coastal-floating-lab (LS2A-C, LS1A)
prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology.
offering_note: Class is only available in Fall semester
notes: Level 3/4

description: This course is designed for juniors and seniors with a solid interest in space. Students must have successfully completed Earth Science and Biology. This course will provide an in-depth study of the universe and technology utilized in studying objects in space. The course will draw upon Physics and Earth Science to develop an understanding of the laws that govern the universe.s. Topics covered include but are not limited to: planetology, cosmology, exploration of space (technology used in exploration), solar systems, deep space objects, and the search for life. Students are expected to take an active role during class time. This class has a blending of lecture and student research. Students will be expected to do research and teach their peers about what they learn.. Besides classroom work, students will complete an observational component as well as a research paper. (ESS1)
prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology
notes: Level 3

description: This course is designed for juniors and seniors who have completed earth science and biology. This course will focus on the many natural disasters humankind may face. From meteorological events such as tornadoes and hurricanes, to geological events like earthquakes, volcanoes, and landslides, the main emphasis will be on how when these phenomena are better understood people have a better chance of minimizing the impacts. The focus will be on project based learning and labs alongside class discussions on the current topic being covered. Students will gain a better understanding of the destructive forces of nature while also gaining a new lens with which to view the world. (ESS2D, ESS3B, ESS3C, ESS3D)
prerequisites: Earth Science/Honors Earth Science and Biology/Honors Biology
notes: Level 3/4

description: This course is designed to give any singer study and experience in Choral music. A wide variety of choral literature will be rehearsed and performed. In addition, the technical aspects of singing, sight singing, and working as an ensemble, will be covered. All participants must perform at all performances scheduled by the Director.
notes: Levels U, 3, and 4; Sub-heading: Music

description: Students in the courses will study a wide range of musical styles and perform music for concert band, marching band and pep band as well as solos and small ensembles. Students will receive regular individual and/or small group instruction in addition to the large ensemble rehearsals. Students are required to participate in all performances scheduled by the director. Band members are eligible to audition for District Music Festivals, as well as for the Vermont All-State Music Festival. This requires outside preparation on the part of the individual. This course is open to students able to demonstrate a strong foundation in basic literacy and performance skills on their musical instrument.
notes: Levels U, 3, and 4; Sub-heading: Music

description: Students in this course will study and perform music from the jazz repertoire, including swing, blues, funk, and latin styles. Students will learn music theory and aural skills while developing the necessary improvisation skills central to the jazz tradition. This course is open to students able to demonstrate a strong foundation in basic literacy and performance skills on their musical instrument.
notes: Level U; Sub-heading: Music

description: Students in this course will study and perform popular music from recent decades, including rock, pop, reggae, hip-hop, rhythm & blues, country, electronic dance music, and other emerging styles. Students will have the opportunity to study the guitar, bass, drums, and/or keyboard as well as vocals and music technology. This course is open to all students.
notes: Level U; Sub-heading: Music

Students have the opportunity to begin learning a new instrument or further skills on a familiar instrument. Lessons are scheduled according to the student’s availability. This course is open to students at all levels.
notes: Level U; Sub-heading: Music

The course work concentrates on technical skills, building a repertoire, and exploring an individual's potential. Lessons are scheduled according to a student's availability.
notes: Level U; Sub-heading: Music

description: This class is for any student interested in theater arts and music, but also integrates visual art, dance and technical theater (set building and light and sound design). This class will primarily work on acting and vocal music skills, as well as introductions to basic dance and visual art for set design. It will additionally offer students the opportunity to train in technical theater through set design and building and light and sound design. Students will be trained on the necessary equipment to help them independently operate light and sound boards. Students will also be offered the student leadership opportunities to work on directing, choreography, vocal music peer assistance, as well as visual set design. This is a class for any student interested in either on or off stage roles in the world of musical theater!
notes: Level U; Sub-heading: Music

description: This course is designed to teach students a deeper understanding of our musical language through rhythm, melody, harmony, form, and more.Throughout the course, students will explore the elements of music notation, including key signatures, time signatures, scales, and intervals. They will develop a strong foundation in understanding harmony and chord progressions, enabling them to analyze and interpret musical compositions across various genres. Additionally, the course will cover the historical context of music theory, allowing students to appreciate how musical conventions have evolved over time. Students will develop skills including sight-reading, ear training, and composition. By the end of the course, students will be able to not only read and analyze sheet music but also compose their own musical pieces, applying the principles learned throughout the curriculum. This Music Theory course encourages critical thinking and creative expression, fostering a deeper connection to the art of music. Whether students aspire to pursue further studies in music or simply wish to enhance their overall musical literacy, this course provides a solid foundation for a lifelong appreciation of the intricate language of music.
notes: Level 4; Sub-heading: Music

description: In this course, students will explore the cultural, historical, and musical background of American Popular Music. Course activities will explore cultural connections, how music reflects social & cultural awareness, and technological developments that impacted the evolution of popular music. Each unit will focus on a different genre musical, or decade, and contain four lessons based on the National Core Arts Standards of Creating, Presenting/Performing/Producing, Responding, and Connecting with variable tasks.
notes: Level U; Sub-heading: Music

description: Art 1 is a foundation course open to all students at all levels. The primary focus in this class is on the foundations of drawing, painting, and basic composition. Using the Elements (color, line, shape, space, texture, value) and Principles of Design (balance, emphasis, proportion, rhythm, unity, and variety/contrast) to guide us, we will explore drawing media (pencil, colored pencils, charcoal, pen and ink, brush and ink) and acrylic paints. Experimentation with printmaking and non-traditional tools and media will be introduced. Basic art history and critical analysis will be addressed weekly. This is the perfect class to take to get your art credit, explore your inner artist and is a prerequisite for any of the advanced art classes/honors credit.
fulfills_text: This is the perfect class to take to get your art credit
notes: Level U; Sub-heading: Studio Art

description: This class is also a foundation course and is open to all students at all levels. This class will focus on using the Elements (color, line, shape, space, texture, value) and Principles of Design (balance, emphasis, proportion, rhythm, unity, and variety/contrast) to create sound compositions. Rather than using traditional art media, students will use their phone cameras, some digital cameras, and alternative photographic techniques, such as cyanotypes. Some very basic photo editing will expand student creative explorations. The willingness for experimentation is heartily encouraged. Basic photographic history and critical analysis will be addressed weekly. This class will meet your art credit requirements, but will not meet advanced art prerequisites.
fulfills_text: This class will meet your art credit requirements, but will not meet advanced art prerequisites.
notes: Level U; Sub-heading: Studio Art

description: This class builds on the foundations and fundamental skills introduced in Art 1. More traditional and non-traditional media will be explored. Sophisticated handling of the Elements and Principles of Design will be a primary focus. Portraiture and the human figure will be a major subject covered throughout this course. Painting techniques, (impasto, grisaille, alla prima, and scumbling) will be experimented with along with different types of water-based paint as students develop their own, personal aesthetics. Students will expand their basic skills and strategies as they develop related bodies of work. Art history and critical analysis will be at a more advanced level than Art 1 and will include some in-depth investigations of certain time periods and artists.
prerequisites: Art 1
notes: Level 4; Sub-heading: Studio Art

description: This printmaking class introduces students to the basic materials, equipment and processes for the production of multiple images from a master plate. The printmaking processes that this class will explore include monotype, relief block, collagraph, and chine colle. Students will create plates out of a variety of materials and then “pull” images by hand or through the use of a hand-run printing press. Emphasis is on design and composition as well as creative use of the materials and techniques of the relief (wood block and linoleum block), monoprint, and serigraph (silkscreen and stencil) printing processes. Experimentation with different kinds of ink, ink application, and handmade paper will also be a focus. Students are expected to explore the role of the printmaker in society and the significance of prints as a vital form of communication. Additionally, the history of printmaking and associated critical analysis will be addressed regularly throughout the course. Honors credit will be given to students who have previously, and successfully completed Art 1 and complete additional assignments.
notes: Level U/4; Sub-heading: Studio Art

description: This introductory course will introduce students to pottery as an art form. Students will learn the basic handbuilding and decorative techniques to create original ceramic pieces. This work will range from traditional, functional ware to imaginative, sculptural forms. Surface decoration and manipulation as well as glazing and underglazing techniques will be covered fully. A variety of historical and contemporary work observed throughout the class for inspiration and appreciation. Students will also experience making pottery on the potter’s wheel. This class offers a creative experience with many challenges, discoveries and rewards. Classes will be limited to upperclassmen (juniors and seniors) with a class size limited to 14. Honors credit will be given to students who have previously, and successfully, completed Art 1 and complete additional assignments.
notes: Level U/4; Sub-heading: Studio Art

description: This course introduces the design and production of relief sculpture and sculpture-in-the round and aims to develop spatial literacy through various 3D design and construction techniques. Students will design and construct realistic and abstract sculptural forms using a variety of materials, tools and techniques. Methods include the additive, subtractive, modeling and casting processes. Students will examine, analyze, and interpret traditional and contemporary works of art and artifacts while their understanding of the elements and principles of design are reinforced. Students explore the structural, compositional and conceptual implications of commonly used materials, such as cardboard, wood, metal, plaster and found objects, and are instructed on the safe use of select hand and power tools. Sketchbook and minor research assignments are a part of this course. Honors credit will be given to students who have previously, and successfully, completed Art 1 and complete additional assignments.
notes: Level U/4; Sub-heading: Studio Art

description: Foods will consist of scaffolded learning from basic to advanced methods of food preparation. Students are responsible for maintaining kitchen safety and sanitation of kitchen areas. Students will work in teams to follow recipes as well as gain competence in creating recipes and menus specific to occasion, dietary restrictions, and lifestyle. Identifying interpersonal skills and character traits necessary for successful collaboration will be part of our daily practice. Kitchen labs will focus on cooking delicious food and social emotional learning will happen through opportunities to participate in community building games and reflective processing. Nutrition, wellness, and a basic understanding of how healthy eating relates to obesity and other preventable diseases is provided. Students will gain knowledge about lifestyle choices and ways to incorporate healthy habits.

description: International Foods is an elective course in Family & Consumer Sciences. Students explore and research the history of food and preparation as it relates to diverse cultures and International cuisines. Students will gain a better understanding of ingredients, agricultural methods, eating utensils, cooking methods and customs of the global society in which we live.

description: Proficiencies for our Health courses are met through a combination of online and in-person workshops to align with State of Vermont requirements. The State of VT defines health literacy as “the capacity of students to obtain, interpret and understand basic health information and service, and the competence to use such information and services in ways that enhance health.” Health topics will include nutrition, interpersonal communication, mental health, healthy relationships, sexual health and substance use. As part of our focus on health, students will also review basic first aid and CPR. In addition to the online (.5 credit) requirement, students can fulfill the remaining .5 BFUHS health requirement through successful completion of related online or in-person courses, including Health Services programs at one of the Tech Centers.

All students are required to complete 1½ credits of Physical Education unless excused by a physician. We recommend that students get involved with P.E. all four years. Listed below are the activities offered in each season of the year. These activities are open to all students. - Fall: Flag Football, Conditioning, Fitness Testing, Frisbee Games, Hocker, Team Handball - Winter: Basketball, Weight Training, Volleyball, Badminton, Table Tennis, Floor Hockey, Pickleball, Snowshoeing and Orienteering - Spring: Softball and Wiffle Ball, Lacrosse, Tennis, Fitness Testing, Rec. Games All Physical Education classes spend about twenty minutes addressing physical wellness before moving to the regular activity unit of instruction. The components of physical fitness are addressed as follows: ● Cardio Respiratory Endurance: Students start by jogging three laps in the gym. One more lap is added each class meeting to build up to the one mile run. Everyone is encouraged to jog, but if unable to, they may walk. ● Agility is addressed by use of several footwork drills such as high knees, backwards running, slide steps or shuffle, and grapevine. ● Flexibility is addressed by several stretching activities. ● Muscular strength is addressed along with muscular endurance at the horizontal ladder, the chinning bar, and the weight room. ● Power is addressed by use of bounding drills or plyometrics. ● Body composition is addressed through the use of a body analyzer. ● Circuit training is also included as a physical wellness activity each quarter.

Assessments will include a research project, tests, written responses, presentations, and class discussions.
fulfills_text: Required in 9th grade year
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.2, Reading 2.1, 2.3 & Writing 3.2, 3.3, 3.4

description: Whether you are a veteran actor or scared on the stage, this class is for all ability levels. The course focuses on the fundamentals of acting, staging, and production. Using acting theory and practice, we will cover the following concepts: Characterization & Development, Improvisation, Movement and Mannerisms, Directing, Costume Construction, Blocking, Scene Development, Vocal control and oral interpretation. This class is an opportunity to explore the performance arts without the pressure of the big stage and audience.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.2, 1.2, Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.1

description: In this course students will read novels, watch the film adaptations, and compare and contrast the two. We will specifically look at plot, characterization, point of view, tone, and literary/film techniques and how these are similar and different in the different mediums. Students will create a variety of products to show how the books and films are similar and different.

description: Contemporary literature focuses on the novels, stories, and poems that are currently impactful and relevant in our world today, focusing specifically on the literature of underrepresented minorities. A variety of literature from diverse authors and experiences will be explored, with a focus on marginalized populations, authors, and experiences. Students will demonstrate their understanding of the universal themes found in literature today in a multitude of ways.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1, Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4

description: This is a course in which students will explore many different types of nonfiction. Specifically, students will examine how the medium of the text suits its message (or not), and how different styles of nonfiction are similar and different. Narrative nonfiction is the main genre of focus. There will also be a small personal nonfiction research project that students conduct. Students are expected to demonstrate their understanding of concepts in a variety of assignments, both written and spoken.
notes: ELA Indicators: Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4

course_name: Digital Media & Performances: The Student Show
description: In this project based class, Lights, camera, collaboration! Students create and produce a live or recorded show featuring original sketches, music, and news segments about issues that matter to them. This course blends journalism, creative writing, and digital production skills—preparing students to inform and entertain their community while developing their media literacy and storytelling voice.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1 & 1.2, Reading 2.2 & Writing 3.4; Project based learning (PBL) course

description: What is the worst-case scenario for our world? This course will allow students to explore issues in the contemporary world through exploration of the dystopian fiction genre. As we analyze the themes of these works, students will make connections to real world issues surrounding government, the environment, and societal inequalities.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1, Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.2, 3.3, 3.4

description: In this course we will read a wide variety of ghost stories including both physical and psychological manifestations. We will examine how ghosts are represented throughout time and across cultures and what that representation reveals about us / what purpose it serves. The spooky, the creepy, and the unexplainable will be common threads through the reading and writing in this course, as well as the inspiration for discussions, presentations, and creative projects.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1, 1.2, Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.1, 3.2, 3.4

description: The graphic novel has become a significant medium for presenting a range of historical, social, personal, and political issues. Students in this course will explore graphic novels and other alternative texts as a means of communicating narrative, using critical media literacy skills as well as traditional text analysis. Through genre study, students will consider graphic novels as literature, examine its formal structure as it relates to content, and trace the development of themes including gender, race, sexuality, justice, and humor. Students will also construct a graphic novel of their own, both independently and collaboratively.
notes: ELA Indicators: Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.1, 3.4

description: This interdisciplinary humanities course will focus on what qualities or deeds make a person a hero or villain, how the characteristics of heroes have changed over time, and the circumstances that make a person a hero or villain.
fulfills_text: NOTE: students may take this course to fulfill either a Global Citizenship requirement OR a Language Arts requirement. Also listed under Global Citizenship (p.33) as satisfying the Social Sciences requirement
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1, 1.2, Reading 2.1, 2.3 & Writing 3.2, 3.3, 3.4; Global Citizenship Indicators: Inquiry 1.1 & 1.3, Hist 2.1 & Social Sciences 5.1,5.2,5.3; Also listed in Global Citizenship department, where it is available to all grades after Foundations

description: Historical perspectives will examine texts where storytelling and history are equally important. Students will look at different perspectives of historical eras, events, and moments. We will also discuss the author's intentions in their portrayal of historical events, and how literary elements can deepen our understanding of the human experience of these events. The goal of this class will be to learn about ourselves through other figures and characters, and the world they experienced by reading a wide range of voices from an equally wide range of times and places.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1, Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4

description: From Shakespeare to Taylor Swift, authors have had a lot to say about love through all eras. In Love Stories, students will explore an array of love stories, including the classics, contemporary YA fiction, essays, and films. Through these texts we will explore characters’ relationships to themselves, the world, and obviously, each other with a focus on theme, characterization, and character development. Get ready to fall in love with reading!
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1 & 1.2 , Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.2, 3.3, 3.4

description: Because they build a sense of identity, community, solidarity, and pride, sports play a vital role in our lives. In this course, students will examine the pivotal role sports play in shaping identity on individual, societal, and global levels. Through a variety of media, students will explore how sports connect to universal topics such as: gender and race, equality and prejudice, honesty and dishonesty, perseverance and disappointment, and heroism and pride. Students will develop their independent, critical thinking skills through analysis of varied media and their treatment of sports and sports related topics.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1, 1.2, Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.2, 3.3, 3.4, 3.5

description: Young adult literature is focused on the teenage experience and the stories that help us navigate our relationship with the world. This course will explore a diverse array of these stories and why they resonate with today’s readers. Students will discuss a variety of novels from the perspectives of genre, theme, characters, representations of adolescence and adulthood, and consider how these stories are relevant in their own lives. Students should expect to delve into some of the most fascinating, compelling, and relatable stories of our world today.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1, 1.2 Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4

description: This is a foundational college credit writing course. The course focuses on understanding the patterns of effective writing through reading, listening, and viewing non-fiction, podcasts, documentaries, letters and speeches, newspaper and magazine articles. Students build their writing skills through developing short essays and a well developed, researched argument on a substantive topic. Students are encouraged to sit the Advanced Placement Exam in May.
notes: ELA Indicators: Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.2, 3.3, 3.4

description: This course is designed for highly motivated students who love literature and enjoy learning through reflection and playing with the written word. Students will read novels, poetry, and drama from the 17th century to the present day, and write their own poetry and short stories. Students are encouraged to sit the Advanced Placement Exam in May.

description: This course is designed for students to explore their own interests and become experts on an author of their choice. In this course, students will examine the biography, works, and legacy of one author. They will share about connections between the author’s life and work through writing assignments and a presentation. Together, students will develop their understanding of what a “literary canon” is and discuss whether their author deserves to be included in it.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1, 1.2, Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, Writing 3.2, 3.4

description: This course will introduce you to creative writing, from generating ideas to revising drafts. Find your voice and develop your craft through writing exercises, as well as discussions of your own and your fellow students’ written work. You will also study models drawn from fiction, poetry, and creative nonfiction, and will be encouraged to try your hand at each of these genres. Students will build a portfolio of work and class will consist of discussion of readings, in-class writing exercises, and workshop discussions.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1, Reading 2.1, 2.2 & Writing 3.1, 3.4

description: This course will focus on literature and art from the victims of the Holocaust. By examining fiction, poetry, memoir, diaries, and art, students will address the historical, religious, sociological, and political impacts of the Holocaust. Among the topics covered: bearing witness and survivor testimony, shaping the collective memory, the second and third generations, propaganda, antisemitism today.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.2, Reading 2.1, 2.3 & Writing 3.1, 3.2, 3.4

course_name: Introduction to College Writing: Dual Enrollment for CCV Credit
description: This class is designed to be an introduction to writing in college. Students will learn about the types of academic writing expected in a variety of college courses, and practice the skills connected to those writing formats. Using the process of brainstorming, outlining, drafting, revising, and editing, students learn to write a variety of well-organized, logical essays and produce writing that is largely free of minimum-standard writing errors. The summative assignment for this course is a 10-page independent research paper in MLA format.
notes: ELA Indicators: Writing 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4; College Credit English Composition - Trimesters 1 & 2 (eligible for CCV credit)

description: This course is designed for students interested in creative reading and writing. The study of poetry and short stories is balanced with the study of language as an art form. Students will read and analyze a wide variety of poetry and short stories. Each student will also write two original short stories and compile an original poetry portfolio.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1, 1.2, Reading 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 & Writing 3.1, 3.2

description: In this public speaking course students have the opportunity to improve their skills in public speaking, oral interpretation of literature, radio announcing, panel discussions, interviews, and storytelling. The course introduces the fundamentals of good public speaking that are applicable in every interview, profession, and discussion. Participants are more confident in their speaking and writing skills as a result. Students will incorporate the video, digital, and multimedia tools to enhance learning and performance.
notes: ELA Indicators: Speaking & Listening 1.1, 1.2, Reading 2.2 & Writing 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 3.4

description: This course is designed to support students with diverse learning needs by integrating key skills in English, world cultures, executive functioning, and daily life. Through engaging lessons and hands-on activities, students will develop reading, writing, speaking & listening skills, explore global traditions and perspectives, strengthen time management and organization strategies, and practice essential life skills for independence. The class fosters a supportive and inclusive environment where students build confidence, enhance communication, and prepare for future academic, personal, and career success. This course is for a select group of students with specific academic needs. Placement decisions will be made by case managers in consultation with students, families, and staff.

description: Placement will be by grade level, with Seniors first, then Juniors, then Sophomores by birth date. If extra spots remain, 9th graders who requested Driver Education on their course requests will be offered spots based on birthday. Students enrolled in this course will acquire a foundation of knowledge and driving skills. They will receive a minimum of 30 hours of classroom instruction, six hours of observation time and six hours of behind-the-wheel instruction time from a certified instructor. Vermont laws and the Department of Motor Vehicles require students to document 40 hours of driving outside of school with an unimpaired adult over the age of 25 with a valid license sitting in the passenger seat. Students must meet all course requirements to be awarded the appropriate certificate from the State of Vermont. Students are responsible for having their permit with them on the first day of class. While enrolled in the class students will need to use some Advisory time for Driver Education. Placement will be by grade level, with Seniors first, then Juniors, then Sophomores by birth date. Students must request Driver Education on their course request form. Because of the demand for this class, students who fail or are removed from class will be eligible to request Driver Education again after a full calendar year. Driver Education will not be offered in the summer. Students who do not request Driver Ed on their Course Request Form may be able to still take the class on a space available basis.
prerequisites: Possession of a Vermont Learner’s Permit.

This time can be linked to the student’s learning goals, or simply part of the career and college discovery process. Discussions regarding career exploration should also include the High School counselors.

The skills are focused around sourcing of information and validity and reliability of information, organized writing, and sharing information through speaking. 9th Grade Foundations also gives an introduction to the content offered in all Global Citizenship courses: Inquiry, History, Civics, Government, and Society, and Social Sciences.

description: This course is designed to allow students to explore the historical development of civilization from the beginnings of civilization to the Renaissance. How do empires rise and what makes them fall? What maintains a civilization? How are we still affected today by events of thousands of years ago? This class will investigate these questions and more, using the nations of the past as the focal points. Areas of study include the first empires, the Greeks, Persians, and Romans, Chinese kingdoms, the empires of Africa and the Americas. Learning is assessed through inquiry lessons, presentation, and an emphasis on communication skills.
notes: Global Citizenship Indicators: Inquiry 1.1 & 1.3, History 2.1, Civics 3.2 & Social Sciences 5.3

description: Students will critically examine the criminal justice system in the US by working a case from the Innocence Project. Students will see how the current and past system have led to many innocent people being wrongfully convicted and imprisoned for crimes they did not commit. Through the investigation of the IP client, students will uncover how something like this can and does occur, noting that there is bias, racism, harsh mandatory minimums, the flaws and malpractice within the prison system, etc. Students will then learn the power of storytelling through a three episode podcasting series that will be marketed and uploaded to Spotfiy to shed light on the injustices that occur with our country. Each segment/episode of the person’s story will highlight a piece of the system, e.g. policing, prosecution/mandatory minimums, - prison life population, demographics, punishment - adjusting after prison, thinking about those who lose their rights as a felon along with mental aspects. This is a team experience and everyone will have a role with the creation, marketing, and production of the series.
fulfills_text: Satisfies Government Requirement
notes: Inquiry 1.1 & 1.3, Civics 3.1 & 3.2

description: "Freedom and Unity" is Vermont's motto. Throughout this course we will see where Vermonters were united as well as where they prioritized their freedom and independence. We will also ask "What does it mean to be a Vermonter?" This course will cover the political, social, and cultural history from indigenous peoples to the present day. It will also explore how the geography of Vermont has effected its past and present. A focus on writing, reading, and researching will be key. This course will take advantage of field trips and read multiple surveys of Vermont History.
notes: Global Citizenship Indicators: Inquiry 1.1 & 1.3, History 2.1, Civics 3.1 & 3.3

description: This course investigates the UN Sustainable Development Goals, why they exist and why they are a global initiative. Students will work in teams to uncover ways in which our school, town, county, or state is not meeting the UN Goals. Teams will then work to come up with unique solutions to the problems they uncovered and will present their solution to the proper stakeholders and then develop an action plan for implementation. The goal of this course is to recognize that we are a part of a worldwide initiative that can be realized within our own community. This class will be part of a global collaborative project where they exchange and connect with students from different countries.
fulfills_text: Satisfies Social Sciences Requirement
notes: Please note this course is available to students in grades 10-12; Global Citizenship Indicators: Inquiry 1.1 & 1.3, Civics 3.2 & Social Sciences 5.3

description: In this course, students will explore the relationship between food, culture, health, and sustainability through hands-on, interdisciplinary learning. They will begin by collecting data and analyzing the types of food they eat, where it comes from, and how it fits into the larger food systems, including production, processing, distribution, marketing, and consumption. The course will cover topics such as healthy foods, balanced diets, malnutrition, and the USDA's MyPlate guidelines. As part of a global learning experience, students will collaborate with peers from different countries to learn about their cultures, food traditions, and celebrations, deepening their understanding of food’s cultural significance. Together, they will share recipes and stories that reflect their diverse backgrounds. Through this exchange, students will compile a class cookbook featuring traditional and meaningful recipes from around the world. The final project will be a community showcase where students present their cookbook, display food items, and provide sample dishes to distribute the professional printing and distribution of their cookbook. This course is for a select group of students with specific academic needs. Placement decisions will be made by case managers in consultation with students, families, and staff.

description: In this project based course, students explore how mental, physical, and social well-being are shaped by systems, environments, and access. Students investigate barriers to mental health care locally and globally and examine how stigma, policy, culture, and community design impact well-being. Through research and community-based projects, students design solutions such as awareness campaigns, advocacy efforts, outdoor wellness experiences, and inclusive “third spaces” that foster belonging and connection. Learning takes place in classrooms, outdoor spaces, and the community, culminating in projects that promote access, inclusion, and well-being.
notes: Global Citizenship Indicators: Inquiry 1.1 & 1.3, Civics 3.2 & Society 5.1; Project based learning (PBL) course

description: This course explores Native American history through inquiry, systems thinking, and public creation. In Unit 1: The Web of Resilience, students examine how land, law, education, culture, and economic systems shaped Indigenous experiences across different U.S. regions. Using their research, students design a collaborative 3-D hallway installation that visually maps these interconnected forces and highlights Indigenous resilience over time. In Unit 2: Abenaki Honors Project, students shift to a focused, place-based study of the Abenaki people. They investigate historical and contemporary experiences, analyze how local systems continue to influence Indigenous presence in Vermont, and design a meaningful public action or recognition project that honors Abenaki history and contributions to the community. Together, these units encourage students to understand Native history as a living, interconnected system while producing work that educates and impacts the wider school community.
notes: Global Citizenship Indicators: Inquiry 1.1 & 1.3, History 2.1, Civics 3.2

description: This course introduces students to the study of human behavior and its history, and allows them to investigate the Essential Question, “Why do we act the way we do?” from multiple perspectives. Each student will design, conduct, analyze and present an experiment demonstrating the scientific method. Students will also develop skills in communication, research, writing and group process.

description: Revolution can mean a change or a turn. This course is designed to explore how our modern world was created through revolutions. How did the discovery of America revolutionize history? How did the French Revolution change our view of rights? How can technology change everything? We will explore these ideas and more in this world history course. Starting at the Reformation and discovering the New World to the Scientific Revolution, the Enlightenment, Colonialism, and the French Revolution. We will look at how events around the world have led to the shape and systems of our world today.
notes: Global Citizenship Indicators: Inquiry 1.1 & 1.3, History 2.1, Civics 3.2 & Social Sciences 5.3

Students design, upcycle, and sell sustainable products—from thrifted apparel to handmade goods—in a school-based store or “Care Closet.” Along the way, they study business management, marketing, and the circular economy while using profits to support social causes.
notes: Inquiry 1.1 & 1.3, Civics 3.2, Social Sciences 5.2 & 5.3; Project based learning (PBL) course

What causes revolutions and change? Why are some revolutions violent while others are peaceful? How are the religions of the world similar?
fulfills_text: Satisfies Social Sciences Requirement

description: The two World Wars were the most deadly conflicts in human history. How could leaders and nations justify these atrocities? How have these two events shaped the world that we live in today? This course will explore how the wars began, the events of each war, and the consequences of global conflicts. Topics will include Pre-war Colonialism and Nationalism, WW1, The Treaty of Versailles and League of Nations, the Rise of Totalitarianism, WW2, and the start of the Cold War. Students will develop skills in research, writing and group work.
notes: Global Citizenship Indicators: Inquiry 1.1 & 1.3, History 2.1, Civics 3.2

description: US History course focusing on the first half of the 20th century. The 20th century was known as “America’s Time” but it didn’t look that way at the outset. How did the United States become a world power? How were we able to weather the Great Depression and World War 1? This course will focus on how the United States changed and adapted as it formed our modern democracy. Topics will include the Progressive Era, World War 1, Roaring 20s and the Harlem Renaissance, the Great Depression, the New Deal, and all the social and political changes in our nation. This course will build off of the skills established in 9th grade foundations, including analyzing sources, writing, and speaking.
fulfills_text: Satisfies US History Requirement
notes: Global Citizenship Indicators: Inquiry 1.1 & 1.3, History 2.1, Civics 3.1, Social Sciences 5.2 & 5.3

description: This US History course focuses on the events of the mid-20th century. At the onset of World War 2, America was placed in a unique position of influence on the world stage. How did America become a world superpower? How did America use this status to influence the world around it? How would these changes affect American society and culture? Topics we'll discuss include World War 2, the Cold War, the Space Race, the Civil Rights Movement, Woodstock, and the Vietnam War. This course will build off of the skills established in 9th grade foundations, including analyzing sources, writing, and speaking.

description: This US History course focuses on the end of the 20th century and the beginning of the 21st century. The 20th century was known as "The American Century." Could the same be said for the 21st century? The course will look at the changes in the United States from the 1980s to today. A focus will be on the importance and changes to American Democracy. Topics include the Reagan Era, End of Cold War, domestic challenges of the 1990s, 9/11 and terrorism, ubiquity of the internet, and the social and political challenges of the 2010s. This course will build off of the skills established in 9th grade foundations, including analyzing sources, writing, and speaking.
