description: Advanced Placement Biology is an advanced, honors level biology program. Topics studied include biochemistry, cellular biology, cell cycle and communication, heredity, gene expression, evolution, and ecology. It is equivalent to 2 semesters of college biology. Depending on the college or university attended, students who do well on the AP exam can earn up to 8 college credits. Students should have a strong background in mathematics and should be proficient in the use of basic laboratory equipment and be familiar with laboratory safety procedures. Students in the course will take the Advanced Placement Examination in Biology given in May of each year. The running of this course is dependent upon sufficient enrollment and staffing.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Biology I, Chemistry I, and Algebra II, and recommendation from current science teacher.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication.

description: This is a challenging, mathematical, laboratory-oriented chemistry course designed for those students with interest in expanding their chemistry knowledge. Topics include extensions of ideas learned in Chemistry I, inorganic chemistry, introduction to organic chemicals, analytical methods, thermochemistry, and chemical kinetics and equilibrium. The class meets for 2 Blocks, is equivalent to 2 semesters of college Chemistry, and can earn up to 8 college credits. Students will take the AP Chemistry Exam in May. The running of this course is dependent upon sufficient enrollment and staffing.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra II & Chemistry I or Chemistry I Honors and recommendation from current science teacher.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity and Curiosity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: Students will study the interrelated parts and connections between earth systems and human impact upon them through laboratory exercises, modeling, debate and independent research. National and local environmental policy, planning, and impact are also explored in depth. Students will study these and other topics in order to prepare for the Advanced Placement exam in May. The course is equivalent to 1 semester of college Environmental Science. Depending on the college or university attended, students who do well on the AP exam can earn up to 4 college credits.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Math I or Geometry, concurrent enrollment in or successful completion of Biology 1 or Honors Biology, and recommendation from current science teacher.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity and Curiosity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: This semester-long class takes an in-depth look at the chemical and biological processes that occur when cooking and fermenting food. We also learn the proper techniques that determine a recipe’s success. We usually make the following foods: jams, salsa, biscuits, frying foods such as french fries and cider donuts, yogurt, homemade cider, and sauerkraut. We learn how to grill food and work in the school garden harvesting food. Finally, you will choose a recipe to cook and investigate as a final project.
prerequisites: 10th-11th graders should be concurrently enrolled in biology, chemistry or physics
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity and Curiosity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: Cookies, cakes, bread, sourdough, chocolate souffles, eggs, meats, grilling, pancakes, waffles, maple syrup and sugaring. This semester will have you baking, cooking, grilling and tapping maple trees producing the best foods all based on proven scientific techniques. Once the snow begins to melt we head out to tap the maple trees and boil off the sap to use on the best pancakes and waffles that you create. Finally, we end the year learning how to grill savory meats and vegetables in the beautiful Vermont spring outdoors.
prerequisites: 10th-11th graders should be concurrently enrolled in biology, chemistry or physics.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication, Creativity and Curiosity; Critical Thinking & Problem Solving.

description: Human Anatomy and Physiology is a challenging year-long course that encompasses the parts of the body and how they work. This course is designed for students who wish to learn how their bodies work or are interested in pursuing careers in the health field after graduation. Topics studied will include the following systems: integumentary (skin), skeletal, muscular, digestive, nervous, cardiovascular, endocrine, and reproductive. Four optional dissections aid in our discovery of the human body.
prerequisites: Concurrent enrollment in or successful completion of Biology.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication.

description: This course aims to provide students with an appreciation and basic working knowledge of our oceans and marine life. The course will focus on both the living and nonliving components in our oceans that contribute to the diverse ecosystems and abundant resources under the sea! In addition to natural ocean phenomena such as currents, tides, plate tectonics, island formation, species diversity and weather, human impacts like pollution, over exploitation of fishing/whaling practices, climate change, and possible career fields will be studied. Demonstrations, labs, videos, and group projects will enhance learning from classroom lectures, articles, and group discussions.
prerequisites: Completion of or concurrently enrolled in Biology
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving; Effective Communication.

description: This semester-long course will introduce students to pathogens that cause human and/or animal disease. Emphasis will be on viral, bacterial, protozoan, and fungal diseases. Students will learn to classify microbes using taxonomic hierarchy. Animal defense mechanisms, disease progression and disease transmission will be primary topics of study. We will review the human response to disease over the centuries. The laboratory component of this course will focus on the basic methods to cultivate, identify and control pathogenic microbial growth.
prerequisites: Completion of or concurrently enrolled in Biology
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving; Effective Communication; Creativity and Curiosity.

description: This semester-long course will introduce students to the field of parasitology. Topics will include parasite diversity, life cycles, host defense mechanisms, and host disease. Biology concepts of immunology, ecology, and evolution will weave throughout our course. Methods for parasite control and treatments with antiparasitic medicines will be explored. The laboratory component of this course will examine and classify parasites of medical and veterinary importance using light microscopy.
prerequisites: Completion of or concurrently enrolled in Biology
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving; Effective Communication; Creativity and Curiosity.

description: Take advantage of this opportunity for a second year of high school physics. Topics include astronomy, optics and light, electricity, magnetism, relativity and other modern topics. Students should have strong reading and math skills and be able to work well in collaborative groups, as well as independently.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Physics I or Honors Physics I and concurrent enrollment in or completion of Precalculus, and recommendation of Honors Physics II teacher.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Critical Thinking & Problem Solving; Effective Communication

description: This course is designed for students who are interested in exploring the cultures of the world languages offered at BHS. This course provides students with an introduction in English to the geography, the culture and to some history of the countries of the languages taught at BHS. The emphasis of the course is not so much on language acquisition but rather on the exploration of cultural topics. The objective of the course is for students to gain some cultural awareness and to gain readiness for any level 1 of world language class at BHS.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: An introduction to the French language and culture, this course offers the building blocks of second language acquisition through the alphabet, number system, basic grammar structures and vocabulary. Students learn to communicate about themselves in such areas as family, school, leisure activities, clothes, etc. and their surroundings. They can identify cultural objects, images, and symbols, and contributions of the target culture. Knowledge in other subject areas (math, social studies, art, etc) is reinforced. Students can identify differences in language and cultural patterns and can identify the target language in their daily lives. They will begin to develop the ability to greet and respond to greetings, introduce and respond to introductions, engage in conversations, express likes and dislikes, make requests, obtain information, understand some ideas and begin to provide information. They can expect to speak in short sentences of directed dialogues, to write simple sentences, to read short passages for comprehension and to listen to patterns of conversations. Stage I proficiency is assessed during the year.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: This course is designed for students who successfully completed level 1 and/or achieved the necessary scoring on the placement exam. Content topics of French 1 are explored in depth. New vocabulary is introduced through authentic and cultural readings. The focus of the texts is the French-speaking world. Cultural behaviors and practices throughout the French-speaking world are studied and discussed. New grammar is practiced regularly in order to improve sentence structure. Conversational skills and practical vocabulary are used daily in class activities. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
prerequisites: B- or higher in French 1 and/or recommendation of middle/high school French 1 teacher
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: At the third level students continue to acquire skills leading to greater proficiency. Content topics of French 1 and 2 are explored in more depth. Students develop the ability to make requests; express their needs; understand and express important ideas and some detail; describe and compare; and use and understand expressions indicating emotion. They will be able to create simple paragraphs when writing; understand important ideas and some details in highly contextualized authentic texts when reading; and use and understand learned expressions, sentences, and strings of sentences, questions, and polite commands when speaking and listening. Progress is assessed throughout the year. Students may participate in the school’s travel/language trip to France.
prerequisites: B- or higher in French 2, successful completion of French 2 final exam and/or French 2 teacher recommendation
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: Students may elect to continue their study of French language and French culture through this course, which continues to foster the enhancement of communication skills through expanding upon the foundations for verbal, listening and writing skills laid in previous French courses. The curriculum focuses on reading, writing, listening and speaking French in class with peers and the teacher and understanding the culture. This will be done by incorporating different strategies in which students will be expected to participate: writing activities, creating projects, and engaging in the target language through music and videos/film.
prerequisites: B- or higher in French 3 and/or recommendation of French 3 teacher
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: In French 5 students increase their knowledge and improve their proficiency engaging in meaningful communication. Pronunciation, expressions, vocabulary and grammar topics are reviewed and practiced using a variety of authentic resources including music, recordings, films, literature excerpts, newspapers and magazines. Skills developed include ability to clarify understanding, express and understand opinions, narrate and understand narration, and identify, state, and understand feelings and emotions. Students read, analyze and engage in class debates, write essays, reflections and reactions, give and critique presentations, present skits and role-play activities, and complete written and oral projects. The course is conducted entirely in French. Students may participate in the school’s travel and language trip to France.
prerequisites: B- or higher in French 4 and/or recommendation of French 4 teacher
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: Students in this introductory course begin to develop: the ability to greet and respond to greetings, introduce and respond to introductions, engage in conversations, express likes and dislikes, make requests, obtain information, understand some ideas and familiar details. In addition students will provide information about topics pertaining to the self and others, family, friends, home, school, schedules, and leisure activities. They can identify Hispanic cultural perspectives and practices beyond the school setting, make connections between Spanish and other disciplines they study, and identify similarities and differences between Hispanic and English language and behaviors. Spanish I students begin to speak in short sentences of directed dialogues, write simple sentences, read short passages enhanced with visual clues and understand some ideas and familiar details presented in clear, uncomplicated speech when listening. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: This course is designed for students who have successfully completed Spanish 1 and/or achieved the necessary standard on the placement exam. Content topics of Spanish I are explored in more depth. Cultural behaviors are studied and practiced. Authentic materials, intended for native speakers, are introduced. Students are able to participate in school-wide multicultural activities in Spanish. Proficiency is assessed throughout the year.
prerequisites: B- or higher in Spanish 1 and/or recommendation of middle/high school Spanish teacher
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: In Spanish 3, students continue to acquire skills leading to proficiency at Stage II. Content topics of Spanish 1 and 2 are explored in more depth. Students develop the ability to make requests, express their needs, understand and express important ideas and some detail, describe and compare, and use and understand expressions indicating emotion. They will be able to create simple paragraphs when writing, understand important ideas and some details in highly contextualized authentic texts when reading, and use and understand learned expressions, sentences, and strings of sentences, questions, and polite commands when speaking and listening. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
prerequisites: B- or higher in Spanish 2 and successful completion of Spanish 2 final exam and/or recommendation of Spanish 2 teacher
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: Students may elect to continue their study of the Spanish language and Hispanic culture through this course which fosters the enhancement of communication skills through expanding content and higher expectations. The course is conducted almost entirely in Spanish. The content will range from self-related topics (family, friends, home, school, activities, likes and dislikes, shopping, clothes, and pets) through less personal concerns (geography, history, directions, weather, cultural/historical figures, places and events, transportation and travel, food and eating customs, and work/professions), to broader topics culturally pertinent to the target language (art, literature, music, current affairs, and civilization). Students begin to analyze cultural behaviors, recognize and use idiomatic expressions, and interact appropriately in realistic situations. Proficiency is assessed throughout the year.
prerequisites: B- or higher in Spanish 3 and/or recommendation of a Spanish teacher.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: In this course, students have intensive exposure to wide ranging and demanding content where high expectations and demanding standards in all skill areas and in all aspects of scholarship will be the rule. Content will range from that delineated for Spanish 4, through topics of broader cultural significance such as the educational system, the government, and political and social issues. Skills developed include the ability to explain and clarify understanding, express and understand opinions, narrate and understand narration in the present, past, and future, and identify, state, and understand feelings and emotions. When speaking, students use strings of related sentences; when writing, they can create simple paragraphs; when reading, they can acquire knowledge and new information from comprehensive, authentic texts; and when listening, they are able to understand most spoken language when the message is deliberately and carefully conveyed by a speaker accustomed to dealing with learners. Preparation for the Advanced Placement examination in Spanish begins at this level. The course is entirely conducted in Spanish.
prerequisites: B- or higher in Spanish 4 and/or recommendation of a Spanish teacher.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: This course is designed for heritage Spanish speakers — students who grew up speaking Spanish in informal settings but may not have had formal instruction. It builds on existing language skills to strengthen reading, writing, and grammar, while expanding vocabulary and cultural awareness. Students will improve their ability to use Spanish confidently in both academic and real-world contexts.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: Latin I exposes students to the language, culture, and history of the Romans. An introduction to the language through the Cambridge Series emphasizes comprehension of the Latin language by reading it and thus understanding the social and political history of the Romans, especially during the first Century AD. The year will focus on Pompeii, the city buried by Mt. Vesuvius in A.D. 79. A variety of cultural topics are explored including family life, entertainment, education, food, slavery, art and architecture (through slide presentations), and religion. In addition, students become familiar with the geography of the ancient world and study the relationship of Latin vocabulary to English. The result of the student’s study of Latin is improved knowledge of both English vocabulary and grammar, an expanded understanding of the relationship of the ancient world to his or her own, and an appreciation for other foreign languages and cultures.
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: The Cambridge Series pursues readings in philosophy, engineering, the legionary soldier, and religion. The Romans abroad in the West, i.e. Britain, and in the East, i.e. Masada, offers further study of social and historical topics. Students will read about Rome during the reign of Domitian and study the art and architecture of the city of Rome with emphasis on the Roman Forum. Students will also study the role of the legionary soldier in the empire. Vergil’s great epic the Aeneid is read in English providing students with a knowledge of the mythology connected with Rome’s foundation. The student will work on mastery of the language by acquisition and understanding of advanced grammar and reading Latin in the original.
prerequisites: Completion Latin II and/or recommendation of the Latin teacher
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: This course is designed for students who have successfully completed German 1. Content topics of German I are explored in more depth. The topics are designed to steer the student to express opinions, ask questions, and participate in simulations of real-life situations.The course is project based in nature where students will use their growing knowledge of German to design and present their notion of the ideal school, compose hip hop music, create board games and even film video projects of an original German comedy series. Other real-life topics are concerned with everyday life such as shopping for groceries and planning meals, purchasing gifts, discussing free time activities and hobbies, eating in restaurants, and finding one's way in a German city. Short stories, poems, films, and cultural readings all help students to further improve their reading, listening and speaking skills. Authentic materials, intended for native speakers, are introduced. Students are able to participate in school-wide multicultural activities in German. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
prerequisites: B- or higher in German 1 and/or recommendation of the German teacher
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: In this course, students continue to acquire proficiency skills, and the content topics of German 1 and 2 are explored in more depth. Subjects such as children’s literature (Grimm’s fairy tales), German history in the 20th century, German politics, German film history, etc. are analyzed and discussed in depth. Students also begin to read, discuss, and debate topics introduced in contemporary literature, including short stories by such authors as Brecht, Borchert and Bichsel. This course is similar to German 2 in that it is project based where, for example, students compose and film their own endings to fairy tales, create their own cooking show, and even organize a German Film festival for the whole school with post-film “talk-backs” organized by students in German 3. Students develop the ability to make requests, express their needs, understand and express important ideas in some detail, describe and compare, and use and understand expressions indicating emotion. They will be able to create simple paragraphs when writing, understand important ideas and some details in highly contextualized authentic texts when reading, and use and understand learned expressions, sentences, and strings of sentences, questions, and polite commands when speaking and listening. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
prerequisites: B- or higher in German 2 and/or recommendation of the German teacher
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: This course continues to foster the enhancement of communication skills through expanding content and grammatical knowledge. Although this course is somewhat organic in that students will be able to help come up with topics they are passionate about at the outset of the year, there are some core topics that will be discussed. For example, students will explore literature, cinema history, and culture, the financial and economic world, environmental concerns and human creativity. Literary works ranging from poetry and short stories, sections of Goethe's Faust to Rilke's poems and Durrenmatt’s post WWII works, generate many opportunities for projects, debates and discussions. A unit on literature, art, and music of the Holocaust, as well as the study of propaganda and its influence on the youth of Germany, is offered during the second semester. This unit includes guest lectures from Holocaust survivors of concentration camps and professors from the UVM departments of Hebrew, German, and Russian. Students begin to analyze cultural behaviors, recognize and use idiomatic expressions, and interact appropriately in realistic situations. Progress is assessed throughout the year.
prerequisites: B- or higher in German 3 and/or recommendation of the German teacher
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: This is a college level course designed to prepare students for success on the AP German Language and Culture exam. Students will continue their exploration of the language, history, culture and practices of the German-speaking world, and will be encouraged to make comparisons and connections with their own culture throughout the year. This course will be taught almost exclusively in German, and students will be required to participate using the target language. Students will engage in activities and assignments focused on Interpersonal, Interpretive, and Presentational modes of communication . As a class, we will address the following interdisciplinary themes of the AP exam in German: Global Challenges, Science and Technology, Contemporary Life, Personal and Public Identities, Families and Communities, and Beauty and Aesthetics . Course materials include authentic reading materials, German video clips, films and podcasts made for a native speaker audience addressing these interdisciplinary themes.
prerequisites: B- or higher in German 3 and/or recommendation of the German teacher
notes: Primary Graduate Expectations: Effective Communication; Cross-Cultural Understanding & Civic Engagement.

description: The Burlington City & Lake Semester (BCL) is an intensive semester program that offers students the opportunity to use the city as their classroom and curriculum for one semester of their high school journey. Students will dedicate their entire Blue Day schedule to explore real world issues, build deeper relationships with a diverse group of 20 peers, and take action alongside adults to improve the community. BCL participants are ambitious and excited for the deeper, student-centered learning that is possible in an experiential program. The curriculum features a cross-disciplinary exploration of five core themes through four units of study. Students may earn one half (0.5) credit each in English and Social Studies, as well as one (1.0) elective credit in Applied Research upon successful completion of BCL. Applications may be submitted here and more information can be found at btvcityandlake.org. *Please note that only the 0.5 English credit is NCAA-approved.

description: Deeper Learning allows students in 10th, 11th, or 12th grade to focus on a specific topic that is not otherwise available at BHS or for students who want to deepen their learning and understanding of content they have been exposed to in a previously completed class. This learning experience will provide all students the opportunity to design in-depth studies based on their interests and passions. These student-designed studies should align with the five Graduation Expectations, which include: cross-cultural understanding and civic engagement, effective communication, critical thinking and problem solving, curiosity and creativity, and personal development. Students may complete Deeper Learning for either core or elective credit in a 0.5 or 1.0 (one-half or one credit) increment maximum in their high school enrollment. The student must identify a minimum of two Graduation Expectations that will align with the study’s objectives. Deeper Learning is available per teacher contract availability. Independent Study courses should not duplicate current offerings and must be supervised by a content area teacher. Students in good academic standing may discuss this option with their School Counselor. Eligible students will then identify a faculty advisor who is appropriately licensed and meet with this personnel to complete an Independent Study Contract together; the student will return this contract to the School Counselor for approval. Please note that while a teacher must agree to serve as an advisor, and be present for the demonstration of learning at the end of the study, no teacher is obligated to serve in this capacity. Only an appropriately licensed teacher advisor can evaluate the demonstration of learning and issue a recommendation as to whether credit should be earned by the student. Final approval and credit award determinations will be made by the Director of School Counseling and/or Principal. Please note: an Independent Study in music will not satisfy requirements for the VYO or state, regional, or national music festivals and organizations.

description: The United States military has gone through vast changes and trials in its 250-year history. From humble beginnings defending private property to a major world power that maintains the balance of power around the globe, America’s relationship with its armed forces has been a statement of the growth of America itself. In this class, you will not just learn about the major conﬂicts our country’s troops have participated in, but also the story of America itself represented in the stories that each conﬂict tells. Among other topics, this course will look at the power of ideas in the American Revolution, the importance of the Industrial Revolution during the Civil War, the treatment of veterans in the World Wars, the desegregation of the Korean War, and the political strife of actions in Vietnam. We will be looking to visit military history museums, battleﬁelds, and historical reenactment troops in New England as well as looking at the evolution of ﬁrearms and other weaponry in the past 250 years. The ﬁnal project of this course will be the creation of a documentary on a key part of America’s military history where you will show your interest and expertise in a ﬁeld of study.

description: Chemistry is the study of matter, which means that literally everything you can see is made of a chemical. Chemicals are, in turn, made of element, and elements are made of protons, neutrons, and electrons. From ﬁreworks, to computer screens, to ph tests, to photography, understanding how chemicals react and the colors they produce has shaped our world. We’ll explore how light and matter interact to create the spectrum of colors in our day to day lives. Understanding elements and the periodic table will be instrumental in our investigation. We’ll also learn about the history of dyes and textiles, and create some really stunning tie dye.
offering_note: Semester II 2025-26 studio; rotates by semester
notes: Studio One. Semester II. Department label in catalog: Chemistry. GX: Creativity. Driving questions: How are colors determined by chemistry? / How can we use predictable chemical reactions to help us understand the world we live in?

description: The focus of many stories is survival, and the word survival can mean many things. It can mean physical survival, like ﬁnding food and water. It can mean emotional survival, like feeling steady in your life. It also can mean the survival of a country or a culture. For this class, we will mostly focus on physical and emotional survival. We’ll be reading and responding to books like Teens at War, Gather, Into the Wild, and Call of the Wild. In addition, we may watch movies like Unbroken. Over the course of the semester, we’ll analyze how characters survive or don’t in these stories. Our other focus will be survival in Vermont speciﬁcally. We will be watching Vermont Department of Fish and Wildlife videos, and we may meet with specialists in various kinds of survival. This class may include some signiﬁcant skill practice outside. Our ﬁnal project will be comprehensive guides to surviving various aspects of Vermont. Students will choose subtopics within this overall topic, and each will create a comprehensive guide that might include sections like hunting, ﬁshing, driving in the winter, avoiding ticks, or other sub-topics that interest them. We will work on this guide over the course of the semester.
offering_note: Semester II 2025-26 studio; rotates by semester
notes: Studio Two. Semester II. GX: Global Stewardship. Driving questions: How can Vermonters best survive local challenges, like weather, a need to hunt, ticks and tick illnesses, etc.? / What do stories about survival tell us about survival, ourselves, and our world?

description: Horror stories have always been a part of human societies for thousands of years, typically providing explanations and physical shapes of the unknown. Each country and culture’s genre varies according to their inﬂuences and experiences and the horror in the United States is a unique experience of its own. This course will get into the origins of American horror and how the events and cultures in America’s history have formed this genre in a distinct American view. From breaking away from a European standard to targeting minorities to addressing political issues, horror in the United States has provided a form of expression that has become one of the country’s most popular outlets. We’ll be looking at more than just media and literature as we’ll be looking at the popularity of themed destinations, holidays, and events. Students will learn to create a representation of horror that reﬂects their own experiences in America today. There will be a variety of group and solo projects, so collaboration is expected to be developed in this course so everyone has a chance to actualize their horror ideals. Appreciation and understanding are the key components of success for this class.

description: This class will be a survey course that provides students a beginner’s insight into the various belief systems around the globe. World Religious and Belief is a course designed to introduce students to different systems of faith and how those faiths have been both shaped by history and culture and how they have shaped history and culture. This religions course will focus on comparison instead of criticism as we look to see common messages and practices of peoples around the world. These religions will vary from early faiths in human world systems to major religions of today to analysis of minority belief systems. We will look at the line between religion and cult and discuss how those differences shape a society. At the end of the course, students will put together a travel brochure of famous sites for someone to visit on a religious trip from one of the religions we have discussed or that falls into the category of the subjects relevant to the course. The brochure will mention each site’s importance to the religion and will display your knowledge of the subject.

description: What do Taylor Swift, Dire Straits, Leonardo DiCaprio, and garden gnomes all have in common? description: This Foundations of Art course covers painting, sculpture, architecture and other media from the following historical eras: Prehistoric, Ancient Egyptian, Aegean, Greek, and Roman. The focus will be on how the ideas of ancient peoples have been built upon over time and are still being used by modern and contemporary artists. The course will also cover modern challenges concerning the preservation and viewing of ancient works of art. Lessons in making art will stem from the ideas of ancient artists and their work. Students will have the opportunity to build technical skills and create their own works in the following media: drawing, painting, printmaking, photography, sculpture, ceramics, and other applied arts.

description: This Foundations of Art course covers painting, sculpture, architecture and other media from the following historical areas: Early Medieval, Gothic, the Italian Renaissance, Fifteenth Century Art in Northern Europe, Art of Sixteenth Century Europe, Baroque, and Rococo. From painting illuminated manuscripts to the construction of light filled cathedrals, the artists of these time periods demonstrated advanced skills and shed light on their subjects during some very adverse and challenging times. Their works of art will serve as the inspiration for students as they develop technical skills and create their own drawings, paintings, prints, photographs, sculptures, and other applied works of art.

description: This Foundations of Art course covers painting, sculpture, architecture and other media from native cultures with a focus on understanding how their world view has shaped their art as they have maintained and/or adapted their culture over time. Cultures considered include those of Asia, Africa, Oceania, and the Americas. Ideas and artifacts from these cultures will inspire the work of students as they hone technical skills and create drawings, paintings, prints, photographs, sculptures, pottery, and other applied works of art.
prerequisites: None
notes: Foundations of Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: This Foundations of Art course covers painting, sculpture, architecture and other media from the following modern historical periods: New Styles in Nineteenth Century Art, Art of Later Nineteenth Century, Art of the Early Twentieth Century, and Modern Art Movements to the Present. Beginning with Picasso, artists rejected traditional views and were driven by new ideas and experimentation. Along with industry and technology, art shaped the fast paced, idea driven world of today in which creativity and invention are highly prized. Students in this class will have the opportunity to be inventive as they develop technical skills in drawing, painting, printmaking, photography, sculpture, ceramics, and other applied arts.
prerequisites: None
notes: Foundations of Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: The focus of this course will be on the processes used in low-fire pottery. Emphasis will be placed on developing vocabulary, skills, and craftsmanship. Three-dimensional drawing, process documentation, procedural writing, historical research, and art criticism will also be a part of the course. Throughout the course, students will trace the history of pottery from ancient times to the present and discover the science behind this art. Students will be encouraged to embrace new ideas and materials, to think of unique solutions to visual problems, to use the processes to achieve their goals, and to evaluate their finished products.
prerequisites: Any of the Foundations of Art courses
notes: Upper Level Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: In this painting course, students will learn techniques associated with watercolor, gouache, ink, and various forms of acrylic paint. If time allows, it could also include explorations of collage, mixed media,and mural painting. It should be understood that drawing is foundational to most other media; therefore, painting preparation will include drawing lessons and exercises dedicated to building the perceptions of edges, space, relationships, lights & shadow, color and gestalt (perception of the whole). Artistic development, and psychobiology of the brain will be discussed in order to understand ourselves and the way we perceive the world around us. We will study the works of the masters and other painters throughout history. The elements of art and the principles of design will be related to both observational and abstract work. Realistic subject matter will include the genres of still life, landscape, and portraiture. As students develop technical skill, there will be an increased emphasis on creativity and pursuit of individual interests through wet media.
prerequisites: Any of the Foundations of Art courses
notes: Upper Level Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: In this course, students will create photographic images, focusing on composition, clarity, and contrast. While digital photography will be the primary process used, it may be possible to include black and white film photography and photo editing with Adobe Photoshop. The photographic processes used will be subject to the available equipment, software, and space. Emphasis will be placed on developing vocabulary, skills, and craftsmanship. The course will cover the development of photography from its inception to current times. Process documentation, procedural writing, historical research, and art criticism will all be part of the course. Students will be encouraged to see the world from a photographer’s point of view, to embrace new ideas and materials, to think of unique solutions to visual problems, to use photographic processes to achieve their goals, and to evaluate their finished images.
prerequisites: Any of the Foundations of Art courses
notes: Upper Level Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: In this sculpture class, students will create three-dimensional works in a variety of media which may include: plaster, ceramics, wood, soapstone, and found objects. They will explore the four sculptural processes of modeling, casting, carving, and assemblage. If time allows, the class may be able to create an installation. It should be understood that drawing is foundational to most other media; therefore, the course will include drawing lessons and exercises dedicated to building the perceptions of edges, space, relationships, lights & shadow, color and gestalt (perception of the whole). These lessons will increase the students ability to communicate three-dimensional ideas. Artistic development, and psychobiology of the brain will be discussed in order to understand ourselves and the way we perceive the world around us. Students will study the works of the masters and other sculptors throughout history. The elements of art and the principles of design will be related to both observational and abstract work. As the course progresses, there will be an increased emphasis on creativity and pursuit of individual interests in three dimensions.
prerequisites: Any of the Foundations of Art courses
notes: Upper Level Art Courses (subheading). Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: This course is for self-motivated, serious art students who wish to pursue studies in art further than other courses have allowed. College bound students may use this time to accumulate work for a college portfolio. Other students may have a particular media that they want to explore in-depth. Projects and topics of study are proposed by the students, although some assignments may be given. In addition to studio projects, students will submit weekly sketchbooks and writing assignments. Writing topics will include art processes, art history, art criticism, current events, and moral/ethical questions in art. Emphasis is placed on skill, creativity, problem solving, experimentation, self-direction and self-critique. The product of the semester’s work will be an exhibition which communicates a progression of skills and ideas.
prerequisites: Students will have taken a minimum of two art courses. More consideration will be given to students who have taken more than one Foundations and all offered Upper Level courses.
notes: Upper Level Art Courses (subheading). Level listed: Honors (Level 3).

It teaches intermediate to advanced skills in word-processing software, presentation software, and database creation and management, placing special emphasis on spreadsheet and data manipulation. The course also addresses the way these applications integrate with one another. Students explore other business applications and technologies, as well, including collaboration, data storage, and content development. The course also helps students develop skills in organization, expressiveness, communication, and creativity. They will also gain an understanding of responsible digital citizenship, media literacy, and the impact of technology on communication and society. Projects will include creating original podcasts, filming and editing short videos, and engaging with industry-standard tools and software.

This course is offered as a component of the Business Administration & Technology (BAT) program or a stand-alone course.

It integrates graphic design, desktop publishing, digital photography, finance, online activities and public relations. The major production is the yearbook and/or supplement to the yearbook. Due to the nature of the product, students taking the course are expected to be responsible and self-motivated. This is a FULL year course.

description: This course will explore the richness of American literature as well as the stories that caused them to be written. The course will explore Native American and early colonial writings and then branch out into the giants of the 19th and 20th centuries before ending with modern American classics. There are too many works to list here, but among the titles considered for this course are The Crucible, The Scarlet Letter, various short works and poetry by Poe and others, The Great Gatsby, To Kill a Mockingbird, Of Mice and Men, The Grapes of Wrath, The Old Man and the Sea, Our Town, Death of a Salesman, and The Things They Carried. Non-fiction reading will come in the form of articles, research, etc. The reading list may change according to the wishes of the class and the availability of texts. A major emphasis will be placed on critical reading and writing. Students will be expected to achieve the standards for 9th grade writing as set forth in the Common Core Standards. Students will be exposed to various types of writing, including informational/ explanatory, argumentative, and narrative. There will be instruction on English mechanics and vocabulary will be geared toward SAT preparation. Frequent homework will be assigned, along with long-term projects. Consequently, students need to be motivated learners. Students are expected to come to class prepared, to do all assigned work, and be ready to learn and to participate. The honors course differs from the standard in terms of the amount and depth of reading, vocabulary and writing assignments. Some literature selections will differ between honors and standard.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: This is a Required Course; American Literature required for graduation
notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: This Foundations of Art course covers painting, sculpture, architecture and other media from the following historical areas: Early Medieval, Gothic, the Italian Renaissance, Fifteenth Century Art in Northern Europe, Art of Sixteenth Century Europe, Baroque, and Rococo. Even in an era dubbed the “Dark Ages”, people produced amazing works of art. From painting illuminated manuscripts to the construction of light filled cathedrals, the artists of these time periods demonstrated advanced skills and shed light on their subjects during some very adverse and challenging times. Their works of art will serve as the inspiration for students as they develop technical skills and create their own drawings, paintings, prints, photographs, sculptures, and other applied works of art.
prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). The catalog prints, as this course's description, the same text as the Art Illuminates the Dark art course (apparent copy-paste error in the source); copied verbatim.

description: In this course, students will focus on developing creativity through original forms of descriptive writing, poetry, drama and fiction. Vivid vocabulary development, and creative writing techniques will be explored while working on essential worldbuilding skills. Students will have opportunities to take part in writing contests and to submit their work on the Young Writer's Project website. Elements of fiction and poetry writing will include character development, setting, plot, sensory details, imagery, figurative language and sound devices. Among the units considered for this course are Modified Fairy Tales, Gothic Literature, Fantasy, Science Fiction, Media Critique, Realistic, and Adventure. (Course is offered in the Fall.)
prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses

description: This course provides an introduction to the principles of writing and organizing stories for publication in print and electronic mediums, as well as getting students ready for the transition into the career world. Students will develop and compose news stories, learn and adhere to industry-standard style guidelines, conduct meaningful and appropriate research, and understand how the ethics, laws, and culture of journalism influence the media. Students will also create a working resume, cover letter, and work on college admissions essays. (Course is offered in the Spring.)
prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
offering_note: Course is offered in the Spring.
notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: This course will explore modern literature from the 20th and 21st centuries. There are too many works to list here, but among the titles considered for this course are The Great Gatsby, To Kill a Mockingbird, The Grapes of Wrath, Death of a Salesman, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, The Devil in the White City and In Cold Blood. The reading list may change according to the wishes of the class and the availability of texts. A major emphasis will be placed on critical reading and writing. Students will be expected to achieve the standards for 10th grade writing as set forth in the Common Core Standards. Students will be exposed to various types of writing, including informational/explanatory, argumentative, and literary analysis. There will be instruction on English mechanics and vocabulary will be geared toward SAT preparation. Frequent homework will be assigned along with long-term projects. Consequently, students need to be motivated learners. Students are expected to come to class prepared, to do all assigned work, and be ready to learn and participate. The honors course differs from the standards in terms of the amount and depth of reading, vocabulary and writing assignments. Also, some literature selections will differ.
prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: This elective upper level course is designed to expand students' literary horizons beyond their English and American heritage to include the study of masterworks of world literature. Students will come to a greater appreciation of and reverence for “foreign” cultural traditions, values, and attitudes, while at the same time identifying those elements which bind all humans together. Students will utilize critical reading and thinking skills, increase their knowledge of vocabulary, develop expository writing skills, produce a research paper, and engage in team learning activities. Students will read a variety of texts, both fiction and nonfiction, from global authors both modern and historical. Reading selections will come from Africa, the Middle East, Latin America, East Asia, and Eastern Europe. The reading list may change according to the wishes of the class and the availability of texts. A major emphasis will be placed on critical reading and writing. Students will be expected to achieve the standards for 11th grade writing and reading as set forth in the Common Core Standards. Frequent homework will be assigned, along with long-term projects. Consequently, students need to be motivated learners. Students are expected to come to class prepared, to do all assigned work, and be ready to learn and to participate. The honors course differs from the standard in terms of the amount and depth of reading and the amount and length of writing assignments. Some literature selections will differ between honors and standard.
prerequisites: Successful completion of two prior English courses
notes: Levels listed: Modified (Level 2), Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3).

description: This course deals with physical, emotional, social and mental well-being. It looks at you as a healthy, whole person. The main topics discussed are: family health, mental health, nutrition, prevention of disease, personal health habits, consumer health, substance abuse, and birth control information. Expectations of the course include: class participation, personal reflection, fitness days, and public speaking.

Special emphasis is placed on graphing and problem solving. Not recommended for college bound students. Honors: This is a fast paced first-year Algebra course designed to help students develop an understanding of variables, exponents, radicals factoring, polynomials, and rational expressions. Special emphasis is placed on graphing and problem-solving skills.
prerequisites: Standard: Score of 60+ on the Algebra readiness assessment 232 on NWEA testing; Honors: Score of 70+ on the Algebra readiness assessment, Pre-Algebra 85%, or 238 on NWEA testing
notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). Standard and Honors descriptions are given separately in the entry.

description: Standard: This course is a continuation of Algebra. The concepts of Algebra I are applied and expanded. Additional topics will include in-depth work with quadratics, polynomial functions, their properties, and applications. Trigonometric functions, logarithms, conic sections, sequences and series, rational equations, probability and statistics will be explored. Not recommended for college bound students. Honors: This course is a continuation of Algebra I Honors. The concepts of Algebra I are applied and expanded. Additional topics include working with basic functions, their properties, and applications, trigonometric functions, analytic geometry, systems of equations, polynomials, relations and functions of the first, second, and third degree, real exponents, logarithms, conic sections, sequences and series, probability and statistics.
prerequisites: Standard: Algebra I (Standard or Honors); Honors: Algebra I Honors - a student who takes a full year or two semester to complete Algebra I is not eligible for Algebra II Honors.
notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). Standard and Honors descriptions are given separately in the entry.

A major goal of the course is to help students develop rigorous and logical, systematic methods of thinking. Therefore, proofs, and constructions are emphasized. The topics also include basic figures, proofs, coordinate geometry, constructions, and trigonometry.

notes: Levels listed: Standard (Level 2), Honors (Level 3). Standard and Honors descriptions are given separately in the entry.

description: Life Skills Math should not be taken for credit after a student passes Algebra 1. It is an introductory course for students that need remediation of basic math skills. Life Skills Math provides learners with math skills related to activities of daily living. Students will participate in a simulation of real-life mathematical issues, including earning money through a job, writing checks and paying bills with other forms of payment. Topics explored include identifying numbers as they relate to daily living, basic computations, understanding money value concepts, budgeting, measurement, time management, graphic representation, and elapsed time.
prerequisites: None

description: This course will inform students how individual choices directly influence occupational goals and future earnings potential. Real world topics covered will include income, money management, spending and credit, as well as saving and investing. Students will design personal and household budgets utilizing checking and saving accounts, gain knowledge in finance, debt and credit management, and evaluate and understand insurance and taxes. This course will provide a foundational understanding for making informed personal financial decisions leading to financial independence.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: This is a Required Course; Personal Finance is required for graduation
notes: Level 2 (Standard). Also listed as a Pre-Tech Foundation Course for Business Administration & Technology (p.59).

prerequisites: None

They will learn how to read rhythms and notes, as well as building chords, writing melodies and composing their own music. ● World Music - students will gain an understanding of music in different world cultures. They will understand how music is important in different communities and gain hands-on experience playing the music in an authentic fashion. ● Music in Media - students will learn how to create music for various forms of media, including movies, video games, and advertisements. They will gain an understanding of techniques used to engage an audience and play with their emotions.

description: Adapted Physical Education is an academic course designed to expose students to various activities and sports (at an adapted level based on the student’s needs) that promote an active, healthy lifestyle as well as are aligned with the Society for Health and Physical Education (SHAPE) academic standards. Students will explore the history, strategies, skills and rules of various recreational activities such as: Locomotor, Spatial awareness, sports skills, and health related fitness. Other sports and activities may be introduced as time, equipment and class size allow. Also, students will understand and employ ways to improve health related physical fitness. Students will become familiar with the components of health-related physical fitness which include cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, body composition and muscular strength and endurance. The “Fitnessgram”or (Brockport Fitness test) battery of tests and various technology products will be used to let students self-assess their health related fitness levels on a monthly basis. Students will be expected to dress in appropriate clothing for physical activities unless otherwise directed by the instructor. Most units will entail some skills recognition assessments, written assessments. Other assignments may include: Internet research, fitness journaling, and best course of action mini-reports related to the PE subject area. Class participation, social maturity and a positive attitude are paramount for being successful in this class. Outside class work will be 3hrs. per week maximum. “Fitness for Life, 6th ed.” will be furnished by the instructor so students can refer to them for clarification and to study for written assessments if appropriate with the students’ needs. If a student could not perform book work, alternate cognitive assignments will be created based on the level of the student.
prerequisites: Be recommended by a Case Manager, Specialist, or Director of Student Services
notes: Level listed: Modified (Level 2).

description: Adapted Physical Education 2 is an academic course that builds on mastering the SHAPE standards indicated in APE - I as well as the principles, strategies and teachings learned in Adapted Physical Education 1. Outside class work for this particular course will be no more than 3 hours per week. Unit study guides and a textbook entitled Aerobic Fitness Everyone will be furnished by the instructor so students can refer to them for clarification and to study for written assignments. If a student could not perform book work, alternate cognitive assignments will be created based on the level of the student. All course materials will be adapted based on the class, or the individual student.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Adaptive PE I, or be recommended by a Case Manager, Specialist, or the Director of Student Services
notes: Level listed: Modified (Level 2).

description: Fitness students will learn about physical fitness, the important role that exercise plays in our lives and how we can safely incorporate exercise into our daily routine. Concepts covered are related to nutrition, proper stretching and cooling down, strength and cardiovascular training, prevention and first aid for sports injuries, and fitness for special populations.

notes: Level 2 (Standard). The course-selection lists (pp.28-31) call it 'Personal Fitness/Sports Skills & Recreational Activities'.

This contract requires the approval of the PE teacher and the principal

Students will be expected to work towards improving skills in all sports studied, as well as designing and running class tournaments. Students will experience opportunities that promote physical literacy and lifetime wellness. Some units will be delivered by the instructor to the students via NFHSLEARN.COM and others will be study guides furnished by the instructor so students can refer to them for clarification and to study for written assessments.
