We will discuss history, composition, lighting, shallow depth of field, long depth of field, and how to bring emotion and mood into photographs in intentional ways. Students will explore editing techniques, and develop techniques to edit batches of photos at a time. This is a tech-based course, however, we will explore photography, mixed media, and other art techniques that can be applied to photographs. This course is very hands on, but requires lots of time on a chromebook to complete classwork on time. Take Photography 1, and see how far you can take your photography!
prerequisites: None
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Arts. Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course.

description: The curriculum will build on techniques and skills covered in Photography 1. We will take a deeper dive into student artwork and fine critiquing while also branching out on our place based learning. Students will explore who they are as a photographer and learn the legal and professional aspects of photography. We will find the limits of DSLR cameras and large format images. This course is for those who are self driven and prepared to take their photography and responsibilities as a photographer to the next level. This course requires permission from the instructor to enroll.
prerequisites: Photography 1 and signature from Instructor
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Arts. Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course.

description: A studio course designed to build on the artistic skills acquired in previous classes. This course provides an opportunity to do concentrated work on unique projects of interest for advanced students who have demonstrated in previous art courses the individual motivation and seriousness necessary to sustain an independent curriculum. A partial list of offerings may include drawing, printmaking, painting, 2D and 3D design, ceramics, metals and nontraditional materials. Students are encouraged to exhibit their projects and write an artist statement explaining and accompanying their exhibit. Sketching and journaling are encouraged throughout the semester. Content should be determined by the student in close consultation with the instructor prior to and throughout the semester.
prerequisites: Previously taken Art courses and signature from Instructor
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Arts. Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: An Art Teacher Assistant “TA” has two main focuses: supporting the teacher and supporting students in the Art Room. TA’s assist the teacher with everyday classroom tasks such as classroom management of supplies/materials, schoolwide art exhibits, and displays, etc. TA's assist students who need extra support in small groups or one-to-one. TA’s will work on their own independent art projects throughout the semester. TA's must have successfully completed art classes, have a passion for art, a positive and patient attitude, and enjoy working with people. This course requires permission from the instructor.
prerequisites: Previously taken Art courses and permission from Instructor
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Arts. Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

course_name: Art and Design 1 (Advanced) / Art and Design 2 (Advanced Placement)
description: This class is for highly motivated, independent students who want to challenge for an Advanced Placement Art credit in the area of 2D Design, 3D Design, and/or Drawing. Students will create a full body of artworks, document their creative process, and write frequent reflections. Keeping an investigative sketchbook is a must. It is a year-long course that focuses on creating a sustained investigation. Students must be prepared to create an inquiry that will allow them to create a body of work. If you are interested in this challenge, see an HHS art teacher to sign up for an interview and be prepared to share examples of previous artwork and/or sketchbooks. Students need explicit permission from the Arts Department prior to enrolling in this course. During the second semester of this full year course you will complete and submit a portfolio to the AP College Board.
prerequisites: Permission from Instructor and Portfolio Review before enrolling in the class
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Arts. Scheduled: 1 Block, Full Year. One year-long course printed under a single heading with two course numbers (Advanced Art & Design 1, AP Art & Design 2); kept as one record. Students submit a portfolio to the AP College Board in the second semester.

description: By State Law in order to get a driver's license before age eighteen, a person must have satisfactorily completed a driver education course. In order to receive credit for this course, a student must successfully complete both the classroom and the behind-the-wheel phases of Driver Education. All students will receive a minimum of 30 classroom hours of instruction, six hours behind the wheel, and six hours of observation time. Enrollment is determined by grade level then date of birth and if the student has obtained a learner's permit.
prerequisites: 15 years old and have a valid learner's permit before August 1st for Semester 1 & before January 1st for Semester 2.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: "This course must be taken in conjunction with either a student created project or physical education course."

description: The opportunity exists to take Driver Education during the summer. The classroom meets 5 days per week, for five weeks, typically from 7:30-9:00 a.m. In addition to the classroom, students participate in daily driving sessions. Students must attend all classes and complete 6 hours of behind-the-wheel instruction. A separate registration will take place during the second semester for the following summer. Enrollment is determined by grade level then date of birth and if the student has obtained a learner's permit.
prerequisites: 15 years old and have a valid learner's permit before June 1st
notes: Scheduled: Summer; classroom meets 5 days per week for five weeks.

description: All 9th graders must enroll in this course and pass. Patterns of Literature is a course designed to provide students with an initial exposure and engagement with the elements of story through the powerful lens of short story, epic, and drama. Learning to properly formulate and support arguments through writing will be a key focus, with lessons in grammar throughout to support those efforts.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: All students need four credits in English—one of which must be Patterns of Literature & Learning and one of which must be Perspectives of Literature unless granted permission from the English Department Chair—in order to graduate.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

course_name: Perspectives in Literature: Modern Human Experiences
description: This course will examine both nonfiction and fiction accounts of people from various places and backgrounds. The goal of the course will be to learn how our cultural and experiential differences can teach us more about the world that we live in and about ourselves. This course will utilize contemporary excerpts and larger works, as well as independently chosen material, to explore a range of cultures. Students will pick only one Perspectives offering.
prerequisites: Patterns of Literature
fulfills_text: All students need four credits in English—one of which must be Patterns of Literature & Learning and one of which must be Perspectives of Literature unless granted permission from the English Department Chair—in order to graduate.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

course_name: Perspectives in Literature: War and Humanity
description: This course will examine both nonfiction and fiction accounts based in the World War 2 and post-World War 2 time period. The goal of the course will be to investigate what a global war taught us about humanity, acceptance, and the importance of valuing people of all backgrounds. This course will utilize excerpts and larger works, as well as independently chosen material to explore the war from a range of perspectives. Students will pick only one Perspectives offering.
prerequisites: Patterns of Literature
fulfills_text: All students need four credits in English—one of which must be Patterns of Literature & Learning and one of which must be Perspectives of Literature unless granted permission from the English Department Chair—in order to graduate.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

course_name: American Literature and Composition: Dreams & Nightmares
description: This course explores themes central to American culture and identity through both classical texts and dystopian and post-apocalyptic literature. Students will use novels, poetry, film, historical documents, and nonfiction writing to enhance their critical thinking and analysis skills. Themes and concepts such as freedom, the realities of the American Dream, society’s influence on the individual, and others will be explored. The course also focuses on elevating voices often left out of the overarching American narrative. This course requires reading outside of class.
prerequisites: Perspectives in Literature (with suggested grade of at least a B) and signature from Instructor
fulfills_text: The following English classes do grant a credit toward the four English credit graduation requirement
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: This course emphasizes developing higher-order reasoning and thinking skills through consideration of such issues as the nature of reality, mind and consciousness, free will, evil, truth, ethics, morality and values. We will read philosophical texts, explore, debate, discuss, and write about contemporary issues using the principles of philosophy as a cornerstone to developing opinions that are specific, complex and refined. There will be a strong emphasis on reading and composition. This course requires reading outside of class.
prerequisites: Perspectives in Literature (with suggested grade of at least a B) and signature from Instructor
fulfills_text: The following English classes do grant a credit toward the four English credit graduation requirement
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: Advanced English & Composition emphasizes the power of clear and articulate language. Here students will implement their knowledge of literary conventions and how they serve to create communicative art forms. There is a heavy emphasis in writing conventions (grammar, usage and mechanics) and their application toward the critical writing of both texts and film: poetic, dramatic, fictional, informational and persuasive. The instructor assumes that all students enrolled will exhibit the motivation and interest of those who are seeking post-secondary education. *There is a pre-reading and writing component to this course that MUST be completed before the course begins-NO EXCEPTIONS.
prerequisites: American Literature (A) or Philosophy Lit and Composition and signature from Instructor
fulfills_text: The following English classes do grant a credit toward the four English credit graduation requirement
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall.

description: Advanced Placement English Literature and Composition is for students who wish to take the AP Literature Exam through The College Board. Poetry, drama and fictional works are the core topics of study and serve as the tools for literary criticism through precise analyses of literature. In order to best prepare students for the AP exam, they will read extensively, become familiar with literary terminology and classifications, and write numerous critical essays. This course is for students who exhibit college level motivation and interest in literature.
prerequisites: 80% or higher in Advanced English & Composition and signature from Instructor
fulfills_text: The following English classes do grant a credit toward the four English credit graduation requirement
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring. Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

description: In this course, students will explore the major literary elements of creative writing through exploration of short stories. Students will complete reading reviews, discussions, and writing practice to explore the different elements. Students will engage in the writing process and will produce an original short story for the final project.
prerequisites: Perspectives in Literature
fulfills_text: The following English classes do grant a credit toward the four English credit graduation requirement
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: In this course, students will be introduced to major film terms, techniques, and narrative structures in order to understand how films are constructed to make meaning. Major films, both classic and contemporary, will be examined for these elements.
prerequisites: Perspectives in Literature
fulfills_text: The following English classes do grant a credit toward the four English credit graduation requirement
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

course_name: Immersed in Verse: Lessons from Poetry
description: This course will explore a variety of poetic styles and themes employed by different writers. In addition to reading, listening to, and understanding poetry, this course will also provide students with an opportunity to write some of their own. All students will create an anthology, showcasing their work and other poetry that caught their attention. This course is perfect for the established poet or for the student who just wants to learn more about poetry.
prerequisites: Patterns of Literature
fulfills_text: The following English classes do grant a credit toward the four English credit graduation requirement
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: In this course, students will be challenged to think critically about the place we live. Students will learn the story of our place in Vermont and the Upper Valley through community-based learning, as well as direct hands-on experiences with the land, people, businesses, and cultural elements of our region. Students will participate in an Exhibition of their learning at the end of the semester, and all students will receive an English and Social Studies credit. A great choice if you like to explore, question, be active, and get outside. Please note, this is a TWO-block course.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: The following English classes do grant a credit toward the four English credit graduation requirement; "all students will receive an English and Social Studies credit"
notes: Scheduled: 2 Blocks, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. Also listed under Social Studies (p.24) with the same course number; one record kept here. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: This course can be taken for college composition credit through dual enrollment with the Community College of Vermont. In this course students will develop communication and composition skills and will work collaboratively to develop their ability to analyze and interpret information, write professional documents, and speak effectively. Students will also pursue research on a question or problem of their choice and produce a paper that reflects a deep understanding of a topic.
prerequisites: Perspectives in Literature
fulfills_text: The following English classes do grant a credit toward the four English credit graduation requirement
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall. College composition credit via dual enrollment with the Community College of Vermont is optional.

description: This course gives students an opportunity to practice and develop public speaking skills through creating individual speeches, logical debate speeches and evidence-based debate speeches. Students will become more effective speakers by working on voice, presentation and organization. The skills that students will practice are research, argumentation, logic, analysis, organization, effective presentation, and teamwork. The purpose in this class is to empower students to become more comfortable with public speaking and present themselves with confidence.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: The following English classes do grant a credit toward the four English credit graduation requirement
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: This course is designed for students who want continued growth in public speaking and debate. Whereas, level 1 students are introduced to public speaking, research, organization and argumentation, level 2 students are expected to improve on these foundational skills and work toward greater proficiency. Level 2 students are also expected to be mentors to level 1 students and assist in debate instruction and rounds.
prerequisites: Public Speaking & Debate 1
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: "The following course will not be counted toward the four English credit graduation requirements" (elective English class).

department: English for Speakers of Other Languages
course_name: English for Speakers of Other Languages
description: This introductory course is offered to newcomers to the United States and to academic English. ESOL I offers individualized support to help students develop the language necessary to succeed in the mainstream high school classroom. In addition to receiving assistance with academic coursework, students will develop a personal vocabulary acquisition plan; acquire the basic social and academic English needed for competence in speaking, listening, reading, and writing through a variety of media; practice reading strategies using graded readers and adapted works of literature; and practice basic grammatical structures and writing conventions. This course counts toward the English graduation requirement.
prerequisites: For students whose native language is not English and who are at a beginning stage of learning English
fulfills_text: This course counts toward the English graduation requirement.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Description refers to the course as "ESOL I".

department: English for Speakers of Other Languages
description: This class focuses on providing ESOL students with the support needed to succeed in their mainstream academic courses. In addition students will work on individual or group projects, keep a vocabulary notebook, and pursue a personal program of reading and writing journals.
prerequisites: For students enrolled in the ESOL program
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

department: English for Speakers of Other Languages
course_name: U.S. Job Applications and Career Readiness
description: This course is designed for students new to the United States to help them navigate the process of applying for a job and beginning a career. Topics may include: types of jobs available to high school students, acquiring and filling out a job application, business communication, job interviews, and social media and work.
prerequisites: For students enrolled in the ESOL program; ESOL II or teacher permission
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

department: English for Speakers of Other Languages
course_name: College Decisions and Applications in the U.S.
description: This course is designed for multilingual students who are new to the United States. The purpose is to help students gain an understanding of the college and university systems in the United States and the college application process. Topics include reasons to go to college, types of colleges and universities, the college application process, college essays, and financial aid. Practical workshops, guest speakers, college visits, and meetings with college admissions counselors will be part of the course whenever possible.
prerequisites: For students enrolled in the ESOL program; ESOL II
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is designed to prepare students for a high school algebra course. The focus of this course is to create a foundation of algebraic thinking. To accomplish this task, students will work with operations on algebraic expressions and equations. Students will learn to use algebra to represent patterns and relationships. The students will be introduced to both algebraic and geometric concepts with an emphasis on understanding number systems and solving basic equations.
prerequisites: 8th-grade Teacher Recommendation
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is designed to build a solid foundation for future success. This course will provide opportunities to apply algebraic concepts to real world applications, to geometric models, and to make connections between concrete models and abstract concepts. This course will develop an understanding of the Language of Algebra, Monomial Operations, and have an emphasis on Solving, Graphing, and Writing Linear Equations and Inequalities, as well as introduce Exponential Functions.
prerequisites: Algebra Prep with a final grade of 60% or better OR 8th grade Teacher Recommendation
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course builds on the foundation set in Algebra A. This course will provide opportunities to add to algebraic concepts and begin to see different patterns and function relationships. These relationships extend into more abstract concepts. This course will begin with solving Systems of Equations and Inequalities, then develop an understanding of Exponential and Quadratic Functions and will further elaborate on Simplifying Radicals, Polynomial Operations, and Factoring Quadratics.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 - Part A with a final grade of 60% or better OR 8th grade Teacher Recommendation
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is designed to provide opportunities to apply geometric and measurement concepts to real world applications, making connections between concrete models and abstract concepts. This course will also emphasize informal proofs and problem solving to integrate review of Algebra 1 concepts. Students will be provided with opportunities to develop and apply properties of lines and angles. They will also build understanding with concepts of parallel/perpendicular lines, congruence and trigonometry as well as utilize relationships among 2-Dimensional and 3-Dimensional figures with emphasis on triangles, polygons, and circles.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 - Part B with a final grade of 60% or better
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is designed to provide students the opportunity to make conjectures about geometric situations and prove in a variety of ways, both formal and informal, that their conclusion follows logically from their hypothesis. Students will justify geometric relationships and properties of geometric figures through congruence and similarity of triangles that will be established using appropriate theorems. Geometry is meant to lead students to an understanding that reasoning and proof are fundamental aspects of mathematics and something that sets it apart from the other sciences. This course will also emphasize problem solving and integrate review of Algebra 1 concepts.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 - Part B with a final grade of 80% or better
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is an extension of Algebra 1, providing a more detailed analysis of operations with real numbers and polynomials. Topics of study include: functions and relations, transformation of functions, linear functions, systems of linear functions, radicals in other bases and inequalities, quadratic functions, complex numbers. Additional topics of study may include: rational expressions and equations and higher degree functions. A graphing calculator will be used regularly.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 - Part B
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is an extension of Algebra 1 - Part A & B, providing a more detailed analysis of operations with real numbers and polynomials as well as graphing rational functions, and conics. It will follow the same curriculum as the standard Algebra 2 course. However, it will go into more depth and detail on each of the topics of study. A graphing calculator is recommended.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 - Part B with a final grade of 80% or better
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Topics covered in this course include trigonometry, exponential and logarithmic functions, polynomial functions as well as Rational Functions and their graphs. This course is preparation for a college general math course.
prerequisites: Algebra 2 with a final grade of 70% or better
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is designed for above average math students. Students will be expected to do longer and more difficult assignments and tests than in the standard Precalculus course. Topics covered include: trigonometry, analytic geometry, exponential and logarithmic functions, polynomial and rational functions and their graphs, and if time, sequences and series. Students will have regular practice in preparing for standardized tests (SAT). This course is a preparation for the successful completion of high school AP calculus.
prerequisites: Algebra 2 Advanced with a final grade of 80% or better
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course satisfies the Advanced Placement Calculus-AB curriculum consisting of all the requirements designed by the College Board and is equivalent to one semester of college level calculus. It is devoted to the 3 Big Ideas: Limits, Derivatives and Integrals/Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. The topics will be presented in a variety of real world problems both from the textbook and released AP materials. Students need to achieve an Enduring Understanding of the concepts which are linked to Learning Objectives and Essential Knowledge designed by the College Board. The course emphasizes multiple approaches to calculus, with concepts and solutions being expressed with graphs, algebraically, tables and in narrative writing and/or verbal presentations.
prerequisites: Precalculus (Advanced) with a final grade of 80% or better
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall. Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

description: This course covers the topics necessary for taking the Calculus AB Exam. Students will take an AP Calculus exam in May and then spend the remainder of the course working on advanced math projects.
prerequisites: Calculus 1 (Advanced Placement) with a final grade of 70% or better
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring. Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

description: This course is an introduction to programming using the Python programming language using JetBrain's Pycharm. After gaining an understanding of the history of computing, programming concepts covered include input, processing, output, loops, conditional statements, functions, data structures and algorithms and file handling. The focus of the course will be to code everyday programs like payroll, cash registers, ATM's and simple games.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 - Part B
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. Applied Maths course. Catalog: advanced credit possible by completing Harvard's Open Courseware CS50 independently; students can earn AP credit by enrolling in and preparing for the AP CS A exam (Java). Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: This course will extend students’ proficiency in mathematics, and apply these skills to technical and/ or industrial situations and problems. Technical Math topics may include but are not limited to technical drawing, rational numbers, systems of measurements, tolerances, numerical language, geometry, algebra, statistics, and using tables, graphs, charts, and other data displays. Students will use the engineering design process while working independently and collaboratively in a course which will be project-based. Students will have to use communication skills when designing their project for the school, a teacher, or community. Given that there will be multiple different projects going at once during a class period, this class is student driven. Students should be self motivated to work independently or within their group to finish projects in a timely manner. Projects will include, but are not limited to, building tables, shelves, chairs, desks, etc. Math will be used during the design and building process to represent pieces of the project like size, diameter, orientation, material tolerance, etc. Students will be asked to demonstrate understanding through reflections of the 8 common core standards of mathematical practices.
prerequisites: Intro to Engineering or Algebra Prep
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Applied Maths course.

description: This project-based course is designed to reinforce general math skills through real life application, extend these skills to include some pre-algebra and algebra topics, and use these skills in a variety of practical, consumer, business, and occupational applications. Course topics typically include rational numbers, measurements, basic statistics, ratio and proportions, basic geometry, formulas and simple equations. Students will be asked to demonstrate understanding through reflections of the 8 common core standards of mathematical practices.
prerequisites: Teacher recommendation only
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. Applied Maths course.

description: This course will extend students’ proficiency in mathematics, and apply these skills to build and solve problems. Students will learn to utilize the engineering design process while working independently and collaboratively in a course which will be project-based. Projects may include, but are not limited to, making mouse trap cars, creating catapults that hit multiple targets, and designing and building of Rube Goldberg machines. In many cases the math process will be done similar to the reverse engineering process with the math learned after the project is completed or during the process. Students will be asked to demonstrate understanding through written reflections of the 8 common core standards of mathematical practices.
prerequisites: Algebra Prep or General Applied Math
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. Applied Maths course.

description: This course is a study of descriptive statistics, probability, and inferential statistics. Students will discover how to collect, measure, display and summarize all types of data. Through the use of probability and inferential concepts, students will find how to describe relationships and make predictions about their data. Applying statistics to real life applications will be the major focus of this course. Data analysis will utilize the graphing calculator (TI-83) and computer software. This course can be taken for college credit through concurrent enrollment with the Community College of Vermont.
prerequisites: Algebra 2 with a final grade of 70% or better
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Applied Maths course. College credit optional through concurrent enrollment with the Community College of Vermont.

course_name: Dollars and Sense: The Mathematics of Personal Finance
description: This course is more than just understanding facts about money—it’s about developing the skills and habits to make financial decisions that lead to long-term success. This course equips students with practical knowledge to navigate real-world financial situations, from budgeting and banking to managing debt and making informed college and career choices. Students will explore key financial topics, including savings, credit & credit cards, loans, investments, emergency funds, and the power of compound interest. Students will also learn to use powerful financial tools, like spreadsheets and financial calculators, that will be useful for the rest of their lives. By the end of the course, students will be prepared to create and follow a personal financial plan, setting themselves up for a stable and secure future.
prerequisites: Algebra 1-Part B or higher
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. Applied Maths course.

description: This course provides students with the opportunity to deepen their understanding of mathematics while developing leadership, communication, and instructional skills. Students enrolled as Math TAs support classroom instruction by helping maintain an organized and productive learning environment. They may create materials for instruction or provide one-on-one or small-group support. Through this role, students strengthen their own mathematical thinking, build confidence in explaining complex ideas, and gain valuable experience in teaching, collaboration, and responsibility. This course is ideal for students who enjoy mathematics, are dependable and organized, and are interested in mentoring others or exploring education, tutoring, or leadership roles.
prerequisites: Completion of AP Calculus
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Better Than Yesterday is designed to give students the opportunity to learn and apply tactical and practical life skills with the goal of discovering the best physical and mental versions of themselves. This course utilizes the “5 Pillars of Health” as a basis for it’s curriculum content. These are: Connection, Mindset, Sleep, Nutrition, & Exercise. A mix of class discussion, hands-on experiences, place-based opportunities, low impact physical activities, and technological resources will provide the conduits that deliver the course material. Students will strive to implement the course content into their daily lives in a quest to achieve their unique & specific goals aimed at a life of purpose and fulfillment.
prerequisites: 1 PE Credit
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course.

description: This course provides students with the opportunity to participate in several team-based sports/games with a high level of intensity. The involvement in specific sports will provide an atmosphere that is competitive, while promoting communication and collaboration among peers. Students will also gain an appreciation for the degree of fitness necessary to participate in these different sports. Units may include; soccer, volleyball, speedball, flag football, kinball, ultimate frisbee, floor hockey, and others.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course focuses on improving the overall fitness capacity of each participant. Although the course is offered in a group setting, the intensity and level of challenge in each workout is specifically modified to meet the individual needs of each student. Each class places a focus on strength, cardiovascular endurance, coordination, power, stamina, agility, and flexibility. The teacher will guide students through a variety of different exercises and movement patterns including weightlifting, conditioning, bodyweight movements, and other mobility endeavors of the body. CrossFit workouts are different everyday. All students will be expected to participate in the group workout everyday. Participants will be guaranteed to sweat each day while embracing the physical and cognitive challenges presented through this program. The goal of this course is to enhance each participants’ fitness capacity in ways that support students to become the best physical versions of themselves.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is designed for students who are looking to embark on a low impact approach to fitness. The goal is to create a daily fitness routine that encompasses a variety of exercises that have proven to be effective for lifetime fitness, health, and wellness. Classes will feature endurance walking and other lifetime fitness activities such as stretching, light strength training, and fitness-based games. In this course we will aim to “Get Our Steps In” each day while operating in a stress-free environment that fosters healthy lifestyle choices. The Lifetime Fitness course promotes time outside whenever weather conditions permit.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is designed to provide opportunities for the students to elect individual and team activities that have carryover value associated with them. These lifetime activities allow for mixed grade, co-educational participation and will provide a variety of life and leisure time offerings. The course objectives include assisting students in the development of physical fitness and motor ability; aiding the student’s physical, mental, and social growth; and offering activities which facilitate meeting these objectives. Activities may include: Tennis, Bowling, Badminton, Table Tennis, Snow Shoeing, Pickleball, bocce ball, croquet, horseshoes, Frisbee golf, Corn hole, etc.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is designed to give students the opportunity to excel in advanced fitness concepts and weight training techniques. This course involves daily training sessions, which will be based on improving athletic performance. Students will work towards improving muscular strength, endurance and explosive power. They will partake in a variety of training techniques such as weight lifting, Olympic lifts, and plyometrics. Students will use pre-designed workouts over the course of the semester and track their progress. They will be expected to complete the given workout with their best effort and provide evidence of improvement at the conclusion of the course. Prior training experience is not necessary but the willingness to train at a high level is.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Personal Fitness is designed to give students the opportunity to learn a variety of fitness concepts and conditioning techniques used for obtaining optimal physical fitness. This course includes active workout/exercise sessions aimed to enhance the fitness capacity of it’s participants. Students will benefit from comprehensive total body training and conditioning with a specific focus on the 10 components of fitness: cardiovascular/respiratory endurance, stamina, strength, flexibility, power, speed, coordination, agility, balance, and accuracy. Students will have the opportunity to explore a variety of approaches to enhance their physical and mental performance in the elements of exercise, nutrition, sleep, relational connections, and mindset. Students will strive to implement the course content into their daily lives in a quest to achieve specific goals.
prerequisites: 1 credit in any P.E. class.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Advanced Personal Fitness is designed specifically for those students who seek to take a deep dive into the cognitive and physical literacy of fitness related content and enhancement of personal fitness capacity. This course requires all students to be physically active participants everyday. YOU WILL SWEAT! This course encompasses all of the integral elements of Personal Fitness with the addition of a series of higher level principals. Students consistently log every workout session and analyze their performance while on a quest to discover the most effective methodologies that bring them closer to their fitness goals. This course will feature a deep dive into various training principles proven to impact the physiology of the human body.
prerequisites: Personal Fitness, CrossFit or Strength and Conditioning and signature from Instructor
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: The focus of the Wellness portion of this course is on the physical, social and emotional aspects of health. Students will research their family's health history in regard to disease prevention. Students will set personal wellness goals in areas of nutrition and fitness. The following topics will also be covered: human sexuality, relationships, substance abuse prevention, and communication skills. As part of the human sexuality unit students will have the opportunity to take care of a "Real Care Baby", a computerized baby simulator. In addition, students will learn how the media influences our choices and behaviors in each of these topics. Guest speakers and videos are used to enhance the curriculum when possible.
prerequisites: None (This is a required course for all entering 9th graders at Hartford High School and must be repeated if a passing grade is not earned.)
fulfills_text: This is a required course for all entering 9th graders at Hartford High School
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block / 1 Term, Fall / Spring. Required for all entering 9th graders. Catalog: "Students are graded on class participation, projects, quizzes, and homework." Graduation requirement: Wellness 0.5 credit.

description: This course is designed for students who are interested in gaining more knowledge and skills in the area of health. Throughout this course, students will have an opportunity to participate in a variety of lessons, activities, and projects with the focus being on their own physical, social and emotional health. Students will also explore the media’s influences on our choices. The following topics will be offered: nutrition, relationships, sexual violence prevention, human trafficking, substance abuse prevention, LGBTQ+ health care needs, stress reduction, lifestyle diseases, and issues in global health. Students will be trained in American Red Cross CPR and will be graded on class participation, projects, and content sharing. Guest Speakers and videos will be used to enhance the curriculum when possible.
prerequisites: Wellness
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Earth & Space Science (ESS) is a laboratory-based, hands-on course which offers a chance to explore a variety of Earth & Space topics while building upon previously learned science concepts and skills. The scope of this course extends from the center of the Earth to the outer reaches of the cosmos. The hands-on component of this course involves experimental gathering, analyzing, and interpreting data to understand evidence in support of scientific knowledge. An emphasis will be placed on exploring Earth & Space concepts through examples of scientific phenomenon, which when possible will be focused on local & regional examples. This course will fulfill the physical science graduation requirement.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: This course will fulfill the physical science graduation requirement.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. Honors option is through the teacher and Department Chair. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: Biology takes an integrated approach to align with the Vermont State Standards, and NGSS targets. Major units of study include characteristics of living organisms, cell structure and function, energy transfer in living systems, cellular reproduction, and how organisms reproduce. Inquiry-based activities and labs will be stressed throughout this course. Laboratory analysis will provide direct opportunities for application of concepts. Emphasis will be placed on the correct use of biological tools such as microscopes, graphic analysis, biological modeling, and scientific writing. This course will fulfill the biology graduation requirement.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: This course will fulfill the biology graduation requirement.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Advanced biology is a rigorous one-semester course that utilizes an inquiry-based lab approach and focuses on four major areas of biology; structures and processes of molecules and organisms, the interactions of chemicals and energy within ecosystems, the inheritance and variation of traits and biological evolution. This course covers all NGSS Life Science High School standards. The scientific practices of critical thinking, supporting an argument with evidence and communicating information are highlighted. This course will fulfill the biology graduation requirement.
prerequisites: None.
fulfills_text: This course will fulfill the biology graduation requirement.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: AP Biology is an advanced placement course. This intensive program is particularly well suited, although not limited to, those students who wish to pursue professional careers in biology, chemistry, bioengineering, medicine, nursing and other allied health fields. Any interested and motivated student, including those who do not typically view themselves as “AP” students, should be encouraged to attempt AP Biology. Upon the successful completion of both semesters, the student is eligible to take the AP exam in biology for college credit. AP Biology includes a deeper examination of the topics from advanced biology, with real world applications and an emphasis on applying scientific information in new contexts. Exam expectation: A student enrolling in this course will take the AP exam in May. There will be an exam fee associated with this course.
prerequisites: Advanced Biology. Algebra 2 or its equivalent (may be taken concurrently) is recommended.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall. Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

description: AP Biology 2 is a continuation of AP Biology 1. Topics not covered in semester I will be completed in this semester. Upon the successful completion of this entire course, the student will take the AP biology exam for college credit where accepted.
prerequisites: AP Biology 1 with a C- or better
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring. Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

description: Bioethics encourages students to explore and understand the ways in which science and technology shape culture, values, and institutions and how such factors in turn, shape science and technology. We will focus on contemporary scientific and policy issues such as pandemic response, vaccine acceptance, climate change, genetically modified organisms, food insecurity, and health justice as it relates to BIPOC, LBGTQ+, persons with disabilities, and other marginalized communities. We will examine the context of historical and contemporary injustices that have led to modern codes of ethics in medicine and research. We will investigate the legacy of colonialism, racism, misogyny, heteronormativity, and ableism which continue to perpetuate bias in our scientific and medical institutions, alongside movements to dismantle mechanisms of systemic injustice. The course will be taught seminar style, with students responsible for reading, preparing for, and participating in student-led discussions. This course is offered subject to enrollment and will not fulfill the biology graduation requirement.
prerequisites: Biology or Advanced Biology
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring. Honors option is through the teacher and Department Chair. Does not fulfill the biology graduation requirement. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: This course is a hands-on elective for students who would like to explore science topics further. This course will investigate topics through all 3 science disciplines, with a specific focus on where they overlap such as polymer formation and behavior, electroplating, and amorphous solids. Additional units and projects may include catapults and trebuchets, forging aluminum, forming alloys, bungee cord theory, design and build boomerangs, design and build kaleidoscopes, making mirrors, and others. There will be an emphasis on meeting the NGSS engineering standards.
prerequisites: 1 Biology credit & 1 Physical Science credit
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course provides a general chemistry foundation. Considerable reliance is placed on laboratory work so that chemical principles are drawn directly from student observation. This course will enable students to better understand: history of chemistry, measurement and data analysis, atomic structure and theory, electrons in atoms, periodic table and periodic law, elements, states of matter and their properties and changes, ionic and covalent bonding and compounds, chemical reactions, the mole, concept, stoichiometry, and chemical reaction rates. Chemistry requires strong math manipulation skills, particularly algebra. This course will fulfill the physical science graduation requirement in conjunction with Physics.
prerequisites: Biology OR Advanced Biology, and Algebra 1
fulfills_text: This course will fulfill the physical science graduation requirement in conjunction with Physics.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Honors option is through the teacher and Department Chair. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: This course is designed to further challenge highly motivated students wishing to prepare themselves for the academic rigors of college. Any interested and motivated student who has completed Chemistry, including those who do not typically view themselves as “AP” students, are encouraged to attempt AP Chemistry. This course is particularly well suited for students interested in pursuing science careers (medicine, nursing, chemical engineering, biochemistry, water resources, environmental science, allied health, etc.) and/or related technologies. This course will be rigorous, detailed, and presented at a fast pace. AP Chemistry 1 will examine topics not covered in Chemistry and will expand upon many topics previously covered in that course. Laboratory exercises and experiments will not only direct the progression of topics to be covered in this course but will be rigorous and similar to that of a typical college course. Topics covered in AP Chemistry are necessary to further prepare students for the rigors of college science courses beyond the general level.
prerequisites: Chemistry, one Biology credit, and Algebra 2
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall. Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

description: This course is a continuation of AP Chemistry 1. Topics not covered in AP Chemistry 1 will be completed in this semester and units including organic chemistry and biochemistry will be expanded upon and/or introduced. Upon successful completion of this course students will take the AP Chemistry exam for college credit where accepted.
prerequisites: AP Chemistry 1 with a C- or better
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring. Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

description: This course will examine Vermont’s environment and the ways humans impact it. Students will closely examine the interrelationships of the natural world. Lessons will focus on identifying and analyzing natural and human-made environmental problems and students will evaluate risks associated with these problems and evaluate alternative solutions for resolving and/or preventing them. This course will include numerous opportunities for project-based learning including collecting data on stream health in local bodies of water, working on developing sustainable practices for the school, and practicing citizen science in the community. Students in this course will work closely with local businesses, nonprofits and educational institutions to develop projects that will positively impact the local environment. Field trips and field research will be incorporated into the course curriculum as well as opportunities to collaborate with other schools to gain a more global perspective on a diversity of environments and ongoing environmental change.
prerequisites: 1 Biology credit & 1 Physical Science credit
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course (per the catalog's list of place-based courses, p.9).

description: This course is designed for any student with an interest in actively doing science. In Physics 1 students will explore the following major topics: Kinematics, Forces, Energy, Momentum, Heat, Electricity, Magnetism, and Waves. Lectures are limited in this course with students learning primarily by performing experiments, observing demonstrations, and participating in problem-solving activities. Lab work and quantitative analysis are emphasized throughout the course. This course will fulfill the physical science graduation requirement in conjunction with Chemistry.
prerequisites: Successful completion or concurrent enrollment in Algebra 1
fulfills_text: This course will fulfill the physical science graduation requirement in conjunction with Chemistry.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is designed for the technical or college-bound student with an interest in science. In Physics 2 (Advanced) students will return to portions of the major topics from Physics 1 including Kinematics, Forces, Energy, Momentum, Heat, Electricity, Magnetism, and Waves for greater in-depth study. In addition, students will explore Rotational Motion, Torque, Fluids, Pressure, and Nuclear Physics. Lectures are limited in this course with students learning primarily by performing experiments, observing demonstrations, and participating in problem-solving activities and engineering design challenges. Lab work and quantitative analysis are emphasized throughout the course.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Physics 1
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring.

description: This course will introduce students to the basic principles of human anatomy. Students will use creative, hands-on instruction to further their knowledge of their bodies and health. Students will explore the major systems of the body using models, investigations, multimedia presentations, and interactive simulations. Regular dissection and analysis of human health is a part of the delivery of this course. This course is offered subject to enrollment and will not fulfill the biology graduation requirement.
prerequisites: 1 Biology credit and 1 Chemistry credit
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Honors option is through the teacher and Department Chair. Does not fulfill the biology graduation requirement. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: This course is meant to serve as a broad overview of the modern world and the challenges it faces. Global Issues begins with an introduction to the different people, religions, governments, regions, and economies found around the globe today. It then takes an in-depth look at the global economy, conflicts around the world, and quality of life experienced by people in various countries. This class emphasizes the development of fundamental academic and personal skills required for success throughout high school and beyond. Specifically, this course will emphasize research, writing, presenting and collaboration with peers. The course culminates in a semester-long project in which students investigate a global issue of their choosing and seek to make an impact in the world they live in.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Upon teacher and guidance counselor recommendation, a student can be placed in a foundational skills section within this class. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

course_name: US History: Civil War to World War II
description: This course provides a general survey of U.S. History. The primary focus is upon the social, economic, and political developments which took place after the 1900's. Citizenship skills are incorporated into the basic objectives of this course. At the option of the teacher, mini-units of concentration may also be included. This course will fulfill the high school requirement for US History.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: This course will fulfill the high school requirement for US History.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Upon teacher and guidance counselor recommendation, a student can be placed in a foundational skills section within this class. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: This course is a study of Modern American history from the end of WWII to the present day. The course will focus on military conflicts, Civil Rights, equality, political issues as well as technology and inventions since World War II. An emphasis will be placed on the United States' role in the world as a result of these topics as well as counterculture that develops. This course will use literature, music and film to interpret the importance of our most recent history. This class will require reading, writing and class participation! This course will fulfill the high school requirement for US History.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: This course will fulfill the high school requirement for US History.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Upon teacher and guidance counselor recommendation, a student can be placed in a foundational skills section within this class. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: There are many ways to learn about our nation's history. History is more than just dates and wars. This course examines US History, beginning with the Westward Expansion era to contemporary times, through a multimedia approach. We will learn our nation's history by examining photographs, newspaper articles, political cartoons, and other publications. We will also listen to and put into historical context music and film from different historical eras. Through this multimedia approach, we will learn about our nation's struggles and successes. We will examine equality and civil rights for all Americans, social and racial injustices, advancements in technology, politics at the national and international level, and American democracy. This course will fulfill the high school requirement for US History.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: This course will fulfill the high school requirement for US History.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Upon teacher and guidance counselor recommendation, a student can be placed in a foundational skills section within this class. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: History is a story; a story that is uniquely experienced by each individual. Civics is how an individual conducts themself and participates in local, state and national activities as a citizen of a nation. This course examines US History from a civic perspective. We will examine what it means to be a citizen. We will look at the rebellion of colonists and the revolution that led to the creation of The United States of America and its experiment in democracy. This course will introduce students to the workings of the American Government at the local, state and federal levels as well as introduce students to national historical documents like the Declaration of Independence, The US Constitution, and the Bill of Rights. We will discuss the role of an individual in society, their community, and the impact an individual can have on society. We will learn our nation's history by examining an array of historical documents and texts, first person accounts, and primary sources. We will learn about our nation's struggles and successes. We will examine equality and civil rights for all Americans, social and racial injustices, advancements in technology, politics at the national and international level, the idea of American democracy, and the stories of individual citizens who lived during the different time periods we study.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: Catalog: "All students in Grade 10 or Grade 11 are required to take either U. S. History or Scholars of U. S. History (Advanced)." (US History credit required for graduation)
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Upon teacher and guidance counselor recommendation, a student can be placed in a foundational skills section within this class. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

course_code: 0122 (Scholars of US History 1 (A)) / 0123 (Scholars of US History 2 (A))
description: Designed for the advanced student, this course will survey the entire history of the United States in great depth. Students must have above average skills in reading and writing as the pace will be accelerated.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: All students in Grade 10 or Grade 11 are required to take either U. S. History or Scholars of U. S. History (Advanced).
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Full Year.

description: This course involves a survey of the history and culture of the Western World from the Mediterranean civilizations to the Renaissance. This course will provide the student with information that will be needed in many college level social science courses. This is a higher level course, requiring average to above average skills in reading comprehension and writing. This course is a must for students considering any of the Social Sciences in college (i.e. Anthropology, Sociology, History, Political Science, Archeology). This course will emphasize research, writing, presenting and collaboration with peers.
prerequisites: 1 US History credit
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall.

description: This course concentrates on Western Europe's modern political, social, and economic development. This course will span from the Protestant Reformation to present day Europe. This is a higher-level course, requiring average to above average skills in reading comprehension and writing. This course is a must for students considering any of the Social Sciences in college (i.e. Anthropology, Sociology, History, Political Science, Archeology). This course will emphasize research, writing, presenting and collaboration with peers.
prerequisites: 1 US History credit
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring.

description: This course will study, analyze and debate the topics of; functions of government, school culture, substance abuse, mental health, teen violence and delinquency, race and gender issues, relationships, hate crimes, legal issues related to technology, current events, and topics that students choose to explore. Students will have the opportunity to present topics that they feel are current social issues. Students will be required to research various issues, work independently and in groups, and participate in class discussions. This course will introduce students to social issues that are currently affecting Americans in various parts of the nation, as well as internationally. The course succeeds when students share and substantiate their opinions, as well as participate in discussion.
prerequisites: 1 US History credit
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: Virtues, ethics, values, fairness, right, and wrong. What exactly is justice? This class aims to explore that question by combining elements of civics, law, criminal justice, and philosophy in the pursuit of an understanding of justice in America. We will consider many questions including: what rights do people have? How should criminals be punished? What makes a law just? Is everyone treated fairly in the United States? Students should be prepared for a lot of reading, writing, and class discussion, as well as interactive activities such as a mock trial.
prerequisites: 1 US History credit
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: This course focuses on how money, markets, and decisions actually work in the real world, and how economic thinking helps explain those outcomes. Students begin with core economic concepts such as incentives, supply and demand, and how markets function, then spend much of the semester developing and running a real business using start-up funds, creating products or services, and working with real customers. Alongside the business project, students learn practical personal finance skills and knowledge they will use after high school, including an understanding of housing and mortgages, investing and retirement, credit and debt, taxes and paychecks, and how marketing and advertising influence people’s decisions when buying and selling. The course also includes career readiness work such as creating a professional resume, practicing job interviews, and reflecting on how economic and financial choices shape outcomes over time. This class is best suited for students who enjoy hands-on projects and want to understand how real-world decisions add up over time.
prerequisites: 1 US History credit or Scholars of US History (A)
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: This course will study the history of genocide from the early 1930's to present day. It will include an extensive study of the Holocaust and its causes as well as post WWII genocides including: Cambodia, Bosnia, Rwanda and Sudan. This course will look at discrimination and intolerance and how it fuels hatred and the destruction of groups of people. This course emphasizes critical thinking, analytical reading, writing, group discussion and self reflection.
prerequisites: 1 Social Studies credit
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Catalog: taught at the standard level; students may earn advanced credit by applying through the teacher/department chair.

description: This course is an introduction into the field of Psychology. We will study the history of Psychology, Psychologists of the 18th-21st centuries, human development, human behaviors, and mental functioning, examine psychological disorders, and Psychology in the 21st century. Throughout the semester we will be examining many aspects in the field of Psychology. We will be looking at the definition of Psychology, the brain and how it functions (or does not function), human and animal behavior, some very influential people who have contributed to the field of Psychology, motivation and emotions, intelligence and different states of consciousness. We will also study specific mental disorders, medications used to treat disorders, how psychological illnesses affect individuals and their relationships, and what YOU can do with or for someone who is suffering from a psychological disorder. This course is designed to be college-like in rigor, independence, and responsibility. Students must complete their work thoroughly and timely. There is an expectation that students will be completing work outside of the classroom, and/or preparing papers and projects for completion.
prerequisites: 2 Social Studies credits (One of which must be taken at the advanced level)
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Turn your ideas into reality. By using the 3D modeling CAD(computer aided design) software SketchUp, learn to create both assigned and original designs. Once your design is complete, learn how to take that design and convert into a 3D printed model using plugins and a 3D printer. Following your design from model to print will allow you to go through real-world problem solving and optimization applications in order to see your vision become a reality.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Taking the skills mastered in 3D Modeling & Printing Technologies, using SketchUp and slicing software learn to take your 3D designs to the next level. Learn how to reverse engineer items and take them from finished products to 3D designs then redesign them to make something new or better. The primary focus of this course will be to complete high quality 3D prints for use or for prototyping and create tutorials for future use. You will also learn how to take your SketchUp model and send those designs to our laser cutter or CNC router to turn your prototype into a usable product.
prerequisites: 3D Modeling & Printing Technologies or teacher recommendation.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course will use the engineering design process of: Identify, Research, Imagine, Plan, Create, Test and Improve. This course focuses on problem solving and uses projects to solve those problems. Projects will include, but are not limited to, making CO2 cars, mouse trap cars, catapults, building classroom workspaces, website design, videography, chain reactions, cardboard escalator, among others. During this course the process is the most important thing, sometimes the builds will not work as planned, but the engineering design process will guide our learning and progress. This course will give you the basics you need to be able to convey your research, ideas and information in a way that can reach the online digital world. Students enrolled in this course can choose to earn either a Social Studies or Technology credit.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: Students enrolled in this course can choose to earn either a Social Studies or Technology credit.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course.

description: In this course, students will team to produce a bi-weekly news broadcast program focused on Hartford High School. Students will learn how to use technology, including video cameras, microphones, and editing software to shoot and edit video stories, assemble scripts, and produce a news program. This course will prepare students for college and careers in a variety of professions by emphasizing 21st century skills involving communication, collaboration, creativity, and critical thinking. The goal by the end of the course is for students to be able to research multiple credible sources, use technology to revise and edit clips, report accurately and clearly to meet deadlines.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course.

description: This sports management course will have students diving into the world of event and game planning and management. Students will learn how to advertise, set up, and run a game or event. There will be a focus on creating digital and printable publications, in-game experiences including announcing and music, and data analysis of the event. Throughout this course we will learn from people who work in or have studied sports management and learn about post-high school opportunities in this field.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Open to Grades 10-12 (Priority by age). Place-based course.

description: Building on the foundations of Sports Management I, this course takes students deeper into the world of event and game planning, management, and execution. Students will take on leadership roles in organizing, advertising, and running sporting events while gaining hands-on experience in digital marketing, event logistics, and game-day operations.
prerequisites: Sports Management 1 (scheduled simultaneously in the same classroom as Sports Management 1)
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course.

description: Students will learn and apply French language skills to talk and write about themselves and to learn about people, places, and cultures in the Francophone world. By the end of the course, students will be able to communicate with memorized or familiar words and talk with others on a most basic level (the ACTFL novice-mid proficiency level). Students will also explore the benefits of learning a world language and practice language-learning strategies.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Students will build on the skills they developed in French 1 as they listen, speak, read, and write about a variety of topics from the Francophone world, including current issues, sports, music, art, food, and geography. By the end of the course, students will be able to create simple sentences and questions (the ACTFL novice-high proficiency level).
prerequisites: French 1 credit or demonstrated proficiency
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course gives students additional tools to communicate in a variety of situations in French while continuing to explore the cultures and communities of the Francophone world. By the end of the course, students will be able to talk about familiar and researched topics and share opinions by creating simple sentences with more detail and by asking questions and follow-up questions (the ACTFL intermediate-low proficiency level).
prerequisites: French 2 credit or demonstrated proficiency
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course focuses on increasingly complex and nuanced aspects of the language and French-speaking cultures. We begin with a thorough review of grammar learned in previous courses. Students practice conversation, improve reading and listening skills, and build vocabulary. The course serves as a bridge to the AP French course offered in the spring, with much of the work designed to prepare students for AP French. It is highly recommended to take French 4 and AP French in the same school year. Students will take the ACTFL Assessment of Performance toward Proficiency in Languages (AAPPL) Exam at the end of the course; this is one path to earn the Seal of Biliteracy.
prerequisites: French 3 credit or demonstrated proficiency
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall/Spring. Open to Grades 10-12 (Grade 9 requires instructor's permission).

description: AP French Language and Culture continues the work students began in French 4. As students prepare to take the AP exam, they learn about a variety of French-speaking cultures and practice interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational communication. The course is comparable to a thirdyear college course. Learning experiences require students to integrate reading, writing, listening, and speaking in order to analyze and synthesize information from authentic French-language sources.
prerequisites: It is highly recommended that French 4 be taken the semester immediately prior to taking AP French.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring. Exam expectation: AP exam in May for a fee of approximately $90 (school covers the fee for students with additional financial need). Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

description: Students will learn and apply Spanish language skills to talk and write about themselves and to learn about people, places, and cultures in the Spanish-speaking world. By the end of the course, students will be able to communicate with memorized or familiar words and talk with others on a most basic level (the ACTFL novice-mid proficiency level). Students will explore the benefits of learning a world language and practice language-learning strategies.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Students will build on the skills they developed in Spanish 1 as they listen, speak, read, and write about a variety of topics from the Spanish-speaking world, including current issues, sports, music, art, food, and geography. By the end of the course, students will be able to create simple sentences and questions (the ACTFL novice-high proficiency level). Students will also explore the benefits of learning a world language and practice language-learning strategies.
prerequisites: Spanish 1 credit or demonstrated proficiency
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This intermediate course gives students additional tools to communicate in a variety of situations in Spanish while continuing to explore the cultures and communities of the Spanish-speaking world. Students will engage with a variety of audio-visual materials, including articles, shows, music and stories to develop their reading, listening, and interpretation skills in Spanish. By the end of the course, students will be able to talk about familiar topics and share opinions by creating simple sentences with more detail and by asking questions and follow-up questions (the ACTFL intermediate-low proficiency level).
prerequisites: Spanish 2 credit or demonstrated proficiency
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course explores a variety of authentic cultural resources from the Spanish-speaking world and includes a thorough review of grammar. Students will engage with a variety of audio-visual materials, including articles, videos, music and stories to develop their reading, listening, and interpretation skills in Spanish. In addition, students will review and apply more advanced Spanish grammar concepts to enhance their writing and communication skills.
