They will write essays and opinion pieces as well as give oral presentations and have interpersonal conversations. Students will refine their fluency, critical thinking, and cultural awareness. By the end of the course, students will be able to talk and write about familiar and researched topics and share opinions by creating a series of connected sentences and by asking a variety of follow-up questions (the ACTFL intermediate-mid proficiency level). Students will take the ACTFL Assessment of Performance toward Proficiency in Languages (AAPPL) Exam at the end of the course; this is one path to earn the Seal of Biliteracy. This course can serve as a bridge to the AP Spanish course offered in the spring. This course is conducted entirely in Spanish.
prerequisites: Spanish 3 credit or demonstrated proficiency
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Open to Grades 10-12 (Grade 9 requires instructor's permission). Place-based course.

description: This course explores a variety of cultures of the Spanish-speaking world and requires students to speak and write at length across various time frames (present, past and future). Students will engage with a variety of primary documents and audio-visual materials, including articles, videos, music, and stories to develop their reading, listening, and interpretation skills in Spanish. In addition, students will review and apply advanced Spanish grammar concepts to enhance their writing and communication skills. They will write 5-paragraph essays as well as give in-depth oral presentations and have lengthy interpersonal conversations. By the end of the course, students will be able to talk and write about a variety of topics and share opinions by creating a few short paragraphs and asking a variety of questions (the ACTFL intermediate-high proficiency level). Students will take the ACTFL Assessment of Performance toward Proficiency in Languages (AAPPL) Exam at the end of the course; this is one path to earn the Seal of Biliteracy. This course can serve as a bridge to the AP Spanish course offered in the spring or students may choose to take this course after AP Spanish. This course is conducted entirely in Spanish.
prerequisites: Spanish 4 credit or demonstrated proficiency
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Open to Grades 11-12 (Grade 10 requires instructor's permission).

description: This course continues the work students begin in Spanish 4 and/or 5. As students prepare to take the AP exam, they will learn about a variety of Spanish-speaking cultures and demonstrate proficiency in interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational communication. In addition, students will have the opportunity to demonstrate understanding of the products, practices and perspectives of the target culture. The course is comparable to a third-year college course. Learning experiences require students to integrate reading, writing, listening, and speaking in order to analyze and synthesize information from authentic Spanish-language sources. By the end of the course, students will be able to write about a variety of topics and share opinions using paragraphs and exchange information and ideas in discussions. (the ACTFL advanced-low proficiency level). This course is conducted entirely in Spanish.
prerequisites: Students MUST take Spanish 4 or Spanish 5 in the fall semester immediately prior to taking AP Spanish
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring Semester. Exam expectation: AP exam in May for a fee of approximately $90 (school covers the fee for students with additional financial need). Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

description: Students will learn and apply German language skills to explore the visible and non-visible aspects of "culture" and encourage students to consider how products and practices differ in their own cultures and in a variety of cultures in the German-speaking world. Students will explore the reasons for learning a world language and discuss and practice language-learning strategies. Recognizing that students acquire language at different rates, students will target the ACTFL novice-mid proficiency level (talking about oneself using memorized or familiar words, expressing likes and dislikes, and talking with others on a most basic level).
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Students will build on the skills they developed in German 1 to explore intercultural perspectives as they listen, speak, read, and write in German. They will use the language to explore a variety of topics from the German-speaking world, including current issues, sports, music, art, food, and geography. Recognizing that students acquire language at different rates, students will target the ACTFL novice-high proficiency level (talking about oneself and familiar topics and asking original questions using simple sentences). Students will explore the reasons for learning a world language and practice language-learning strategies.
prerequisites: German 1 credit or demonstrated proficiency
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course expands upon work begun in previous levels and gives students additional tools to communicate in a variety of situations in German. We will continue to explore the cultures of the German-speaking world and begin something that interests them. Recognizing that students acquire language at different rates, students will target the ACTFL intermediate-low proficiency level (talking about familiar and researched topics and sharing opinions by creating simple sentences with more detail and asking appropriate follow-up questions). Students will explore the reasons for learning a world language and practice language-learning strategies.
prerequisites: German 2 credit or demonstrated proficiency
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: This course is an intermediate-level course that focuses on themes relevant to daily life in Germany, especially topics helpful to our exchange trip with our partner school in Germany. We look at German homes and towns, living with a host family, food, and school. We improve on ways to compare German culture to our own, describe how we're doing, and recount what has happened recently. We also focus on themes such as German history, architecture, sports, art, film, literature, Fascism, Communism, and Democracy; architecture and innovation; and other specific themes that interest the class. German 4 begins with a review of grammar and previously-learned vocabulary themes. Students build on reading and listening skills, as well as new vocabulary and expressions through various themes and topics covered throughout the semester. Students will take the ACTFL Assessment of Performance toward Proficiency in Languages (AAPPL) Exam at the end of the course; this is one path to earn the Seal of Biliteracy. The course can either stand alone or serve as a bridge to AP German. Our German program is designed to prepare students for two weeks of immersion in Germany living with families from our partner school. Students are expected to be enrolled in (or have completed) German 4 at the time of the trip during the years that this trip is offered.
prerequisites: German 3 credit or demonstrated proficiency
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall.

description: AP German Language and Culture continues the work students begin in German 4. As students prepare to take the AP exam, they learn about a variety of German-speaking cultures and practice interpersonal, interpretive, and presentational communication. The course is comparable to a third-year college course. Learning experiences require students to integrate reading, writing, listening, and speaking in order to analyze and synthesize information from authentic German-language sources.
prerequisites: It is highly recommended that German 4 be taken the semester immediately prior to taking AP German.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring. Exam expectation: AP exam in May for a fee of approximately $90 (school covers the fee for students with additional financial need). Students enrolled in an AP course are expected to take the AP exam in the spring (fee); failure to take it changes the transcript identification to "Advanced" and the grade value from weighted to unweighted.

description: This course opportunity offers a hands-on introduction to the field of education with a focus on world language instruction. It is designed for students with strong interest in leadership, communication, and a world language. This experience supports growth in instructional skills, student mentorship, and classroom collaboration. Students will work with the teacher to create a course syllabus that meets the student’s learning objectives.
prerequisites: Completion of French 3, German 3 or Spanish 4 or demonstrated proficiency AND teacher permission.
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring.

description: Each and every Hartford student will have a different, unique, and personalized path through our school. Students will develop their Personalized Learning Plan (PLP) during Personalizing Pathways. Students will engage in activities designed to support their understanding of setting goals that are specific to their dreams and the creation of a living PLP that will allow them to drive their learning throughout their high school career.
prerequisites: None (This course will be taken the opposite term of Wellness.)
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block / 1 Term, Fall / Spring. Required half-credit course for every grade 9 student (see graduation requirements).

description: This course provides high school sophomores the opportunity to explore their post-high school goals. Students will reflect upon their strengths, interests, values, and goals by focusing on three key questions – Who am I? What are the habits of effective people? What will I do after high school? You will explore some of your post-high school options and learn skills to succeed in college, business, or the military. This course also provides students with an introduction to online learning, including an overview of CCVs portal environment. In addition, you will have Sophomore meetings with your school counselor, leading to next steps for your high school career and beyond. Other topics covered: time management, personal budgeting, and communication skills.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall. Title includes "(CCV ICC)"; the description mentions an overview of the CCV portal environment; the catalog does not say whether college credit is earned.

description: An opportunity to explore your future in higher education! You will spend the semester reflecting upon your strengths, interests, values, and goals by focusing on three key questions -- Who am I? What are the habits of effective people? What could college look like for me? This course opportunity offers a hands-on introduction to the field of education with a focus on world language instruction. It is designed for students with strong interest in leadership, communication, and a world language. This experience supports growth in instructional skills, student mentorship, and classroom collaboration. Students will work with the teacher to create a course syllabus that meets the student’s learning objectives. This class focuses on the skills necessary to apply for and succeed in higher education academic settings (including community, junior, and four-year colleges, trade and technical schools), and includes Junior meetings with your school counselor. Using the CCV platform in a hands-on environment, we will examine a variety of topics (driven by class interest), such as time management, interviewing, college searches and applications, personal budgeting and communication skills.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Spring. Title includes "(CCV ICC)"; uses the CCV platform; the catalog does not say whether college credit is earned.

description: This course embraces Student-Created Projects to expand learning experiences geared towards personal interests and goals. Students are encouraged to identify their passions and create their own authentic learning opportunities. Students will guide their own learning through connecting to and accessing resources to aid their endeavors. Teachers in this program serve as guides and resources for students to access experts in the community as much as possible; therefore, the experiences available are not limited to the walls or traditional schedule of Hartford High School. Students wishing to pursue this type of education must be able to work independently, collaborate with others and be willing to document and demonstrate their growth in Transferable Skills. They will show this growth using progress reflections, a final reflection and a public exhibition of their learning. Students enrolled in this course will receive an elective credit and may earn content-specific credit based on their project and collaboration with members of the appropriate department(s). This course may be repeated for multiple elective credits with the prerequisite of the instructor's permission. Some students may choose to participate in community-based learning. These learning opportunities may include: Volunteering, Internships, Job Shadows, or Work Experience. Students engaged in Student-Created Independent Projects with a focus on Community-based Learning will be required to reflect on their learning through the Transferable Skills standards as well as professional standards in accordance with their aligned profession or field. These students will partner with a mentor/supervisor who can assist them in developing their career-specific skills and will simply add these components to their final exhibition presentation. These students will receive an elective credit.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. May be repeated for multiple elective credits with the instructor's permission.

description: This one-credit elective course is designed to help students venture outside of their comfort zones to improve their mental and physical well-being. Through the cultivation of a growth mindset, students will engage in various activities, discussions, and individualized projects. Participants will learn strategies for managing stress, building resilience, and fostering a mindset that embraces challenges for self-improvement. By exploring topics such as selfcare, emotional intelligence, and physical wellness, students will develop practical skills for maintaining a balanced and healthy lifestyle. Through student-centered experiential learning, this course prepares participants to navigate and embrace life's challenges with curiosity and confidence while equipping them with skills to thrive in areas of life deemed most important.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course.

description: WBL 1 (Employment Prep) is an educational program that combines classroom instruction with practical work experience that is directly related to student interests. The program’s mission is to enhance student knowledge by combining classroom learning with hands-on work experience. This includes opportunities such as interviews, job shadows, work experience, internships, apprenticeships, etc. Students will be required to reflect on their learning through Transferable Skill standards as well as professional standards in accordance with the aligned professional field. These students will partner with a mentor/supervisor who can assist them in developing their career-specific skills and will simply add these components to their portfolio for a final exhibition presentation. This class is Pass/Fail and students will receive an elective credit.
prerequisites: None
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. Pass/Fail; elective credit.

description: WBL2 (Work Study) is a course where students who are currently employed will be fully immersed in a work-based educational experience. Students will collaborate and create educational goals with an employer and the Work Based Learning Coordinator to allow them to work four days a week while learning skills in their current occupation to prepare them for post secondary life. Students will create a plan on what topics, skills, and goals that will be needed for the career focused experience and will meet with the Work Based Learning coordinator weekly for check in and discuss Transferable skills. They will participate in all Work Based Learning scheduled trips and activities, such as business panels and mock interviews and will gather evidence of their learning from the course and create a product for a final exhibition presentation. This class is Pass/Fail and students will receive an elective credit.
prerequisites: Demonstrated skills as reflected in WBL-Employment Prep or school counselor recommendation
notes: Scheduled: 1 Block, Fall / Spring. Place-based course. Pass/Fail; elective credit.

description: Edmentum is an online learning platform that provides the opportunity for students to learn anywhere they have access to Wi-Fi and a computer at any time. Students can enroll in these online courses (referred to as QUEST classes) if (1) the course does not exist in name or content in the Hartford High School Program of Studies or (2) the student has failed the equivalent course and in doing so exhausted teachers who teach the course or (3) the student is unable to schedule a course that exists as a link in a sequence of courses that will prohibit the student from attaining the highest level possible in the sequence or (4) the student's counselor and/or case manager identifies that the online version of the course better serves the student's individual learning needs.
notes: program; individual online course titles are not listed in the catalog. Online courses are referred to as QUEST classes.

description: Hartford High School recognizes that there can be occasions when a student’s educational interests are best served by engaging in an independent study with a teacher in the appropriate content area. The student will identify appropriate proficiency-based standards, including the transferable skills, which they will work toward achieving through their Student-Created Independent Project experience. Students will work closely with a sponsoring professional/teacher in the content area appropriate for their project. The individually developed project will be supported through regular contact with a high school teacher and will result in an exhibition or display of learning as a culminating presentation.
notes: program

department: Guidelines for Obtaining Credit for Alternative Coursework
description: This represents an excellent opportunity to get a head start on accruing college credits, as well as obtaining credit applicable to high school graduation. In order to participate in a dual enrollment course students need to complete the dual enrollment process with their school counselor.
prerequisites: Students must identify their desire to take a Dual Enrollment course through their Personalized Learning Plan - PLP.
notes: program. Catalog: two courses may be taken and paid for by the state of Vermont/local district; students may take courses beginning the summer of their sophomore year until graduation; the course must be at a participating Vermont college; the college grade appears on the HHS transcript. Elsewhere the catalog says dual enrollment is for juniors and seniors (p.4) and a PLP must be in place for 11th/12th graders (p.5). A full-term three- or four-credit college course equals one one-credit, semester-long high school course (p.8).

department: Guidelines for Obtaining Credit for Alternative Coursework
course_name: Dartmouth College Courses (Special Community Student Program)
description: This unique opportunity is provided through the Special Community Student Program and is for advanced students who want to take one or more classes at Dartmouth College while earning college credit in high school. Students interested in learning more about this program should contact their high school counselor.
prerequisites: Second semester juniors and all seniors who meet the eligibility requirements
notes: program. Students may take as many as 4 courses at Dartmouth College; HHS transcript shows "P" (Pass) or "F" (Fail); the "P" is not calculated into the GPA.

course_code: 1623 (Autobody, Motorsports & Customs 1) / 1624 (Autobody, Motorsports & Customs / Math 2) / 1625 (Autobody, Motorsports & Cust. / Science 2)
description: Students will be introduced to the fields of Autobody, Motorsports and Customs (AMC). Students in AMC get to use top-of-the-line equipment and technology like the DeVilbiss semi-downdraft paint booth, PPG Aquabase paint mixing system, and commercial quality vinyl cutting machine. The curriculum focuses on mechanics, body repair and replacement, sanding, masking, painting, and use and care of high tech spray equipment. Students gain hands-on experience as they prepare for career opportunities in autobody repair, metal fabrication, painting, graphics, motorsports, restoration and customization of vehicles, and more, depending on student interests. With permission from the instructor, students may work on “live jobs'' brought in by the local community. This program is ASE Education Foundation certified. After completing this program, students have had success entering directly into the workforce or going on to post-secondary education.
fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Math credit or 1 Science credit
notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Automotive and Collision Enthusiasts Club (ACE). Industry Certifications: Non-structural Analysis and Damage Repair ASE entry level certification test; Maintenance and Light Repair ASE entry level certification; Painting and Refinishing ASE entry level certification; S/P2 online safety training; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

description: Automotive Technology trains and prepares students to become successful automotive technicians, for jobs in related fields or post-secondary education. Students are trained both in the classroom and on HACTC shop vehicles. Our emphasis is on safe, honest, ethical and professional work habits and skills. We follow a best practices approach to automotive repair. Units are aligned with the National Institute of Automotive Service Excellence (ASE), and students have the opportunity to take an ASE exam and earn an entry-level Industry Recognized Credential (IRC) at the conclusion of each unit. Students will utilize individual skills as well as team based learning to become proficient at problem solving and time management. Qualified Level 2 students will have the opportunity for a Cooperative Education placement with local automotive employers.
fulfills_text: Embedded Credit: 1 Science credit
notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Automotive and Collision Enthusiasts Club (ACE). College Course Option: None at this time. Industry Certifications: 9 ASE Entry Level Certifications; Lift it Right Certification; WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

description: Students get hands-on access in the professional trades while they work to build a house from the ground up. This two-year program guides students through building a brand new energy-efficient house from beginning to end. This is a real world/life experience for students to safely practice and learn work ethic and a new skill set. During this process, students will learn everything from beginning tool safety, skill techniques, and blueprint reading through residential plumbing and electrical. Students also have the chance to work with subcontractors who are hired to work at the house throughout the building process. Safety is our goal 100% of the time. Students are also exposed to real world experiences on field trips, job shadowing and Cooperative Education learning experiences. Upon program completion, students are qualified to walk into most entry-level positions within the Building Trades arena, pursue apprenticeships, or further their education.
fulfills_text: Embedded Credit: 1 Math credit
notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: None at this time. College Course Option: None at this time. Industry Certifications: NCCER Core and Carpentry Modules; OSHA-10; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

description: Business, Entrepreneurship and Marketing (BEM) students are people who want to develop their business and communication skills for use in a variety of contexts. This program leads students through all aspects of the business world, from accounting and personal finance to marketing and professional communications. Students develop their own sharp business skills through individual and group projects, Cooperative Education placements, and guest lectures from industry professionals. BEM students have the opportunity to participate in Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA), earn up to 12 college credits and four industry recognized certifications, and build a professional business and communications portfolio.
fulfills_text: Embedded Credit: 1 English credit
notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA). College Course Options: River Valley Community College - Introduction to Business (3 credits); Small Business Management (3 credits); Accounting 1 (3 credits); and Personal Financial Management (3 credits). Industry Certifications: CareerSafe OSHA-10 Certification; Ergonomics; Quickbooks Online Pro Advisor; WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

course_name: Career & Technology Exploration Program (Sophomore Students Only)
description: CTE is a unique program to the HACTC, open only to high school sophomores. This classroom model is meant to offer a unique and holistic learning experience. Students are referred for admission to the CTE program by their school counselor. Small-group and one-on-one instruction are at the heart of helping Career Technology Exploration (CTE) students reconnect to their own educational experience. The more individualized, hands-on and supported instruction is vital in helping students find success in school and improving their overall educational experience. The CTE program helps students earn traditional high school credits while providing early exposure to Career and Technical Education. Students cycle back and forth between time in the CTE classroom and placements in the HACTC technical programs, giving students an up close and hands-on introduction to HACTC opportunities. While in their own classroom, CTE students focus on high school math, English, and art credits. Upon successful completion of the CTE program, students will have the opportunity to apply to an HACTC program for their junior year.
fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Math credit, 1 English credit, and 1 Fine Art credit
notes: program. Open only to high school sophomores; students are referred for admission by their school counselor.

description: The HACTC Cosmetology Program provides students the skills and experiences they need to become licensed Cosmetologists. Completing 1,000 hours of study, students will master skills in hair design, nail and skincare, personal appearance, communication, and business management. Students learn and put into practice these skills through demonstrations on mannequins and by working with fellow students and live clients in a salon setting. Students have the opportunity to earn their Cosmetology licensure in the State of Vermont by successfully completing this rigorous college-level program.
fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Science credit
notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA). Industry Certifications: Vermont Cosmetology Licensure, S/P2 Cosmetology Safety and Sanitation Certification; Barbicide Certification; Conover Workplace Readiness; Lucacide/Sol Certification; Pivot Point International Units of Measurement, and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC). Program involves 1,000 hours of study.

description: The Culinary Arts program is a fast-paced learning environment grounded in food science, safety, sanitation, customer service and the basic principles of cooking. With our cafe-style restaurant named The Getaway, students are exposed to a practical application of skills in a dynamic, rigorous curriculum. Students will demonstrate a basic knowledge of the food service industry, including: organizational flow, Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP), sanitation practices, personal hygiene, equipment and utensil identification and use, basic first aid, nutrition, customer service, basic food and bakeshop techniques, as well as storage, handling of food and math applications.
fulfills_text: Embedded Credit: 1 Science credit
notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Hospitality Club. College Course Option: Lakes Region Community College - Culinary Fundamentals (3 credits); Sanitation and Safety (3 credits); and Bakery Production (3 credits). Industry Certifications: American Culinary Federation Secondary Graduate Certification; ServSafe Manager; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

description: The Design and Illustration and Media Arts (DIMA) program at the HACTC is full of creative thinkers. Students in both levels work through projects that introduce them to technical skills in this exciting industry while still exploring their personal interests through self-directed projects. Students use industry standard Mac platform software with the most up-to-date Adobe hardware. Students work through projects that introduce them to many different aspects of digital illustration, digital video production, digital photography, 2-D animation, and motion graphics. Students also accept “live jobs” from the public sector and must learn how to create professional quality work products, follow real-world timelines and work with clients. Students will prepare themselves for endeavors after high school by creating a professional online portfolio, resume and cover letter that they can use for post secondary education or the workforce.
fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Fine Art credit
notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Future Business Leaders of America (FBLA). College Course Option: Lakes Region Community College - Introduction to Digital Photography (3 credits); Digital Illustration (3 credits); Foundations of Design (3 credits); and Design Software Essentials (3 credits). Industry Certifications: Adobe Photoshop CC; Adobe Illustrator CC; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC) Vermont Arts Portifolio.

description: Are you interested in helping people, working in healthcare, and making a difference in your community? Health and Human Sciences is a fast-paced, hands-on program where students will learn skills, explore careers and earn both a license and certification before graduating high school. Students will have the opportunity to earn their Licensed Nursing Assistant (LNA) license and Phlebotomy certification. Students will practice skills in the classroom as both patient and provider, and in healthcare settings. This means students need to be comfortable being touched by peers, as well as using real needles to draw blood. Students may also earn college credits in each year of the program, and complete Cooperative Education rotations in various health care settings.
fulfills_text: Embedded Credit: 1 Science credit
notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: Future Health Professionals (HOSA). College Course Option: River Valley Community College - Introduction to Psychology (3 credits); and Supportive Communication Skills (3 credits). Industry Certifications: Licensed Nursing Assistant (LNA); Certified Phlebotomy Technician (CPT); Basic Life Support (BLS) for Healthcare Providers: CPR and AED; First Aid; Bloodborne Pathogens; Stop the Bleed Certification and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

description: This course exposes students to a wide range of topics designed to instill general fabrication skills combined with technical subjects. The course prepares students for a wide range of occupations such as welding, electrical, machining, and mechanical trades. Students routinely use math and science skills and interact with STEM, Automotive Technology, Natural Resources and Autobody, Motorsports and Customs programs while working on projects. Students are prepared for a career or post-secondary education with technical skills, a positive attitude and a strong work ethic.
fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Science credit
notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Industry Certifications: S/P2 Environmental Safety Training Certification; American Welding Society 1G Structural Steel Certification; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

course_name: Information Technology (One-year course in the P.M.)
description: The Information Technology program is designed for students who are interested in exploring a career in the growing tech industry. Over the course of the year, students will gain valuable hands-on experience in computer repair, user support, and networking and have the opportunity to obtain two valuable industry certifications as well as six college credits. Students will also explore careers across the field and practice the skills necessary to earn a job in this growing sector. Lastly, students will spend some time each week discussing topics of interest like cybersecurity, big data, artificial intelligence and the impact these technologies have on our modern world.
fulfills_text: Yearlong Credits: 1 Technology credit, 0.5 English credit, 1.5 elective credits
notes: program (one-year course). College Course Options: Community College of Vermont - Concepts of PC Hardware (3 credits) and Desktop Operating Systems (3 credits). Industry Certifications: COMPTIA A+; and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC). Sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses.

course_name: Software Engineering (One-year course in the A.M.)
description: The Software Engineering Program will give students the foundational skills necessary to pursue a career in software development, or dev ops. Students will be given a thorough introduction to Python, one of the world’s most popular programming languages, and learn valuable software development skills along the way. At the end of the year students undertake a substantial project where they will have the opportunity to learn a new technology or framework, taking an idea from requirements to implementation.
fulfills_text: Yearlong Credits: 1 Technology credit, 0.5 Math credit, 1.5 elective credits
notes: program (one-year course). College Course Option: River Valley Community College - Introduction to Python (4 credits). Industry Certifications: WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC). Catalog does not say whether sophomores may enroll (it names STEM and Information Technology courses for sophomores).

description: The Natural Resources program is a practical application of skills in a hands-on learning environment. Students will discover and explore the many careers that Natural Resources has to offer through field experiences, community projects, and exposure to experts in various fields. Students will be prepared for a career or further education with technical skills, a positive attitude and a strong work ethic. Qualified Level two students will have the opportunity for Cooperative Education placements with local businesses.
fulfills_text: Embedded Credits: 1 Science credit
notes: program (two-year sequence; Level 1 / Level 2). General HACTC rules: eligible incoming juniors and seniors (sophomores may register for STEM or Information Technology courses); programs occupy 1 1/2 blocks daily; separate HACTC application required; upon completing both levels a student receives 5 elective credits in the career program and 1 embedded credit. Leadership Club: FFA. College Course Option: None at this time. Industry Certifications: Game of Logging 1 and 2 (for Level 1 students); Game of Logging 3 and 4 (for Level 2 students); LEAP Certification and WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC).

course_name: Introduction to Engineering Design (STEM) (One-year course in the P.M.)
description: Using the Project Lead the Way curriculum, Introduction to Engineering Design (IED) students are introduced to the engineering design process. This program focuses on applying math, science, and engineering standards to identify and design solutions to a variety of real problems. Students will work both individually and in collaborative teams to develop and document design solutions using engineering notebooks, 2D and 3D modeling software, a laser engraver, a 3D printer, and a CNC router, as well as a host of traditional tools. Students develop skills in problem solving, manufacturing, research and design process documentation and presentation. IED is a one-year long course offered in the P.M.
prerequisites: Concurrently enrolled in Algebra 1 or have completed it with a C- or better
fulfills_text: Year-Long Credits: 1 Engineering credit, 1 Technology credit, 1 Physical Science credit
notes: program (one-year course). College Course Option: St. Cloud State University - Introduction to Engineering Design (3 credits). Industry Certifications: WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC). Sophomores may register for STEM courses.

course_name: Principles of Engineering/Physics (STEM) (One-year course in the A.M.)
description: While using the Project Lead the Way curriculum, Principles of Engineering (POE) students work through problems that engage and challenge, while exploring a broad range of physics and engineering topics, including mechanical and electrical design, developing sustainability, the strength of structures and materials (civil engineering), and the application of robotics using computer programming in Python. Students continue to refine skills in problem solving, manufacturing, research, and design, while learning strategies for design process documentation, collaboration, and presentation. POE is a one-year long course offered in the A.M.
prerequisites: Concurrently enrolled in Algebra 2 or have completed it with a C- or better
fulfills_text: High School Credit Option: 1 credit Physics, 1 credit Engineering, 1 credit Technology
notes: program (one-year course). College Course Option: St. Cloud State University - Principles of Engineering (3 credits). Industry Certification: WorkKeys National Career Readiness Certification (NCRC). Sophomores may register for STEM courses. The course-number table lists 1645 and 1646 separately but only one description is printed.

description: Windows and Mirrors, your 9th grade English class, begins with you, the student. What makes you unique, and how do you fit into your local and global communities? We will investigate ourselves and others through a range of literature. We will learn how to use communication skills to create the change we want to see in the world. In this course, we will learn to closely read and analyze texts, participate in student-led discussions, write effectively, listen actively, and use evidence, reasoning, and elaboration to support our thinking.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (9th grade English)
notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

description: In Sports and Adventure Literature, students will learn about themes that transcend specific texts, develop analytical and descriptive writing skills, understand the formal techniques and structure of sports and adventure texts and work individually and collaboratively to explore themes and techniques used by writers. Roughly one quarter will be dedicated to sports literature and the second quarter will focus on adventure literature.
prerequisites: None
notes: Listed as an elective for grades 9-12 in the English department chart (semester).

description: Intergenerational Book Club is a project-based class partnering Harwood students with seniors in the community to choose, read, and discuss books. The course is designed to build bridges across time and space, connecting young and more experienced community members around the acts of reading, talking, and writing about books. Students should expect to play an active role in their learning by designing, planning, and facilitating community bookgroup meetings. We will balance class time between working with books, corresponding with community partners, planning upcoming events, and reflecting on how we are meeting our goals.
prerequisites: None

description: What does it mean to be American? What are the values that we share versus the enduring tensions in our society? In this discussion-based course, students will study American fiction, non-fiction, poetry, and plays to better understand our nation and its heritage. We will examine the historical context of each piece that we read, and will often consider how the ideas of the authors speak to or contrast with current events.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th grade English
fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (10th grade English)
notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

description: The primary goal of this semester-long English course is to become leaders in the design and practice of Harkness pedagogy and bring student-driven inquiry to the greater Harwood community. Just as important are the life skills you take away from this class, including honing your critical thinking (in reading, writing and reflection), public speaking, and ability to work as a team to innovate and problem solve.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th grade English
notes: Department chart lists it as an elective for grades 10, 11 and 12 (semester only); course entry states Grade: 10, 11.

description: Why does news matter? In this course we explore its importance to democracy, its relationship to the First Amendment, and media ethics. This is a hands-on course; we will read and evaluate news in many forms, but we will also put out our own products in digital editions of “Common Ground,” photo essays, and podcasting. These pieces will reflect the interests of you, your classmates, and our greater Harwood community. The philosophy for our journalistic efforts can be summed up in one simple phrase: for students, by students, about things that students care about.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th grade English

description: This year-long course is designed to build your creative writing and reading skills with a focus on creative nonfiction, short-fiction, and poetry. You will be asked to read, discuss, and analyze exemplary works of literature as well as create and respond to your own and your classmates’ work. In this class, you will explore a variety of ways to create meaningful pieces of writing. You will also have the opportunity to extend your audience beyond the classroom.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English OR a recommendation from a 9th grade English teacher
notes: Department chart: requires teacher recommendation (10th grade).

description: In this hands-on class, students will be actively learning how to write for business. They will analyze and write about business transactions as well as reading literature about famous businessmen and women and historical booms and collapses. We will look at socially responsible companies such as Ben & Jerry's and Darn Tough Socks Vermont and analyze their advertising and marketing communication through media literacy messaging.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English or a recommendation from 9th grade English teachers (10th graders)

description: This semester-long course examines master storytellers of mystery fiction and the art and craft of writing mystery fiction in its many forms, including detective stories, thrillers, and suspense. The goal is to understand and model the concepts of adventure, keeping secrets, and high octane suspense. Students can expect to read, discuss, and write mystery fiction in this course.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English

description: How can ancient stories inform our world today? What commonalities do we see among combatants and non-combatants in the stories told across eras? War Stories begins with the foundational Western war story, Homer’s Iliad, and then follows war storytelling to contemporary society. In this course, we uncover the tragedy and glory of the Greeks’ epic battle with Troy and its parallels to contemporary warfare. Our materials include Stanley Lombardo’s translation of Iliad paired with Gareth Hinds’ graphic adaptation of it; Lysistrata, by Aristophanes; All Quiet on the Western Front, by Erich Marie Remarque; The Things They Carried, by Tim O’Brien; City of Thieves, by David Benioff, along with multiple short stories, excerpts, poetry, and films. Students are expected to take ownership of their own learning, do the work, and drive our classroom discussions and discoveries. We will look at our texts through six themes: courage and cowardice; women’s roles in war; old men say, young men do; brotherhood and bonds; good leadership/bad leadership; and honor and dishonor. With every source we read, view, or discuss, we will return to these themes. As an elective course, there will be LESS homework than a core content course, but do expect to read outside of class time. Be mindful that the course will read about and discuss difficult and mature content that is often uncomfortable.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English

description: Whose stories are worth telling? Which parts of our lives are important? In this Harkness-based course, we will read, discuss, and write about the work of women writers. We will explore a variety of poems, song lyrics, short fiction, essays, videos, and novels. Discover what women’s voices have to teach you, and develop your own voice as you consider their impact!
prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English

description: The AP English Language and Composition course aligns to an introductory college-level rhetoric and writing curriculum, which requires students to develop evidence-based analytic and argumentative essays. Students evaluate, synthesize and cite research to support their arguments. Throughout the course, students develop a personal style by making appropriate grammatical choices. Students also discover and analyze rhetorical elements in non-fiction texts from many disciplines including: speeches, biographies, contemporary non-fiction, business, sports, graphic images and historical periods. Students who take the AP English Language and Composition course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
prerequisites: A 3.3 or higher in your current English class OR a recommendation from an English teacher with a sample of literary analysis; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

description: This course is designed to replicate an introductory college-level literary analysis course. Its goal is to engage students in the close reading and critical analysis of imaginative literature, thereby deepening their understanding of the ways writers use language to provide both meaning and pleasure. The class is inquiry based and encourages students to delve deeply into the material, take ownership of their learning and drive our classroom discussions.In this course, students can expect to read novels, plays, short stories, and poetry, and discuss those works through student driven inquiry such as Harkness. Writing assignments include expository, analytical, and argumentative essays that require students to analyze and interpret literary works. Students who take the AP English Literature and Composition course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
prerequisites: A 3.3 or higher in your current English class OR a recommendation from an English teacher with a sample of literary analysis; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

description: The Global Studies experience begins with you, the student. What makes you unique, and how do you fit into your local and global communities? We will investigate our identities, our historical moment and how we got here, and how to use communication skills to create the change we want to see in the world. In this course, students will learn to closely read and analyze texts, participate in student-led discussions, write effectively, listen actively, conduct research, and use evidence and reasoning to support their own thinking. The goal of this course is to help students build communication, research, and critical thinking skills while developing their own sense of what it means to be a Global Citizen.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (9th grade social studies)
notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

description: What does it mean to be a citizen in a republic? In Three Democracies, we learn about the rise and fall of democracy in ancient Athens and Rome, making connections to the United States and the challenges that we face. Students consider timeless and timely questions about justice, leadership, political division, empire, and more. Importance is placed on applying lessons from the past to the present. This course features a combination of reading, reflection, discussion, projects, and writing.
prerequisites: U.S. History or equivalent
fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (11th grade): Three Democracies, or Creating Sustainable Communities, or AP U.S. Government
notes: One of three 11th grade required options (Three Democracies, Creating Sustainable Communities, AP U.S. Government with a U.S. History course score of 3.3 or greater).

description: U.S. History helps students learn about the past events, peoples and ideas that make up the United States of America, from the Native American civilizations to the founding documents drafted in Pennsylvania to the Civil and the World Wars, always taking into account the rich and vibrant tapestry of people whose roots and culture hail from all over the world and thus contribute to the unique American story. Students will learn to research and evaluate evidence, including primary sources; they will learn how to put information and ideas into context and how to compare sources and various accounts of the past. Students work alone and together as they deepen their ability to read closely and annotate texts, engage in civil discourse, write short texts and longer essays, and create and teach each other with multimedia presentations. Finally, students will not only learn about the past; they will reflect on the issues facing the country in the present, always inspired by the question: “How does learning about the past help us better understand the present and make more informed choices about the future?” The course makes extensive use of primary and secondary readings, textbooks, and videos. Successful completion of U.S. History is a graduation requirement.
prerequisites: None
fulfills_text: Successful completion of U.S. History is a graduation requirement.
notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

description: CSC is designed to help students understand how the U.S. political system really works (political literacy), how the media influences the political system (media literacy), how to develop and communicate an educated opinion on important public policies (critical literacy, argumentative writing, and civil discourse), and how to use the tools they have available to them to make change in their local and/or state-wide communities (action civics). Students should expect to do the following in this course: ●​ Analyze, mark-up, and annotate a variety of written and recorded texts and media sources ●​ Thoughtfully consider multiple perspectives through civil discourse, active listening, note-taking, and deliberative dialogue ●​ Communicate an educated opinion on a variety of current events and political issues ●​ Develop a plan for taking action on an issue they care deeply about and/or addressing a need in the community through active citizenship or social entrepreneurship This course is unique to Harwood Union High School. It is designed to be deeply relevant and responsive to both current events and student interest. The goal of this course is to help students become the type of citizens who are able to create more resilient, more equitable, more joyful, more just, and more sustainable communities, now and in the future.
prerequisites: US History or Equivalent
fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (11th grade): Three Democracies, or Creating Sustainable Communities, or AP U.S. Government
notes: One of three 11th grade required options.

description: Who are you? Why is your behavior similar to or different from other humans? Psychology is a social science that seeks to answer questions about human behavior and this course explores the latest, peer-reviewed research in an attempt to shed light on the mysterious world inside your head. In particular, we will explore what science has discovered about learning, memory, emotions, creativity, sensory perception, and much more. In the end, you’ll understand how your brain really works—and how to get the most out of it. Class activities, readings, and assignments are designed so students can reflect upon personal experiences and how psychology applies to all aspects of human life. Harkness dialogue and presentations are common summative assessments in this course. Psychology is a vastly broad topic encompassing a wide range of areas of study. Behavior, learning and memory, childhood development, language, and internal mental processes are just a few examples. Students should leave this course with an understanding of the brain and its processes, human behavior, the scientific method and ethics of experimentation, and the history and differing perspectives within the study of psychology.
prerequisites: None

description: Students will explore how advertising shapes culture, identity, and values — and how it can also promote health, well-being, and the common good. Through student inquiry and hands-on projects, students will learn to research, design, and launch media campaigns that make a positive social impact. Students will begin the semester by exploring how marketing and advertising have evolved over time before moving on to issues in contemporary media and advertising. Students will then work with a community partner to develop a media and marketing campaign, including some students who will work to “market” Harwood Union High School. Note: the idea for this course, as well as the curriculum, was co-created in collaboration with a number of current Harwood students who will also be serving as teaching assistants next year.
prerequisites: None

description: History on Film is a course where students view and analyze feature films and movies, documentaries, and other audio and visual media, along with printed source material. The purpose is to gain historical knowledge, ask probing questions, and develop an informed opinion on topics that increase one’s understanding about past, present, and future issues and events. The primary forms of assessment are film analysis and class discussions to evaluate student learning and understanding. Students will need to be comfortable respectfully sharing ideas, supported by evidence, within a large group. Other types of assessment include detailed film notes, written reflections, and individual and group projects and presentations.
prerequisites: None

description: This course explores major events and contemporary issues in the news, while seeking to understand how they have developed from a historical perspective. Students analyze news accounts in various sources: mainstream and more independent media, social media and other venues. Context is always important so the historical roots of these problems will be examined and questioned. As historians and critical media consumers we will also consider: What is the role of media in a democratic society? What makes the “news” and how do reporters and editors interpret events? Can we believe what we read, see, hear and “click”? Students will help guide the directions we take and we’ll look at and critically consider all of it: the mainstream TV channels and “newspapers,” credible “alternative” media outlets, original documents, social media, radio and podcasts and even some of the less-than credible sources, to make sure we understand how peoples’ ideas and opinions are shaped. Class activities are discussion-based, and students will be able to demonstrate their learning through class dialogue, reaction papers, original projects, and digital presentations.
prerequisites: None

description: Economic decisions impact our everyday lives. Understanding economics means thinking about how limited resources require us to make choices and evaluate one option against another. In this course, you will come to recognize that there are examples of economics all around you. You will see how these economic choices, from larger groups such as state and federal governments, to individual consumers, impact us every day. This course will examine the basic concepts of economics, the pros and cons of capitalism, communism, and socialism, the federal and state budget-making process, our growing national deficit, income inequality, the role of the government during a recession, as well as economics-related current events stories.
prerequisites: None

description: Street Law explores the laws in our streets, cities, and states. This course provides a general overview of law and the role that it plays in our society. Areas of focus include constitutional law, criminal law, civil rights, contract law, civil law, and family law. Students are given practical information, helpful in our law-saturated society. The textbook and the U.S. Constitution provide the basic framework for our understanding of laws. Current events provide realistic examples of how the law applies to human actions. Discussions and note-taking are expected, and student presentations on law-related topics are required. Students will also be expected to participate in a series of mock trials.
prerequisites: None

description: AP U.S. Government and Politics provides students with the skills and knowledge to be active citizens in our American Republic, as well as to prepare them for success in taking the AP Gov Exam. Students can expect to discuss current events, analyze graphs, write argumentative essays, complete projects, read Supreme Court cases, participate in Harkness discussions, and take practice AP Gov tests. One major goal in AP Gov is for students to learn about how our government is designed to operate in theory and to develop a clearer understanding of how it operates in practice.
prerequisites: A 3.3 or higher in your current English class OR you may submit a written appeal to the History Department to take the course; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework
fulfills_text: Counts as an 11th grade required option (AP U.S. Government with a U.S. History course score of 3.3 or greater).

description: AP European History is a survey overview of the development of modern Europe. The time period covered by the course is 1450 - the present day. The following is taken from the College Board’s Course Description: AP European History is designed to be the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university European history course. In AP European History, students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in four historical periods from approximately 1450 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical comparisons; and utilizing reasoning about contextualization, causation, and continuity and change over time. The course also provides six themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: interaction of Europe and the world; poverty and prosperity; objective knowledge and subjective visions; states and other institutions of power; individual and society; and national and European identity. Students who take AP European History are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
prerequisites: Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

description: This course addresses fundamental math concepts in the areas of algebra and functions, statistics and probability, and trigonometry. Learn to find heights of tall objects. Explore problems about data. Solve problems using constraints. Students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Algebraic fluency skills ●​ Using properties of similarity and trigonometry to solve problems ●​ Methods to collect, represent, and analyze data ●​ Methods for writing and graphing linear equations ●​ And more! The goal of this course is to give students a foundational understanding of algebra, trigonometry and statistics.
prerequisites: None

description: This course is designed for students who want to double up on math courses to provide additional challenges or to provide more opportunity for electives later in their high school career. This course addresses fundamental math concepts in the areas of algebra and functions, statistics and probability and trigonometry. These strands are unified in themed units and students will develop math habits of mind through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Algebraic fluency skills ●​ Using properties of similarity and trigonometry to solve problems ●​ Methods to collect, represent, and analyze data ●​ Probability & expected value The goal of this course is to give students a foundational understanding of algebra, trigonometry and statistics.
prerequisites: Must take this course concurrently with Integrated Math 2; Must have an Quarter 3 course score of 3.3 or above in 8th grade math; Must successfully complete a set of online prerequisite tasks and a formative assessment. This will be assigned digitally in March and due in early April.; Must have STAR score in the 70th percentile or higher in most recent testing period; Teacher recommendation will be considered in this decision
notes: Must be taken concurrently with Integrated Math 2 (in person).

description: This course addresses intermediate math concepts in the areas of algebra and functions and geometry. Explore exponents with Alice in Wonderland. Blast off some quadratic equations with fireworks. Maximize your geometric potential with the corrals unit. Students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Three forms of linear functions ●​ Methods for solving systems of equations ●​ Exponential relationships, properties of exponents, and logarithms ●​ Creation and transformation of quadratic functions to solve problems ●​ Surface area, volume, and trigonometry, and other elements of Euclidean geometry The goal of this course is to give students an intermediate understanding of algebra and geometry.
prerequisites: Students must have a proficient course score in either Integrated Math 1 (or be concurrently enrolled in IM 1 online and meet the criteria for the online course)

description: This course addresses math concepts including functions, trigonometry, and the real number system. These strands are unified by common themes and students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. This course is designed to be taken concurrently with Integrated Math 2 in person. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Function definition, notation, families, operations, transformations, and problem applications ●​ Use of circle and coordinate geometry to solve problems ●​ Trigonometric functions ●​ The real and complex number systems The goal of this course is to improve upon students' understanding of algebra and trigonometry with a special emphasis on families of functions and their transformations.
prerequisites: Must take this course concurrently with Integrated Math 2; Must have an overall course score of 3.3 or above in Integrated Math 1; Must have a self direction of 3.3 or above; Must have STAR score in the 70th percentile or higher in most recent testing period (and/or Harwood math teacher recommendation)
notes: Designed to be taken concurrently with Integrated Math 2 in person.

description: This course addresses math concepts including functions, trigonometry, and the real number system. These strands are unified by common themes and students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Function definition, notation, families, operations, transformations, and problem applications ●​ Use of circle and coordinate geometry to solve problems ●​ Trigonometric functions ●​ The real and complex number systems The goal of this course is to improve upon students' understanding of algebra and trigonometry with a special emphasis on families of functions and their transformations.
prerequisites: Students must have a Proficient course score in Integrated Math 2

description: Do you dream of being an independent, financially stable adult? This will be one of the most important courses you will ever take. This course introduces the fundamentals and skills of personal finance including budgeting, types of credit, managing credit, investments and savings. Use of the calculator and computer technology is emphasized. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Behavioral Finance ●​ Income & Taxes ●​ Banking: Checking & Savings ●​ Paying for College ●​ Types of Credit ●​ Managing Credit ●​ Investing ●​ Risk Management ●​ Budgeting The goal of this course is to introduce students to financial topics and to give students the skills to make thoughtful financial decisions now and in the future. Personal Finance for College Credit: For the 2026 fall semester, there will be the option to take this course for college credit. Students must meet all the class requirements as the student taking this course for Harwood credit plus the following: ●​ Use one of their dual enrollment vouchers ●​ Complete two independent learning units/projects on insurance and budgeting ●​ Answer additional questions on each of their three in-class summatives Students taking the class for college credit will be enrolled in the same PF classes as those taking it for Harwood credit. This is a great opportunity for students to use their dual enrollment vouchers for an in-person class without having to leave our campus!
prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Math 1 OR Integrated Math 1 Online
notes: For the 2026 fall semester there is an option to take this course for college credit using a dual enrollment voucher (details in description).

description: Why is math important to you? How will it apply to your areas of interest and your future? Come explore these ideas in a project-based learning environment where you choose the math application that directly impacts you and the things you care about. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Math topics that are relevant to their interests ●​ Techniques and processes to solve complex scenarios ●​ Connections between different mathematical disciplines The goal of this course is for students to apply mathematical logic, problem solving techniques, and a variety of math content to solve applied problems. Students will see the relevance of math in their own lives!
prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Math 1
notes: Duration: Semester 1 Only

description: This course is designed for students who plan to take Calculus at Harwood the following year. This course is a continuation of algebra and geometry topics required for the study of Calculus. Particular emphasis is given to topics that are fundamental to a first course in calculus including trigonometry, logarithms, function notation and transformation, and graphing calculator techniques. This class is a condensed and fast paced version of precalculus. Students can expect to: ●​ Increase fluency in interpreting math representations including tables, graphs, equations, situations ●​ Increase fluency in algebraic manipulation of equations ●​ Learn about applications and properties of Logarithms, Inverse functions, Rational Functions and Trigonometric Functions The goal of this course is to prepare students for Calculus or AP Calculus. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
prerequisites: Students are currently enrolled in Integrated Math 3 and are maintaining a proficient score OR have completed Integrated Math 3 with a proficient course score
notes: Duration: Semester 2 only

description: This course is designed for students who have completed three experiences of Integrated Mathematics and are seriously interested in further exploration of mathematics. Throughout this course, students will continue to engage in mathematical habits of mind while gaining a deeper understanding of function behavior, algebraic modeling and manipulation. This course can serve as a prerequisite class for Calculus (either at Harwood or at college) or as an advanced math elective. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Transformations and manipulations of functions as related to the four mathematical representations of functions (graphical, tabular, algebraic, verbal) ●​ In depth analysis of the following types of functions: Trigonometric functions, Polynomials, Rational functions, Exponential functions, Logarithmic functions, and Inverse functions The goal of this course is to prepare students for further studies of mathematics, such as Calculus, as well as other college level maths. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3

description: This is a course in one-variable Calculus for college-bound students. The course includes graphical, numerical, and algebraic techniques of both derivation and integration. Generally, concepts are presented informally and intuitively as well as proven more formally. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ The concept of a derivative and its applications ●​ How to find the derivative of most two variable functions ●​ The concept of an integral and its applications ●​ How to find the integral of most two variable functions ●​ The connection between Integral and Derivative Calculus (The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part I and Part II) The goal of this course is to prepare students for college level math classes. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 AND Bridge to Calculus OR Precalculus

description: Do you want to be able to watch the news or read an article and understand what’s really going on? This course will teach you to develop critical thinking and analytic skills in order to act as an informed consumer. This course will introduce students to four broad conceptual themes of statistics: exploring data, sampling and experimentation, anticipating patterns, and making statistical inferences. Topics may include: ●​ Exploring and understanding data by describing patterns and departures from patterns ●​ Exploring relationships between variables ●​ Planning a study and gathering data ●​ Exploring randomness and probability ●​ Making inferences about situations by estimating population parameters and testing hypotheses The goal of this course is to introduce students to the major concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing and drawing conclusions from data.
prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 OR Advanced score in Integrated Math 2

description: This is a course in one-variable Calculus for college-bound students. The course includes graphical, numerical, and algebraic techniques of both derivation and integration. Topics are covered at a faster pace than the other Calculus course to prepare students to take the Calculus AB Advanced Placement Exam in May. Students enrolling in AP Calculus are strongly encouraged to take the AP exam. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ The concept of a derivative and its applications ●​ How to find the derivative of most two variable functions ●​ The concept of an integral and its applications ●​ How to find the integral of most two variable functions ●​ The connection between Integral & Derivative Calculus (The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part I & II) ●​ Preparation for the AP Calculus Examination The goal of this course is to prepare students for the AP Calculus exam and other college maths. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 AND either Bridge to Calculus OR Precalculus; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework; If students are not proficient in AP Calculus by the end of Quarter 1, they will switch to regular Calculus.

description: The AP course in statistics will introduce students to four broad conceptual themes of statistics: exploring data, sampling and experimentation, anticipating patterns, and making statistical inferences. Topics are covered at a faster pace than the other Statistics course to prepare students to take the Statistics Advanced Placement Exam in May. Students enrolling in AP Statistics are strongly encouraged to take the AP exam. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Exploring and understanding data by describing patterns and departures from patterns ●​ Exploring relationships between variables ●​ Planning a study and gathering data ●​ Exploring randomness and probability ●​ Making inferences about situations by estimating population parameters and testing hypotheses ●​ Using inferences to determine when variables are related The goal of this course is to prepare students for the AP Statistics exam and provide a general understanding of statistical analysis. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 OR Advanced score in Integrated Math 2.; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework.; If students are not proficient in AP Statistics by the end of Quarter 1, they will switch to regular Statistics.

description: This performance-based class will study a variety of genres of music and participate in various concerts throughout the year. Together we will learn the fundamentals of music literacy, meaningful & expressive singing, and composition! All grades and experience levels are welcome. Students will also have the opportunity to audition for local, state, and regional music festivals, as well as an after-school honors choir.
prerequisites: None
notes: Department note: all music classes are available to students of all grades.
