description: AP Language and Composition is an introductory college-level composition course. Students cultivate their understanding of writing and rhetorical arguments through reading, analyzing, and writing texts as they explore topics like rhetorical situation, claims and evidence, reasoning and organization, and style. Completion of a summer assignment is mandatory for enrollment in the course. Students will sit for the AP Language and Composition exam in May.
prerequisites: High engagement and excellence in prior English courses and the completion of the summer assignment
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: research papers, essays, academic journals, other written work, oral presentations, tests, final projects, exam

description: This semester class focuses on questions of what it means to be American and an exploration of the American dream. By looking at a variety of ethnic, religious and cultural identities that are a part of America, students will see how current events are linked to the past. Additionally, students will unpack the concept of the American dream and debate if the dream is the same, and attainable, for all. Readings include both fiction and non-fiction texts; students are encouraged to engage in a variety of projects to pursue their own interests. This class includes work towards upper level writing and speaking and listening proficiencies as students continue to develop their personal portfolios.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th & 10th grade English
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: Reading and writing proficiency assessments are offered as students build portfolios of their work for college and career readiness. A final project assesses speaking, listening, and presentation skills.

description: Creative Writing is a writing intensive course. Students will study poetic forms and work through the writing process to write their own original poetry. Additionally, students will analyze the elements of the fairy tale and then write their own original or fractured tale. Word games, writing prompts, and classroom discussions are daily classroom activities.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th & 10th grade English. Open to 10th graders with a teacher recommendation
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: projects, presentations, homework completion, writing portfolio

description: This upper level English course will help students focus their creative writing on pieces that are meant to be performed. It will be an English course that involves the study, analysis and creation of writing that is meant for television, radio, film, stage or even social media. Students will analyze texts and create their own pieces of writing, including a monologue or dialogue, a video recorded scene for film or TV, and a 10 minute play that could potentially be performed by a theatre class or performing arts group.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th & 10th grade English
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: projects, presentations, homework completion, writing portfolio

description: Students will read and examine science fiction, utopian, and dystopian literature and film. Discussions will emphasize themes dealing with the imagining of possible futures, including post-nuclear apocalyptic societies and the modern world. Because science fiction and utopian/dystopian literature expresses what an author sees as possible, hopes is possible, and fears is possible, it is inherently a political and social critique. We will discuss the causes and effects of these critiques. Texts will include various novels, short stories, and films.
prerequisites: Two successful high school English experiences. Open to 10th graders with a teacher recommendation
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: essay writing, presentations, and homework completion

description: In English 9, students will explore their identities and place in the world through literature and other forms of media, such as film, song, and visual art. Students will build on their understanding of themselves and apply their knowledge to the greater world through coming of age stories. Students will build on their skills throughout the year through multi-modal instruction, learning how to make their writing clear and powerful, have discussions respectfully and with confidence, and read for information, understanding, connection, and deeper meanings.
prerequisites: None
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: projects, essays and other writing exercises, assignment completion

description: This year-long course will cover fictional and nonfictional works. Students will read a variety of literature, including short stories, novels, drama and articles, to explore social issues in modern society. Students will improve their writing skills through reflective journals, a persuasive essay, and other various writing exercises. An on-going portfolio of students’ achievements will be compiled to document proficiency and to proceed to further study. Since learning is not limited to the classroom students will be expected to complete assignments outside of school. All students are required to and are expected to use Chromebook in lieu of personal devices for assignments and to access Schoology, our online learning platform. Students will be assessed through essays, quizzes/tests, projects and participation in class as well. Please note that Self-Direction is an important part of student evaluation.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 9
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: projects, presentations, homework completion, writing portfolio

description: This course will begin with a discussion of the origins of fantasy, and a quick look at world mythologies that have helped to shape archetypal characters and plot structures that are still commonly used in fantasy today. After this introduction, the course will explore the development of modern fantasy, explain what “high fantasy” is, discuss the things that make the supernatural world so important to this genre, and explore some texts where this supernatural world is prominently featured. After this, we will discuss JRR Tolkien, some of his influences, his thoughts on fantasy and its place in literature, and we will examine some of his works for their obvious contributions to modern high fantasy. After Tolkien, we will examine several other works of high fantasy that came afterward, such as Ursula LeGuin’s “Earthsea” novels, and several other stories that center around wizards fulfilling their heroic journeys and destinies through their experiences at wizarding schools. Throughout all of this reading and discussion we will be reading accompanying nonfiction texts that contain elements of history, mythology, and essays by various authors about fantasy, its importance, and its impact.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th & 10th grade English
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: journal assignments, presentations, essays, quizzes

course_name: Film & Fiction: Stephen King Author Study
description: In Film & Fiction students will read the Stephen King novellas The Body and Rita Hayworth and The Shawshank Redemption and perform a literary analysis of theme, symbolism, and characterization. The class will watch the film adaptations, Stand By Me (Reiner) and The Shawshank Redemption (Darabont) and study the films for their cinematography, theme, and characterization. Students will work on analysis and critical thinking skills in critiquing directorial choices in content and style. Students will read, write and engage in discussion.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th & 10th grade English and an additional English
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: reaction/opinion and research papers, projects, media reviews, tests/quizzes, class participation, midterm and final exams

description: Literature of the Theatre is designed for students who would like to explore different elements of theatre. It involves reading plays, analysis, script work and in-class performance. Students will also learn vocabulary and terminology of the theatre. It is imperative to be an active student in class. Students are not expected to have any prior acting experience; a curiosity or desire to read, write, study or act in plays is preferred.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th & 10th grade English and an additional English
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: writings, analysis, vocabulary, script memorization and performance, original works

description: In Media Literacy students will be asked to question, research, analyze and report on the world around them and the issues that dominate our media. These skills will be developed through project based deep dives into a topic that interests them pertaining to media. As a class we will explore the history of media to the current day, analyze the various media types, with a deep dive into the media titans Meta, Amazon, and X. Students will practice rhetorical and persuasive techniques while honing their critical independent thinking and research skills. Attendance and participation are a must and students will work on critical thinking skills to prepare them to navigate a technology and media dominated world.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th & 10th grade English and an additional English
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: reaction/opinion and research papers, projects, media reviews, tests/quizzes, class participation, midterm and final exams

course_name: Rock, Pop & Hip Hop in Literature
description: This course invites students to explore the rich tapestry of popular music, specifically rock, pop, and hip hop, as a vital and evolving form of literature. Moving beyond simple entertainment, we will delve into the historical contexts that shaped these genres, analyze the poetic and narrative qualities of their lyrics, and examine the critical lens through which music journalists have interpreted and influenced our understanding of this art form. Students will develop their analytical skills, deepen their appreciation for various musical expressions, and hone their own critical writing abilities.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th & 10th grade English
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: reaction journals and listening notes, tests, quizzes, written critical reviews, biographies, research projects and presentations, class discussion, participation and attendance

description: Through a project-based learning format, students will learn what it’s like to be a part of video and television production in a practical environment. Working together with Green Mountain Access Television located at the GMTCC, students will plan, create and produce various videos and segments for television. This class will involve analyzing informational texts, writing scripts, covering live events, creating, producing, filming and editing. Students will be able to take an idea that starts in a classroom and bring it to life in the studio. They will also produce and implement a short, televised program that will be broadcasted into classrooms each week. Students will take turns being on-camera talent, while others will be able to collaborate as a whole class; contributing to script writing, camera operation, switchboard operation, managing the studio floor, and editing. description: Driver and Traffic Safety Education is designed to teach safety practices involved in the use of a motor vehicle. In this course, students will learn decision making skills behind the wheel; how to navigate various traffic problems; what to do in adverse weather conditions/emergencies; responsibility for passengers and other roadway users; and basic car control, maneuvers, ownership, and maintenance. This course will prepare students to take their Vermont driver's license test. Drive time is a required component of this course. Students will be placed in driving groups to gain experience behind the wheel with the Driver's Education instructors. Students enrolled in Driver's Education must have a study hall in their schedule so they can engage in the driving portion of the course. Students may request Driver's Education as part of the standard course request process. They will need to produce their Vermont learner's permit before the class begins. Enrollment in the LUHS Driver's Education course is a privilege. Because you are required to operate a motor vehicle, you must demonstrate the maturity to do this safely and responsibly. LUHS may remove students from Driver's Education, at any point in the semester, for violating our Substance Use policy, and for behavioral infractions that create safety concerns.

description: The AP Environmental Science course is designed to be the equivalent of a one-semester, introductory college course in environmental science. The AP Environmental Science course provides students with the scientific principles, concepts, and methodologies required to understand the interrelationships of the natural world. We can work with, not against, the natural world to meet our needs and build a life of meaning. In this half-day EPIC experience, you’ll chart a new path into the wild spaces of our campus, braving the elements in all their extremes and committing to learning by doing. From friction fire, survival shelters, and species identification to restorative agriculture, food preparation, and personalized nature-based projects, we’ll build knowledge, skills and community in an uncultivated classroom. Like our ancestors, we’ll circle around fire to discuss big ideas, share our stories, and reflect on our experience. If you’re hungry to build agency and science proficiency in the great outdoors, join us for the adventure of EPIC: Rewild.
credits_text: Students can earn 1.0 credit of science in this 2-block experience.
prerequisites: This adventure requires a strong commitment to participation in discussion, reflection, self-directed learning, and the challenge of trying hard things in all of the weather and wildlife conditions Vermont throws at us. If you’re up for it, we want to rewild with you.
fulfills_text: Students can earn 1.0 credit of science in this 2-block experience.
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: students will be able to build key survival skills including plant, fungus and animal identification; water sourcing, filtration, and purification, shelter construction, field first aid, fire making, and food preparation; Credit statement from EPIC: Rewild program page (p. 6); half-day, two consecutive blocks on blue or gold days

description: This single block, semester-course takes learning from EPIC Rewild to the next level. Students who have already earned credit in Rewild and demonstrated consistent safety, responsibility, and kindness will apply their understanding of natural systems and wilderness survival to address complex real world problems of resource use and sustainable living. Please note: This adventure requires a strong commitment to participation in discussion, reflection, self-directed learning, and the challenge of trying hard things in all of the weather and wildlife conditions Vermont throws at us. If you’re up for it, we want you to rewild with you.
prerequisites: Successful completion of EPIC Rewild and demonstrated consistent safety, responsibility, and kindness
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: demonstrations of skills, reflections, engagement in discussions, field notebooks

description: Co-teachers from the history and science departments will help to unwrap the mysteries of human bodies preserved through the ages. We will explore the history and culture of the dried mummies of Ancient Egypt, the frozen mummies of the Incas of Peru, the bog bodies of early Europe, and the modern chemical mummies of communist leaders Lenin & Mao. We will examine the science related to the study of mummies and ancient cultures, including how mummies are preserved and the tools and techniques used to analyze them.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Biology & US History
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: homework, classwork, projects, lab; Also listed in Social Studies (p. 42); Catalog course length printed as 'Semester 2'

description: Meteorology is a course designed for the study and investigation of the Earth’s atmosphere, weather and climates. Topics of study include: air and its properties, wind, atmospheric moisture, precipitation, air masses, weather fronts, climates, control of weather, observation of weather, measurement of factors affecting weather, the weather map, forecasting, and human influence upon the atmosphere. Methods of study include discussion of topics, observation and measurement of weather factors and the use of weather maps. An individual project will be done as well, engaging with the scientific method to investigate topics in Meteorology.
prerequisites: None
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: testing, laboratory exercises, quizzes, research presentation, exam, weather measurements

description: This full year course engages students in a variety of physics topics through active exploration and mathematical practice. Emphasis is placed on guiding students to a firm conceptual understanding of the principles of physics by means of a guided series of laboratory experiences. There will also be ample opportunity for guided practice which helps the student to apply mathematics to gain an understanding of physical principles. This is a lab credit course, and the following units will be covered: linear motion, projectile motion, forces, momentum, energy, rotational motion, gravitation, waves, electrostatics and circuits. Additional topics in magnetism, sound, light, thermodynamics and fluids will be introduced as time allows. Readings will be assigned which introduce the student to ideas in physics beyond the usual introductory course. This course will provide students with opportunities to meet all of the performance indicators related to physics within the physical sciences graduation requirements.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra I
fulfills_text: This is a lab credit course
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: quizzes, guided study sheets, lab activities, class participation, readings, writing article summaries; Grades printed as: 10-12 (9th grade with math teacher recommendation)

description: Through an engineering approach, this one semester course introduces students to engineering principles, mechanical design, and programming. This course will involve daily challenges and a large individual semester ending project. Students' outcomes will be to understand the engineering design process, basics of programming, and mechanical principles such as torque and forces.

description: Through an engineering approach, this one semester course introduces students to engineering principles, mechanical design, and programming. Students from the class will be members of the Lamoille Robotics team that will build a robot and compete in the Vermont FIRST robotics competition. Participation in the competition on a weekend in February is mandatory. FIRST robotics is an international organization that challenges students to accomplish a different task with their robot every year. Students' outcomes will be to understand the engineering design process, basics of programming, and mechanical principles such as torque and forces.
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: daily contribution to design and building process; group projects; demonstration of program

description: Psychology is the scientific study of behavior (how we act) and mental processes (how we think). This course is organized around six major units of study: research methods, biological bases (foundations) of behavior, cognition, development and learning, social psychology and personality, and mental and physical health. Students will explore how psychologists use evidence to evaluate claims, interpret data, and share their findings. Instruction will focus on applying psychological concepts to real world scenarios, analyzing research, and drawing conclusions based on evidence. This course is equivalent to an introductory college level psychology course.
prerequisites: Successful completion of U.S. History is required. Self-motivated sophomores, juniors, and seniors. Must take national AP exam at the end of the year. Summer assignment required.
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: homework, psychological case studies, multiple choice and free response questions, quizzes, tests, projects

description: This course is a college-level introductory survey of the nation’s cultural, political, economic, and social history from the pre-Columbian period (1491) to the present. The course is taught in accordance with The College Board’s AP US History curriculum framework, with the focus of preparing students for the APUSH exam in May. Some essential questions that will be asked are: Who is an American? How has the United States made efforts to form a “more perfect Union?” How can the use of historical thinking skills help us better understand the present and orient ourselves to the future?
prerequisites: Successful completion of U.S. History is required. Self-motivated juniors and seniors, and sophomores with special permission from teacher. notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: daily homework, analysis of primary and secondary sources, tests, quizzes, multiple-choice questions and written response questions from The College Board’s bank of AP test materials, and projects.

description: This course covers the period from the origins of civilization to the 14th century. It includes a study of the early river valley civilizations such as Egypt and Mesopotamia. It introduces the classical civilizations of Greece, Rome, India, and China. It introduces the world’s major religions, and concludes with the medieval world of castles, the Black Death, and the Silk Road.
prerequisites: Successful completion of U.S. History
notes: Formative and Summative Evaluation Methods: may include but are not limited to quizzes, tests, projects, oral presentations, essays, journals, and participation

description: This course provides students an understanding of the foundations of American democracy, the three branches of the federal government, and the system of checks and balances. It provides an opportunity to examine the civil liberties and civil rights that all American citizens have under our system of laws. And finally the course looks at our right to vote and examines the American political system and different positions taken on various issues by the different political parties. The ultimate goal of the course is that students will develop the knowledge and skills necessary for active participation in a democratic society.
prerequisites: Successful completion of U.S. History
notes: Formative and Summative Evaluation Methods: homework, news articles, quizzes, tests, projects

Students will collaborate with each other doing current and historical research to develop their own answers to these questions. Students will demonstrate their knowledge and skills by creating a public product or presentation for a real audience.
prerequisites: Successful completion of U.S. History
notes: Formative and Summative Evaluation Methods: homework, news articles, quizzes, tests, projects

description: Economics is the study of how societies, governments, businesses, households, and individuals allocate their scarce resources. The study of economics can also provide valuable knowledge for making decisions in everyday life. It offers a tool with which to approach questions about the desirability of a particular financial investment opportunity, whether or not to attend college or graduate school, the benefits and costs of alternative careers, and the likely impacts of public policies including universal health care and a higher minimum wage.
prerequisites: Successful completion of U.S. History
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: may include but are not limited to quizzes, tests, projects, oral reports, cooperative assignments, essays, journals, current events, and participation

description: This course will examine the history of several authoritarian regimes, how those regimes came to be and resistance to them. Nonfiction and fictional works analyzing these regimes will assist with the understanding of larger concepts and hallmarks of totalitarianism.
prerequisites: Successful completion of U.S. History or Modern World History
notes: Formative and Summative Evaluation Methods: tests, essays, projects, and class discussions.

description: This course will introduce students to the practice of ancient slavery around the world, including the Atlantic slave trade and slavery in the American South. It will include a study of modern slavery, including debt bondage, forced labor, domestic servitude, descent-based slavery, and child marriage. It will explore both continuities and changes in slavery over time, and explore strategies to combat and abolish modern slavery.
prerequisites: Successful completion of U.S. History is required. Self-motivated sophomores must have approval of previous social studies teacher and a proficiency grade of 3+.
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: homework, news articles, quizzes, tests, projects, essays, and participation

description: Introduction to Philosophy will introduce students to the history of Western philosophical thought from the Greeks to contemporary thinkers. Students will be exposed to big ideas and questions including, but not limited to: Who are you? Where did the universe come from? Is there a God? What is death? Is morality relative? Can computers think? How do you know what you know? Do animals have rights? What is justice? How should we govern ourselves? What should we eat? Students will also be asked to apply what they learn to modern societal, and personal ethical questions. Students will be introduced to the material through assigned readings, role play, class discussions, and lecture.
prerequisites: Successful completion of U.S. History; open to 10th graders with permission of the instructor
notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: may include but are not limited to quizzes, tests, projects, oral reports, cooperative assignments, essays, journals, current events, and participation

description: By the mid-eighteenth century, the world had become smaller. The New World was no longer new, their native populations subjugated by European powers. These same empires dominated a network of trade and power that extended to nearly every corner of the Earth. But something was about to change… Students taking this course will apply historical thinking skills and concepts to analyze historical narratives of our modern world. The course begins with an overview of these skills, then will move into the outbreak of revolutions that sparked around the globe. Next, we will explore the origins of industrialization and its impact on labor, race and gender. From there we will discuss the impacts of colonialism and imperialism, followed by their eventual collapse during and after the World Wars. The course ends with an exploration of the Cold War and the emergence of a highly technological, globalized society.
prerequisites: Successful completion of United States History

Students at this level will gain a greater understanding of France and her “offspring”—the many other regions of the world that use French as a primary or secondary language. Students are given the opportunity, and are expected, to work independently and have much choice in the selection of projects.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Advanced French with a recommended minimum 3.0 or teacher permission

description: The AP French Language and Culture course is designed to challenge students at a level equivalent to a college level curriculum. This demanding course helps students fine tune the language skills acquired over the five years of language study. The six themes (Global Challenges, Science & Technology, Contemporary Life, Personal & Public Identities, Families & Communities, and Beauty & Aesthetics) based on the College Board's Curriculum Framework, will be the focus of the teaching and learning through the entire year. Students will be exposed to a number of authentic materials so that they may develop a higher level of understanding in interesting and relevant contexts. The students and teacher will use French at all time in the classroom. Exploration of facets of the Culture of the French-speaking world will be an integral part of the course throughout the year. Culture will be the 'prism' by which students deepen their understanding of the Francophone world. Students will be expected to take the AP French Language and Culture Exam at the end of the course.

notes: Formative & Summative Evaluation Methods: active classroom participation, discussions & debates, writing of emails and persuasive essays, projects, quizzes, tests, translations and/or analysis of selected poems or readings, final project after the AP exam.

description: How do we read closely, think deeply, write effectively, and communicate clearly? This required 9th-grade English course prepares students for high school-level writing while exploring questions of identity, voice, and power. Students will strengthen writing fundamentals, including vocabulary, punctuation, grammar, and narrative essay structure, and develop habits and organizational skills to transition to high school with confidence. Through a variety of readings and discussions, students will reflect on what shapes their identity—society, peers, family, community, gender, and race—and discover their own voice. Writing will be approached as a multi-step process, including prewriting, drafting, proofreading, self-editing, and revision, fostering thoughtful discussion, personal reflection, and effective communication. Possible texts include The Hate U Give, by Angie Thomas; The Outsiders, by SE Hinton; The 57 Bus, by Dashka Slater; The Body, by Stephen King; short fiction and nonfiction
fulfills_text: Level-1 English credit
notes: Sub-heading: Level-1 Courses (Grades 9-10); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course examines how systems of power and identity—including racism, sexism, anti-Semitism, homophobia, and classism—shape our school, community, and world, while exploring how literature promotes justice, dignity, and self-discovery. Students will engage with diverse texts including memoirs, graphic novels, plays, poetry, and short stories, and selections from the Facing History curriculum, “Holocaust and Human Behavior.” Themes of justice, resilience, and social change are central to the course, fostering connections across global experiences and perspectives. Possible texts include Night by Elie Wiesel; In the Sea There Are Crocodiles by Fabio Geda; graphic novel selections including Persepolis, Fun Home, They Called Us Enemy, and Maus; various memoirs, anthologies, short stories, and poetry.
fulfills_text: Level-1 English credit
notes: Sub-heading: Level-1 Courses (Grades 9-10); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: A true journalistic product has credibility with its audience; it contains facts and can be used for record-keeping; it covers all aspects of the school year, good, bad, happy, or sad; it also strives to include every person in the school. A journalistic approach will teach you skills in business, graphic design, visual communication, writing, photography, and collaborative relationships. These skills will serve you in whatever field you decide to pursue in the future and in producing the school newspaper.
fulfills_text: Level-1 English Credit OR Elective Credit; may be repeated for elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Level-1 Courses (Grades 9-10)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: In the first half of the course, students will write 10-minute plays–sometimes called bolts of theatrical lightning– that reflect their own ideas and attitudes. To begin, students will read plays and study the craft of playwriting; then, they’ll draft, revise, and polish their own short plays. At the end of the unit, students’ efforts may culminate in staged readings of their plays for an audience. In the second half of the class, students will learn about the elements of screenwriting and create their own screenplay for a short film. First, we’ll study the artistic and technical aspects of movies–we’ll watch a number of short films and clips from longer ones–and we’ll consider the ways in which they tell stories through images and sound. As a culminating activity, students will collaborate with peers to create and screen a short film produced from a student screenplay. Then we’ll invite an audience to attend a screening! Texts may include A Younger Ten: Writing the Ten-Minute Play, Filmmaking for Teens, and a number of published and unpublished short plays and screenplays.
fulfills_text: Level-1 English Credit OR Elective Credit; may be repeated for elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Level-1 Courses (Grades 9-10)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course is intended to be equivalent to a college first-year English course and is designed to fulfill the curricular requirements of the AP English Course Description of the College Board. We will study a broad range of representative works from a variety of genres and periods and build on students’ analytical and interpretive skills. Literature both informs and enriches our lives as it continually calls into question what we think we know about ourselves and our world. Accordingly, students will be expected to examine characters and themselves with the aim of self-knowledge in mind. The course emphasizes close reading of texts, meaningful discussion of texts, ideas, and literary movements, and clear, concise writing of timed and untimed essays. The course is taken for two semesters (both required). The AP Exam in English Literature and Composition, given in May, is required for all students enrolled in AP English.
prerequisites: Minimum grade of 3 in Level-1 courses and teacher recommendation
fulfills_text: Level-2 English credit
notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Students will explore children's literature through a critical lens, examining themes and motifs that are both universal and specific to the genre. Through close reading and analysis of popular children's literature books, students will refine their literary analysis skills and gain a deeper understanding of the genre. In addition, students will engage in creative writing activities that encourage them to think deeply about the role of children's literature in shaping our understanding of the world including creating their own picture book and engaging in independent projects.
fulfills_text: Level-2 English credit
notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Designed to be a dual enrollment for Vermont State Colleges, students will read and think critically, write effectively, and learn the fundamentals of literary analysis and grammar. We will use essays, stories, and two or more novels to explore various themes – as students build skills in communication, critical thinking, and research. Students will write daily and revise often, in a variety of genres, including satire, reviews, literary analysis, and personal narratives. We will take inspiration from a variety of writers, as students hone their hone their own writing voice. Students will learn how to find and assess effective sources and how to effectively incorporate research. A research paper with 10 sources, including scholarly research, is the final project. Possible texts: Catcher in the Rye; Handmaid’s Tale; others to be determined.
fulfills_text: Level-2 English credit; Dual-Enrollment for VT State Colleges
notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Creative writing is a process that takes courage. This class is an opportunity for students to be open to the joys of writing and to be willing to take risks as they try out many types of writing–from poetry, spoken word, and memoir to screenplays and short stories. What makes a good story? What is a poem, and how do we write one? What are the literary tools that writers use? What do we have to learn from other writers? What does your writing voice sound like? What does it mean to read like a writer? What writers inspire you? Students will decide on a format for sharing their writing–perhaps a zine, a blog, or spoken word performance. Texts will include a self-chosen novel, much short fiction, poetry, memoir, and screenplays.
fulfills_text: Level-2 English Credit; may be repeated for Elective Credit
notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This interdisciplinary, project-based course empowers students to explore, analyze, and address critical issues in the American criminal justice system. Using an EL Education framework, students will engage in sustained inquiry into mass incarceration, the school-to-prison pipeline, police reform, and systemic inequities, with a focus on real-world applications. Throughout the semester, students will read diverse texts, examine multiple perspectives, and collaborate to develop solutions to systemic problems. The course culminates in an authentic final project: students will create and present policy proposals to local or state stakeholders, using research and persuasive skills to advocate for change. This hands-on approach fosters critical thinking, civic engagement, and the belief that young people have the power to make a difference.
fulfills_text: Level-2 English Credit; *may complete additional work to earn social studies elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); Also listed in Social Studies Elective Courses (p.13) as 'PBL Expedition: Justice in Focus' (Grades 11-12; 'Social Studies credit; *may complete additional work to earn English elective credit'); same description, one record kept

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
course_name: Friending, Crushing, and Othering in Literature
description: This course will examine the theme of friendship–and all the complicated relationships–as students develop analytical reading and writing skills. We’ll ask questions about one of the most important relationships we have, using examples from a variety of novels, films, and excerpts from psychology, anthropology, and journalism. We’ll ask questions about the forces that impact friendships, love, and belonging and how these relationships have evolved throughout history.
fulfills_text: Level -2 English Credit
notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This interdisciplinary, project-based course explores the profound impact of war on individuals, societies, and the human condition through the lenses of literature and history. Combining English Literature of War and a social studies elective in Military History, the course examines how writers, historians, and soldiers have captured the complexities of war across time and cultures. Through engaging with novels, memoirs, poetry, historical documents, and films, students will analyze themes of power, sacrifice, resilience, and justice. This course emphasizes critical thinking, historical inquiry, and literary analysis, while fostering collaboration and creativity through project-based learning. Possible texts include Fallen Angels, Things Fall Apart, Where Angels Fear to Tread, Farewell to Arms, View from the Bridge, The Things They Carried, Julius Cesar, Richard III, Slaughter-House Five, Night, Diary of Anne Frank, The Art of War
fulfills_text: Level-2 English Credit; *may complete additonal work to earn social studies elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: How has the world of sports played a role in American society throughout history? What impact do sports have on building communities? What does our participation in sports reveal about the human spirit? Explore the past, present, and future of sports in the United States, and assess the good, bad, and ugly sides of professional sports from the perspectives of players, coaches, and fans. Possible texts include journals, articles, essays, and videos; readings from Sports Illustrated and other news columns; Friday Night Lights by Buzz Bissinger
fulfills_text: Level-2 English Credit
notes: Sub-heading: Level-2 Courses (Grades 11-12); grade_levels from Level-1/Level-2 section heading or course title (no grade line)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
course_name: America and World History in the 19th Century
description: A required course for ninth grade students and a prerequisite to other history courses. This course will focus on historical events that happened both nationally and globally into the 19th century. Including topics such as the French Revolution, Post Napoleonic Europe, the Industrial Revolution, American Civil War, and Imperialism. These events will be looked at through different lenses: geographic, economic, civic and historical. In this course, students will develop research, reading, and writing skills, by completing a major research project. Students will read a variety of materials, including newspaper articles and primary and secondary sources.
fulfills_text: Social Studies credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
course_name: America and World History in the 20th Century
description: This course starts with causes of World War I and goes through the interwar years into World War II. The course continues to cover topics relevant to world history up until the war on terrorism in the early 2000s. Students will learn and develop the skills of inquiry and research. In this class, students strengthen research, critical analysis, writing, reading, and presentation skills.
prerequisites: Previous participation in America and World History in the 19th Century.
fulfills_text: Social Studies credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This rigorous course offers 9th-12th grade students the opportunity to engage in college-level academics early in high school. Replacing both 19th and 20th Century courses, it examines global cultural, economic, political, and social developments from c. 1200 CE to the present. Students will analyze primary and secondary sources, evaluate evidence, contextualize historical events, and craft well-supported historical arguments. All students are expected to take the AP exam, with credit awarded at the end of the second semester. (Description adapted from the College Board)
prerequisites: 9th graders need approval from the course teacher and a recommendation from their 8th-grade teacher. 10th graders have no prerequisites, but highly recommend completing 19th Century Hist before enrolling.
fulfills_text: Social Studies Credits

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This one-semester foundational course will focus on American citizenship and government. The main topics of the class will be the history of the government’s creation and change over time, civic life, and government. Students will investigate the US government’s separation of powers, and the responsibilities of federal, state, and local governments. Promoting civic virtues and enacting democratic principles will also be priorities.
prerequisites: Previous participation in 9th and 10th grade social studies or AP World History
fulfills_text: Social Studies credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: AP U.S. History is designed to be the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university U.S. history course. In AP U.S. History students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods from approximately 1491 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical comparisons; and utilizing reasoning about contextualization, causation, and continuity and change over time. The course also provides seven themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: American and national identity; migration and settlement; politics and power; work, exchange, and technology; America in the world; geography and the environment; and culture and society. All students will be expected to sit for the AP US History exam in May. This two credit course will replace Civics and count as an elective.
prerequisites: Summer work completion
fulfills_text: Social Studies credit
offering_note: 26/27 School Year; scheduled every year (catalog p.2 note 2)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Students learn and apply the principles of micro and macro economics to current social issues and their own lives. Topics include the role of scarcity in economics, the Federal Reserve, different economic systems, supply and demand, inflation and unemployment, Gross Domestic Product, fiscal and monetary policy, and the Federal Reserve and inflation. Students will also learn about financial literacy and consumer life skills.
fulfills_text: Elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Elective Courses (Elective Credit, NOT Social Studies)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course focuses on the military history of the United States from World War II until the present. Topics include World War II, the Korean War, the Vietnam War, the U.S. War on Drugs, and military actions in the Middle East. The emphasis of the class will be on strategy, technology, motivation, and impact of the U.S. military abroad and at home. Students read, research, analyze, discuss, write, and present their views based on facts, principles, and beliefs.
fulfills_text: Elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Elective Courses (Elective Credit, NOT Social Studies)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Based on student and teacher interest, controversial issues will be chosen to study. Students will research, determine reliability, identify bias, and describe evidence supporting varied perspectives on issues. Students will be expected to articulate opinions and support perspectives with meaningful and trustworthy evidence. Constitutional law and Supreme Court cases will be studied when applicable to help understand the legal status of each issue.
fulfills_text: Elective Credit
notes: Sub-heading: Elective Courses (Elective Credit, NOT Social Studies)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This class focuses on introducing students to the thinking, vocabulary, and foundational ideas of psychology. The class begins with a look at the six main perspectives of psychology. The class then moves to units focused around nature vs nurture, neuroscience, learning and human behavior, memory, thinking and intelligence, human development, states of consciousness, motivation and emotion, personality, social psychology, disorder and treatment, and happiness. The course focuses on using demonstrations and active learning of the content. Students will do several research presentations and simulations to learn and apply the content.
fulfills_text: Elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Elective Courses (Elective Credit, NOT Social Studies)

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course is a combination of applied mathematics, project based learning (PBL), and individual proficiencies. Applied mathematics shows first hand how students can use mathematics to make better decisions and to solve real world challenges. Students work on a project over an extended period of time that engages them in solving a real-world problem. For individual proficiencies students will be assessed with diagnostic tools in order to create a personalized action plan for each student to differentiate instruction, fill individual knowledge gaps and facilitate meaningful progress.
prerequisites: Concurrent enrollment in HOME program

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Students participate in student-centered instruction focused on gaining fluency in operations in the Real Number System. Instruction will also be provided in graphing data, identifying and using functions, applying and comparing geometric relationships, and most importantly, recognizing and seeking algebraic expressions and equations to solve problems. Successful completion of this course will allow students and teachers to reevaluate their multi-year plan with regard to meaningful and appropriate courses to follow.
prerequisites: Teacher recommendation or multi-year plan for mathematics

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Discovering Algebra is designed for the student who has learned the basic mathematics and computational procedures from earlier years, but may lack the number sense to use these skills in a meaningful or creative way. These students may not be quite ready for Algebra I Part 1. Students will develop organization, clear thinking, and strategizing, all important prerequisite skills for success in high school mathematics. Topics include: variables, expression, and integers, solving equations, and inequalities, factors, fractions, and exponents, ratios, proportions, and probability, and linear functions. All topics are focused to develop basic equation solving skills. Success in this class would support enrollment in Discovering Geometry or Algebra I Part 1.
prerequisites: Teacher recommendation or multi-year plan for mathematics

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Following the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum, Algebra I part 1 continues to develop number sense, proportional thinking, and fluency with the real number system. It further develops the language and process of the algebra studied in the earlier grades by manipulating more sophisticated expressions and equations. Emphasis is on working with linear functions with one and/or two variables. Students learn the basics of a graphing calculator as part of learning to create, manipulate, solve, and/or graph linear functions and systems. Additionally, the concepts of probability will be extended. Curriculum used is Illustrative Mathematics.
prerequisites: Pre-algebra, teacher recommendation, or middle schooler commitment to accelerate
notes: Catalog states: Grades 8-12

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Following the Illustrative Mathematics curriculum, Algebra I part 2 starts with a quick review of linear functions and then develops the rules for exponents in order to engage in factoring and the solution of quadratic functions. Connections are made to those rules and simplifying square roots. Students learn additional solution methods and applications for quadratic functions. Inverse functions are taught and students learn to solve radical equations. Data analysis concepts are extended.
prerequisites: Algebra I Part 1

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course is an introduction to the practical aspects of geometry. Students complete a variety of two- and three-dimensional hands-on projects. This practical application prepares students for theoretical concepts and problem-solving in Euclidean Geometry. Topics include the properties of angles, triangles, quadrilaterals, circles and other two-dimensional shapes, area, perimeter, volume, ratio and proportion, geometric construction, and right angle trigonometry. The text used is Discovering Geometry: An Intuitive Approach (Key Curriculum).
prerequisites: Algebra I Part 1 or Discovering Algebra

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Students demonstrate high-level reasoning by writing proofs and solving problems dealing with points, lines, angles, triangles, quadrilaterals, circles, and other shapes. Students study area, perimeter, and volume and the connections between the three dimensions. Students complete a variety of two- and three-dimensional hands-on projects. The texts used are Geometry (Houghton, Mifflin)
prerequisites: Algebra I: Part II

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course extends the study of previous algebra courses and assumes a strong working knowledge of those topics. It encompasses the study of functions including logarithmic functions, irrational and complex numbers, polynomial equations, analytic geometry, conic sections, and series and sequences. Concepts in trigonometry are extended to include circular and inverse functions. The text is Algebra II (McDougall, Littell).
prerequisites: Algebra I part 2, Euclidean Geometry or Disc. Geo. with teacher recommendation

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course completes the preparation for college-level calculus. Students develop skills in advanced function analysis and the use of these functions for modeling applications. Analytic trigonometry is studied to apply in vector, parametric, and polar applications. Conic sections are reviewed and extended, as are topics in discrete mathematics. Students use graphing calculators on a daily basis.
prerequisites: Algebra II and Geometry

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course is a broad introduction to the concepts of probability and statistics. Probability consists of collection display, analysis of data, permutations, and combinations. Statistics involves binomial, normal and t-distributions, percentile rank, and standard deviation. Learning objectives include demonstrating statistics encountered in everyday life as well as showing how statistics lend credibility to an argument.
prerequisites: Algebra II or teacher recommendation

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This full-year course prepares students for The College Board Advanced Placement Examination, level AB, which is equivalent to one semester of college calculus. This course includes a brief review of the most important algebraic and transcendental functions and a study of topics in the differential and integral calculus. Students taking this class participate in the AP Calculus exam. Second semester, the course will run every day until the AP Exam in May. The primary text is Calculus: Graphical, Numerical, Algebraic, 3rd ed. (Finney, Demana, Waits, Kennedy).
prerequisites: Pre-calculus and teacher recommendation

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course is designed to inform and educate students in concepts of personal finance and money management. Students will begin to develop the skills and strategies that promote personal and financial responsibility related to: financial planning, savings, and investment. Five broad topics will be the foundation of the course: college and/or career planning, money management, savings and investing, income, and spending. There will be several projects incorporated into the curriculum.

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course is a study of the Earth and its place in the universe. Students will explore the origins and geological evolution of Earth, interactions between Earth systems, and the impact of human activities on natural systems, including global climate change. Methods of learning can include hands-on investigations, research reports, projects, and analysis of local and global data.
fulfills_text: Science credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Students learn to understand the similarities and differences among organisms, genetics, evolution, human anatomy, and physiology. Methods of learning can include fieldwork, laboratory experiments, class discussions, research reports, and self-directed projects. The text is Basic Biology: An Ecological Approach.
prerequisites: Earth Science
fulfills_text: Science credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course is designed for any student wanting a solid grounding in chemistry concepts. Students engage in lab experiments regularly. Topics include atomic theory, the periodic table of the elements, properties of matter, types of chemical reactions, and applying chemistry to everyday materials and events. Upperclassmen may earn 4 college credits from Northern Vermont University for successful completion of this course.
prerequisites: Biology and Algebra I (both parts)
fulfills_text: Science credit; May take as 4-credit dual-enrollment class*

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: In this class students will explore how matter and energy interact in the universe. Major topics of study will be motion, forces, energy, momentum & collisions. Students will learn about the physical properties of our universe by engaging in lab investigations and developing mathematical problem-solving skills. Students signing up for this course should be prepared to work outside of class and meet with the teacher as needed to understand challenging material.
prerequisites: Biology and Algebra I (both parts)
fulfills_text: Science credit - dual enrollment pending

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Meteorology is the science that deals with the phenomena of the atmosphere, specifically weather and weather conditions. Students investigate how the atmosphere interacts with solar energy to create dynamic weather systems and apply basic meteorological and climatic principles to the study of local, regional and global weather patterns. This course includes an in-depth unit of global climate patterns and changes as well as field trips and guest speakers. Upperclassmen may earn 4 college credits through Northern Vermont University for successful completion of this course.
prerequisites: Earth Science and Biology
fulfills_text: Science credit – 4 credit Dual enrollment option

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course will examine the geology, weather, wildlife, stream ecology and flora of the Green Mountain State and how all these factors make Vermont, well, Vermont. We will look at the many microclimates of Vermont and how these climates fit into the bigger picture of the Northeast. Comparisons will be drawn from what is occurring in the present day to that of times past. This course will require field work.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Earth Science and Biology and an understanding of basic algebraic concepts.
fulfills_text: Science credit - dual enrollment pending
notes: Catalog states: Grades 11-12 or permission of the instructor

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: In this course, students will be introduced to the basic concepts of both theoretical and applied chemistry and physics. The goal of this course is to provide a basic foundation in each discipline while focusing on the real-world applications of each. This will be a lecture/lab-based class and will apply for a student’s third required science course for graduation.
prerequisites: Earth Science and Biology
fulfills_text: Science credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: In this course, students deepen their understanding of the human body. They compare structures and functions of the musculoskeletal, neurologic, cardiac, respiratory, digestive, renal, immune, endocrine, and reproductive systems. Students apply concepts to real-life situations in health, injury, and disease.
prerequisites: Earth Science and Biology
fulfills_text: Science credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course is intended to provide an introduction to understanding the science behind crime detection. Course topics are drawn from the fields of chemistry, physics, and biology. The laboratory exercises will include techniques commonly employed in forensic investigations. Examples of topics include fingerprinting, blood splatter analysis, DNA, hair/fiber comparisons, and death investigation. The course will span all ability levels and will be especially valid for those interested in a career in Law Enforcement or Criminal Justice.
prerequisites: Earth Science and Biology
fulfills_text: Science credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Wildlife Ecology will introduce students to ecology and New England wildlife. Topics of study include biodiversity & evolution, ecosystems, species interactions, population dynamics, conservation biology, and state and local ecological issues. Students will be expected to participate in field work. Visits from professionals from a variety of careers in wildlife science will be able to provide insight on career paths and options.
prerequisites: Earth Science and Biology
fulfills_text: Science credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: In this course students will explore our solar system and the human endeavors that have allowed us to reach our current levels of understanding. Topics of study include tools & methods of astronomy, night sky observations, the Earth-Sun-Moon system, the solar system, and the search for exoplanets. Students learn by completing activities, labs, projects, and simulated telescope observations. Upperclassmen may earn 4 college credits from Northern Vermont University for successful completion of this course.
prerequisites: Earth Science and Biology
fulfills_text: Science credit – 4 credit Dual enrollment option

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course is offered every other year, alternating with Astronomy: The Solar System. In this astronomy course, students will focus on the universe beyond our solar system, covering topics such as tools & methods of astronomy, stars, galaxies, cosmology, and the search for extraterrestrial life. Students learn by completing activities, labs, projects, and simulated telescope observations. Upperclassmen may earn 4 college credits from Northern Vermont University for successful completion of this course
prerequisites: Earth Science and Biology
fulfills_text: Science credit – Dual enrollment option

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This class is designed for students with little to no prior experience in the visual arts. The course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to both 2D and 3D mediums, allowing students to develop basic knowledge and skills in the world of visual expression. Throughout the semester, students will engage in hands-on activities and projects that explore a variety of artistic techniques. The curriculum is structured to foster creativity, critical thinking, and artistic confidence. Students will learn how to pursue independent projects that align with their artistic interests and goals. Emphasis will be placed on building a strong foundation in fundamental art concepts.
fulfills_text: Fine Arts credit
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This class is for students who have already completed a beginner-level course or possess equivalent skills and knowledge in the realm of visual arts. This course delves deeper into the exploration of 2D and 3D mediums, challenging students to expand upon their previous experiences and skills. Throughout the semester, students will engage in advanced projects and activities that push the boundaries of traditional artistic techniques. Students will explore independent projects based on their artistic interests and goals. The curriculum is designed to foster a greater depth of understanding, creativity, and mastery in the field of visual expression.
prerequisites: Art & Design 101 or any other art class. May be repeated
fulfills_text: Fine Arts credit
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Students wishing to create a portfolio for consideration in the AP Studio Art examination and possibly earn college credit enroll in this course. The portfolio exam consists of three sections, breadth, quality, and concentration. This program provides the opportunity to earn college-credit and/or advanced placement in college. Those enrolling in this course should plan to work all year on their art, including time outside of school and the summer prior to the beginning of the course.
prerequisites: Foundations of Art, Ceramics and Sculpture, or Painting Exploration and teacher recommendation
fulfills_text: Fine Arts credit
offering_note: AP Art and Chinese are held with sufficient enrollment; otherwise students may enroll as independent studies (catalog p.2 note 2)
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Beginning with basic tools of imagination, pencil, and paper, students will draw, script, and storyboard their ideas, which will then be used to create a 2D animation. With an introduction to photography, using tools in Adobe Photoshop, students will garner a basic understanding of composition and photo manipulation. Building on the previous lessons, students will then learn about and use Non-Linear editing tools found in Adobe Premiere Pro, WeVideo, and personal devices. Students will then be prepared to create and refine their ideas into completed projects. The class will also examine the impact of film and animation and the subtle and not-so-subtle ways it affects American culture.
fulfills_text: Fulfills the Fine Arts credit requirement
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course builds from the Video and Animation course and involves working with more advanced software programs such as Studio-Max and Autodesk Maya. Three-dimensional design software provides modeling, animation, simulation, and rendering for motion graphics artists. Students complete short animations for films or games. This is an opportunity to meet the demands of a professional artist.
prerequisites: Video and Animation or permission of the teacher

notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This hands-on course for 9th through 12th graders empowers students to pursue their project ideas, fostering engagement with the content. Through individual projects, students develop practical skills in storytelling, documenting their project journey, and utilizing Design Thinking and Systems Thinking methodologies to address real-world problems. Emphasis is placed on communication skills, with students learning to convey their project experiences and outcomes through various media effectively. Opportunities for collaboration with outside organizations provide authentic learning experiences, while assessments are based on communication standards aligned with transferable skills. Students are expected to demonstrate curiosity, an exploratory mindset, and perseverance. By participating in this course, students enhance their presentation and storytelling skills, develop project-specific skills, and gain a deeper understanding of Design Thinking and Systems Thinking methodologies.
fulfills_text: Elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Technology

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Project Bike Tech offers an immersive experience in bicycle mechanics, technology, and entrepreneurial skills. In this dynamic course, students not only learn the ins and outs of bicycle maintenance and repair but also gain invaluable insights into running a business and mastering shopcraft. Students delve into the fundamentals of bicycle mechanics, from diagnosing common issues to mastering advanced repair techniques. Through hands-on workshops and classroom instruction, participants gain confidence in using specialized tools and equipment to keep bicycles in top condition. Through simulated business scenarios and real-world projects, students learn how to manage inventory, provide excellent customer service, and market their services effectively. They also develop proficiency in honing their craftsmanship and attention to detail as they customize and refurbish bicycles to meet customer needs. By combining practical skills with business savvy, Project Bike Tech empowers students to not only excel in the bicycle industry but also make a positive impact in their communities. Join us on this exciting journey of discovery, creativity, and entrepreneurship through the world of bicycles!
fulfills_text: Elective credit; students may repeat this course for elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Technology

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Band is for students with at least one year of experience on a band instrument who meet the school band entry requirements. Participants perform in two annual concerts, solo festivals, chamber ensembles, and pep band at varsity basketball games. Instruments can be rented locally. Students also attend 20-minute rotating private lessons throughout the year.
fulfills_text: Fine Arts elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Music

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Students study and perform choral music from various periods and cultures, focusing on singing techniques and music reading. They perform in at least two school concerts annually and participate in community events. Students also attend 20-minute rotating private lessons throughout the year.
fulfills_text: Fine Arts elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Music

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This class provides instruction in playing technique, chord charts, sheet music, tablature, tuning, and composition. Students learn to play both guitar and ukulele. Depending on the experience levels of enrolled students, the class may be divided into beginner and intermediate/advanced sections.
fulfills_text: Fine Arts elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Music

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of hand tool woodworking, from understanding wood as a resource and developing skills to creating designs and scale drawings for self-directed projects. It also includes antique restoration, where students repair and restore 19th and early 20th-century furniture, focusing on structural issues, veneer repair, and cosmetic restoration. No prior experience is required, and students may repeat the course for additional credit with more challenging projects.
fulfills_text: Fine Arts elective credit
notes: Sub-heading: Woodworking

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This program is for students serious about woodworking, offering nearly 1000 hours of instruction and self-directed work. Students learn joinery, furniture construction and repair, and antique restoration. Students will keep a detailed journal of their skills, and upon completion, students will have a strong foundation in hand tool use, a portfolio of crafted pieces, a juried exhibition, and a Fine Woodworking Apprenticeship certificate of completion.

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Chinese I introduces the language and culture, focusing on listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students learn the Pinyin system, intonation, Chinese writing with strokes and radicals, and typing for digital communication. Cultural activities enhance language learning and awareness, while characters, vocabulary, and grammar are taught through communicative contexts.
fulfills_text: Elective credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Chinese II builds on the four language skills—listening, speaking, reading, and writing—for effective communication. Students expand their knowledge of Chinese characters, grammar, and culture while practicing comprehension, speaking drills, and writing short essays. They also explore proverbs and idioms through basic stories.
prerequisites: Chinese I
fulfills_text: Elective credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Chinese III advances students' skills in listening, speaking, reading, and writing. They practice immersive listening and engage with authentic materials like movies, books, and posters to deepen cultural understanding and language proficiency. Students also explore Chinese literature through reading books, articles, and poems.
prerequisites: Chinese II
fulfills_text: Elective credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Chinese IV is the advanced level of the Chinese language and culture study. The course is intended to further develop the four communication skills: listening, speaking, reading and writing with advanced grammar. This comprehensive curriculum is implemented in an immersion environment where students are encouraged to speak only Chinese in class to ensure and enhance their learning effectiveness. Students will participate in a variety of speaking and writing activities.
prerequisites: Chinese III
fulfills_text: Elective credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This year-long AP course, equivalent to a college sophomore class, develops advanced listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills aligned with the five goals: communication, cultures, connections, comparisons, and communities. Students engage with diverse materials like signs, advertisements, books, films, and contemporary texts from Chinese-speaking communities. Cultural elements are integrated to deepen understanding of China's national and international issues, daily life, and more.
prerequisites: Chinese IV
fulfills_text: Elective credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: In Spanish I, students learn the basics of speaking, listening, reading, and writing. They focus on grammar, including present tense verbs, sentence structure, and formal vs. informal language. Vocabulary development enhances speaking, comprehension, and understanding of Latin roots in English and Spanish. By the end of the course, students can discuss functional topics such as greetings, dates, food, sports, school, and family.
fulfills_text: Elective credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Spanish II builds on communication skills, expanding speaking, listening, reading, and writing abilities. Students study vocabulary related to household items, clothing, technology, and leisure activities. They learn grammar, including regular and irregular preterite tense, stem-changing verbs, present progressive, imperative, and object pronouns, enabling them to express opinions, share information, and narrate in Spanish with increased confidence.
prerequisites: Spanish I
fulfills_text: Elective credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Spanish III intensifies linguistic challenges, with more classroom time conducted in Spanish. Students engage in tasks like asking for directions, describing daily routines, and discussing past events. They study reflexive verbs, preterite, imperfect, imperfect progressive, and reciprocal verbs, along with pronouns and possessive adjectives. Reading stories, news articles, and vocabulary exercises enhance language use. Cultural exploration and linguistic development culminate in presentations in various formats, including spoken, written, and artistic.

fulfills_text: Elective credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: In this advanced Spanish class, students continue building on previous years of study with a focus on complex grammar, including present perfect, impersonal expressions, imperative, future and conditional tenses, and subjunctive forms. These structures are applied in tasks like expressing opinions, concerns, recommendations, and wishes. Students engage in spoken and written narratives about past, present, and future events, further refining their linguistic, cultural, and vocabulary skills while taking greater responsibility for their mastery of Spanish.

fulfills_text: Elective credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course is designed to prepare students for taking the Advanced Placement Exam administered by the College Board in May. Students attain an advanced level of fluency in Spanish through an integration of speaking, listening, reading, and writing while performing multiple linguistic and analytical tasks. This course parallels the rigor and commitment of a third-year college level course, and is conducted entirely in Spanish. Course materials include AP Spanish exam texts, listening exercises, and workbook activities and practice tests.

fulfills_text: Elective credit

description: All freshmen must take the Fitness Foundation course as part of their two-credit requirement. This course develops physically literate individuals with the knowledge and confidence for lifelong healthy activity. Students assess their fitness, set S.M.A.R.T. goals, and create a personal fitness plan. Activities include jogging, hiking, yoga, Pilates, shadow boxing, and more, with options often chosen by students. IHT heart rate technology tracks progress, and students use the PLT4M online program to design and implement fitness plans.

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This course is an extension of Fitness Foundation and focuses on students’ increased knowledge of how to care for their wellness. Topics covered include nutrition and stress management education. Students will become physically literate individuals who value physical activity and its contributions to a healthy lifestyle. Project-based work will include developing a personalized plan and working to achieve their S.M.A.R.T. goals. Students will have a choice in how to achieve their goals through options such as mountain biking, snowshoeing, hiking, basketball, yoga, resistance training, walk/jog/run, volleyball, and racquet sports. Students will also have access to an online program, PLT4M, which helps design programs for use in the classroom.
