fulfills_text: Physical Education credit

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School

Students will explore the qualities of a good leader, and work on developing their own leadership skills with the opportunity to become proficient at leading and participating in all the challenges of a low and high ropes course from group initiatives, team building, cooperation, and healthy risk-taking activities.

description: This life skill course introduces students to the complex decision-making skills necessary for the driving environment. It teaches how healthy choices support learners in achieving a lifetime of collision-free driving. The in-vehicle course component may necessitate driving after school. Practice driving with a parent or guardian is required throughout the course. description: Spend the semester looking at the ways in which we rely upon the land. Explore food systems, commodities, land based tourism, wilderness skills through an experiential and project based curriculum. After taking a deep dive into ways the landscape influences our lives here in Vermont, we will spend six weeks traveling outside the state exploring ways in which other cultures and communities build and sustain their lives in tandem with the natural world. Will include domestic and international travel.

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Senior Survival guides students through the transition from high school to adulthood. Modules include orientation, career exploration, professionalism, job applications, resume writing, cover letters, mock interviews and informational interviews. Students will learn specific skills and strategies as well as transferable skills. Senior Survival is embedded within the Financial Literacy course. Senior Survival will meet once per week during each semester, Through collaborations with faculty and community members, this will be a true community effort resulting in a comprehensive look at how to be prepared for life as an adult. This course IS required for graduation.

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: Based on diagnostic assessments resulting in prescriptive instruction in reading and writing, IEP goals and objectives are created to address targeted students’ significant deficits and gaps in the various basic skills areas. Students are assigned to the appropriate lab(s) where they receive specialized instruction. Depending on the need, instruction is either 1:1 or in a small group with a special education teacher. For some high school students, these labs may be used for content area credit through a multi-year plan/personal learning plan.

school_name: Leland & Gray Union Middle & High School
description: This yearlong special education program for Middle and High school students meets daily for four periods/2 Blocks. Using the student’s IEP as a guideline, students develop practical life long skills based on projects, service-learning activities, and expedition planning and execution. The skill of boat building has been a theme of past projects, such as kayaks of plank on frame, stitch and glue, skin on frame, and cedar strip construction. Using the Circle of Courage model, Special Education students learn to cooperate as a team, develop strong work ethics, and learn the value and satisfaction of volunteer service to the community. Students are placed in this course by their IEP Teams.

course_name: Dual Enrollment - College Credit for L&G Courses
description: In 2013, the Vermont Legislature adopted Act 77 - Flexible Pathways in order to allow for greater individualization of secondary school programs as well as to provide opportunities for students to earn college credit while in high school. The Dual Enrollment Program includes college courses offered on a campus of an accredited post-secondary institution and college courses offered by an accredited post-secondary institution on the campus of a secondary school (which can include online courses). Dual enrollment offers eligible students the opportunity to experience college-level classes, take coursework not offered at their schools, and explore possible pathways to their post-secondary futures. Students who successfully complete a dual enrollment course also earn both secondary and college credits. Vermont colleges approved for providing dual credit courses include: VT State University, Landmark College, Community College of Vermont, College of St. Joseph, SIT Graduate Institute, University of Vermont, Norwich University,Bennington College,and Champlain College. Students in grades 11 and 12 are eligible for two vouchers to pay for the course costs. Vouchers can be requested at https://dualenrollment.vermont.gov/vtde. If a student is in the 10th grade or has used both vouchers, they may take additional courses, but may have to pay the course fee out of pocket. LGUHS may also have funds available to cover the course cost. For additional information regarding Dual Enrollment courses at L&G, please contact Terry Davison Berger.

course_name: Fundamentals of Language and Literature, MYP Year 4
description: Students in this course study novels, plays, short stories, memoirs, rhetoric, and poetry. Basic composition skills, sentence structure, analytical paragraphs, essays, vocabulary, and usage are integrated with the texts. Literacy activities, organization techniques, and study skills are emphasized.
fulfills_text: Each student must enroll in the 100-level course (MYP Year 4 Language & Literature) and the 200-level (MYP Year 5 Language & Literature) course during their first two years at MUHS.

description: This course centers on the development of students’ writing strategies by continuing the work of MYP4. Students study graphic narratives, speeches, epistles, op-eds, plays, and novels to develop analytical and creative abilities both in reading and writing. Students build skills in analyzing, organizing, producing text, and using language.
fulfills_text: Each student must enroll in the 100-level course (MYP Year 4 Language & Literature) and the 200-level (MYP Year 5 Language & Literature) course during their first two years at MUHS.

description: This course promotes the ability to form independent literary judgments and develops an understanding of the techniques involved in literary criticism. Over the course, the formal analysis of texts and wide coverage of a variety of literature—both in the language of the subject and in translated texts from other cultural domains—is combined with a study of the way literary conventions shape responses to texts. Students completing this course will develop a thorough knowledge of a range of texts and an understanding of other cultural perspectives. They will also develop skills of analysis and the ability to support an argument in clearly expressed writing, sometimes at significant length.

This course will cover all of the topics covered in the Literature SL course, plus additional topics and required texts. The HL course moves faster and covers more content, and contains more DP assessments. The Higher Level Essay is completed in the spring of Year 1.

This course aims to develop skills of textual analysis of both literary and non-literary texts from a variety of sources, genres, and media. A key aim of this course is to encourage students to question the meaning generated by language and texts, which, it can be argued, is rarely straightforward.

This course covers all of the topics covered in the Language and Literature SL course and also includes additional topics and students will be required to read additional texts. The HL course moves faster, covers more content, and contains more DP assessments.

course_name: Popular Fiction: Science Fiction, Fantasy & Horror
description: In this course, students will explore speculative fiction. Students will read a variety of short- and long-form fiction, including books of their own choosing, in three different genres. Literary conventions and social contexts will be explored through discussion, creative writing and formal analysis.

course_name: Popular Fiction: Real Life, Then & Now
description: In this course, students will explore realistic fiction, historical fiction, memoir and travelogues. Students will read a variety of texts that illustrate ordinary life and extraordinary circumstances, personal journeys, and the past. Literary conventions and genre terminology will be instructed, and students will produce reflective, narrative and analytical assessments.

This course examines the major themes of our nation’s earlier writers, and emphasizes analysis in discussion and writing. The course aim is to heighten the student’s awareness of the literature reflective of American culture prior to 1900. Students will read selected novels, poems, plays, stories, and essays from writers like Edgar Allen Poe, Henry David Thoreau and Walt Whitman.

This course examines the major themes of 20th and 21st century writers, and emphasizes analysis in discussion and writing. The course aim is to heighten the student’s awareness of the literature reflective of American culture after 1900. Students will read selected novels, poems, plays, stories, and essays from writers like F. Scott Fitzgerald, Ernest Hemingway and Sylvia Plath.

description: Creative Writing I is a workshop-based course for 11th- and 12th-grade students interested in exploring their own writing in a collaborative environment. Students focus on creative nonfiction, memoir, personal narrative, and short fiction, using peer and teacher conferences to support experimentation, free expression, and revision.The course incorporates a variety of media and models, including literary nonfiction, literary fiction, and selected graphic or digital narratives, to highlight different approaches to voice and structure. Throughout the semester, students complete a series of writing projects, participate in workshops, and maintain a learning portfolio of drafts and polished pieces that they share with their peers.

Creative Writing II is an independent, workshop-based course open to all 11th- and 12th-grade students, with no prerequisite. This course emphasizes poetry, drama and dialogue, and oral storytelling, while also inviting students to experiment with additional forms such as thriller elements, dramatic scenes, and graphic or hybrid narratives. Students engage in writing projects, readings, and performances that foreground image, rhythm, subtext, and pacing, using peer and teacher conferences to refine their work. As in Creative Writing I, students assemble a learning portfolio that documents multiple drafts and finished pieces across genres and are expected to share selected work with classmates through workshops, readings, or informal performances.

In Exploring Film Genres, students will delve into the world of film’s various cinematic aspects (such as cinematography, mise en scene, composition, and narrative structure), while simultaneously exploring how different genres of film (comedy, horror, noir, documentary, action, etc.) use these aspects in distinct ways. Students will “read” a wide variety of films from different genres, interpreting filmmaker choices and analyzing films’ meanings and qualities.

Critical Studies in Cinema gives students a great deal of practice in critically watching, reading about, and writing about film. By looking at film as a text to be studied and interpreted, students will consider elements such as setting and cinematography, narrative strategy and point of view, character development, dialogue, and pacing. Thematically, students will learn how to apply a different critical lens to film by studying theories such as race, gender, and class, among others. Additionally, students will be instructed on technical aspects (camera angle, blocking, mise en scene, focus, etc.) of film.

Mythology, history, culture and language are all explored in this beginning course designed as an introduction to the ancient Romans and their language. Emphasis is placed on acquiring the skills needed to read elementary Latin texts. The influence of Roman civilization on modern society is examined through a study of Roman mythology, culture, history, art, and archeology. Southern Italy and the city of Pompeii are heavily featured in geography. In addition, students expand their English vocabulary through a study of Latin root words.

Emphasis is placed on acquiring the skills needed to read intermediate Latin texts. Further study of Roman colonial expansion, civilization, culture, and religion through an examination of adapted readings in Latin increases the students' awareness of the debt of western civilization to ancient Greece and Rome. Roman settlements of Greece, Egypt, and Britain are heavily featured in geography. Students continue to develop their English vocabulary through a study of Latin roots. In DP Latin, students complete their study of Latin grammar through authentic reading of Livy’s ab urbe condita and other topical texts. Through this course, students will continue to translate Latin works in context, examining the ideas the ancients expressed, and their artistry within their historical, political and cultural contexts. All students in DP Latin Year 1 have an opportunity to explore a classical area of interest through the completion of the IB internal assessment. Prerequisite: Demonstrated proficiency in Latin 2.

Students will use French to communicate on a variety of novice level topics including introducing themselves, talking about their free time activities, school life, making plans with friends, discussing families, their home, and their larger community. Students begin to explore the cultures of France and francophone countries, by examining and analyzing the products, practices and perspectives from these communities. Students will also explore the reasons for learning a second language and strategies for success when learning a new language.

They look at travel, food, shopping, and celebrations in the French speaking world. Students learn to talk about activities in the past tense. Students describe and compare, provide and obtain specific information, express likes and dislikes, and learn to express their needs. Students begin to explore the cultures of France and francophone countries by examining and analyzing the products, practices, and perspectives from these communities. Students also further develop strategies for success when learning a new language. Prerequisite: Demonstrated proficiency in French 1.

Students use French to communicate about a variety of everyday situations such as our use of technology, discussing household responsibilities, reading children’s fairy tales and expressing opinions. These conversational topics can now be expressed in appropriate tenses (present, past, future). Students continue to explore the cultures of francophone countries by examining and analyzing the products, practices, and perspectives from these communities. Short reading selections and authentic literature samples are used to introduce or reinforce vocabulary and grammar structures as well as for their cultural and historical relevance. Students explore modern and historical issues such as revolution and war, access to education, art, the environment, and immigration within a global context. Students expand the range of their communication skills by understanding and producing a wide variety of oral and written texts for audiences, contexts, and purposes associated with academic and personal interests. description: This course is designed for students who need more time to build the knowledge and skills presented at the middle school, have not taken Spanish previously, or moved into the district without previous language experience. In this introductory course, students learn to express themselves in Spanish using basic structures and vocabulary in units organized around everyday themes (i.e. Who I Am and My School, Pastimes and Favorite Activities, Cities and Towns, etc.) with a cultural content. Proficiency at this level is attained by developing the modes of communication (interpersonal, presentational and interpretive) within the thematic contexts. In addition, there is a strong focus on language connections and comparisons in order to interact with cultural competence and to become a lifelong language learner. It is expected that students will attain a novice proficiency level at the end of the course.

description: This is an entry level course designed to provide students that are interested in career and technical programs an alternative pathway to success in Language Acquisition at MUHS. The course equips students with field-specific language skills that expand their preparedness to enter the workforce. Students can expect to engage in direct whole group instruction on basic conventions of Spanish such as commands, impersonal expression, present tense, and simple past tense. During this time, students will also build foundational skills across all modes of communication (interpersonal, presentational, and interpretive) in order to strengthen conversational and cultural competence in a way that is directly applicable to their integration into the workforce. At the same time, students will follow a personalized curriculum focused on specific vocabulary to help them reach their career goals.

description: Students continue to expand their arena of conversation to include animals and their habitats, daily routines, childhood, food in the market, and travel. Students talk about their daily routines and learn to talk about past activities. Students describe and compare, provide and obtain specific information, express likes and dislikes, and express needs. Students listen to and read to understand and write or tell a simple story in the past tense. Proficiency at this level is attained by developing the modes of communication (interpersonal, presentational, and interpretive) within the thematic contexts. In addition, there is a strong focus on language connections and comparisons in order to interact with cultural competence and to become a lifelong language learner. description: This is a pivotal year of study for students on the road to language acquisition and communication. Students are expected to express themselves in simple contexts in the past, present, and future tenses. In addition, Spanish 3 introduces students to the most common uses of the subjunctive and its forms. Much new vocabulary is acquired as students talk about themselves and others, household chores, travel, geography, cooking, legends and fairy tales, and other everyday topics. Short reading selections and authentic literature samples are used to introduce or reinforce vocabulary and grammar structures as well as for their cultural and historical relevance. Communication is evidenced through receptive, productive, and interactive skills across a range of contexts and purposes that are appropriate to the level of the course. In this course, students build upon the grammatical foundations of the previous levels while exploring deeper linguistic and cultural themes of global importance. Students explore modern and historical topics such as fashion, health, immigration, the environment, identity, revolution and war, and art, all within a global context. Students expand the range of their communication skills by understanding and producing a wide variety of oral and written texts for audiences, contexts, and purposes associated with academic and personal interests. For the development of receptive skills, students must study authentic texts that explore the cultures of the target language. Prerequisite: Demonstrated proficiency in Spanish 3.

course_name: Roots of the Modern World, MYP Year 4
description: Roots of the Modern World uses a thematic approach in exploring history, allowing for substantial connections to be made between historical events and the world today. The course explores themes including urbanization, sustainability and world religions. Roots of the Modern World is designed to develop the student in a holistic manner by emphasizing transferable skills that will be of use in other areas of academics and beyond. Throughout the course, students are asked to deeply engage in their own education as inquirers and problem-solvers and reflect upon their process and growth as they do so.
fulfills_text: All 9th and 10th graders must complete the MYP Year 4 and Year 5 courses or equivalent.

description: This course explores the formation and transformation of the United States from its earliest Indigenous civilizations through the end of Reconstruction. Students examine how geography, culture, conflict, and ideology shaped the roots of American democracy and identity. Through inquiry, discussion, and analysis of primary and secondary sources, students investigate key turning points from colonization and revolution to reform and civil war that defined the nation’s early character. The course emphasizes multiple perspectives, the inclusion of historically marginalized voices, and the evolving meaning of freedom and equality. Students will use disciplinary thinking from history, civics, and economics (C3) to evaluate change and continuity over time, build evidence-based arguments, and connect the past to contemporary questions about democracy and justice in the United States.
fulfills_text: All 9th and 10th graders must complete the MYP Year 4 and Year 5 courses or equivalent.

description: This engaging course is designed to deepen students’ understanding of the pivotal events, influential personalities, and transformative ideologies that shaped the 20th century on both a global and national scale. In this class, students explore the interconnectedness of world events and their impact on the United States, examining the social, political, economic, and cultural changes that have defined modern history. Through a thematic and chronological approach, we delve into the major historical milestones and analyze the complex relationships between nations, ideologies, and individuals. Students engage in critical analysis, research, and discussion to develop historical thinking skills. By examining primary and secondary sources, students gain a nuanced understanding of the complexities of historical narratives, encouraging them to think critically about the world around them. Students draw connections between past and present, make informed decisions, and become active, engaged citizens in an ever-changing global landscape.

This course explores the events and realities of the world today through the lens of various approaches to the Social Studies. Students will engage in learning activities that ask them to analyze and understand the world around them. The units include media analysis, the justice system, and other topics that will shift from year to year; skills that students will be developing and the focus on the modern world will be consistent. Students will develop skills in analysis and critical thinking, research, reflection, communication, argumentation, and collaboration, among others.

This course explores world history up to 1500 CE focusing on the question: what happens when cultures come into contact? The course covers cultural interactions through global trade, the impact of disaster on communities, and how the Age of Exploration shaped the roots of the modern world. Students develop skills in historical thinking, comparative analysis, communication, and critical thinking.

Psychology is the study of the human mind and its functions. This course provides an introduction to the basics of that study. Students will learn about topics like nature versus nurture, sleep and dreams, memory, learning and conditioning, psychological ethics and experimentation, and developmental psychology and psychological disorders. Students engage with psychological concepts through reading and reflective writing, research projects, and will even develop and conduct their own psychological experiments.

Because sports play a dominant role both in American society and in the culture of American high schools, it is important for students to understand and appreciate the deeper significance of sports as a major influence on American culture. The purpose of this course is to learn what sports can teach us about issues of race, gender, and violence in American society. Students examine both the historical record and current trends and events that highlight these issues. Students read widely from a variety of scholarly and popular sources, discuss and debate issues with classmates, and conduct significant in-depth research on a case study related to the themes of the course. Students are required to complete several position papers as well as informal and reflective writing about the topics that are covered in class.

This course explores fundamental political concepts such as power, equality, sustainability, and peace in a range of contexts. It allows students to develop an understanding of the local, national, international and global dimensions of political activity and processes, as well as to explore political issues affecting their own lives. The course helps students to understand abstract political concepts by grounding them in real-world examples and case studies. It also invites comparison between such examples and case studies to ensure a wider and transnational perspective. The foundational unit of the course, which comprises the first semester, explores the concepts of power, sovereignty, legitimacy, and interdependence through both theoretical and practical, real world lenses. The Human Rights unit is explored during the second semester. Also in the second semester, students will complete a political engagement activity which requires research, active engagement, and reflection on a political issue. The engagement activity is a DP internal assessment. Recommendation of teacher and successful completion of MYP 4 and 5 required.
This course covers the same topics as Global Politics SL Year 1 but in more depth. Recommendation of teacher and successful completion of MYP 4 and 5 required.

The DP Business Management course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of business theories, concepts, and tools, enabling them to analyze business activities at local, national, and international levels. The curriculum covers key areas such as business organization, human resource management, finance, marketing, and operations management, focusing on their interconnections. Students explore core concepts like change, ethics, globalization, and strategy, developing a holistic view of the business environment. Emphasis is placed on ethical decision-making, strategic thinking, and long-term planning, while students build critical thinking and financial analysis skills. The course encourages exploration of global business issues, equipping students for the international business world. Prerequisite: Successful completion of MYP 4 and 5 required.

course_name: Earth Systems and Physics, MYP Year 4
description: This course explores the origins and connections between physical and geological processes of the Earth system. Students develop their skills in experimental design, data collection and analysis, and scientific communication. The curriculum supports learning through inquiry-based laboratory investigations. The content is aligned with the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS). The earth science curriculum includes geology, plate tectonics, and astronomy. The physical science curriculum includes gravity, forces, motion, and heat transfer. This course provides the knowledge, skills, and habits of mind needed for problem-solving and ethical decision making in the 21st Century.

Biology is a laboratory course designed to further develop skills learned in Earth Systems and Physics. Particular focus will be given to observation skills, experimental techniques, data collection and analysis, reasoning from experimental data, and reflecting on the impacts of science in modern society. Classroom activities will include many opportunities for hands-on, experiential learning. Topics include biochemical and cellular processes in plants and animals, heredity, evolution, taxonomy, and ecology. This course will connect the local natural world to the classroom, including studies of the Otter Creek and other nearby ecosystems.

Chemistry is an experimental science that combines academic study with the acquisition of practical and investigational skills. This course introduces students to the fundamental principles of chemistry, emphasizing theoretical understanding, practical laboratory skills, and quantitative chemistry. Students explore topics such as atomic structure, bonding, stoichiometry, reactions, and thermochemistry, while also examining the role of chemistry in real-world contexts. The curriculum is designed to develop critical thinking, scientific inquiry, and problem-solving abilities, with an emphasis on inquiry-based learning. Students will be expected to build upon previous skills in experimental design, data collection and analysis, and scientific communication.

This course provides students with in-depth knowledge about a broad-range of topics including biochemistry, cell biology, metabolism, genetics and evolution. This in-depth knowledge is the foundation for essential understanding of broader relationships between structure and function, matter and energy, biological evolution, and the interdependence of organisms. The course focuses on developing students' communication, lab, and critical thinking skills. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Earth Systems and Physics - MYP Year 4, and Chemistry.

description: This course provides students with in-depth knowledge about a broad range of topics and extends on the content in SL Biology to include biochemistry, cell biology, metabolism, genetics, evolution and ecology. This in-depth knowledge is the foundation for essential understandings of broader relationships between commonality with diversity, form and function, interaction and interdependence and feedback for regulation. The course focuses on developing students’ communication, lab, and critical thinking skills. The DP internal assessment begins at the end of the academic year. description: This course examines a variety of local and global environmental issues facing our present and future generations. Students study ecological principles and engage in field work throughout the year as they investigate Vermont’s soils, wildlife, forests, and aquatic systems. Students look at environmental and sustainability issues through the lens of our food system and how it impacts the environment such as water and air pollution. As students learn about the food system and the associated environmental issues, they learn to grow their own food as well as grow food for the MUHS school cafeteria using the MUHS greenhouse. Research projects include a river study of the Otter Creek, Vermont Fish and Wildlife fur bearing project, and community based projects throughout the Middlebury area. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Earth Systems and Physics - MYP4, and Biology - MYP5, Chemistry, or equivalent.

Science, technology, engineering, and math concepts (STEM) are embedded in all of the units. Concepts such as reverse engineering, Newton’s laws of motion, and simply machines are covered. Students pick an engineering design project that focuses on solving a problem in the community as their final summative assessment for this course. Because it is an interdisciplinary course, it can count as either a science credit or an Individuals and Societies credit (or as both, by splitting the credits between the two years). The topics for this course are aligned with the Common Core Standards for mathematics and include the following: factoring, computation with rational numbers, writing and solving linear expressions and equations, inequalities, direct variations, and properties of rational numbers including exponents.

The topics for this course are aligned with the Common Core Standards for high school mathematics and include the following: linear, exponential, and absolute value functions, direct and inverse variation, linear equations and inequalities, systems of linear equations and inequalities, rules of exponents, and quadratic equations.

The topics for this course are aligned with the Common Core Standards for high school mathematics and include the following: deductive reasoning, coordinate geometry, properties of triangles, quadrilaterals & polygons, congruence and similarly, right triangle trigonometry, circles, surface area and volume, one & two variable statistics, Venn diagrams, set notation, and probability. The topics for this course are aligned with the Common Core State Standards for high school mathematics and include the following: functions, quadratics and quadratic equations, exponents and exponential equations, logarithms and logarithmic functions, inequalities, and topics in geometry including similarity, trigonometry, circles and volume and surface area. description: This course engages students with real-world financial applications while maintaining deep mathematical rigor. Each of the course’s 10 units blends one core personal finance topic with one relevant math concept. Financial topics include taxes, checking, savings, budgeting, investing, managing credit, and insurance. Relevant math topics include: linear equations, systems of linear equations, inequalities, exponential equations, modeling functions, statistical analysis, probability and an introduction to calculating with spreadsheets. Prerequisite: Algebra 2 with Geometry (MA225) or Geometry, Probability and Statistics (MA215).

description: Enrollment in this course will be by audition in the spring. This select group will ideally consist of five saxophones, five trumpets, four trombones and five rhythm instruments. Students are required to be enrolled in Band (with the exception of the guitar and bass). Students are expected to improvise and learn concepts of improvisation such as major/minor scales and modes. Students may be asked to learn jazz standards and stylize them, arrange jazz charts and compose jazz melodies. Students are expected to attend adjudications and competitions as well as public performances throughout the school year.

description: In this Visual Arts course, students engage in a variety of materials and methods in order to build and strengthen art-making skills, including: collage, drawing, pen & ink, printmaking, zine-making, watercolor, acrylics, digital tools, ceramics, jewelry, graphic design, sculpture, and more. Students practice the fundamental concepts used to create effective artwork and then work to create final pieces that demonstrate their learning. Students participate in research and inquiry to understand the factors that influence the creation of artwork, and practice creative thinking skills to develop and use their creative voice. Students also receive and populate a multimedia sketchbook, chronicling their creative journey.
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

description: This is an advanced studio course designed to offer students the opportunity to develop ideas and technical skills at a higher level. Investigating established artists' works and understanding the context and meaning behind these artworks will contribute to students' own artmaking and idea development. The course will begin with guided practice in art-making skills. As the semester progresses, students will gain independence as they develop their own ideas, practice skills, and complete resolved independent artworks. Students participate in the annual art exhibition, developing and carrying out an independent exhibition of their own artworks. Prerequisite: Students must have completed 1 credit of visual art coursework prior to enrolling in this class.
prerequisites: Students must have completed 1 credit of visual art coursework prior to enrolling in this class.
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

description: Through demonstration, practice, and observation, students in this course work to strengthen their drawing skills. Students learn and apply the fundamentals of composition, art, and design to their drawings. Students work with a variety of drawing mediums and practice new techniques as part of coursework. Students use a variety of drawing materials, including graphite, drawing, and pen and ink, as they work to refine their technique.
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

description: The course is designed to introduce students to the fundamentals of painting using a variety of painting media. Students learn to control their values, edges, color, and composition. This course explores a variety of subject matter and painting techniques. Prerequisite: Students must have completed either Drawing or Creative Process in Studio Art prior to enrolling in this course.
prerequisites: Students must have completed either Drawing or Creative Process in Studio Art prior to enrolling in this course.
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

description: This course covers the fundamentals of art and three-dimensional design. Students apply these concepts in creating three-dimensional artworks. Students have the opportunity to work with a variety of materials and methods used in creating sculpture, including clay. Students investigate the definition of sculpture, its origin and history, and its evolution over time to understand the factors that influence the creation of artwork.
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

description: This course introduces students to digital imaging techniques. The course is taught from a fine art perspective with a continual focus on artistic composition and photographic communication. Students gain a deeper understanding of the elements of art and principles of design as they relate to artistic decision-making and photographic aesthetics. The work of great photographers and movements is integrated to support these aims. This is a hands-on art course that requires students to engage with digital technology and computer literacy. A digital camera is provided for in-class use.
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

description: In this course, students explore the use of materials to create well-designed objects that adorn the body. They learn techniques of metalworking including, forging, cold connections, and soldering. Through the study of ancient and modern techniques, students also explore the history of this craft and its contexts in culture.
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

description: This course is designed for students who have a solid foundation in the basics of jewelry making and are eager to explore more complex and challenging designs. Students delve deeply into the creative design process to produce sophisticated and personalized jewelry pieces. Students cultivate a personal design aesthetic and effectively communicate their designs through sketching, rendering, and prototyping. Prerequisite: Students must complete Jewelry and Metalwork before enrolling in this course.
prerequisites: Students must complete Jewelry and Metalwork before enrolling in this course.
notes: Sub-heading: Visual Art

description: This course may be taken as a one-year advanced art course or combined with Year 2 of the course for students interested in the IB Diploma Program or certificate. The course encourages students to challenge their own creative and cultural expectations as artists. It is an intensive and thought-provoking course in which dedicated students apply the creative process to develop technical proficiency and confidence as art-makers. In addition to creating art, students learn how to formally analyze artworks from a variety of contexts while reflecting on how these artworks impact their own art-making practices. At the end of Year 1, students will have completed the research and writing of the comparative study (an IB-required assessment task), in which they compare artworks from different cultures through a written report. Additionally, students will have developed a portfolio that demonstrates growth and proficiency in a wide range of artistic concepts, skills, and techniques. Prerequisite: Portfolio review or successful completion of 1 fine art credit required.
prerequisites: Portfolio review or successful completion of 1 fine art credit required.

description: This course expands upon DP Visual Art SL with additional assessment requirements at HL that allow for breadth and greater depth in the teaching and learning. The assessment tasks require HL students to reflect on how their own work has been influenced by exposure to other artists and for them to experiment in greater depth with additional art-making media, techniques, and forms. HL students are encouraged to produce a larger body of resolved works and to demonstrate a deeper consideration of how their resolved works communicate with a potential viewer. This rigorous course encourages highly dedicated art students to challenge their own creative and cultural expectations and boundaries. Prerequisite: Portfolio review and successful completion of 1 fine art credit required.
prerequisites: Portfolio review and successful completion of 1 fine art credit required.

description: This course is an intensive course for students who have completed DP Visual Art Year 1 or portfolio review and are working towards either an IB certificate or the IB Diploma. In Year 2, students are working towards completion of the IB DP requirements: the comparative study, process portfolio, and exhibition. This course requires students to be self-directed and demonstrate an ability to manage long-term and complex assignments, while working towards technical proficiency and confidence as art-makers and thinkers. The course culminates with an independent exhibition of the student’s own work and submission of all IB assessment criteria. Prerequisite: Successful completion of DP Visual Art Year 1 required.
prerequisites: Successful completion of DP Visual Art Year 1 required.

description: Artisan Studio invites students to explore craftsmanship as a form of creative expression in a world increasingly dominated by mass production. Through woodworking, leatherworking, 3D printing, and laser fabrication, students learn to design and create original handmade works that emphasize quality, artistry, and attention to detail. Projects focus on aesthetic decision-making, creative problem-solving, and material exploration. Students leave the course with a strong foundation in craftsmanship and an understanding of how these skills connect to real-world applications where handmade, well-crafted products are highly valued.

Artisan Studio 2 builds upon the creative and technical foundations established in Artisan Studio 1, challenging students to apply their knowledge to larger, more complex artistic problems. Students engage in advanced projects and design challenges that integrate woodworking, leather, laser fabrication, and 3D design. The course emphasizes independent inquiry, refined craftsmanship, and artistic innovation. Students also explore how their skills and creations can connect to real-world opportunities—developing an appreciation for the growing market that values handmade, high-quality, and sustainably crafted goods. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Artisan Studio 1.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Artisan Studio 1.

description: In this hands-on, project-based course, students will learn the fundamentals of computer programming while exploring the tools and technologies used to create computer and video games. Through engaging activities, students will gain experience in block coding, text-based programming, and the dynamic field of artificial intelligence (AI). Additionally, the course provides opportunities to work with robotics and drones, offering practical insights into their real-world applications. The robotics and drone components focus primarily on coding, creativity, and design—not mechanical engineering—helping students understand how software brings digital and physical designs to life. No prior programming experience is necessary, making this course accessible to beginners.

All students in grade 9 take this course. This class explores a variety of lifetime activities, introducing fitness skills and concepts and aesthetic movement through dance. The physical education curriculum uses national and state standards to guide instruction in order to provide students with opportunities to develop knowledge and skills in a variety of activities which will improve fitness levels and foster personal growth and confidence. Each standards based unit is designed to teach the students the concepts and skills necessary for them to participate successfully and safely.

All students in grade 9 take this course. This course will explore how to incorporate health components and skills into the increasingly independent lives of adolescents. Standards based instruction is used to provide students with opportunities to develop knowledge and skills in a variety of topics, which will foster personal growth and confidence. Each unit is designed to teach the concepts and skills necessary for students to take care of different components of their wellness. These units include motivation for individual wellness, substance education, interpersonal relationships, sexual wellness, mental wellness, and the taking care of the physical body. This course plays an integral role in the well-rounded growth and learning of all students and will help them to develop the foundation for a healthy lifestyle.

All students in grade 10 take this course. This class combines physical activity with learning about healthy lifestyle practices. Students further their knowledge and understanding of how to develop personal wellness through fitness, nutrition, sleep, hydration, and mindfulness habits in order to positively impact how they feel and perform. Students explore lifetime activities in order to promote wellness and complete an aesthetic movement unit which will include yoga, Tai Chi, pilates, and step aerobics.

All students in grade 10 take this course. Students will learn and apply healthy lifestyle practices through a variety of engaging activities–such as self reflection, guest speakers, group collaboration, and independent project assessments. This course aims to provide structured and natural exploration of all areas of wellness. This course will cover the following topics: mental wellness, substance education, diversity/sense of belonging, healthy relationships/communication, sexual wellness, diseases, and first aid. This course plays an integral role in students’ abilities to understand and access community resources, make informed and practical decisions, and develop a sense of autonomy surrounding their own health and wellness.

This course builds on content and knowledge learned in MYP4 and MYP5 PE to improve students' fitness levels through a variety of fitness activities. Students experience different ways to develop fitness as well as participate in a self-designed fitness routine based on their personal goals. This course facilitates a greater understanding of how to condition appropriately, and demonstrates that there are many ways to develop a physically active lifestyle. Students are challenged to develop good habits of exercise, nutrition, hydration, and rest, as well as make connections between regular physical activity and their social, emotional, and cognitive wellness. The independent and individualized nature of this course helps students develop the foundation for a lifetime of physical activity and wellness.

The primary purpose of this course is to teach students the skills and understanding required for successful, high-level academic research and writing. Topics explored include choosing relevant sources, citing sources appropriately, academic honesty, determining appropriate methodology across different subject areas, and writing using academic language. Additionally, full DP candidates will learn about extended essay requirements and receive guidance on choosing a subject and topic, as well as crafting a feasible research question. This course is required for DP candidates.
fulfills_text: This course is required for DP candidates.

description: Theory of Knowledge is a course focused on the question, “How do we know what we know?” In TOK, students explore how we produce, acquire, share, revise, and verify knowledge in real-world contexts. The curriculum comprises the exploration of themes such as knowledge and the knower, eight ways of knowing, and areas of knowledge. Students can take this semester-long version of TOK in either grade 11 or 12. TOK Part 1 or Midd Core TOK Part 1 is required for graduation.
fulfills_text: TOK Part 1 or Midd Core TOK Part 1 is required for graduation.

description: In this elective course, an extension of the required TOK Part 1, students continue to focus on the question, “How do we know what we know” by diving deeper into knowledge questions via five areas of knowledge and the respective organizational framework of four elements: scope, perspectives, methods and tools, and ethics. This course allows for and requires students to explore individual knowledge topics. Prerequisite: Successful completion of 300: MC TOK Part 1.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 300: MC TOK Part 1.

description: In addition to covering the same topics as the Midd Core TOK, this class centers on exploring knowledge questions that are organized into a framework of four elements: scope, perspectives, methods and tools, and ethics. In Part I, students focus on the core and optional themes in preparation for the IB internal assessment, the TOK Exhibition. Following the Research and Writing Readiness for the Extended Essay course in semester 1, DP candidates begin TOK Part 1 during the semester 2 of grade 11. This course runs over two years. The second half takes place during semester 1 of grade 12. Successful completion of this course is required for all DP candidates.
fulfills_text: Successful completion of this course is required for all DP candidates.

description: This course is an extension of the first semester, from the previous year. Students focus on examining Areas of Knowledge in preparation for the culminating IB external assessment, the TOK Essay. This course is only offered first semester of the grade 12 year in order to allow full diploma candidates to meet the timeline for submitting their two required IB diploma assessments.

In this course, students explore all aspects of dealing with their own finances. This includes learning about budgeting, checking accounts, savings accounts, credit cards, loans, insurance, apartment renting, car buying, investing, financial aid for post-secondary education, and other important financial skills. The class challenges students to look at their own personal spending habits now and in the future. This is a class for everyone who wants to be a better informed consumer and be able to make educated decisions about what to do with their money.

What happens after high school? What are the options available to students once high school is finished? This course helps students determine career interests and research the different paths that can lead to different careers. Whether headed to college, vocational school, an apprenticeship, or into the job market after high school, it is important to be on the right path. Students do interest inventories, research different career clusters and post-secondary institutions, hear a variety of speakers from different areas, and find out what it takes to get hired in today’s competitive job market.

This course is designed for students who want to explore the tools for successful small business ownership. In this class, students develop a business plan for the business of their choice. Students choose a product or service that interests them and develop their business plan from there. This is a great course for anyone who is involved in a family business or would like to start a business in the future.

Learn the four P’s of Marketing: price, product, place, and promotion. Students develop a marketing plan for a product that they determine on their own. Students then conduct a market research project on the products to see if and how they will sell in the marketplace. Students decide where their products will be sold, for how much, and how to market their products. The course culminates with a segment on how business and marketing firms target young people so that everyone becomes a better-educated consumer. This is a great introduction to the world of marketing and business.

Where does Middlebury fit into the world economy? How does the world economy affect us here in Vermont? These questions and many more are answered in this course on how the world of international business works. Students learn how the economies of the world work together, why they work together, and what happens when they do not work together. Each student focuses on one country and how that country’s economy is affected by the globalization of business that affects us all.

Take the opportunity to interact with a business or organization and acquire in-depth information about a career or special interest by participating in an internship. Students attend their internship when they are not scheduled for a class or after school. Requirements include attending the internship on a weekly basis, turning in timesheets that explain what the student does on a daily basis at the internship, and meeting regularly with the Work-based Learning Coordinator. Academic credit is given based on the number of hours engaged in the internship. This opportunity is open to all students.
notes: program

description: This class stresses basic food preparation techniques and basic nutrition. Students use their knowledge to plan and prepare nutritious meals that they enjoy serving and eating. Students also have the opportunity to explore new foods.

Students use the same skills and knowledge gained in beginning foods. In addition, students travel around the world using their taste buds, exploring the foods of Asia, Greece, France, Mexico, Germany, etc. This is a fun class full of wonderful tastes and aromas. The students prepare all the meals themselves. Prerequisite: Successful completion of Beginning Foods.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Beginning Foods.

description: Students work at a job-site and receive elective credit along with a paycheck. This program teaches students workplace skills that will help any person succeed and grow in any area of work and/or career exploration that the student chooses. The work-site supervisor and the Work-based Learning Coordinator work with students to teach these essential skills. Requirements include working at the job-site and agreed upon set of hours, meeting regularly with the Work-based Learning Coordinator, and turning in paycheck stubs. Credit is determined by the amount of hours put in at the work-site each academic quarter. This opportunity is open to students age 14 and older.
notes: program

description: Students may do volunteer work in a variety of social service agencies such as Special Olympics, Elderly Services, the Better Middlebury Partnership, local elementary schools, libraries, Equestrian Challenges, etc. They may also design their own individual volunteer projects in coordination with the Community Service Coordinator. In doing this work, students participate in the life of the community, learn about career possibilities, gain knowledge and skills needed for responsible membership in their communities, and understand more about social issues. To receive credit, students attend one group meeting to share their experiences with others, keep a journal, and complete a final project about the organization they served. All grades are Pass/Fail. The hours completed in community service can apply toward the CAS requirement of the IB Diploma Program.
notes: program

description: Students in this class will have multiple opportunities to practice skills needed for independent living, employment, community participation, and post-secondary education/training. Students learn and work at mastering key transition skills for the following areas: employment, independent living, community participation, and post-secondary education/training. description: The focus of this course is to improve the student’s overall spiritual, emotional, and physical health through modifications designed to meet the individual needs and abilities in participation through lifetime, recreational, and fitness activities. Lifetime and recreational activities include archery, golf, soccer, basketball, badminton, softball, Bocce, and gymnastics. A fitness program is implemented based on the individual’s FitnessGram Assessment in the beginning of the course. Health topics in this course include male and female anatomy, adolescence, puberty changes, conception, stages of pregnancy, contraceptive methods, and sexually transmitted diseases. A focus for students with high needs may include personal hygiene, safety, and daily living skills.
notes: Sub-heading: Academic Curriculum; Special Education course. Credit determination for Special Education courses is an IEP Team decision.

description: Food Systems Science is a course designed to educate and empower students to make informed decisions about their bodies. Students will learn about the three pillars of Human Sustainability - Mind, Body and Fuel. They will learn about the interconnected parts and their relationship to the industrial food system and more sustainable alternatives. It will include information on food's impact on human health, biodiversity and the environment. Students will examine the food system’s affects on consumers and their communities. The course will culminate with a “Food System Action Project”, where each student will identify a food system problem and design an intervention to address it. A large component of the course will include active learning in context through growing greens in the MUHS greenhouse and managing the student-run Hidden Brain Cafe. Prerequisites: MYP4 or EPIC, with teacher recommendation and IEP Team approval.
prerequisites: MYP4 or EPIC, with teacher recommendation and IEP Team approval.

description: In Work Experience, grade 10-12 students are placed in 1-2 supported work experiences per semester at businesses in the Middlebury community. Students are coached in the keys of the working world. They are supported on work-sites by a job coach, with the goal of fading supports to just transportation as the student grows in independence. Those decisions are made on an individual basis, as some students and sites require constant supervision or support. Students are evaluated by the work-site supervisors and their job coach. Classroom work includes maintaining an updated resume, practice searching for jobs, and filling out applications. Students who complete an additional portfolio may receive 0.5 Language/Literature credit. We have amazing community partners around Middlebury! Possible internship sites include retail, restaurant, technology, agriculture, automotive, and manufacturing.

description: Students travel to the Lake Champlain Maritime Museum (LCMM) in Ferrisburgh, Vermont, every other afternoon to build a 32-foot Pilot Gig Longboat. Students learn about the history, science, and design behind these boats, as well as how to work as a team to accomplish a common goal. Students demonstrate proficiency through individual and group projects, along with self-reflection on “I can” statements connected to course criterion. At the end of quarter 3, families are invited out to the boat-shop where each student demonstrates one aspect of the building process. On launch day, students give a brief presentation on their experience before embarking on the first row in the new boat.

description: EPIC provides students an opportunity to explore careers in the service industry while gaining basic employee soft skills and daily living skills. Students begin by taking career interest assessments, which guide our community-based explorations. Instruction in science is embedded in units on nutrition, food safety, and food chemistry. Students learn through completing personalized projects, preparing food in a commercial kitchen, and touring local businesses.

description: On MUHS Career Crew, students form a service learning team that completes projects for local community members and businesses. Projects include landscaping, construction, agriculture, plumbing, painting, and general property maintenance. Instruction in work-site communication, safety, and preparing for work is provided. Embedded math topics include measurement, geometry of construction, and estimating / billing. Science lessons include introductions to forestry, agricultural and electrical sciences.

description: The ability to understand, speak, pronounce, read, and write basic English is critical to the social and academic participation of any American high school student. Beginning ELD introduces students whose primary language is not English to the basics of the language. Students practice listening, speaking, reading, writing, and viewing English through drills, dialogues, skits, discussion, tasks, guided reading, dictation that emphasize comprehensible input and communicative competence. ML students practice conversing in a variety of situations and develop basic reading and writing skills and strategies. They also gain a working knowledge of school and community culture and how to use technology to produce classroom work. Language and Literature credit may be awarded with administrative approval.
fulfills_text: Language and Literature credit may be awarded with administrative approval.

description: In Intermediate ELD, students continue to build on previously acquired English Language proficiencies and work to improve their use of the strategies and resources available to them as they move into full participation in the academic and social life of the school and the community. Using the key language uses of argue, narrate, inform, and explain, Intermediate Multilingual Learners, using academic vocabulary in class discussions, related writing exercises that emphasize U.S. writing styles and discourse analysis, and individualized reading assignments that include analysis of various schemata. They also improve their listening, speaking and pronunciation skills through classroom dialogues, video analysis, drills, discussions, and projects. Language and Literature credit may be awarded with administrative approval.
fulfills_text: Language and Literature credit may be awarded with administrative approval.

description: English 9 includes three units of study that reinforce the exploration, relevance, and critical analysis of the following themes: Labels, Labeling, and the Impact of Naming; Storytelling Tropes (like the Hero’s Journey) and Subverting The Tropes; and Conflicts and Connections (Compare and Contrast). Units consist of modern and classic literature along with the teaching and practice of specific writing genres including Informational/Explanatory, Argument Techniques and Narrative Techniques through writer’s workshops, journals, On-demand prompts, and a variety of other mediums. Within each unit, students will participate in various discussions, create, read, compose, and find who they are as learners. Independent Reading- In addition to the required readings and student choice, students will select books from a variety of library lists including, but not limited to: Ultimate Reads, Best Fiction, Quick Reads, Community Book Discussion and many more. Within both semesters of this one-year course, there will be student-led choice of various texts.

description: Building on English 9’s focus on self-discovery, English 10 expands students’ understanding of identity by looking at the ways in which our identity is linked to our sense of power or agency, to act in the world. Students will be introduced to the concept of narrative identity and explore and deepen their understanding of agency, social status, and privilege. Students will be challenged to further their knowledge of the elements of an author’s writing style and their analysis of how those choices create meaning to help the author achieve their purpose for writing. Working both as readers and writers of complex texts, students will be challenged to compare and synthesize across texts, compose essays on demand, and discuss interpretations in dialogue with peers to ensure their preparation to reach their future goals. Independent Reading- In addition to the required readings and student choice, students will select books from a variety of library lists including, but not limited to: Ultimate Reads, Best Fiction, Quick Reads, Community Book Discussion and many more. Within both semesters of this one-year course, there will be student-led choice of various texts.

description: AP Language and Composition is a college-level rhetoric and composition class that develops the ability of students to do the following: read critically and evaluate sources of information to meet the expectations of higher education; fulfill the civic responsibilities of our democracy; and discover the beauty of our world. As readers, students learn the structures and purposes of non-fiction texts applying their understanding as writers through inquiry, explanation, criticism, and argumentation. The understanding of language and texts students gain, leads to significant growth in skill and confidence in writing. Students also expand their literary knowledge by reading classics and poetry as they explore topics including American myth and identity, economic power, race, gender and society, and the relationship between humans and nature.
fulfills_text: Juniors and Seniors must choose between an AP course or Seminar course to meet the graduation requirement.
notes: The AP course and AP Exam must be completed in its entirety for AP credit to appear on your transcript. Early withdrawal will result in no AP credit on the Transcript.

description: AP Literature and Composition is a college-level literature and composition class. Students will focus on big ideas related to character, setting, structure, narration, figurative language, and literary argumentation. As a result of the extensive reading, students will experience classics and contemporary works that are often mentioned on the exam and will be given detailed instruction on how to write appropriate responses to literature at the AP level. Formal essay assignments on major works will further develop their analytical and interpretive skills. Topics covered: the power of storytelling; identity and power; the nature of tragedy; fate and free will; personal freedoms, and social issues.
fulfills_text: Juniors and Seniors must choose between an AP course or Seminar course to meet the graduation requirement.
notes: The AP course and AP Exam must be completed in its entirety for AP credit to appear on your transcript. Early withdrawal will result in no AP credit on the Transcript.

description: Speculative fiction, a term first used by Robert A. Heinlein in 1947, encompasses various genres that “speculate” about imagined worlds. In this course, students will survey branches of speculative fiction such as fantasy, dystopian, and science fiction, exploring their respective conventions. The course will delve into the role of technology, magic, armageddon, and more in literature from the 19th century to the present day. Additionally, students will consider how this literature reflects and deflects from reality.
fulfills_text: Juniors and Seniors must choose between an AP course or Seminar course to meet the graduation requirement.
notes: Offerings list shows course number 01061

description: This semester-long course surveys and explores our history through the many forms of literature used for protest from novels and speeches to art and film. Students will study issues relevant and important to them in the context of historic and current systems of injustice and the civic and democratic ideals of America’s founding freedom and liberty for all. Students will learn how prejudice based on race, class, and gender formed and consider its impact on individuals, groups, and society. Students will examine multiple factors that impact marginalized groups and how those groups led movements for social change. This course will create opportunities for students to gain a greater understanding of varying perspectives and experiences of people throughout the United States. Students will develop high level critical thinking, reading, research and composition skills and have the opportunity to apply their knowledge and skills as they collaborate to act on an issue of concern to Vermonters and our nation.
fulfills_text: Juniors and Seniors must choose between an AP course or Seminar course to meet the graduation requirement.

description: Students explore the literature of war considering how it reflects the values and beliefs as individuals and as a nation as well as the responsibility we have as citizens especially as it relates to the impact of war on soldiers. Students develop their critical reading skills studying and comparing the many types of texts used to tell war stories including novels, short stories, photos, poetry, film, and non-fiction texts. Students further their inquiry skills in research projects on topics they choose. The projects challenge students to understand and explain the factors that lead to war, to effectively evaluate sources, and to explore many perspectives before drawing conclusions. Discussions are an anchor for learning in class. They ensure students understand how to listen and engage in civil discourse exploring current and timeless topics related to war and violence as well as healing and reconciliation.
fulfills_text: Juniors and Seniors must choose between an AP course or Seminar course to meet the graduation requirement.

description: Students in this course will engage with stories that have been adapted into some sort of retelling, whether it be for stage, screen, or other revitalized formats. We will read and view adaptations of ancient stories (such as Greek mythology and fairy tales) and famous plays (such as Shakespeare), as well as assorted short stories (such as “Supertoys Last All Summer Long”) and choice novels. In addition to critiquing the similarities and differences between the originals and the adaptations, student will consider key ideas in literary analysis such as how some pieces of literature can reflect and comment upon the society from whence they came and also how some pieces of literature hold timeless life lessons that are equally relevant in our world today. Through writing, discussions, and various projects such as creating unique adaptations of transformed source materials themselves, students will engage with the art of adaptation as a powerful facet of storytelling.
fulfills_text: Juniors and Seniors must choose between an AP course or Seminar course to meet the graduation requirement.

course_name: Social Issues in Young Adult Literature
description: Young adult literature has increasingly become a vehicle for young people to explore social issues. As students explore themes including the myriad ways people experience justice and belonging, they will build the skills to plan and facilitate Socratic Seminar discussions, taking ownership of the direction of the class. Key topics may include mental health, substance abuse, family, community, identity, violence and justice, immigration and home. As young adults studying young adult literature, students will consider what conclusions can be made about power, the individual in society, and the nature of community through these works.
fulfills_text: Juniors and Seniors must choose between an AP course or Seminar course to meet the graduation requirement.

description: Students will explore Gothic literature and its influence on the mystery and horror genres. Through close examinations of several texts, we will identify the unique aspects of each genre in addition to their commonalities. Beware of ghosts, murderers, and monsters as we seek to understand all things that go bump in the night. Students will also identify the themes and common Gothic tropes utilized by genres such as: mystery, thriller, horror, science fiction, and fantasy and determine what truths are revealed about human nature and society. Some film presentations will also be analyzed, focusing on the translation from print to film.
fulfills_text: Juniors and Seniors must choose between an AP course or Seminar course to meet the graduation requirement.

description: Spend a quarter exploring current Young Adult Reads for next year’s Community Book Discussion list. Read from award winning books and share your findings with the rest of the class. Read from your favorite genres and try new ones! It’s up to you!

Spend a quarter exploring your interests by reading books that matter to you. Put together a list of books that you want to read and knock them out one at a time. Become an expert on vampire literature or figure out what makes an excellent graphic novel. Read different fantasy novels and understand how to make an imaginary world or discover Victorian England. Tackle the classics; prepare for AP courses and college reading. You will read and share your findings with the rest of the class. Read from one genre or across a range of genres! It’s up to you! Just read, read, and read some more, and then share it with the world.

description: Spend a quarter completing your college application, college essays, and college mini-essays before your college deadline. This nine-week course is structured as a writing workshop where you will make goals weekly to accomplish the day you hit “submit.”

In this course, students strengthen their writing skills by learning how to express their ideas and experience in convincing, meaningful, and beautiful ways. Students will develop their understanding of different structures and forms and how they support an author’s purpose in writing. They will analyze model texts, practice writing in different genres, and develop their capacity to give and receive feedback on writing. This will prepare students to develop a piece of writing that they will publish as part of their final project. Throughout the course, they will consider the questions: How do audience and purpose influence writing? What are the differences between drafting, revising, and editing? How can I engage my readers’ attention? Students read and discuss examples of effective writing as a way to hone their skills. At the end of the course, students participate in a public reading or public publishing as part of the final exam.

Literacy Lab provides a systematic and structured reading approach that will help students improve in the areas of comprehension and fluency. Our primary focus in the program is to ensure that students have an opportunity to read with competence, confidence, and understanding. Daily, students monitor their fluency rate, comprehension, and crucial reading skills (vocabulary expansion, fact and opinion, sequence of events, inferences, and main idea) as well as their growth, mastery, and areas that desire improvement. Throughout the year – different genres are addressed, writing on self-selected topics, and question-response sessions are incorporated. Formal assessment is administered to all students in the program (pre and post testing) in order to identify strengths and weaknesses. Assessment scores are shared with parents, the student, and the academic team for accountability. Students who enroll in this program learn to celebrate reading and learn more about the world.
