description: A.P. Psychology is an exploration into the human mind. Why do we think the things that we think? Why do we do the things that we do? Do we change over time or stay the same? Are we a product of nature or nurture? While these questions and many others like it will be examined, this course is designed to introduce students to the systematic and scientific study of the behavior and mental processes of human beings and other animals. Students will be exposed to the psychological facts, principles, and phenomena associated with each of the major subfields within psychology. Students will also learn about the ethics and methods psychologists use in their science and practice.
notes: The AP course and AP Exam must be completed in its entirety for AP credit to appear on your transcript. Early withdrawal will result in no AP credit on the Transcript.

course_name: AP United States Government and Politics
description: This course, which will prepare a student for the Advanced Placement Exam, provides an analytical perspective on government and politics in the United States. The course will include both the study of general concepts used to interpret U.S politics as well as specific case studies. The various institutions, groups, beliefs and ideas that constitute U.S. political reality will be explored. The following specific topics will be studied: Constitutional Underpinnings of the U.S. Government, Political Beliefs and Behaviors, Political Parties and Interest Groups, Institutions of the National Government, Public Policy, Civil Rights and Civil Liberties. All AP students are expected to take at least one AP exam.
prerequisites: Completion of U.S. History
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION; The AP course and AP Exam must be completed in its entirety for AP credit to appear on your transcript. Early withdrawal will result in no AP credit on the Transcript.

description: Criminal Justice is a nine-week elective course that examines the U.S. criminal justice system. Topics of study will include the constitutional foundations of the legal system, methods of investigation, the criminal court process, theories and types of punishment, and the juvenile justice system. Explorations of various careers in the criminal justice system will be a part of the course. Students will have the opportunity to explore topics of interest, and the class may elect to conduct a mock trial.
notes: Offerings list shows course number 15051A

description: At times, the subject economics has been termed the dismal science, but economics is anything but dismal as we make many economic decisions regularly. Economics is about human behavior, especially how people choose to use resources. In this course we will examine some principles of economics through a modern lens of knowledge, technology, entrepreneurship, and innovation. This course will examine what is needed for economic growth and how new ideas, new technology and entrepreneurial skills work in today’s world.

Geography is divided into two main branches: Human geography and physical geography. Human Geography is the study of people in place, including the various political, economic, and social factors that create place. Physical Geography studies the processes and patterns in our natural environment. Human geography and physical geography provide an opportunity to examine how humans interact with their environment and how the surrounding environment can impact people. This course is designed to explore geographic processes, such as the physical and human systems that shape our world, and geographic tools, such as maps, geospatial technology, and other forms of data. Geography is a semester-long social studies elective available to 11th and 12th-grade students.

There is more than one way to study and engage in history. History through Film offers an exciting opportunity to access historical narratives and social trends by screening films, analyzing their content and messages, and using film as a springboard to authentic socio-political discourse. In addition to screening films from around the world, students will engage in Socratic discussion, research historical accuracy, and collaborate to better understand some of the cultural, religious, political, and social movements of human history.

Philosophy means the “love of wisdom.” In this class students have the opportunity to further develop their sense of wonder. What makes an action right or wrong? Who am I? What is the meaning of life? What makes a word mean anything? How can we know if there is anything outside of our own minds? People’s analytical capacities are highly developed before a great deal about the world is known. Many people start to think about philosophical problems on their own—about what really exists, or whether we can know anything. The main concern of this class is to question, argue, try out new ideas, and find understanding about common ideas that all people use every day.

Applied Psychology will take students on an exploration of the many ways that psychology is part of their everyday lives. Psychological research underlies many areas of life that impact people and this class will address how issues such as money, the law, sports, health, technology, school, work and family are influenced by the study and application of modern psychology. Psychology is a diverse field that has much to offer society in terms of both theoretical and practical knowledge. Students will change the way they think about themselves and the world around them as they apply the practical concepts from this course.

The goal of Personal Finance is to help students become financially responsible and conscientious members of society. This course develops students' understanding and skills in such areas as career selection, budgeting, proficiency in student and auto loans, the wise use of credit, and the understanding of how to invest in various securities. This course will give students the tools and resources needed to make wise financial decisions. Students will analyze their personal financial decisions, evaluate the costs and benefits of their decisions, and apply the knowledge learned to financial situations encountered later in life. This course will provide a foundational understanding for making informed personal financial decisions.

description: This course is intended for 11th and 12th-grade students. One focus of this course is on civic and political institutions, specifically, how the U.S. Constitution establishes a system of government that has powers, responsibilities, and limits that have changed over time and that are still contested. The second focus of this course is processes, rules, and laws. Students will analyze how people use and challenge local, state, and national laws to address a variety of public issues. Students will also analyze historical, contemporary, and emerging means of changing societies, promoting the common good, and protecting rights. This course is complemented by the frequent aid of elected and public officials to enrich course content.

This class is a study of the language, concepts, and techniques of algebra that will prepare students to approach and solve problems following a logical succession of steps. Skills taught in this course lay groundwork for upper-level math and science courses and have practical uses.

description: This course is intended for the student who has a thorough knowledge of college preparatory mathematics, including Algebra, Geometry, Trigonometry, Analytic Geometry, and Pre-Calculus Mathematics. The curriculum will follow the College Board Advanced Placement (AP) curriculum. The course covers elementary functions, limits, the derivatives and integrals of basic algebraic and transcendental functions and their applications. The student choosing this course must understand that he/she is making a commitment to a consistent amount of hard work and more than a normal amount of outside-of-class preparation.

description: This course is intended for the student who has a thorough knowledge of college preparatory mathematics, including algebra, geometry, probability, and functions. Statistics is divided into four major themes: exploratory analysis, planning a study, probability, and statistical inference. Students will be provided the opportunity to understand and interpret data, look at various sampling methods, understand sampling bias, and design and carry out sampling methods. Successful completion of this course will prepare students for the Advanced Placement Statistics exam. All AP students are expected to take at least one AP exam.

The course topics will also include derivatives, antiderivatives and integration techniques. This course is designed for the student who isn’t ready to commit to an AP level math class and its rigor but would like some experience with calculus before moving on to college.

It is a dual enrollment course and, as such, will require you to use one of your dual enrollment vouchers. It will provide the skills necessary to be successful in technical mathematics. It is designed for students who have taken two years of high school algebra, have scored at least a 2 on the SBAC, in the 50th percentile for the STAR assessment and have a math SAT/PSAT score of at least 480. Topics covered include fundamental algebraic concepts; geometry; right triangle trigonometry; factoring and algebraic functions; systems of equations; quadratic equations; radicals and exponents. description: Statistics is the art of distilling meaning from real world data. No matter what path a student ends up exploring, understanding and using statistics and probability will give them the edge in that career. In this course, real world data will be gathered and analyzed to discover meaning that is not apparent. Students will be given the tools to critically understand and evaluate statistical conclusions, to be able to interpret the validity of the information they will encounter in everyday life. Topics in the course include: - Interpreting categorical and quantitative data - Making inferences and justifying conclusions - Using conditional probability - Using probability to make decisions
prerequisites: Completion of Algebra I.

Students who are looking for an option to improve their conceptual understanding in a more hands-on, discussion-format, problem-based course would benefit from taking this course. Students who’ve taken EMC^2 will feel more confident in math and about taking future math courses. This course is designed to increase the postsecondary enrollment rates for students due to their increased competence and confidence in math. Upon successful completion of this course a student will be able to enroll in one of the VSC system schools (CCV, Castleton University, Northern VT University at Lyndon or Johnson, and Vermont Technical College) without the need for remediation in math. This saves the student money and moves them into their program of study seamlessly. This course typically runs every other year alternating with Principles of Mathematics.

Students also learn to count money and make correct change in preparation for work experience. Vocabulary and math language are incorporated into instruction. This course is by teacher recommendation.

description: In the first unit students use mathematical and computer models to determine the factors that affect the size and diversity of populations in ecosystems, including the availability of resources and interactions between organisms. In the second unit students make a model that links photosynthesis and respiration in organisms to cycles of energy and matter in the Earth system. They gather evidence about the linked history of Earth’s biosphere and atmosphere. They also explore the macronutrients in our diet and the energy transformations that occur as they eat and process food. The third and fourth units focus on how organisms grow, maintain themselves, and pass along genetic information. In the fifth unit students develop a model about how rock layers record evidence of evolution as fossils. Building on their learning from previous grades, they focus on effectively communicating this evidence and relate it to principles of natural selection. The final unit focuses on ecosystem stability and the response to climate change. Required of all 9th graders. This is a Lab Science.
fulfills_text: Biology (Required); Science (Biology/Physical-Earth/Chemistry) 3 Credits

description: Physical and Earth Science is a foundation course of the high school science pathway. This survey course exposes students to some of the major concepts that they will encounter in the physical/earth sciences course of study. Through problems that engage and challenge, students explore a broad range of affiliated topics, including forces and motion, Earth’s system, geology, climate change, waves, and the origin of the universe. The course applies and concurrently develops secondary level knowledge and skills in mathematics, science, engineering, and technology. Required of all 10th graders. This is a Lab Science.
fulfills_text: Physical & Earth Science (Required); Science (Biology/Physical-Earth/Chemistry) 3 Credits

description: Chemistry is the third foundational course designed to provide the chemistry and earth science background necessary to understand the effect of human action on local and global climate. Chemistry topics include the structure of matter, the relationship between the subatomic structure of matter and the properties that matter exhibits, conservation of matter and energy, chemical reactions, and nuclear reactions. Earth science topics include atmospheric composition, the greenhouse effect and the way matter cycles in the environment (especially the carbon cycle). In addition to understanding why environmental problems like climate change are occurring, students will analyze potential solutions. This is a Lab Science.
fulfills_text: Chemistry (Required); Science (Biology/Physical-Earth/Chemistry) 3 Credits

description: The AP Biology course is designed to be the equivalent of an introductory biology course usually taken by biology majors during their first 2 semesters of college. The goals of the course are to prepare students for a college level workload, while building college level lab-science skills and to develop college-level content knowledge. However, extensive high school supports are offered to help students build success. Students who are interested in pursuing biology careers may earn college credit with a score of 3, 4, or 5 on the May exam which will allow them to begin college with higher-level classes. However, most students looking to major in biology choose to take intro biology classes in college and find this a perfect course to prepare them to excel in those classes. Students pursuing other science majors or non-science majors should consider AP biology as a way to demonstrate college level skills in diverse fields and earn college credits to satisfy college liberal arts requirements. During the first semester, students study biochemistry and cellular biology. The second semester explores genetics, evolution, and ecology. Students will spend approximately 20% of class time engaged in laboratory activities. This class is intended to be taken by juniors or seniors and does not require chemistry as a prerequisite.
prerequisites: Completion of 9th grade science. This is a Lab Science.
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION; The AP course must be completed in its entirety for AP credit to appear on your transcript. Early withdrawal will result in credit for “Advanced Biology” on the Transcript.

description: AP Physics 1 is a year-long algebra-based, introductory college-level physics course that explores topics such as Newtonian mechanics (including rotational motion), work, energy, and power. Regular physics is not a requirement for being successful in this course. Through inquiry-based learning, students will develop scientific critical thinking and reasoning skills. All AP students are expected to take at least one AP exam. Students pursuing other science majors or non-science majors should consider AP physics 1 as a way to demonstrate college level skills in diverse fields and earn college credits to satisfy college liberal arts requirements.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th and 10th grade science, as well as a B or better in Pre-calculus and/or Trigonometry. This is a Lab Science.

description: This second part of the Chemistry course is designed for the student with a keen mind and a strong drive to excel in the field of science or math. This course will be a continuation of the first semester of Chemistry and will cover gas laws, intermolecular forces, stoichiometry, acid/base chemistry and thermochemistry.

description: This project-based course will help students develop an engineering mindset, which can be used to design and promote sustainable solutions to some of the world’s largest problems. Students will learn how to combine the knowledge and skills of multiple academic disciplines into an approach that can be used to effectively meet the needs of the 21st century. This is a student driven course, allowing students to pursue interests in many different engineering fields, ranging from mechanical engineering to the Internet of Things, to agricultural engineering via hydroponics.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th and 10th grade science.

description: This course allows students to investigate and study the structure, shape, and function of the human body. Using a systems approach, we will focus on the relationship and interactions between the 11 organ systems to maintain a balance (homeostasis) by responding to internal and external stimuli. There will be an emphasis on normal physiological function and clinical aspects of disease and injury. Laboratory work is included in this course.
prerequisites: Completion of Biology.
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

description: This course is a continuation of Human Anatomy I that allows students to investigate and study the structure, shape, and function of the human body. Using a systems approach, we will focus on the relationship and interactions between the 11 organ systems to maintain a balance (homeostasis) by responding to internal and external stimuli. There will be an emphasis on normal physiological function and clinical aspects of disease and injury. Laboratory work is included in this course.

description: This course is designed to introduce physics to students with a wide range of backgrounds and abilities. It shows students how physics is related to their lives and the world around them. This course offers a unique balance of conceptual development and quantitative applications, covering fields of physics that are of interest to the students. Knowledge of algebra is required for this course. Understanding the basic principles involved and the ability to apply these principles in the solution of problems is the major goal of the course.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th and 10th grade science, geometry, and statistics. This is a Lab Science.
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

description: Food Science is designed to reinforce and enhance your knowledge of scientific principles and processes through the study of foods and nutrition. Within a hands-on lab approach, students will learn the chemistry of cooking. Chemical/biochemical reactions of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, and other constituents in fresh and processed foods are discussed with respect to food quality. Reaction conditions and processes that affect color, flavor, texture, nutrition, and safety of food are emphasized.

Passionate researcher, teacher, and author, Ann Wigmore once said, “The food you eat can either be the safest and most powerful form of medicine or the slowest form of poison”. Students will study the vast science and connection involved in growing, preparing, and eating food. The curriculum applies knowledge in plant biology, ecology, chemistry, and environmental science to real systems that students can relate to whether or not they plan to enter into a science-based job or program after high school. These include connections between those who eat and those who produce food, between our own health and the health of our environment, and between what happens in the classroom, the cafeteria, and the community. Student strengths are leveraged to help the group to meet our collective goals. Our goals are to produce a good amount of food for our local community. In addition, our goals are that every student learns more about the food they eat and to see themselves as empowered producers as well as knowledgeable consumers. Activities are mostly outside, mostly hands-on, and entirely completed during class time. As our “lab”, we will use the school garden and growing spaces. Students will never look at food the same way!
notes: Not in the course offerings list; offered in quarter 4

description: Introduction to Forensic Science is a nine-week hands-on investigative science course designed to expose students to the field of forensics. In this course students will learn how to apply the processes and technologies of science to problems associated with identifying and analyzing evidence in criminal events. Some of the topics that will be covered will include analysis of fingerprints, DNA, hair and fiber, blood, glass, and soil. A strong emphasis will be placed on developing scientific inquiry principles and skills. This is a Lab Science.

Take your interest in forensic science further. Students will consider additional techniques for collection and analysis of forensic evidence. Students will also take a deeper dive into the science behind blood analysis, chemical analysis and illuminate the many uses of DNA evidence. We will continue to consider true crime analysis to see how forensic scientists are working in the real world. Students will continue to focus on the scientific method and use of comparison and controls.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Introduction to Forensic Science I

description: We use natural resources to power our homes, create our consumer goods, and feed ourselves. Managing our natural resources is important in order to see that we are meeting our needs while maintaining the resource base for future generations. Our resources include fossil fuels, metals, water, minerals, soils, forests, as well as our hunting grounds and fisheries. This class is offered in quarter 3 and will grow the seedlings that will be transplanted into the garden by the quarter 4 Food systems class.
notes: Offerings list shows course number 21024

description: Want to know how your brain works? Neuroscience is the study of the nervous system and how it regulates behavior. This one-quarter course is designed as a “users manual” to introduce concepts about how your senses communicate with your brain, how your brain communicates with your muscles and how the many parts of your brain communicate with each other. We consider the evolution of the human brain, the differences between the human brain and other animal brains and admire the intelligence of non-human brains. Students will consider the benefits of exercise on our cognitive functions both now and as we age. In addition, we look at the structure of the brain and nervous system and understand the structure of brain cells and how they communicate messages to each other. Students will learn about how we pay attention, why we struggle sometimes to pay attention in class and the brain characteristics commonly known as ADHD. We discuss the effect of stress and anxiety on our brains as well as brain injuries and diseases. Students interested in pursuing biology in college will find this class useful in addition to (either before or after) AP biology and Anatomy and Physiology. However, students who are pursuing non-biology fields in college may also enjoy understanding more about how their brain works (AP biology and Anatomy and Physiology are not required). Students may even be inspired to pursue a career in neuroscience!
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th grade science, completion of (or concurrent with) Chemistry.
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

description: Want to know EVEN MORE about how your brain works? Students that have completed the Introduction to Neuroscience class may wish to take this follow up class. In addition to going deeper into topics from the Introduction to Neuroscience class, in this course, we will also consider: ● the impacts of food, medicines and drugs on the brain’s function. ● what happens to our brains as we sleep and dream ● parasites that can infect our brains ● Short term and long-term memory formation ● Neuroplasticity and how we can change our brain We will continue to learn about how we study the brain including with scientific experimentation as well as with use of new technology. Students interested in pursuing biology in college will find this class useful in addition to (either before or after) AP biology and Anatomy and Physiology. However, students who are pursuing non-biology fields in college may also enjoy understanding more about how their brain works (AP biology and Anatomy and Physiology are not required). Students may even be inspired to pursue a career in neuroscience!
prerequisites: Successful completion of 9th grade science and Intro to Neuroscience (or permission of instructor).

description: In this introductory course, students will begin to express themselves in French in practical real-life situations, as outlined by the ACTFL Standards for Foreign Language Learning (Communication, Cultures, Connections, Comparisons and Communities). Students will develop their listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills through functional and proficiency-based activities. Students will learn to understand and manipulate the structures of the language necessary for basic communication. They will become familiar with francophone cultures around the world. Students should obtain the level of Novice Low (ACTFL) or A1.2 (CEFR) in French by the end of this course.

Students will continue to build on the foundation that they have established previously. They will further develop their language skills, refining their ability to communicate in French in a variety of practical situations. This course focuses on expanding vocabulary, improving conversational fluency, and deepening the understanding of more complex grammar structures. In addition, students will continue to explore francophone cultures utilizing their growing language skills. Students should obtain the level of Novice Mid-High (ACTFL) or A1.3 (CEFR) in French by the end of this course.

Students will continue language study in the five areas as outlined in the ACTFL Standards for Foreign Language Learning (Communication, Cultures, Connections, Comparisons and Communities). They will continue to develop their listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills begun in French I. They will become more proficient in spontaneous use of the language and will continue to make real-life and functional applications. Students will also develop the functional skills necessary to use the language for work, travel, academic, and personal goals. Students will engage in a more in-depth study of francophone cultures around the world. Students should obtain the level of Novice High (ACTFL) or A1.4 (CEFR) in French by the end of this course.
prerequisites: Recommended grade of C+ or higher in French I Part 2

description: The focus of this class is on oral comprehension and speaking fluency in French. Students will communicate at a more advanced level as they expand their vocabulary and become proficient with more complex grammatical structures. French III uses a thematic approach to present vocabulary and grammar in context. In addition, students will research relevant cultural and social topics in the francophone world. Students are expected to communicate in French during class. Students should obtain the level of Novice High to Intermediate Low (ACTFL) or A2.2(CEFR) in French by the end of this course.

Activities focus on the five areas outlined in the ACTFL Standards for Foreign Language Learning (Communication, Cultures, Connections, Comparisons and Communities). Connections with the greater community are highlighted. Students should obtain the level of Intermediate Mid (ACTFL) or B1.1 (CEFR) in French by the end of this course.
prerequisites: Grade of B or higher in French III and a commitment to speaking French is essential.

description: This course will have an emphasis on literature from the French- speaking world, composition, and speaking. The curriculum will continue to support the five areas as outlined by the ACTFL Standards for Foreign Language Learning (Communication, Cultures, Connections, Comparisons and Communities). We will continue to develop and hone the students’ breadth of language structures in French and will build upon their prior language skills through authentic texts and speech. description: This course is intended for students who want to gain confidence and improve their fundamental computing skills. We will discuss the history of computers and different computing devices that are commonly used today. Students will work with the most frequently used software tools (email, documents, slideshows, spreadsheets) and learn advanced features that are useful to workflow and productivity. The course will end with a personalized investigation of a professional computer application that connects to our other electives.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

description: This course is intended for college-bound juniors and seniors who are considering a career in computers, math, science and/or engineering. This course will cover the foundations of programming in Java and build into topics such as designing solutions, object-oriented programming, debugging, data structures and abstractions. This is a challenging course that will require you to re-evaluate how you approach and solve problems, but the skills that you gain in computational thinking can be applied to all content areas.
prerequisites: Completion of Algebra II. The motivated student does not need prior programming experience.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art
notes: The AP course and AP Exam must be completed in its entirety for AP credit to appear on your transcript. Early withdrawal will result in no AP credit on the Transcript.

description: This course will cover the basics of creating 2D and 3D digital art and how to develop animations using both styles. This is a project-based course where we will learn by doing. Throughout the course students will develop a portfolio of work that can be easily transferred or shared. No artistic talent is needed to succeed in this course, and we will work to improve your skills at any level.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

description: In this hands-on course we will examine the application of computer-controlled physical systems. We will start with a look at binary counting and its link to electronic systems before diving into basic electrical components. The bulk of this course will focus on using these components as building blocks to mimic simple systems (ex. Automatic door, remote control), and will wrap up with students constructing a complex system of their choice.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

description: Enjoy playing video games, board games or card games? Have you ever wanted to create your own? In this course we will look at the way digital games are created. Students will learn to use Unity, a popular free game engine, to make simple games and the course will finish with students applying their skills to construct a personalized game.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

description: Interested in computer programming but don’t know where to start? This course serves as an introduction to writing code to perform a variety of computer functions. We will cover the foundations of programming including variables, conditional statements, loops, and functions. This course is designed for beginners and will be taught using the Python programming language.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

description: This is the course for students who have completed Computer Literacy and want to gain real-world work experience. This could include assisting with a computer literacy course or working with the school IT department. The students benefit by examining the use of technology from both an educational perspective and a business perspective. Students will be able to gain experience that expands existing skills and may lead to a reference for future work. Independent projects with detailed documentation are also considered. This work will help you stand out from the crowd on your college applications.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

description: Discover the artistic and technical aspects of web design. This course will primarily focus on front-end development using the Big 3 (HTML, CSS and Javascript) to create and style personal websites. We will learn how to write websites from scratch and look at modern tools that can assist the process. By the end of the course students will have developed and launched a webpage.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

description: This course will focus on the art and impact of documentary filmmaking. Students will learn from some of the great documentary filmmakers around the world, covering issues that matter most. The course will balance screening particular powerful documentaries, with learning how to make short documentary films of their own. Students will work collaboratively to seek out local stories, develop story concepts, capture interviews, balance archival footage with new footage, and edit it all together into a powerful piece of new media. This class will culminate with a film festival, and individual DVDs of student projects for college applications. This class is brought to you by the Milton Creative Media Lab.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

description: This is an introductory course to digital filmmaking and is a prerequisite to Filmmaking II as well as a foundation course for those interested in being involved in YJTV. Students will learn the language and skills to create their own short films in this 9-week course using digital HD cameras, gimbals and drones as well as Apple’s Final Cut Pro and Adobe Premier. Students will work individually and in groups to write, direct, light, and edit their own original productions. We will analyze scenes from groundbreaking films, understand the technology of filmmaking today, and work together to entertain and enlighten the world. This class will culminate in a film festival, and individual DVDs of student projects to use in college applications. This class is brought to you by the Milton Creative Media Lab.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

description: This is an advanced course in filmmaking and requires that participants successfully complete Filmmaking I. Students will work in crews to write screenplays, direct, and edit short films using digital HD cameras gimbals and drones, as well as Apples’ Final Cut Pro and Adobe Premiere. The concept of this course is to use this time to create films that we can submit into local and national student film festivals. This class will culminate in a film festival, and individual DVDs of student projects will be provided to use in college applications. This course is brought to you by the Milton Creative Media Lab.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

course_name: Gold Records and Glory: Audio Engineering Technique
description: This is a multi-level audio engineering course designed to teach students how to use digital audio recording technology to make music. Whether you are a trained musician or someone who just loves music, but does not play an instrument, this course is designed for everyone. Students will be introduced to recording technique and theory and work to complete a variety of individual and group projects using Apple’s Garageband, Logic Pro, and the Protools Recording Suite. We will culminate in a listening party and CDs will be made available for participants. This course is brought to you by the Milton Creative Media Lab.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

description: YJTV is an opportunity for students to create a monthly news and variety show to be screened for the entire student body, as well as made available online. This class is for any student interested in camera operation, sound mixing, content editing, or on-air talent such as anchorpersons, weather experts, and sports commentators. This is a unique opportunity for dedicated students to produce a valuable resource to the school and broader community, and to become a star both in front of, and behind the camera. No prior broadcasting experience necessary, however completion of Filmmaking I is a plus. This class is brought to you by the Milton Creative Media Lab.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED: .5 Credit in Computer Science Electives, Creative Media Electives or Digital Art

description: In this quarter foundational course, students will explore several different artistic media and techniques. The elements and principles of design are studied through drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture, and other media. Projects will incorporate the study of historical and contemporary artists while allowing students freedom to explore their creativity. This course is required for those students desiring to pursue any of the advanced courses offered in the fine arts.
fulfills_text: REQUIRED

description: This quarter course is designed to further the exploration of various media while learning advanced techniques. We will explore drawing, painting, printmaking, and sculpture. The course will focus on developing observational skills while fostering creative imagination. Students will examine the styles of both historical and contemporary American Artists while developing their own personal style of expression.

AP Art is intended for highly motivated students who wish to pursue art in college. Observational drawing will be stressed as students continue to develop personal visual imagery through intensive work in drawing, painting, mixed media, printmaking, and sculpture. As with other art courses, the projects will be based on artists from contemporary and historical times as a springboard for creativity.
notes: The AP course must be completed in its entirety for AP credit. Early withdrawal will result in no AP credit on the Transcript.

description: In this class you will learn about art and artists from the 1400’s to the present. We will discuss these famous works of art and artists in depth, learning about why they made specific works of art and who they were as people. We will also use the techniques these artists used to make art, through our own projects. This class is both a lecture and a hands-on art making experience.

In this quarter course, the student will express him/herself in clay to make functional pottery. Students will explore line, shape, form, color, texture, and pattern as tools of expression and use basic building techniques including pinch, coil, slab, sculpting and wheel.

Clay and Pottery II is an extension of Clay and Pottery I with an emphasis placed on creativity and individual interests. Projects, which may be thrown on the potter's wheel or hand constructed, will include sculptural and functional forms traditional to clay. Experimentation with techniques will be encouraged, as will works of depth and complexity.
prerequisites: Completion of Clay and Pottery I
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

description: Drawing is highly recommended as a foundation for every type of art. Students will learn about the fundamental skills of drawing. This class will focus on drawing from images, realistic shading, shadow, perspective, etc. We will use different drawing mediums such as pencil, charcoal, ink, as well as digital Procreate.

In this class, we’ll explore the foundations of jewelry making and metalworking. You’ll learn essential techniques like cutting and filing metal, soldering, stone setting, creating linkages, and crafting glass pendants. Along with hands-on projects, you’ll discover the history of jewelry design, and each student will research and present on an influential jewelry designer to share with the class.
prerequisites: One art class or permission of instructor.
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

description: In this class, we’ll dive into the fundamentals of 3D sculpture using materials like wood, metal, glass, paper, and wire. You’ll explore various techniques, from carving and building forms to fusing glass, bringing your creations to life in three dimensions. Alongside hands-on projects, you’ll also learn about the history of sculpture, and each student will research and present on a notable artist to share insights with the class.
prerequisites: One art class or permission of instructor.
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

description: In this class, students will develop their painting skills and techniques using watercolor and acrylic paint. Students will explore the style of many artists throughout history, while developing their own paintings. The subjects considered and studied will include landscapes, still-life, the figure, and abstraction.
prerequisites: Art 1
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

description: Art Studio is an opportunity for students who have taken at least two classes of art to pursue independent work with the support of an Art teacher. Credit will be based on portfolio review.

description: This course is designed to appeal to students coming from various musical backgrounds and is a springboard to greater understanding of music. This course explores parts of the guitar, riffs and melodies, open chords, and scale patterns. Students will learn songs that are related to their specific music interests as well as explore basic elements of songwriting with the guitar. This course concentrates on acoustic guitar. Note: Students may bring their own acoustic guitar.

This course focuses on intermediate guitar techniques that include barre chords, fingerstyle, picking, and playing across the fretboards. This course focuses on both acoustic and electric guitar styles. Students will learn chords and melodies in a variety of styles as well as styles that are related to their music interests. Note: Students may bring their own acoustic guitar.
prerequisites: Permission of instructor, completion of Guitar 1 or equivalent mastery of the guitar.
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

description: Music Theory and Composition is a course designed for motivated students interested in learning about music language: scales, keys, chord structure and harmony. Students will study and analyze musical elements and be given opportunities to compose and arrange their own music.

course_name: Modern Band: Piano, Guitar, Bass, Drums and Vocals
description: Modern Band is a course designed to get students, regardless of experience, involved in music. Throughout this course, students will learn many aspects of music, including how to play multiple musical instruments (guitar, bass, drum set, piano, etc.). Students will be given the opportunity to collaborate musically with one another and perform for others. By the end of this course students will be able to play songs in a rock band style.

This course is designed for students from a variety of musical backgrounds and serves as a foundation for understanding and performing music through the piano. Students will explore essential piano techniques, note reading, rhythm, scales, and chord progressions. The course emphasizes performance, creativity, and personal connection to music. Students will perform individual and ensemble pieces, learn songs relevant to their musical interests, and engage in basic songwriting and composition. Instruction will primarily utilize electric keyboards. This is a beginner level course and no experience is necessary.

This course is an advanced co-curricular offering of the music department. Advanced vocal music will be emphasized. Students will perform at least 4 times per year in a variety of settings. Rehearsals are held outside of school time at least 1 time per week.
prerequisites: Successful vocal audition including sight reading, commitment to weekly rehearsals, and prior Middle School or High School vocal experience.
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

description: This course is designed to give the student an opportunity to study and perform advanced band literature of various styles. The student will learn to appreciate, to understand, to perform, and to criticize with discrimination within the area of instrumental music. Members from this group may audition for the District, All-State, and New England Music Festivals. The Music Department acknowledges the importance of these music festivals and views them as a reward for excellence and a means to obtain excellence in musicianship. STUDENTS WILL PERFORM AT LEAST THREE TIMES A YEAR. ATTENDANCE AT PERFORMANCES IS MANDATORY.

The Milton High School Chorus is for all students who like or would like to sing. The course is designed for students who wish to extend their knowledge of music through performance of vocal music. Music selections will include a variety of styles stressing regular choral repertoire including classical, spirituals, sacred, madrigals, and pop music. There will also be opportunities for students to do solo and small group work, as well as to audition for and participate in a variety of music festivals. The goals for students who are members of the chorus experience are to learn to sing as a group in multi-part harmony, to develop the ability to read music, to gain an understanding for basic music theory, to gain the knowledge of various styles of music, to perform as often as possible, to contribute to the musical life of the school and community, and to participate in special events and festivals. Homework: Extensive rehearsal and practice - occasional written work. Method of Evaluation: Teacher observation, participation in class and lessons, aural exams, quizzes, and occasional tests.

This course is a performance organization, which explores jazz, pop, and rock music in a small instrumental group. This is a half-credit course, which meets once per week after school. Students must audition to participate.

Students will use a skills based approach to investigate healthy behaviors and environments that impact them, their family, peers, community members, fellow citizens, global citizens and the earth. Using the social-ecological model as a framework, students will identify the multiple levels that influence health behaviors while investigating and analyzing the Youth Risk Behavior data from the MTSD district, the State of Vermont and other reliable sources to determine areas of strength or improvement. Students will also identify reliable sources of information and evidence-based resources that can contribute to decision-making around personal and community health. Students will be able to practice behavioral modification strategies for themselves based on personal reflections and in depth analysis of health factors beyond individual control. As a summative assessment, the students will be afforded the opportunity to interpret data, and advocate for personal, community or political change on a topic of their choosing.
prerequisites: Grade 10
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION

description: The Driver Education course is designed to develop the student driver and teach traffic safety, to assist drivers in the study of traffic crash prevention, and to acquire knowledge and skills leading to the safe operation of motor vehicles. The class consists of classroom instruction and behind-the-wheel driving/observing. Students are required to drive outside of class for at least 20 hours during the course to obtain a “yellow card”. Students should expect to spend about 1 hour outside of class (each week) on reading and various worksheets to enhance their learning. There is a mandatory parent/student meeting near the beginning of the class to help aide parents/students about their roles in this process. Students must have a learner’s permit before the course begins and ideally have 10 hours of driving practice. This is NOT OPEN TO FRESHMEN without the permission of the school counselor. Students can miss a maximum of 8 classes and still meet the attendance requirement; more than 8 classes missed, and students are removed from the class and need to skip a semester before taking the class again.
This course is designed to provide support to students in completing the homework portion of the class and may need extra time to practice skills.
prerequisites: Permission of Driver’s Ed Instructor
notes: Catalog labels this a RECOMMENDATION; (Students enrolled in Driver Education)

description: This course promotes lifelong fitness, teamwork, and personal well-being. Students will explore fitness concepts, build collaboration skills through team and cooperative games, and develop self-awareness with social-emotional learning (SEL) and mindfulness activities. Non-traditional, low-organization games encourage creativity, inclusion, and fun while enhancing movement skills. By the end of the course, students will understand the value of staying active, building trust and cooperation with others and maintaining a balanced, healthy lifestyle. This class meets everyday for one quarter.
fulfills_text: Required for Grade 9

description: The purpose of this class is to expose students to activities that can lead them toward healthy active lifestyles after high school. Some of the activities may include Archery, Badminton, Basketball, Circuit Training, Cross Country Skiing, Dance, Lawn Games, New Games/Name Games/Trust Activities, Pickleball, Racquetball, Snowshoeing,Tennis, Ultimate Frisbee, Volleyball, Walk/Jog/Run, etc. This class meets every day for one quarter.

The purpose of this class is to offer students opportunities to develop new skills through participation in activities and games. It is our goal to expose students to activities that can lead them toward healthy active lifestyles after high school. Some of the activities that may be used as a vehicle towards fitness and wellness are Archery, Badminton, Basketball, Circuit Training, Cross Country Skiing, Dance, Field Hockey, Flag Football, Floor Hockey, Lacrosse, New Games/Name Games/Trust Activities, Pickleball, Racquetball, Snowshoeing, Soccer, Team Handball, Tennis, Ultimate Frisbee, Volleyball, Walk/Jog/Run, etc. This class is suitable for those with a competitive spirit.

This class is designed for 11th and 12th grade students to dive deeply into the components of fitness and involves academic and hands-on ways to achieve personal fitness. The students will be assessing, refining, and maintaining a comprehensive personal fitness plan based on personal performance on a nationally recognized fitness assessment. They will show knowledge of physiological effects and adjust their physical activity to achieve the physiological response. Through class discussions, readings, hands on experience and reflections the students will learn how to implement the four components of fitness into their lives.
notes: Prose says designed for 11th and 12th grade students; offerings list shows 10-12

description: The objective of this course is to prepare students to be coaches. Each Student will have the opportunity to engage in hypothetical and real situations that arise when coaching sports and activities. Students will have the chance to analyze and discuss topics involved in coaching that include coaching certifications, gender, culture, sportsmanship, ethics, officiating/refereeing, careers in sports, and building and implementing practice plans. Students will gain knowledge from experienced coaches through guest speakers, interviews, and/or mentoring. Students may also have the opportunity to coach a youth sport during the class, and work toward collecting community service hours. This class will have some in-class lessons, as well as lessons in the gymnasium and on the fields. The goal of this class is for each student to leave with one or more coaching certifications, a coaching resume, and hands-on experience.

Students will enjoy a very welcoming and non-competitive atmosphere during this experience. The class will focus on health, fitness, and wellness implementation to create a symbiotic and harmonious relationship with the mind, body, and soul. Students will have the opportunity to take part in breathing exercises, mindfulness, meditation, mobility, moving meditation, Pilates, low aerobic intensity, and impact exercises, embracing nature, wellness goals and plans, some non-competitive fun activities, and nutrition information. The overall goal of this course is to create an alternative to traditional PE class and allow students to embark on a personal journey toward holistic health and well-being. This class will focus on the dimensions of wellness that include, but are not limited to, physical, social, emotional, spiritual, intellectual, environmental, and occupational wellness.

This physical education program integrates students of all abilities into the gym for sports, fitness, and other physical activities. The goal is to foster inclusion, build friendships, develop athletic skills, and promote a school-wide culture of understanding and acceptance by providing a shared, positive experience. The model focuses on teamwork and meaningful participation for all students, using rule modifications and higher-ability partners as mentors to ensure success. Examples of activities include basketball, lawn sports, bowling, bocce, dance, general fitness concepts, riding a bike, and other activities that enhance abilities for life now and in the future.

description: Students who participate in two years of any varsity sport may seek a waiver, which grants them .5 credits for their athletic experience. The waiver request form is available from the guidance office and must be signed by members of the school and athletic administration. Students will be asked to reflect upon their athletic experience through the lenses of both current PE standards and PBGRs to secure the waiver and the associated credit.

Step into the world of 3D design! In this hands-on course, you’ll learn how to bring your ideas to life using modern CAD software, 3D printers, and laser cutters. You’ll design and model your own creations — from custom games to detailed prototypes — while exploring how art, engineering, and technology connect. No experience needed — just your creativity and curiosity. By the end, you’ll have real 3D projects you can hold, share, and be proud of

Ready to take your creativity to the next level? In this class, you’ll dive into vector graphics and wearable design — making your own custom apparel, stickers, signs, and patches! Learn how to use professional design software to create bold, original graphics and then turn them into real products using vinyl cutters, embroidery, and direct-to-film printing. It’s your chance to design and wear your own ideas — or even start a brand!
notes: Previously known as Design Studio II

course_name: Intro to Wood and Metal Fabrication
description: If you love to design, build, and make things that last, this is the class for you! In this hands-on course, you’ll explore how to design and create custom projects using wood, metal, and mixed materials. You’ll learn the basics of woodworking, welding, CNC routing, and CNC milling — and discover how digital design tools connect with real-world fabrication. From furniture to small product design, you’ll develop craftsmanship, creativity, and problem-solving skills while bringing your ideas to life in the shop.

Turn your ideas into reality — and maybe even a business! In this course, you’ll explore what it takes to launch a product, service, or brand. You’ll learn how to build a business plan, develop your brand identity, and use real design tools to prototype your ideas. Work in teams to pitch your project to local professionals and community partners, gain feedback, and connect your creativity to real-world opportunities. Whether you want to start a business, enter a pitch competition, or just learn how innovation works in the real world, this class gives you the skills and confidence to make it happen.

description: Photography & Visual Storytelling at the Milton Innovation Center empowers students to explore the art and science of photography while developing technical skills and creative expression. With access to professional-grade equipment and editing software, students will create high-quality work for digital and print platforms and build a personal portfolio through hands-on projects and critiques. Guest speakers and workshops with professional photographers will offer real-world insights and career exploration opportunities. This course fosters artistic confidence and technical expertise, equipping students to communicate compelling visual stories in an increasingly image-driven world.

description: Internship/Service Learning provides each Milton High School student the opportunity to design and carry out a personally meaningful educational experience. This experience includes making connections with the community beyond school. Volunteering can help students gain confidence by giving them a chance to try something new and build a real sense of achievement. Volunteering can have a real and valuable positive effect on people, communities, and society in general and allow students the opportunity to learn new skills, gain experience and possible qualifications. Through volunteering students can challenge themselves to try something different, achieve personal goals, practice using their skills and discover hidden talents. This graduation requirement's guiding principle is that all students must demonstrate the ability to research a subject of their own choosing, take part in a meaningful internship or service project directly related to that subject, and demonstrate learning through keeping a record of learning and the creation of a final presentation. Exploration of a student’s internship/service learning may begin in the first year of advisory. Students will map out interests and begin exploring opportunities for completion of the project. Requirements include: 1. Meeting with the Service-Learning coordinator to discuss possibilities for the internship/service experience and to finalize logistics and details. Presentation of the project to their Teacher Advisory group and the Service-Learning Coordinator along with a written reflection of the experience. Students may earn elective credit by assisting teachers with classroom responsibilities, course preparation activities and/or tutoring fellow students. course_name: ENGLISH 9: INTRODUCTION TO LITERATURE AND WRITING
description: This course prepares students for success in high school level reading, writing, speaking, listening, and work habits. The course's essential question is “Who am I?”; students will explore who they are and who they want to become. The following skills are the prioritized learning for 9th grade students: citing textual evidence to support an analysis of a text, integrating useful evidence from credible sources, engaging thoughtfully in conversation about diverse topics and perspectives, and producing clear writing appropriate to task, purpose and audience. Instruction is differentiated by student learning style and ability, as well as student interest.

Students develop and refine the skills necessary for expository and argumentative writing for real-world audiences. Research methods and independent reading are integrated into the course.

description: In this semester-long course, students will examine different monsters across various texts (literature, graphic novels, film, art) in order to answer the question, “How do monsters reflect the fears of a society?” Students will explore who and what a society determines to be a monster and, in turn, what this says about the culture that created it. Students will close-read written and visual texts to discover who or what the monster is and evaluate why it exists. Students will write a variety of creative and essay assignments to deepen their understanding of genre, specific readings, and common themes found in literature with monstrous characters.

description: This course is designed to help students develop an appreciation and understanding of cultures, religions, people, and events through history and make connections to their present day lives. The first half of the year is focused on developing an understanding of cultures from around the world, while learning how to construct an argument using claim, evidence and reasoning. In the second half of the year students are developing inquiry projects and forming solutions to global problems. Students will have an opportunity throughout the year to make choices about how they show their understanding of the key skills while at the same time focusing on issues and topics of interest.

description: This standards-based college preparatory course will provide students with an understanding of the important trends in the history of our nation and state. Focus is on citizens’ rights, change over time, inquiry, and key events such as the Civil War, Westward Expansion, Industrialization, the Great Depression, and the World Wars. Emphasis is on the skills of writing, discussion, and making connections over history.
fulfills_text: Required Courses (Social Studies)

description: This course is a capstone to a student's social studies experience at MVU, designed to bring together the previous five years of learning to ensure they are prepared for adult life. Students must demonstrate their ability to be an informed and engaged citizen, to manage a budget and navigate a ballot, and to be part of a successful family, town, state, and nation. Field Trips, discussions, class simulations and games, independent research, and community projects will help students gain the knowledge and understanding needed. Class materials will include Town Reports, federal budgets, Town Meeting ballots, zoning by-laws, Vermont Bar Association's Your Legal Rights @ Eighteen, and various other government and legal documents. 10 hours of community service will be completed during the course within class-designed projects and field trips. Since much of the course requirements are in-person and hands-on, timeliness, attendance and participation are essential to receiving credit. *This course is required for graduation.
fulfills_text: This course is required for graduation.

description: The Green Mountain State has a unique and storied history. In this class students will learn about Vermont's links to events that are covered in Social Studies classes all over the country. The Revolutionary War? It happened here. The Civil War? Vermonters were key combatants in that conflict. The Prohibition Era? It unfolded right here in Vermont. Rail History? There were railroads in Vermont before they were out west! In this course, students will learn about Vermonters who changed the course of history.

This course is designed to expose students to the enormous amount of local history that exists in Franklin County and Vermont. Students will learn how large national events unfolded here at home, and conduct group and individual inquiry projects using local resources such as historical societies, archeological digs, and historians or experts. Students will be expected to participate in numerous class discussions and hands-on learning opportunities. Some work will also be done using Ancestry.com and online sources to trace local family lines. The class will also explore the Abenaki/NativAmerican history of the region.

This course is an exploration of the role of war throughout history. Students will research topics of personal interest related to war, and discuss current conflicts in the world. Students will complete small scale inquiries, as well as an in-depth historian project. Movies, music and other media will be used to show the impacts of war on soldiers, veterans and their families, civilians, leaders, and the environment.

This course is designed to examine historical and contemporary subjects through modern film, music, and art. The media will investigate how society changes or informs our perceptions of ourselves and our society. This is a discussion-based class with the opportunity to learn how to develop, articulate, and argue opinions and positions. Students will examine politics, climate, urban development, food, war, government, art, animal rights, and contemporary issues related to high school students and their interests.

This course is designed for those who are interested in college level work, but need more support in time management, organization, test and note taking skills. The first semester will focus on those college skills and will gradually build in the content of U.S. government and politics. The second semester will focus on both the study of general concepts of U.S. government and politics, and the analysis of specific examples of current events, policy, media, and court cases, including those from local and Vermont government.Topics covered will be: The Constitution, Political Beliefs and Behaviors, Political Parties, Interest Groups, Mass Media, Institutions of National Government, Public Policy, and Civil Rights and Liberties. *Dual enrollment option for 3 college credits with CCV.

description: Advanced Placement courses are overseen by the College Board and are designed to be rigorous, college like experiences. AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines. Advanced Placement Psychology focuses on the evolution of modern psychology, different approaches to psychology, and advanced topics like abnormal psychology. The course follows the rigorous AP curriculum established by the College Board, including in-depth study of a variety of concepts, issues, and theories in the field of Psychology. Students will use a scientific approach to investigate human behavior and mental processes. Specific topics of study include memory, sensation and perception, personality, psychological disorders and treatments, and social psychology. The culminating activity of the course will be the AP examination by which students may earn college credit for their work. Students who are considering careers in social services or in psychology are encouraged to take this class. *Dual enrollment option for 3 college credits with CCV.
notes: Dual enrollment option for 3 college credits with CCV

AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines. AP United States Government and Politics is a year-long course that will give students an analytical perspective on government and politics in the United States. This course includes both the study of general concepts of U.S. government and politics, and the analysis of specific examples of current events, policy, media, and court cases, including those from local and Vermont governments. In the preparation of the AP exam, topics covered will be: Constitutional Underpinnings of United States Government, Political Beliefs and Behaviors, Political Parties, Interest Groups, and Mass Media, Institutions of National Government, Public Policy, and Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, Community Service is a requirement for this class as well.
offering_note: This course is only offered every other year, running in 2026-27

description: This course is only offered every other year, running in 2027-2028 Advanced Placement courses are overseen by the College Board and are designed to be rigorous, college like experiences. AP students will be expected to complete assignments outside of scheduled class time, attend additional study sessions, complete long term projects, take exams, and meet firm deadlines. AP U.S. History is designed to be the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university U.S. history course. In AP U.S. History students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods from approximately 1491 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical comparisons, and utilizing reasoning about contextualization, causation, and continuity and change over time. The course also provides seven themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: American and national identity; migration and settlement; politics and power; work, exchange, and technology; America in the world; geography and the environment; and culture and society. The course follows the rigorous AP curriculum established by the College Board. The culminating activity of the course will be the AP examination by which students may earn college credit for their work. Sophomores must get a teacher's recommendation.
offering_note: This course is only offered every other year, running in 2027-2028 (not offered 2026-27)

description: This course addresses fundamental math concepts in the areas of algebra and functions, statistics and probability, geometry, and discrete mathematics. These strands are unified by common themes and students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum.

Geometry topics include constructions, circle properties, similarity, algebraic reasoning, trigonometric ratios, properties of quadrilaterals and triangles, proofs of theorems, transformations. Course instruction includes investigations that are designed to help students apply geometry concepts as they explore problems and make connections with other areas of mathematics.

Algebra II is a continuation of Algebra I. Advanced Algebraic reasoning is emphasized in this course. Topics include solving equations and inequalities, solving polynomial and rational functions, as well as a catalog of elementary functions including but not limited to linear functions, absolute value functions, piecewise functions and square root functions.

This course is designed for students who wish to take AP Calculus or AP Statistics by their senior year. Algebra II will be held daily for Semester 1 and Pre-Calculus will be held daily for Semester 2. Algebra II requirements must be met by the end of semester one in order to continue to Pre-calculus semester 2. Upon completion of Pre-Calculus you will receive 2 credits. A math teacher must recommend a student.
prerequisites: Teacher recommendation
notes: Scheduled as 2 periods

description: This course is designed for those students who are planning to take calculus or other advanced math courses. Topics covered include linear and nonlinear functions, analytic geometry, trigonometry, logarithms, complex numbers, and sequences and series. * Dual enrollment option for 3 college credits with CCV.
prerequisites: Passing completion of Algebra II or Math in Action Recommendation
notes: Dual enrollment option for 3 college credits with CCV

description: This course builds on the foundations of Algebra 1 and Geometry through a project-based approach that emphasizes real-world applications, collaboration, and problem-solving. Students will explore key practical math concepts—including geometric construction, scale drawings, systems of inequalities, and exponential growth—by engaging in hands-on projects that connect mathematics to authentic contexts.
prerequisites: Passing Completion of Algebra and Geometry

description: This course covers the basics of statistics and data analysis. Students will learn how to collect, organize, and interpret data using graphs, charts, averages, and simple probability. Emphasis is placed on real-world examples and developing a practical understanding of how data is used in everyday life. No advanced math skills are required beyond basic algebra.

Explore how trigonometry is used in the real world to solve practical problems in science, engineering, architecture, navigation, and design. Focusing on topics that show up in various careers, such as Construction, Electrical work, Architecture, Surveying, Engineering, and more. Learn about angles, right triangles, Laws of Sines and Cosines, and trigonometric functions through real-life applications like measuring distances, modeling waves, and interpreting data. This course emphasizes problem-solving, critical thinking, and the use of technology to connect math to everyday life.
prerequisites: Passing Completion of Algebra and Geometry

A student in this class must be prepared to spend 1 ½ to 2 hours of study time for each hour of class time. This course requires the use of the TI-84 plus graphing calculator for technology support.
prerequisites: Passing completion of Pre-Calculus
