Students will write and illustrate their own fictional and informative picture books that they can share with the elementary schools in our district. The class is designed for students who are interested in Early Childhood Education, nostalgic for the days they spent reading picture books, or considering a career in writing, as well as those who would benefit from writing intervention services.
notes: English Intervention, Elective 8-10

description: In this class, students will develop their reading, writing, speaking and listening skills by exploring short stories, novels, nonfiction, and poetry. They will investigate how social issues like oppression and poverty affect individuals and communities, and how people come together to find joy and hope despite these challenges. Students will write analytical and persuasive essays as well as creative and personal narratives; discuss. Skills building will focus on active reading strategies and productive writing processes. A range of texts will be used, including short stories, poetry, fiction and nonfiction.

In this class, students will develop their reading, writing, speaking and listening skills by exploring short stories, novels, nonfiction, and poetry. They will investigate how social issues like oppression, poverty, and hierarchies affect individuals and communities, and how people come together to find joy and hope despite these challenges. Students will write analytical and persuasive essays as well as creative and personal narratives; discuss. Skills building will focus on active reading strategies and productive writing processes. A range of texts will be used, including short stories, poetry, fiction and nonfiction.

Advanced Placement Language and Composition is a year-long, college-level English Language Arts course designed to prepare highly motivated students for success on the AP Language exam. It is intended to teach students how to read, analyze, and write about the rhetorical strategies embedded within a broad and challenging range of non-fiction texts. Through frequent informal and formal performance tasks, students will develop the skills necessary to intelligently synthesize arguments from multiple texts into persuasive essays in which they establish strong claims, support them with convincing evidence, thoughtfully explain how their evidence supports their claims, and acknowledge and respond to the most compelling arguments refuting their logic and reasoning. To give shape to the course’s content, readings are organized around themes addressing key cultural, social, and political issues that shape and define our culture today. This class will prepare students for the demanding reading and writing they will encounter in college. Most importantly, though, students will engage in deep critical inquiries into aspects of our world that will help them realize their full potential as active participants in our democratic society. Upon successful performance on the Advanced Placement exam, students may earn up to three college credits and advanced placement in college English. A summer reading and writing assignment is required for enrollment in this course.
notes: Junior/Senior English Courses; Full Year Course (with summer work); summer reading and writing assignment required for enrollment

description: Advanced Placement Literature and Composition is a year-long, college-level English Language Arts course designed to prepare highly motivated students for success on the AP Literature exam. Students will read, analyze, talk, and write about imaginative literature from the Greek and Roman classics to the present to deepen their understanding of how writers use language to cultivate meaning and explore the human condition in their art. They will read texts as authorial constructions—intentional acts of other humans trying to communicate something important to them. Students will understand how crucial it is to respect writers by reading their texts as they expect them to before deciding to what extent they want to embrace, adapt, or resist the writer’s visions. To that end, the key question students will ask throughout the year is: How do writers reveal their thoughts, beliefs, and feelings through their writing? In other words, how do they use writing conventions and literary elements and devices to communicate their ideas? What kinds of changes are writers working to produce in their readers and the world—and why? What points of view or perspectives are writers representing—and why? What are writers encouraging readers to know, believe, or do after reading their texts—and why? This is an engaging and rigorous reading, writing, and discussion-based course of study that requires on-time completion of all formative and summative assessments. Upon successful performance on the Advanced Placement exam, students may earn up to three college credits and advanced placement in college English. A summer reading and writing assignment is required for enrollment in this course.
notes: Junior/Senior English Courses; Full Year Course (with summer work); summer reading and writing assignment required for enrollment

description: The American Dream is a slippery concept. Some argue that every American can experience economic prosperity, social mobility, and personal freedom and happiness if they are willing to apply themselves. Others argue that systematic barriers—such as racism, sexism, the exploitation of the lower and middle classes, and class rigidity—prevent many Americans from achieving it despite their considerable efforts. In this one-semester English Language Arts course, students will analyze the ways in which American authors have questioned their society’s most deeply rooted assumptions and values. While doing so, they will explore and develop intelligent, well-defended responses to the following questions (among others): To what degree is the American Dream real, an expression of nostalgia for a disappearing past, or an idealized narrative of the American experience as a promised land filled with limitless resources and boundless opportunities? To what degree is the American Dream (and its notion of upward mobility) available to everyone in our society or only to those from specific socio-economic backgrounds, races, and sexes, etc.? To what degree has the American Dream evolved? To what degree does American literature shape, respond to, and challenge vital social, political, and cultural conversations? To what degree does American literature compel its readers to become well-informed, active participants in our democracy? With these inquiries in mind, students will read, write, and argue through a variety of performance tasks (e.g., close-reads, class discussions, Socratic seminars, essays, and quick-writes, etc.) grounded in complex texts that may include The Great Gatsby , Of Mice and Men , Death of a Salesman , A Raisin in the Sun , or Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas . Non-fiction texts will augment the study of those mentioned above.
notes: Junior/Senior English Courses

course_name: Narrator Reliability in Literature, Media, and Film
description: In this semester-long English Language Arts course, you’ll examine narrative perspectives to better understand how they shape our notions of truth and reality. Through the lenses of literature, media, and film, you’ll explore how unreliable narrators intentionally and unintentionally manipulate content to influence their audiences’ perceptions—i.e., to persuade them to think or behave in specific ways. The essential questions that will guide instruction are: To what degree can we trust someone else’s (or our own) perception of reality, and how can we discover whether the stories we are told are true? By consistently applying these questions to course materials, you’ll develop a heightened and nuanced awareness of the power dynamics inherent in storytelling. You’ll also cultivate the critical thinking skills necessary to interrogate a variety of narrative texts for implied bias, thereby empowering you to navigate our increasingly complex world with insight and discernment.
notes: Junior/Senior English Courses

description: We’re all storytellers—even if we haven’t published our writing in a magazine or online journal. We’ve heard and told stories since we were babies and learned about life through them. Understood by the young and old, Once upon a time … and then … and then … and then …and the end are common phrases for signaling a story. Here’s a complication, though: telling a story is one thing—writing one is another. It takes a high level of awareness to understand how stories are formed and how they shape people's perceptions of the world, their sense of self, and their relationships with others.
notes: Junior/Senior English Courses

description: Dystopian fiction often imagines bleak, apocalyptic futures controlled by totalitarian regimes, subjugated by technology run amok, devastated by environmental disasters, and blighted by plague-like contagions. As depressing as these imagined worlds may seem, they do productive work. By focusing on and exaggerating contemporary social problems, dystopian literature can affect healthy cultural change. In this one-semester English Language Arts course, students will analyze the ways in which dystopian authors turn inquisitive eyes on their societies to improve them. While doing so, they will explore and develop intelligent answers to the following questions (among others): What are the defining characteristics of dystopian fiction? In other words, what themes, symbols, and images recur in the genre? How does dystopian literature respond to, challenge, and shape vital social, political, and cultural conversations? How do governing authorities use propaganda to control the masses, and what responsibility does the individual have to question them? To what degree does dystopian fiction compel readers to become well-informed and active social critics—to realize their potential to change the worlds in which they live? Students will read, write, and argue through various performance tasks requiring them to comprehend, analyze, and evaluate complex, provocative fiction and non-fiction texts that are intended to serve their intellectual, social, and emotional needs.
notes: Junior/Senior English Courses

course_name: The Hero's Journey in Literature and Film
description: The hero’s journey paradigm is a storytelling structure that, at various levels, informs much of the fiction we read and watch. In this one-semester English Language Arts course, students will apply Joseph Campbell’s version of it to a wide range of narratives. This interpretive work is designed to lead students to a deeper understanding of the texts they experience (e.g., the hero’s journey symbols and patterns often embedded in literature, film, music, television, and advertising, etc.), the world in which they live (e.g., its values and ideals), and, ultimately, themselves (e.g., their psychological and emotional struggles and transformations). More than anything, students will cultivate an appreciation for storytelling as a reflection of humankind’s innate longing to create structure, and thus meaning, out of the complex materials of human experience.
notes: Junior/Senior English Courses

description: In this class, students will explore the history of the United States from the pre-colonial era through the Civil War. Students will learn basic geographical and historical facts about our nation while also exploring broader questions of American identity and rights through a comparison of historical and contemporary events. The course will approach this content from the perspective of multiple socioeconomic classes, races, ethnicities, and genders. This class will also focus on the development of oral proficiencies through classroom discussions, as well as writing skills needed for success at higher grade levels. The course will culminate in a research project, the completion of which is required to complete the course.

Modern World History is a global history course aimed at tenth-grade students that provides a cohesive approach to learning and understanding the history of the world. In this course, students will explore the transformations that created our modern world, beginning in the long nineteenth century and ending in our present moment. This course will help students learn how to use stories about our connected human past to orient themselves to their present moment and prepare for the future. We’re going to cover a lot of ground (and almost 300 years), but this course is not a typical march-through-time history class that covers one thing after another. Rather, this course uses a set of overarching inquiry problems and narrative frames, situated at a variety of scales, to organize and facilitate teaching and learning. Along with presentation summative assessments, students will also complete three document-based writing assignments and a 3-5 page research paper.

This course explores American history from the Reconstruction period through the present day. Using case studies, role plays, seminar discussions, oral history interviews, and independent research, students will explore the events and historical forces that shaped the world we live in today, and evaluate various perspectives about the lessons we should learn from these events to help us make sense of the problems we face today. This class will focus on developing research and writing skills to prepare students for Senior Project, and on developing the knowledge and skills to be informed, engaged citizens.
notes: catalog's typical course sequence places US History II in 11th grade

description: AP U.S. History is designed to be the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university U.S. history course. In AP U.S. History, students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods from approximately 1491 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; making historical comparisons; utilizing reasoning about contextualization, causation, and continuity and change over time; and developing historical arguments. The course also provides seven themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: American and national identity; migration and settlement; politics and power; work, exchange, and technology; America in the world; geography and the environment; and culture and society.

The AP World History course focuses on developing students' understanding of world history from 1200 CE to the present. Students investigate the content of world history for significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in four historical periods, and develop and use the same thinking skills and methods employed by historians when they study the past. The course also provides five themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places encompassing the five major geographical regions of the globe: Africa, the Americas, Europe, Asia, and Oceania. Students will focus much of their energy on preparation for the National Advanced Placement Examination in May.

World Religions takes a look at various belief systems throughout human history, and focuses on five major world religions being practiced today: Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Students in this course have the opportunity to read and interpret religious texts, discover unfamiliar cultural practices, and identify the significance of religion in shaping the world in which we live. Summative assessments allow students to choose topics of interest within each major religion for deepdive research and presentation, in order to teach the rest of the class about their findings. This is a great elective for students who wish to learn more about history, the power of myth, and its ability to organize culture around the world.

This course provides an introduction to archaeological theory and methods through the study of the Ancestral Puebloan (Anasazi) peoples of the Four Corners Region. Students will explore the development of their civilization from the Archaic era up through Modern Puebloan societies, including the cliff-dwellers of the Pueblo II era. Students will think critically about pseudoarchaeology, focussing on how interpretations of the past that ignore or misrepresent scientific evidence , often promote sensationalist ideas The class will travel to the Crow Canyon Archaeological Center in Cortez, Colorado in October.

This course presents an introductory overview of the history of Western art from the Renaissance to the present. It covers works in a wide array of media, such as painting, sculpture, architecture, prints, photography, and performance. Emphasizing significant stylistic movements in Europe and the Americas, this class introduces students to visual analysis and other interpretative tools of art historical research. Students will also learn how the art pieces of a particular time and place relate to historical circumstances and values of their respective societies. The skills developed in this course provide important tools for navigating and interpreting media and visual representation in the twenty first century.

course_name: Sociology: Nature and Nurture; Rights and Wrongs
description: Once you have taken Sociology, you will never look at the world the same way again. This is because Sociology is not a body of knowledge, but a way of thinking about how human societies function. We’ll ask (and attempt to answer) questions like: “What attributes do all cultures share?” “Are we born with our morals, or do we learn them?” “What are the unwritten rules of social interaction and what happens when they are broken?” and “Under what conditions will ordinary people behave in extraordinarily evil ways?” If you take this course, expect to read, write and share your ideas in class on a regular basis; I promise it won’t be boring, but this is not an elective you can coast through. The final exam will be a research project in which you investigate a topic that interests you, collect and interpret data, and present your findings.

You may think it’s all graphs and numbers. You may think that Economics is boring. You may think that you could never understand terms like “collateralized debt obligations” or “aggregate demand” and that even if you could, it would never help you in your life. But you’d be wrong. This course is tough, but it is also practical, interesting and extremely relevant. By the end of the semester, you will be able to use economics to predict how gas and food prices might change over time, decide how best to pay for college or a car, evaluate politicians’ plans to fix the economy, invest your time and money most effectively, and decide for yourself how worried you should be about our national debt. Completing homework, studying for quizzes and actively participating are keys to success in this course.

In this course students will examine the full scope of Vermont history. We begin with the natural history of the land and the forces that shaped Vermont’s landscapes, and lead into an examination of Vermont’s indigenous populations. From there we look at the arrival of Europeans, and formation of the United States. We will explore Vermont’s role in the greater developments of the nation and the world, while discovering how our local communities reacted to those events. This course will rely heavily on primary sources, allowing students to discover the images and writings from our local history. This course will appeal to students who are interested in their local history, and will ask students to make their own discoveries and evaluations from primary sources, rather than relying on secondary sources or others’ interpretations.

This first class in our series of three courses uses a rigorous integrated problem solving approach to enhance student learning habits through investigation of related topics and skills, much like those one could find in real life. Students develop mathematical reasoning and computation skills through collaboration, critical thinking, and related skills practice. This instruction is supported through an online digital skills support program called Mathia. The content included in AGS 1 includes analysis and manipulation of functions, systems of equations and inequalities, coordinate graphing, one-variable statistics, constructions, and rigid motion congruence theorems.
prerequisites: 8th grade math, pre-algebra or equivalent

description: This second of three course series continues development of the integrated content. Students further develop mathematical reasoning and computation skills through collaboration, critical thinking, and related skills practice. The content includes algebraic analysis of geometric shapes and relationships, trigonometric relationships and applications, and probability.
prerequisites: AGS 1 or equivalent or teacher permission

description: This third of our series of integrated courses. This course includes the structure of algebraic patterns and quadratics, comparisons of polynomial equations and models, rational and irrational functions with logarithmic expressions and modeling, further applications of trigonometry, and data interpretations and arguments using these previous tools.
prerequisites: AGS 2 or equivalent or teacher permission

description: This course is offered as a prerequisite for those students interested in taking Advanced Placement Calculus and college Calculus. The course finishes the study of functions of two variables: polynomial, exponential, logarithmic, trigonometric and the conic sections. Mathematical reasoning, problem solving, understanding multiple perspectives, and use of graphing calculators will be stressed.
prerequisites: AGS 3 and AGS 2 or teacher permission

description: This elective course is equivalent to a first-semester college statistics course. Students will learn concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing and drawing conclusions from data. Students learn under four broad conceptual themes: 1) Exploring Data: Describing patterns and departures from patterns, 2) Sampling and Experimentation: Planning and conducting a study, 3) Anticipating Patterns: Exploring random phenomena using probability and simulation, and 4) Statistical Inference: Estimating population parameters and testing hypotheses. Due to the rigor of the AP curriculum, a non-AP version of statistics will be concurrently offered. Please see the instructor to determine which course placement is most appropriate for you.
prerequisites: AGS 1 or equivalent
notes: Description says the course is equivalent to a first-semester college statistics course; a non-AP version is offered concurrently with the AP curriculum (AP Statistics is listed among available AP courses)

description: This elective course is equivalent to a first-semester college calculus course. Students will engage in the following behaviors to achieve conceptual understanding: reasoning with definitions and theorems, connecting concepts and representations, implementing processes, building notational fluency, and communication of ideas. As prescribed by the College Board, students will study three main ideas: limits, derivatives, and integrals. The notion of a limit helps us understand the behavior of a graph near a point and serves as the basis for determining continuity. In a hopeful sense, limits are much less about what things are and much more about what things should be. Derivatives give us the language of covariation: describing the rate of change of one variable in terms of another variable. Applications of derivatives include, but are not limited to, slopes of tangent lines at a point, analyzing graphs, rectilinear motion, Mean Value Theorem, related rates, optimization, and growth and decay. Integrals allow students to use the language of limits to solve problems involving area, volume, rectilinear motion, and accumulation. Students will study the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus as means to translate between the languages of derivatives and integrals. Due to the rigor of the AP curriculum, a non-AP version of calculus will be concurrently offered. Please see the instructor to determine which course placement is most appropriate for you.
notes: Elective; a non-AP version of calculus is offered concurrently

description: AP Computer Science Principles is an introductory college-level computing course that introduces students to the breadth of the field of computer science. Students learn to design and evaluate solutions and to apply computer science to solve problems through the development of algorithms and programs. They incorporate abstraction into programs and use data to discover new knowledge. Students also explain how computing innovations and computing systems—including the internet—work, explore their potential impacts, and contribute to a computing culture that is collaborative and ethical. The following are the major areas of study, or big ideas, that serve as the foundation of the course, enabling students to create meaningful connections among concepts and develop deeper conceptual understanding: Creative Development: When developing computing innovations, developers can use a formal, iterative design process or a less rigid process of experimentation, and will encounter phases of investigating and reflecting, designing, prototyping, and testing Data: Data are central to computing innovations because they communicate initial conditions to programs and represent new knowledge. Algorithms and Programming: Programmers integrate algorithms and abstraction to create programs for creative purposes and to solve problems. ■ Computing Systems and Networks: Computer systems and networks are used to transfer data. Impact of Computing: Computers and computing have revolutionized our lives. To use computing safely and responsibly, we need to be aware of privacy, security, and ethical issues. During this full year course students will create many programs using JavaScript which is considered by many experts to be the among the most commonly used computer language in the world today.
notes: Description states 'full year course'

description: This course provides an introduction to robotics for students with no programming background using Vex Robotic kits. Using the CCSS math practices, students will learn to construct, control and program these robots through investigative and exploration activities. Research projects will expose the students to the engineering process.

This course will continue the development of the engineering skills necessary to advance previous robot programs and design. Students use mentoring to increase their understanding of required programs. More rigorous research projects or activities will be expected. Students may partake in the regional Vex Robotics competition.
prerequisites: the successful completion of Robotics I or equivalent experience

description: Students in this class build their numeracy skills, hone problem-solving strategies, and work with resources geared to, and differentiated for, individual needs. Common Core Math Practice Standards are reinforced throughout this course. Along with increased mathematical competency students will practice their organizational skills, note-taking strategies, personal management skills, productivity, reflection and revision. Areas of focus include financial literacy, architecture, and foundational skills.

course_name: Integrated Science I: Earth Science with Chemistry
description: This course serves as an introduction to Earth science with an emphasis on the chemistry of and human impact on the environment. We will examine surface and atmospheric processes including, but not limited to, the relationships between resource extraction, natural hazards, and climate change and human development. We will use hands-on investigations and real world examples to explore these key concepts.

course_name: Integrated Science II: Biology with Chemistry
description: This course offers an introduction to the principles of biology with emphasis on biological chemistry, ecology and homeostasis, cell structure and function, gene expression, and patterns of inheritance. We will be using hands-on labs and real-world examples to explore the key concepts in biology.
prerequisites: Integrated Science I: Earth Science with Chemistry

description: This course considers questions such as “how did the Universe begin? How do stars generate the different elements that make up our world? How did the Earth form, and how does energy from the Sun’s core arrive here?” This course provides an introduction to the principles of physics through the lens of space. We will be using hands-on investigations to analyze the phenomena of space. ( RU students at RTCC also take the semester of Integrated Science III to help ensure coverage of standards and help with their readiness for the 11th grade assessment.)
prerequisites: Integrated Science I: Earth Science with Chemistry Chemistry Full Year Course This course offers a foundation in chemical concepts and focuses on physical chemistry. Students will learn how the atom and its particles determine the nature and properties of compounds that make our world work. This course has a heavy emphasis on science skills including explanations and argumentation, developing and conducting investigations, and reading informational texts. Basic algebra skills will be employed to better understand the content; dimensional analysis is the backbone of most calculations. This course will help students who wish to take AP Physics and AP Biology. Prerequisite: Integrated Science 1 and AGS 1 or instructor approval

This course has a heavy emphasis on science skills including explanations and argumentation, developing and conducting investigations, and reading informational texts. Basic algebra skills will be employed to better understand the content; dimensional analysis is the backbone of most calculations. This course will help students who wish to take AP Physics and AP Biology.

description: This course follows the College Board Curriculum for AP Physics 1. It offers both hands-on and theoretical approaches to understanding forces, momentum and energy and applying them to everyday situations. Topics covered include kinematics, projectile motion, statics and dynamics, rotational mechanics, pressure and fluids. Algebra is used throughout this course as mathematics is the backbone of physics. Students who are interested in engineering, technical or science careers are encouraged to take this class.
prerequisites: AGS 1

description: AP Environmental Science is an interdisciplinary course that focuses on ecological processes, human impacts on the earth, and how to resolve or prevent natural and human-made environmental problems. Students who complete the course will be expected to apply scientific concepts, principles, and methodologies to real-world examples and problems.

Applied Science is a hands-on, project-based course that explores how scientific concepts are used in the real-world. Students investigate a variety of fields including health sciences, environmental science, engineering, diversified agriculture, forensic science, and skilled trades through practical applications and problem-solving experiences. Each unit is organized around a specific career pathway, allowing students to engage in authentic tasks such as designing solutions, conducting experiments, analyzing data, and using industry-relevant tools and techniques. Emphasis is placed on developing transferable skills including critical thinking, collaboration, communication, and scientific/technical literacy.

This semester-long course will introduce students to forensic science, and skills and practices used in crime scene investigation and other applied sciences. Students will learn how to investigate, and problem solve with lab activities and mock crime scenes, as well as explore the many careers paths and applications of this science.

In this semester-long course, you will learn how CORAL REEFS, SEAGRASS BEDS and MANGROVE FORESTS support specialized forms of ocean life and how they support one another as well. Also, learn how we, as humans, can contribute considerably in the preservation of marine organisms/systems that support overall EARTH-HEALTH. This course may culminate in a week-long marine biology field-trip.

This semester-long course will take you on a walk through the human body seeing human tissues magnified 400 times with HIGH-POWERED MICROSCOPES and learn how your many billions of cells work together to allow you to do all the interesting things you do. Everything from seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and the way your body parts work together to perform exercise will be explored.

The goal of this course is to help students develop a foundation in college-level biology. Students will engage as scientists in systematically investigating the world around us and building on the understanding of prior scientific work. In addition to appreciating the inherent beauty and elegance of living beings, throughout the course students will make connections between ideas in the course as well as to current societal issues. Daily use of scientific thinking will help students explore concepts in an authentic context while honing key skills. Students will be expected to take the exam in May.
prerequisites: Proficiency in science standards 1 - 3 or approval from the instructor.

description: French I is a beginning level language course designed to develop basic speaking, reading, writing and listening skills. Students will focus on building vocabulary and grammar, as well as an awareness of the history, geography, culture, and ways of life in various French-speaking countries of the world. The cultural focus of this class is meant to highlight France and their cultural heritage. Students will be able to ask simple questions, talk about themselves and their environment and will be able to grasp the meaning of simple texts, videos, and songs in French.

This course reviews and expands on the basic communicative skills taught in French I. Students will be capable of more complex conversational exchanges in the present tense. Students will progress from memorized words and phrases to “sentence-level” dialogue to “paragraph-level” conversations and will become comfortable reading and responding to longer texts in French. Students will focus on building vocabulary and grammar, as well as an awareness of the history, geography, culture, and ways of life in various French-speaking countries of the world. Students will use more complex structures to ask questions and express opinions. The course will have a cultural and linguistic focus on music and food.

Spanish I is a beginning level language course designed to develop basic speaking, reading, writing and listening skills. Students will focus on building vocabulary and grammar, as well as an awareness of the history, geography, culture, and ways of life in various Spanish-speaking countries of the world. The cultural focus of this class is meant to introduce students to the world’s many Spanish-speaking countries and their cultural heritage. Students will be able to ask simple questions, talk about themselves and their environment and will be able to grasp the meaning of simple texts, videos, and songs in Spanish.

This course reviews and expands on the basic communication skills and cultural knowledge from Spanish I. Students will be capable of more complex conversational exchanges in the present tense, and will develop their listening comprehension skills and be encouraged to increase their speaking skills. They will progress from “sentence –level” dialog to “paragraph –level” conversations and will become comfortable reading and responding to longer texts in Spanish. The course will have a cultural and linguistic focus on music and food.

Students in this course will review the grammar principles learned in Spanish I and II and consider new themes not presented there. Reading, writing and conversational skills will be sharpened as we study the history, geography and culture of several of the twenty Spanish-speaking countries in the world. Using Spanish in class is a priority at this level and students will be reading and responding to stories, films, podcasts, songs, and other authentic media from the Spanish-speaking world. Students will create dialogues, videos, and presentations in which they talk about the past, present, and future. Students will continue developing their ability to communicate in Spanish, expanding on the grammar and vocabulary from previous years through thematic cultural units that deepen their knowledge of history and culture and address current issues. In addition, students will focus on improving written communication. They will write short essays in response to cultural events and issues in the United States and Spanish-speaking countries. Readings, films, class discussion and music will facilitate their understanding of the language. The class will also incorporate group activities and accessible technology. At the end of the year students will have deepened their understanding of the language and have a broader knowledge of the cultures, art, history and literature of the Spanish-speaking world.

This class is designed to expand upon the material covered in French I and II, as well as begin to use more authentic texts and resources to expose students to a wider variety of topics beyond personal environments and relationships. Reading, writing and conversational skills will be sharpened as we study the history, geography and culture of several of the 29 French-speaking countries in the world. Using French in class is a priority at this level and students will be reading and responding to stories, films, podcasts, and authentic media from the French-speaking world. Students will create dialogues, videos, and presentations in which they talk about the past, present, and future. Through the study of authentic sources, students gain an appreciation for the breadth of cultures, beliefs and customs across the francophone world.
