description: This course explores the government and politics in China, Iran, Mexico, Nigeria, Russia, and the United Kingdom. Throughout the course, students will learn how different governments solve similar problems and will gain a clear understanding of the comparative method by analyzing data and text-based sources, making comparisons and applications, and developing evidence-based arguments.
prerequisites: Successful Completion of US History, Civics or AP US Government. Or with Teacher/Department Chair Approval.

description: AP US History will cover the content and skills required for the AP exam, which all students are required to take in May. Students will use a college-level textbook and read and write extensively. The course will refine critical thinking techniques and expose students to alternate perspectives on history through print and visual media. The class will move at a quick pace and a considerable amount of independent work will be expected of students.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Humanities History and US History, or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval.
fulfills_text: 1 History, 1 Elective

description: AP United States Government and Politics will cover content for the AP exam and introduces students to key political ideas, institutions, policies, interactions, roles, and behaviors that characterize the political culture of the United States. The course examines politically significant concepts and themes, through which students learn to apply disciplinary reasoning to assess causes and consequences of political events, and interpret data to develop evidence-based arguments.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Humanities History and US History, or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval.
fulfills_text: including embedded Civics credit

description: This survey course explores the economic, political, cultural, and social developments in world history from the rise of civilization to 1500 CE in Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Americas. The course highlights geography, cultural and political movements, and human interactions that influenced the historical evolution of various world societies and their interrelationships within a global context.
prerequisites: Acceptance to CCV as a Dual Enrollment Student. Students should show evidence of college readiness by earning 3.5 or higher in English 10, US History or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval. Note: this course has an attendance requirement.
notes: CCV concurrent/dual enrollment course

description: A survey of the basic issues, concepts, theories and methods of psychology. Students will increase their awareness of the scientific approach to understanding human behavior through a study of sensory processes, perception, emotion, motivation, intelligence, learning and personality formation.
prerequisites: Acceptance to CCV as a Dual Enrollment Student. Students should show evidence of college readiness by earning 3.5 or higher in English 10, US History or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval. Note: this course has an attendance requirement.
notes: CCV concurrent/dual enrollment course

course_name: CCV Society and Environment in History
description: An exploration of the response to environmental challenges by various societies in history and why societies fail and perish, or succeed and survive. Students will describe strategies employed by societies that survive environmental challenges and analyze the relationship and interaction between society and environment in the development of sustainable communities.
prerequisites: Acceptance to CCV as a Dual Enrollment Student. Students should show evidence of college readiness by earning 3.5 or higher in English 10, US History or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval. Note: this course has an attendance requirement.
notes: CCV concurrent/dual enrollment course

description: This course is a survey of human growth and development throughout the life cycle including physical, cognitive, linguistic, ethical, and psychosocial dimensions. Students will identify and discuss issues in human growth and development arising from differences in gender, race, and socioeconomic status.
prerequisites: Acceptance to CCV as a Dual Enrollment Student. Students should show evidence of college readiness by earning 3.5 or higher in English 10, US History or their equivalent or with teacher permission and Department Chair approval. Note: this course has an attendance requirement.
notes: CCV concurrent/dual enrollment course

description: This course will cover topics in military leadership, citizenship, interpersonal communications/relations, public speaking, written communications, and physical fitness, with emphasis in personal responsibility. Students will develop their leadership skills during class time through drill and ceremonies (D&C), and physical training (PT). Additional leadership opportunities are available outside the classroom. Students will experience a hands-on learning environment using a military model, with extensive intra-curricular service learning opportunities. Students are required to attend a weekly “formation” conducted at 0730 in the gym on the first school day each week, wearing the prescribed uniform. Additionally, students are required to participate in the Barre Veterans Day parade.
notes: JROTC

description: This course description is similar to LET1, however units are as follows: military drill, physical training, "You the people" (a citizenship-skills foundation of the American political system), creating the constitution, shaping American institutions, and practices for citizen roles in American democracy.
fulfills_text: 0.5 PE, 0.5 Elective
notes: JROTC

description: This advanced level course capitalizes on the training received in LET1 and LET2 to allow cadets to assume senior level non-commissioned officer and junior officer ranks in the cadet organization. The course reviews, reinforces and expands on each of the subject areas with emphasis on career development and the pursuit of higher education.
prerequisites: Successful completion of LET 2
notes: JROTC

description: Primary emphasis will be placed on the practical application of the cadet organization. Therefore, the LET4 year is structured to allow cadets to perform their assigned command or staff duties and act as a class instructor or assistant instructor for selected LET 1 through 3 subjects. Academic instruction for LET4 will consist of self-paced study, suggested readings, seminars, vignettes, case studies, and special assignments.
prerequisites: Earn Partial Proficiency in LET 3
fulfills_text: 0.5 Civics, 0.5 Elective
notes: JROTC

description: These advanced level courses are available to cadets having successfully completed the program and who wish to continue to develop leadership and managerial skills in the program by becoming teacher assistants in the LET 1 through 4 classes. Students are expected to perform duties as assigned to include: special projects, tutoring, classroom instruction, coaching of the various extracurricular activities, and to act as cadet mentors.
prerequisites: Permission of Instructor
fulfills_text: 0.5 Elective, 0.5 Financial Literacy
notes: JROTC

description: In this quarter-long elective course, students will be introduced to basic conversational French, focusing on the vocabulary and phrases they would most need if traveling to a French-speaking country or region. In addition, they will learn about French, African, Quebecois traditions, geography, and history. This course can be taken as a one-time exploratory elective or used as a springboard into the more formal study of the French language.

This course is for students with no exposure to French. Students are exposed to facets of language through mostly storytelling. With an online platform, students engage with the stories by using all the skills of reading, listening, speaking and writing. Interactive activities, music, videos, game play are used to reinforce the material. This is a highly social class where interpersonal exchanges and cooperative work and conversation with peers are practiced daily. Emphasis is on comprehension and application of the stories and questions in a variety of modes along with exposure to the culture of the French speaking world. Embedded Honors available.

This course is a continuation of French 1 storytelling and comprehensible input. It is designed for the student with a solid grasp of the fundamentals of French 1. Basic skills are reviewed before progressing into new material. Students learn more complicated grammatical concepts through the stories, acquire more essential vocabulary and continue to practice their reading, writing, listening, and speaking skills through interactive activities, games, projects and classwork. Emphasis is on asking and answering questions in order to create meaningful dialogue.
prerequisites: Successful completion of French I or demonstrated proficiency

description: A continuation of language acquisition, this course stresses more grammar, which is used in writing exercises and short compositions. It also focuses on acquiring language through storytelling but progressing to the past tense. New vocabulary is presented along with short stories and students use this in both oral and written expression. Speaking is emphasized at this level, with students being able to converse more spontaneously. Students make cultural connections through the online platform, stories, music, and authentic materials.
prerequisites: Successful completion of French II or demonstrated proficiency

description: Through more storytelling and comprehensible input, this is an accelerated and intensive course providing a more complete and thorough coverage of the French language, in which speaking proficiency, listening comprehension, vocabulary acquisition, reading, and writing are brought to a level enabling students to use the language actively in everyday situations. This course is especially designed for the student who has the capability to function at a higher level of language acquisition and is self-directed and highly motivated.
prerequisites: Successful completion of French III or demonstrated proficiency

description: This course is normally offered as an independent study. Students who attain this level of study are self-directed and motivated. Before beginning the course, students will outline the areas of culture, vocabulary and reading that they wish to explore. They will continue with more advanced grammar and use their studies to improve their writing in more complex projects and essays.
prerequisites: Successful completion of French I, French II, French III, and French IV or demonstrated proficiency

description: This course is for students with little to no exposure to the Spanish language. Listening, speaking, reading and writing will be the main focus in this class and will be practiced within thematic units. Students are exposed to the mechanics of the language through highly interactive activities, reading short dialogues, stories, Q+A practice and writing short responses. This is a highly social class where interpersonal exchanges and cooperative work and conversation with peers are practiced daily. Emphasis is on vocabulary acquisition, basic grammar skills, and being able to interact with others. Exposure to, research and awareness of the Spanish speaking world at large will help students become more globally minded citizens.

This course is a continuation of the work that has been covered in Spanish I. The main focus is being able to keep up with listening, speaking, reading and writing proficiencies. Students are expected to read and retell stories, easily converse in Spanish with peers using key verbs and vocabulary and be able to move through meaningful Q+A scenarios with peers on a daily basis. There will be a heavy focus on reading short stories, retelling these shared stories and listening. Writing will consist of short narratives and various comprehension activities. As in Spanish I, this is a highly social class where interpersonal exchanges and cooperative work and conversation with peers are practiced daily.
prerequisites: Spanish I or demonstrated proficiency

description: This course is a continuation of the work that has been covered in Spanish I and II. The main focus is being able to keep up with listening, speaking, reading and writing proficiencies in a more in-depth capacity with the language. Literacy is a strong focus in this class. This course stresses key vocabulary acquisition as well as more complex grammar that will be used in various writing exercises and compositions, as well as in shared exchanges between peers and speech. Reading includes short cultural stories and the ability to engage in more lengthy readings and dialogues. Speaking is emphasized at this level, with students being able to converse spontaneously with key language structures. Students will continue to make cultural connections through films, music and authentic materials.
prerequisites: Spanish II or demonstrated proficiency

description: Through more conversation, readings, storytelling and comprehensible input, this is an accelerated and intensive course providing a more complete and thorough coverage of the Spanish language, in which speaking proficiency, listening comprehension,vocabulary acquisition, reading, and writing are brought to a level enabling students to use the language actively and spontaneously in everyday situations. This course is especially designed for the student who has the capability to function at a higher level of language acquisition and is self-directed and highly motivated.
prerequisites: Spanish III or demonstrated proficiency

description: Students who attain this level of study are self-directed and motivated. Before beginning the course, students should be able to outline the areas of culture, vocabulary and reading that they wish to explore within the Spanish speaking world. Self-directed projects and research along with accelerated language acquisition will be a heavy focus during this course. Students will continue to be expected to gain, use and maneuver more advanced grammar and use their independent and collaborative studies to improve both their speaking and writing in more complex dialogues, projects and essays.
prerequisites: Spanish IV or demonstrated proficiency

description: This hands-on course introduces students to the fundamentals of art-making through exploration, creativity, and self expression. Students will learn foundational skills in drawing, painting, sculpture, and mixed media while developing an understanding of the elements of art and principles of design. Through guided projects and open-ended challenges, students will experiment with materials and techniques, engage in creative problem solving, and reflect on their artistic process. Emphasis is placed on fostering a supportive studio environment where students are encouraged to take creative risks, share ideas, and appreciate diverse perspectives.

As an introduction to digital photographic techniques, students will use Adobe Lightroom throughout the course to produce and edit their photographs. Emphasis will be placed on the elements and principles of design and how they contribute to strong composition in photography. Students have the opportunity to learn the mechanics of digital photography, lighting techniques and digital image manipulation. Students will be required to take photographs outside of class time.

Advanced Art is an upper-level studio course designed for students who are ready to deepen their artistic voice, technical skill, and creative independence. Through sustained investigation, students explore a variety of media - including drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture, mixed media, and digital tools - while developing personal themes and concepts in their work. Students engage in increasingly rigorous studio practice, including sketchbook development, collaborative critiques, and reflective writing. A key focus of the course is portfolio development. Students will produce a cohesive body of work suitable for college applications, exhibitions, or personal artistic growth. This class fosters a supportive and challenging environment where each student pushes their skills, takes ownership of their process, and discovers deeper meaning in their artmaking.
prerequisites: Art Studio Introduction and/or Teacher Approval

description: Since the invention of the motion picture humans have been fascinated by the experience of cinema. While many of us carry a video camera everywhere we go, that doesn’t mean that we are using them to their fullest potential. This quarter-long class will introduce you to the filmmaking process. Students will learn strategies for creating stories by shooting, editing and manipulating sound to create short films.
prerequisites: None

description: Clay + Fire = Stone. The ceramic process has been used by humans for over 20,000 years. Whether you prefer to make functional pottery or decorative sculpture, Ceramics will allow you to build spatial reasoning and fine motor skills as you form, refine and complete artworks. Students will use a variety of tools including (but not limited to): extrusion, firing, glazing, hand building, modeling and wheel throwing. Students are expected to create a body of finished work and participate in either the Winter or Spring SHS Art Show as a requirement for achieving Proficiency. This course may be repeated If the student wants to continue building their skills.

3D printing, laser cutting and digital illustration are a few of the media that you will have the opportunity to learn in I.D.E.A. & Craft. If you prefer traditional, analog artmaking carving foam, wood and stone are options for your creative expression as well. Students will be able to embrace their creativity in whichever mode they prefer in this quarter long course.

Dive into the rich and versatile world of fiber arts in this engaging and hands-on course. Students will learn a variety of techniques such as embroidery, felting, crocheting, and sewing while exploring the cultural and historical significance of textiles across the globe. This course emphasizes creativity, craftsmanship, and self-expression as students create unique, functional, and decorative pieces. Open to all skill levels.

This course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental principles and techniques of drawing. Through a series of hands-on projects, students will explore various drawing mediums, such as pencil, charcoal, ink, and pastels. Emphasis will be placed on developing observational skills, understanding proportions, shading techniques, perspective, and composition. Students will study both traditional and contemporary approaches to drawing, with opportunities to experiment and express their individual creativity. Critiques and discussions will foster a collaborative studio environment, encouraging students to analyze and reflect on their own work and that of their peers. By the end of the course, students will have gained a solid foundation in drawing and created a portfolio to showcase their artistic development. This course is open to all skill levels and aims to inspire a lifelong appreciation for the art of drawing.

Explore the dynamic possibilities of mixed media in this hands-on studio course. Students will experiment with combining various materials and techniques, such as drawing, painting, collage, printmaking, and found objects to create unique works of art. Emphasis will be placed on creative problem-solving, personal expression, and the interplay of texture, color, and form. Through guided projects, open-studio time, and critique, students will develop their technical skills, artistic vision, and understanding of communal studio practices. No prior experience necessary- just curiosity and willingness to create!

The Spaulding Band meets every day during our AM block. The band is open to all students. Prior experience is not required. Students will gain experience in both marching and concert band settings. Band members will also work independently on developing their skills and abilities at their own pace. Band members are expected to perform at 2 concerts, all home football games and local parades and Pep Band Events. Embedded Honors available.
notes: Credit stated per semester; course length not stated

description: This course meets everyday during AM block. Chorus is open to all students with a desire to learn to sing. Prior singing experience is not required. Students will gain exposure to a wide variety of styles and genres of music including classical, pop, broadway, folk, and world music. Students will learn the fundamentals of singing, sight reading, and music notation. Attendance at public performances that take place outside of the school day is expected. Embedded Honors available.
notes: Credit stated per semester; course length not stated

description: The Popular Music Ensemble performs popular music, including, but not limited to Blues, Country, R&B, Hip Hop, Funk and Soul Music. Rehearsals are conducted as coaching sessions, where both instrumentalists and singers perform together and blend sounds of musical instruments including piano, guitar, bass, percussion, wind instruments and MIDI devices. Students will be expected to participate in the written preparation of original and arranged music. This class is designed to provide students with a hands-on learning experience of music in a non-traditional format.
prerequisites: Teacher recommendation required prior to enrollment.
notes: Credit line reads "1.0 credit / Honors"

description: This is an honors level class. Students will refine the basic skills learned in Chorus. This class is ideal for students looking for more challenging music and individual attention. In addition to more advanced repertoire, students will work on individual vocal development, sight-reading, and further developing their literacy in music theory. Students are expected to attend multiple performances throughout the semester including Baccalaureate and SHS graduation.
prerequisites: Concurrent enrollment in Band or Chorus, recommendation or invitation by instructor

description: This course is designed for music students who wish to gain an understanding of the form, structure, and sound of music. This course will provide a background in the basics of music and how it is organized. Topics include reading bass and treble clef, intervals, scales, triads, rhythms, and more. Students will be taught music theory and offered practice in theory concepts through computer assisted compositions.

This course is for the beginning guitar student with or without previous music experience. The class will consist of a survey of musical styles with emphasis on note reading. Limited to 15 students, priority is given to juniors and seniors.
prerequisites: Students are urged to supply their own acoustic guitar. If this is not a possibly, the Music Department does have a limited number of guitars for student use.

description: This class is designed for students that have successfully completed Beginning Guitar (FNA 302) or have previous experience with Guitar playing. Students will receive guidance and direction in solving problems related to playing the guitar on an intermediate level and will learn many of the different styles, skills, and techniques required to become a successful musician.

This course is designed for students who wish to gain an understanding and appreciation of World music. This course will provide a background in the techniques and traditions of World drumming. The class will be taught aurally and students will not read music. No prior drumming experience is required, nor is the ability to read music. A willingness to try new things and have fun is required! Course limited to 15 students.

This Course traces the development of American popular music from its roots in the blues, through jazz and early rock and roll, continuing through contemporary styles of rock music. It will involve lecture, listening, discussion, student research, presentations and written work. Assessments are largely project based.

This course is designed for the beginning music student who is interested in developing basic piano and music reading skills. No previous experience required. Students will learn the concepts and fundamentals needed to play piano. This class operates largely on an individual basis. The curriculum is developed in a sequential manner - moving from simple to more complex concepts. There is ample opportunity for practice and review in order for the student to gain understanding and appropriate skill development. Weekly performances in class are the primary means of assessing proficiency and skill development. Performances are made only to the instructor and not to the entire class. Limited to 15 students.

This class explores the ways we experience and interact with music in our lives and how it can impact us. The general topics we will focus on in this course are music in our everyday lives, how music affects our brain, and music in film, as well as creating our own music using online software. There is no performance component to this class, but this class is an opportunity to be creative. Assessments are largely project based.

Students will enjoy a very welcoming and non-competitive atmosphere during this experience. The class will focus on health, fitness and wellness implementation to create a symbiotic and harmonious relationship with the mind, body and soul. Students will have the opportunity to take part in breathing exercises, embracing nature, and wellness goal planning. The overall goal of this course is to create an alternative to a more traditional physical education class setting and allow students to embark on a personal journey toward holistic health and well-being. This class will focus on the dimensions of wellness which include, but are not limited to, physical, social, emotional, spiritual, intellectual, environmental, and occupational wellness.
prerequisites: Wellness and/or Introductory PE

description: This section is the prerequisite course for all other PE courses. Students will gain understanding of games by participating in a variety of recreational sports, lifetime activities, and non-traditional games. 3-4 days per week students will experience games like badminton, floor hockey, cornhole, and wiffleball where they will work towards better understanding game play concepts, rules, and strategies as well as motor skill development/refinement. In addition to learning games, students will also gain an understanding of and participation in basic fitness programs focused on the ‘5 elements of fitness’(Cardio, Muscle Strength, Muscle Endurance, Flexibility and Body Composition). 1-2 days per week students will experience genres of fitness like Yoga, Performance Training and various Cardio & Resistance Training methods.

Want to get stronger, feel better, and improve your overall fitness? In this Personal Fitness class, you'll get the chance to set your own fitness goals and work toward achieving them in a fun and supportive environment. You'll participate in a variety of workouts, including strength training, HIIT, and circuit training, to build muscle, boost endurance, and increase energy. On other days, enjoy recreational sports, yoga, stretching, and recovery techniques that help you stay balanced and healthy. Whether you're new to fitness or looking to take your training to the next level, this class will help you feel your best, both physically and mentally.
prerequisites: Introductory Physical Education

description: Get ready for action and teamwork in the Team Games class! This course is designed for students who love playing sports and working together as a team. You’ll have the chance to compete in a variety of team-based games like basketball, soccer, volleyball, and more. Throughout the class, you'll develop your skills in strategy, communication, and leadership while staying active and having fun.
prerequisites: Introductory Physical Education

description: If you love sports that involve strategy, teamwork, and quick reflexes, the Net Games class is for you! In this class, you’ll play and improve your skills in exciting net game sports like: volleyball, badminton, and pickleball. You'll learn the rules, techniques, and strategies needed to succeed in each game while staying active and having fun. Whether you're a beginner or have some experience, this class offers a great opportunity to improve your hand-eye coordination, communication, and sportsmanship.
prerequisites: Introductory Physical Education

description: This honors level PE class will offer the opportunity to teach and mentor students that are part of the life skills program in a variety of physical activities.The mentor's responsibility will be to guide, assist and teach their partner through a variety of skills and strategies during activities. Emphasizing teamwork, respect for others, problem solving will also play a strong role in the relationship between the mentor and the mentee when participating in activities.
prerequisites: Completion of 2 PE classes (Intro and another), Proficient or higher for final grade.

description: This a required, semester-long course focuses on developing skills for lifelong personal health. These skills include analyzing influences, accessing health resources, interpersonal communication, advocacy, decision making, goal setting, and practicing health behaviors. Health topics include disease prevention, relationships, alcohol and other drugs, nutrition, and stress management.
fulfills_text: required

description: This semester-long course focuses on developing skills for lifelong personal health. These skills include analyzing influences, accessing health resources, interpersonal communication, advocacy, decision making, goal setting, and practicing health behaviors. Health topics include disease prevention, relationships, alcohol and other drugs, nutrition, and stress management. This course is designed for students who have not completed the first-year Wellness course. Preferred level is 11th and 12th grades.

This quarter-long course introduces students to the fundamental concepts of nutrition, focusing on a weight-inclusive approach that prioritizes health and well-being. Students will explore how different nutrients affect the body and learn how to make informed choices based on personal needs, activity levels, and health goals. This course encourages students to develop a healthy relationship with food, promoting physical and mental well-being all while exploring the physical, emotional, and cultural importance of food.
prerequisites: Health or Wellness

description: This course prepares novice drivers to drive safely on America’s highways and empowers teens to manage high risk situations using the most appropriate highway user attitudes, responsible driving skills, and traffic safety principles available. Course topics include the driving task, zone control, reference points, driving in urban traffic, rural areas, and on expressways, handling emergencies and adverse conditions, insurance and liability, legal issues, and the effects of driver impairment on driving. This program requires students to show respect and tolerance.
prerequisites: A valid Learner's Permit prior to the first class and Sophomore status.
notes: listed under MISCELLANEOUS

description: This course will cover core concepts of maple syrup production. Maple syrup production is a very important aspect of Vermont life and history. Every year in the early spring people of all ages find their way to the woods to tap trees, collect sap, and participate in the great tradition of producing maple syrup. Vermont is the largest maple syrup producer in the United States and maple is an essential industry from a historical, cultural, agricultural, and economic perspective. As the industry continues to grow, it creates potential employment opportunities for people of all ages, including recent high school graduates.
notes: Maple Program

description: The class will spend much of its time in the field learning how to and installing maple tubing. The students will learn how to operate basic tubing installation tools once completing basic training and completing a basic OSHA course. Once tubing is installed the class will gather data on the 3 tubing systems sap yield based on environmental conditions and the weather. When the students are not in the field students will compile and analyze the data to determine a theory on which system yields the most sap and why. The second component of the course will involve multiple site visits to large sugaring operations around the state. While on these site visits students will observe techniques used to gather and process maple sap into maple syrup. These large scale operations will also provide the students with the opportunity to view and understand the business/marketing side of the Maple Industry.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Maple Program Class
notes: Maple Program

description: This is an introductory course on Work Based Learning that enables students to gain the necessary skills and knowledge of being a part of the workforce. Topics will include Career Readiness & Professionalism in the Workplace, workplace safety, and exposure to various work settings through the Central Vermont area. Students will also have the chance to participate in an activity in the nonprofit sector, and spend the remaining semester in a Work Based Learning opportunity off-site.
prerequisites: A valid driver’s license and access to reliable and insured transportation. If interested in a medical placement, additional requirements are needed. For some placements, one must be 18 years of age prior to placement.

description: Work Based Learning will be offered in the format of a semester class helping students make clear, informed choices about their futures by learning about what education, experiences, and training (E2T) they can obtain with a post secondary institution, such as a 2 or 4 year college/university. This has been especially meaningful for students who may seek out a post-secondary education at a technical or community college, students who are seeking a four year college education and ask “WHY college?”, or for students who may be interested in exploring a particular career immediately after high school.

This elective is a semester-long course (internship) that enables students to gain practical skills and knowledge about a particular field, along with learning about the aspects of a workplace. It allows students to gain first hand knowledge and determine if this particular career/field is still of interest to them. Components of the course include: preparation and professionalism in the workforce, climate and confidentiality, required written assignments, training agreement, evaluations, and a final product, along with meeting the standards outlined in the curriculum map
prerequisites: Earned Proficiency in WBL200A. A valid driver’s license and access to reliable and insured transportation. If interested in a medical placement, additional requirements are needed. For some placements, one must be 18 years of age prior to placement.

description: Early College is a full year rigorous alternative to the traditional senior year of high school. Students enroll in college level courses, typically taking four to five courses per semester, which allows them to complete both their senior year of high school and their first year of college simultaneously tuition free. While tuition is covered, families/caregivers and students are responsible for associated fees required by the participating institution. Several institutions offer Early College programs including Norwich University, Community College of Vermont, and Vermont State University. Students interested in Early College should meet with their school counselor and 504/IEP case manager to determine whether the program is an appropriate fit. It is recommended that students begin exploring Early College options during the first semester of their junior year as application deadlines vary by institution.

This option can be relevant for students looking for classes not offered at SHS, for areas of scheduling conflict with required courses, or to supplement a student's schedule outside of the regular school day.

notes: program

description: In Cosmos “U,” students work with teachers across designated content areas, including English, Science, Social Studies, Math, Physical Education, and Art. This course is designed to offer a variety of flexible pathways to earn credit towards graduation or for enrichment purposes. The selection of particular content or transferable skills to be mastered will be decided collaboratively by the student, counselor, Flexible Pathways Coordinator, and teacher. As a central hub for flexible pathways, Cosmos “U” offers an adaptable environment tailored to each student's needs. Learning activities through Cosmos “U” provide a comprehensive range of options, which can include Dual Enrollment and Early College for higher education credit, independent passion projects and capstones, online learning through VTVLC and other approved programs, and hands-on internships or work-based learning experiences, alongside other Expanded Learning Opportunities tailored to student interest. Whether a student requires daily structure for credit recovery or a flexible schedule for advanced study, Cosmos "U" provides the resources and teacher oversight necessary for success.
notes: program; Note: See content departments for related offerings

description: Students who enroll in Work-Based Learning (WBL) have the opportunity to take part in a job shadow(s) or internship(s) after spending time researching their career(s) of interest, writing a resume and cover letter, participating in mock interviews, and/or looking at the trends and outlooks in the job market. Through a combination of meetings with the WBL Coordinator, real-world application, and experiential learning, students will gain valuable insights into various industries, develop essential employability skills, and make informed decisions about their future careers.
prerequisites: Recommended completion of Adulting 101 or Google Classroom Intro to Work-Based Learning Course
notes: program; Work-Based Learning (WBL)

description: Dual enrollment, one of the Cosmos “U” Flexible Pathways opportunities, allows students to earn college credit and high school graduation credit simultaneously. Courses can be taken on-campus at SHS or directly through a participating Vermont or New Hampshire college.

description: Online learning, one of the Cosmos “U” Flexible Pathways opportunities, is open to any SHS student if it is determined that the format is a developmentally and academically appropriate fit, provided policy requirements are met. This format is designed to enhance learning experiences beyond those available within the walls of SHS through the Vermont Virtual Learning Collaborative (VTVLC) or other approved online providers. Generally, online courses are permitted only if they are not accessible to students via other reasonable means.
provider: VTVLC or other approved online providers
notes: program; Vermont Virtual Learning Collaborative (VTVLC) or other approved online providers

description: Through the State of Vermont Flexible Pathways Initiative, Springfield High School students are eligible to participate in Vermont's Early College Program during their senior year of high school. This allows students to complete their last year of high school (earning their diploma) while simultaneously completing their first year of college. Students may not enroll in any SHS classes as an early college student. However, they can still receive support (counseling, college advising, etc.) and may participate in SHS-based activities (sports, prom, senior trip, etc.). After early college acceptance, a student may request to complete early college work at SHS. With administration approval, these students must sign in and out at the office, work only in the library for half of the day, and arrange their own transportation. Funds are available to students accepted into full-time programs through participating colleges throughout the state and covers the cost of tuition for 12-15 college credits. Currently, the following Vermont Colleges have approved Early College programs:
notes: program; approved Vermont colleges: Community College of Vermont, Norwich University, Vermont State University; seniors only

description: In this course students will learn to become competent and responsible drivers who are committed to improving driver performance throughout their lifetime. Topics will include alcohol and drug education, seat belt usage, zone control method of operation, risk management and other topics. All concepts and skills to be practiced in the car, will be first presented in the classroom. A partnership will be formed between the instructor, student, and parent/ guardian to help support driving skills. This course will build a foundation of driving skills that students can use throughout their lifetime of driving.
credits_text: 0.5 elective credit upon completion of both classroom and in-vehicle requirements.
prerequisites: Proof of an official driver permit (physical card present) is REQUIRED to be on file with the SHS registrar prior to August 15th for fall semester course enrollment and prior to January 5th for spring semester course enrollment. Temporary paper permits and/or email confirmations WILL NOT BE ACCEPTED. Students who do not produce an official permit (physical card) to the registrar on or before these dates will be unenrolled from the course in compliance with Vermont state regulations. Enrollment in Drivers Ed is based on Date of Birth and proof of a valid Vermont drivers permit. Due to high enrollment numbers and required driving hours, this course is limited to 30 students per semester.
notes: Note: Daily participation and attendance are required.

description: This course introduces students to high-school English through structured support in reading comprehension, vocabulary, writing conventions, and analytical thinking. Students read accessible versions of grade-level texts centered on the theme “Coming of Age” and build foundational skills in annotation, paragraph writing, and text-based discussion. Emphasis is on developing confidence and proficiency in reading and writing skills.
prerequisites: Placement based on prior performance, assessments, and teacher recommendations

description:
This course introduces students to high-school English through a series of thematic units that explore identity, growth, and the challenges of coming of age. Students read a blend of whole-class texts, short stories, poems, and paired nonfiction articles to deepen comprehension and build a foundation in literary analysis. Students will also practice developing claims, refining sentences, and improving writing through the full drafting and revision process. Daily independent reading is expected to strengthen fluency and stamina. This course prepares students for the demands of English 10, which will include the expectation of nightly homework completion. Throughout the course, students learn to:
• Annotate and analyze fiction and nonfiction texts
• Identify and trace central ideas across text sets
• Write narrative, analytical, and explanatory pieces
• Cite evidence effectively in their writing
• Participate in structured discussions and collaborative activities

This course challenges students with complex independent readings, literary criticism, and accelerated writing expectations. Students study the “Coming of Age” theme through high-complexity texts and produce analytical, argumentative, explanatory, narrative, and creative work. Students participate in advanced discussions and must submit required summer work before the first day of school. Independent reading and homework will also be a nightly expectation of students in this course.
prerequisites: 8th Grade English teacher recommendation & completion of summer work

description: This course continues foundational literacy development while exploring themes of tragedy, control, and catharsis. Students read accessible versions of anchor texts, develop structured analytical writing, and strengthen grammar, vocabulary, and reading comprehension. This course prepares students for English 11.
prerequisites: Placement based on prior performance, assessments, and teacher recommendations
notes: Duration: One Semester, meets daily

description:
This course challenges students to examine how individuals respond to conflict, power, tragedy, and societal pressures. Through text sets that include drama, novels, informational texts, and primary-source documents, students explore themes of control, justice, rebellion, and moral choice. Students develop vocabulary, reading comprehension, and writing proficiency while engaging in inquiry-based projects. Independent reading and homework continue to be a core expectation.
Students build on English 9 skills by:
• Analyzing complex characters and themes across multiple genres
• Comparing perspectives across paired readings
• Writing clear, well-structured analytical, argumentative, and explanatory essays
• Incorporating research and nonfiction evidence into writing
• Delivering presentations and participating in Socratic-style discussions
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 9

description: This course extends the English 10 curriculum through more complex texts, advanced writing expectations, and AP-aligned reading lists. Students produce sophisticated analytical and argumentative writing, participate in sustained discussions, and will be asked to work and read independently at home. Summer work must be submitted by the first day of school for weighted honors credit.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Advanced English 9 or English 9 + teacher recommendation
notes: Additional Requirement: Summer work

description: This course supports students as they study American literature with scaffolding and accessible texts. Students analyze how culture, history, and identity shape the American story while strengthening vocabulary, reading comprehension, and structured writing. The course prepares students for English 12.
prerequisites: Placement based on prior performance, assessments, and teacher recommendations

description:
This course examines American literature and thought through units that connect historical eras with modern issues. Students read text sets that include novels, memoirs, speeches, poetry, short fiction, and paired nonfiction to explore themes such as freedom, identity, justice, and the American Dream. Students also build college- and career-ready writing skills by producing polished drafts and practicing revision routines. Independent reading and homework continues to be a core expectation.
Across the year, students will:
• Analyze how historical context shapes literature and cultural conversations
• Compare arguments and ideas across primary and secondary sources
• Write argumentative, analytical, and narrative essays with increasing sophistication
• Develop research questions and integrate credible sources
• Participate in discussions that challenge them to evaluate multiple viewpoints
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 10

description: This course mirrors a college-level literary analysis course. Students engage in close reading of complex texts, exploring structure, style, themes, figurative language, symbolism, and tone. Students write expository, analytical, and argumentative essays and prepare for the AP exam in May. Summer work is required for weighted credit. Independent reading and homework continue to be a core expectation.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Honors English 10 and summer work

description: This course focuses on essential reading, writing, research, and communication skills. Students explore British and world literature using accessible texts and paired nonfiction. Writing instruction emphasizes paragraph structure, thesis development, practical/workplace writing, and evidence-based reasoning.
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 11 and/or teacher recommendation

description:
This course is a capstone course that brings together world literature, British literature, and contemporary global texts. Students explore broad themes such as power, morality, identity, cultural conflict, and the search for meaning through curated text sets, paired readings, and literary/nonfiction connections. This course emphasizes critical thinking, academic writing, global awareness, and preparation for college-level reading and communication. Independent reading and homework continue to be a core expectation.
Students will:
• Analyze how authors across time and cultures address universal human questions
• Compare multiple texts that express different perspectives on similar themes
• Write sustained analytical, argumentative, and explanatory essays
• Conduct guided and independent research
• Participate in structured debates, Socratic seminars, and presentations
prerequisites: Successful completion of English 11

description: This course emphasizes academic writing, research, information literacy, and revision. Students write college essays, literary analysis, reviews, and a research paper, while practicing the full writing process. This is the most advanced senior-year English option
prerequisites: English 11 and teacher recommendation
notes: Note: Potential college credit through Vermont State University

description: This course provides students with a strong foundation in news writing, reporting, and media literacy. In this writing intensive course, students learn the fundamentals of journalistic style, including news values, interviewing strategies, source verification, Associated Press Style conventions, and the structure of hard news, features, sports, and opinion writing. Throughout the course, students practice reporting techniques, write publishable articles, analyze professional models, and participate in peer editing workshops. Students also learn the basics of layout, design, and newsroom ethics, as well as how to evaluate sources, avoid bias, and understand the role of journalism in a democratic society. Students who demonstrate strong writing, responsibility, and collaborative skills have the opportunity to earn a staff position the following year, where they will take on leadership and production roles within the Greenhorn student newspaper.
notes: Section: English Electives (do not count toward the core English requirement)

description:
Advanced Journalism functions as the newsroom and editorial staff of the Greenhorn, Springfield High School’s student newspaper. Students in this writing intensive course take on increasingly complex reporting, writing, editing, and production responsibilities, working under real deadlines to publish multiple issues throughout the year. Returning staff members may serve as section editors, senior reporters, or managing editors, guiding Intro Journalism students, coordinating story pitches, designing pages, and shaping editorial direction. This course is ideal for students interested in writing, media, communications, public relations, broadcasting, or any field requiring clear, persuasive communication.
Advanced Journalism students deepen their skills in:
• Investigative reporting and in-depth interviewing
• Multimedia storytelling
• Associated Press Style mastery
• Copyediting, fact-checking, and headline writing
• Layout and design using digital publishing tools
• Editorial leadership and newsroom management
• Ethical decision-making and responsible journalism
prerequisites: Intro to Journalism
notes: Section: English Electives (do not count toward the core English requirement)

description: In this course, students will develop their critical thinking abilities, argumentative skills, and listening skills. Students will also practice and improve their research skills, while learning to write and present speeches. Students will gain experience in both giving public presentations and learning from the presentations of others. By the end of the course students will be able to prepare for and participate effectively in a range of classroom conversations and debates. This course will prepare students for college and careers that demand the following: logical thinking, clear spoken expression, active listening skills, an ability to conduct research, and adaptation and collaboration working in teams. This course will provide a forum for students to practice and develop effective communication skills for the purpose of addressing diverse audiences with confidence and competence. Using a variety of instructional strategies students will learn to research, outline, and deliver speeches appropriate for the setting and population. Students will study speech fundamentals and delivery strategies and learn to adapt purpose and message based on audience analysis. Special attention will be given to critical listening skills and ethical considerations.
prerequisites: English 10
notes: Section: English Electives (do not count toward the core English requirement)

description: In this course, students will learn the principles and techniques of creative writing and actively participate in writing workshops. Students will read and discuss the styles and techniques of various writers and will begin to develop their own sense of style and voice in their own work. Students will have a choice of genre, theme, and topic to focus their study on. This course will focus on the creative writing process through the study of fiction and creative nonfiction. Students will analyze examples of varying genres and will have daily critical discussions. Writing workshops will deepen the students' understanding of the writing process, and will provide students with additional time to craft and share their work. Students are expected to participate in meaningful class discussions and formal/informal presentations. Students will write creative pieces daily, revise and edit consistently, and frequently read independently. Independent reading and homework are a core expectation.
prerequisites: English 9
notes: Section: English Electives (do not count toward the core English requirement)

description: Students will explore the dramatic arts through script analysis, performance, and production. They will bring the page to the stage by delving into acting, directing, technical theater, and playwriting. This course emphasizes creativity, collaboration, and confidence-building, culminating in a final production. This course is designed for motivated students who are eager to learn on-stage and backstage techniques and develop strong problem-solving skills. Throughout the year, students will learn to analyze, write, read, and produce plays while strengthening their public speaking, social, and collaborative abilities. Students will participate in a Fall production during the first semester and a One-Act performance during the second semester, performed for the school and community. Students taking the course in the second semester will focus more on playwriting and smaller productions. There is a required after-school/weekend commitment of 5–10 hours for dress rehearsals and performances. Additionally, students must attend live theatrical productions or watch films, culminating in play/film reviews.
notes: Section: English Electives (do not count toward the core English requirement)

description: This course offers a flexible, student-driven environment where students can earn English credit through non-traditional pathways. Specific English standards are mastered through a plan decided collaboratively by the student, counselor, Flexible Pathways Coordinator, and English teacher. This adaptable model supports a variety of goals, ranging from credit recovery for missed core requirements to enrichment opportunities such as independent passion projects, capstones, or advanced studies that extend beyond the standard curriculum. Additionally, Cosmos “U” can provide targeted support for students engaged in career-based internships or online courses, ensuring they have the guidance needed to navigate external learning. Whether a student needs daily structure to catch up or a flexible schedule to dive deeper into a specific area of study, Cosmos "U" provides the teacher oversight and resources necessary to succeed.
notes: Section: English Electives (do not count toward the core English requirement)

description: This ninth grade course is comprised of a comprehensive health curriculum, which covers concepts of wellness, assessing the various dimensions of wellness. Instructional units include: Goal Setting, Mental Health, Nutrition, Substance Abuse Prevention, Interpersonal Communication, Decision Making, and Fitness. Students will use critical thinking skills to discover ways for enhancing wellness, reducing risk of disease and promoting healthy behaviors for themselves and their families. Students will demonstrate their learning achievement through performance and/or cognitive assessments. Health Education prepares students to make healthy decisions and take healthy actions on matters concerning personal, family and community health. The goal is for students to become health literate and to use such information/skills in health-enhancing ways.

This course teaches students the skills necessary to weigh options, make responsible decisions and to develop behaviors that promote healthy and balanced lifestyles. Instructional units include: Healthy Human Sexuality, Analyzing Influences, Accessing Valid and Reliable Information/Products/Services, Sleep, Mindset, and Motivation. All students will learn the lifesaving techniques of Adult First Aid/CPR/AED through the American Red Cross (CPR certification is optional). By the end of the course students will be able to demonstrate the ability to practice health-enhancing behaviors that reduce risk and promote health. Students will demonstrate their learning achievement through performance and/or cognitive assessments.
prerequisites: Intro to Wellness

Throughout the course, students explore real-world problems and attempt to describe relationships between quantities using mathematical models. This course includes the following proficiencies: Algebra, Functions, Modeling with Algebra & Functions.

description: In Geometry, the concepts in this class can include: geometric vocabulary, angles, logic, geometric figures such as triangles, quadrilaterals, lines, etc., transformations, congruence and similarity,and aspirationally trigonometry, and circles. This course includes the following proficiencies: Geometry, Modeling with Geometry .
prerequisites: Algebra I

description: In Honors Geometry, the concepts in this class will include: geometric vocabulary, angles, logic, geometric figures such as triangles, quadrilaterals, lines, etc., transformations, congruence and similarity, trigonometry, and circles. This class is designed to move at a faster pace in order to cover more content. This would be a great option for students who took Honors (previously Accelerated) Algebra I or are ready for more after Algebra I part 1 and 2. This would allow more exposure to concepts such as trigonometry, circles and special right triangles to better prepare students for encountering these topics again in Algebra II and beyond. This course includes the following proficiencies: Geometry, Modeling with Geometry.
prerequisites: Algebra I (recommended: Honors Algebra 1)

description: This course includes a brief review of Algebra I and can include: irrational, imaginary, and complex numbers; operations with polynomials; graphing polynomials; exponential and logarithmic functions; rational and radical functions; and trigonometry extended to the unit circle. This course includes the following proficiencies: Algebra , Functions.
prerequisites: Geometry and teacher recommendation

description: This course is designed to prepare students for a calculus course. Topics include polynomial, rational, exponential, and logarithmic functions. It includes a thorough study of trigonometry. Other topics introduced include conic sections and limits. Students are encouraged to have a graphing calculator. This course contributes to academic distinction in STEM. This course includes the following proficiencies: Algebra, Functions, Number and Quantity, Geometry.
prerequisites: Advanced Algebra 2 or Algebra 2 with teacher recommendation

description: This is a college level introduction to differential and integral calculus. A TI-83+ or TI-84 graphing calculator is required for this course. Students continuing on in the spring are required to take the AP Exam. Students must take a math assessment for placement purposes prior to registration. The curriculum is aligned with the expectations of the College Board AP Calculus course. This course contributes to academic distinction in STEM. This course includes the following proficiencies: Calculus.
prerequisites: PreCalculus

description: AP Calculus AB is an introductory college-level calculus course. Students cultivate their understanding of differential and integral calculus through engaging with real-world problems represented graphically, numerically, analytically, and verbally and using definitions and theorems to build arguments and justify conclusions as they explore concepts like change, limits, and the analysis of functions. This course includes the following proficiencies: Calculus.
prerequisites: PreCalculus
notes: Note: Students must also enroll in Calculus AB Lab the following semester.

description: AP Calculus AB Lab is a second semester course which makes final preparations for the AP Calculus AB test in May. In this course, students learn the remaining topics in the AP Calculus AB Curriculum and work to perfect their understanding of differential and integral calculus as mentioned in the AP Calculus AB description. Students will interact more with The College Board AP Classroom website to facilitate this work and testing preparation. This course includes the following proficiencies: Calculus.
prerequisites: PreCalculus; Calculus AB (Advanced Placement)

description: An introduction to the basic ideas and techniques of probability and statistics. The use of a TI-84 is required .The curriculum is aligned with the expectations of the College Board AP Statistics course. This course contributes to academic distinction in STEM and Research. This course includes the following proficiencies: Statistics

description: Personal Fitness is primarily a self-directed course with focus on goal setting, fitness concepts, and basic nutrition and overall healthy habits. Students will teach weight training exercises and techniques to their peers. Students will use both the weight room and fitness room to conduct personal fitness plans. Students will be graded on the following: their proficiency level based on the Four National Physical Education Standards, Fitnessgram testing, written assignments, and most importantly, their participation.. The students will learn muscular anatomy and how to develop stronger muscles through proper mechanics of lifting free weight dumbbells and the machines we have available in the gym. The students will learn the different types of weight training and how it relates to particular developmental goals. Students will also use the cardio room to enhance their cardiovascular endurance. Each student will design a fitness program they will follow throughout the semester. This course will include some or all of the following proficiencies: Psychomotor, Cognitive, Social, and Affective.
prerequisites: Physical Education
notes: Note: Daily participation is required. Participation includes: changing into athletic clothes/shoes and moving for class.

description: Biology is the study of life. By the end of the course, students will have an understanding of the following ideas: structure and function; ecosystems, ecology, heredity, and biological evolution. Students will learn Life Science content, as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
prerequisites: Grade of 1.5 or higher in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science
notes: Note: Recommended for 10th grade

description: In this course students will learn about the origin of the universe, the life cycles of stars, and about Earth’s history during the Precambrian Era. Students also learn about Earth systems and how energy is transferred through these systems. Students will learn Earth & Space Science as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
prerequisites: Grade of 1.5 or higher in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science
notes: Note: Recommended for 11th or 12th grade

description: In forensics, students will discover how science plays a role in solving crimes. We will cover topics like collecting evidence, analyzing DNA, studying blood types, autopsies and dissection, and exploring past and current events. By the end of the course, you will be able to analyze and understand data from crime scenes, and you'll learn how to solve crimes using forensic science. We will use models, conduct experiments in the lab, and engage in discussions to apply science to real-life situations. This will help you sharpen your critical thinking skills and give you a glimpse into potential careers in forensic science. Students will learn Life Science and Physical Science content, as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
prerequisites: Passing grade in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science
notes: Note: Recommended for 10th-12th grade

description: This general physics course introduces the student to basic kinematic physics. Topics include Newtonian mechanics, forces, circular, rotational and planetary motion. Students will learn Physical Science content, as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
prerequisites: Algebra II (can be taken concurrently)
notes: Note: Recommended for 11th or 12th grade

description: This course is an introduction to the concepts, principles and applications of chemistry. Topics of study will include: atomic structure, periodicity, structure of matter, thermochemistry, solutions, and equilibrium. Lab sessions will illustrate the principles of quantitative interpretation of data. Students will learn Physical Science content as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
prerequisites: Passing grade in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science; Algebra II (can be taken concurrently)
notes: Note: Recommended for 11th or 12th grade

description: This course is a continuation of the introduction to the concepts, principles and applications of chemistry. Topics of study will include acids/bases, redox reactions, introduction to organic chemistry, and nuclear chemistry. Lab sessions will illustrate the principles of quantitative interpretation of data. Note that this course is reflected as Introductory Chemistry on the college transcript from Vermont State University. Students will learn Physical Science content, as well as Science and Engineering practices.
prerequisites: Chemistry I

description: AP Biology is a year-long introductory college-level biology course. Students cultivate their understanding of biology through inquiry-based investigations as they explore the following topics: evolution, cellular processes, energy and communication, genetic information transfer, ecology, and interactions. Students will learn Life Science content, as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
prerequisites: Grade of 3.0 or higher in Biology
notes: Recommended: Chemistry I

course_name: A Walk on the Wildside: Nature, Community, and Environmental Research
description: In this class, we'll head outdoors to discover and study the local Vermont environment. We'll do research in the SHS Forest, look into how climate change affects Vermont communities, and explore the ideas of biomimicry--that is, engineering based on how living things are structured and what they do. Students will learn Earth & Space Science and Engineering content, as well as Science and Engineering Practices.
prerequisites: Grade of 1.5 or higher in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science; the willingness to go outside for class in almost any weather.
notes: Note: Recommended for 11th and 12th grade.

description: In this course, students will explore cosmetics design through a hands-on DIY (do-it-yourself) approach. Using chemistry and the engineering design process, students will design and make cosmetics products such as soaps, lip products, scrubs, perfumes, and makeup. Students will learn Physical Science and Engineering content, as well as Science and Engineering practices.
prerequisites: Passing grade in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science

description: In this class, you'll get a taste of the world of engineering. We'll dive into designing and creating things like bridges, rockets and self-powered vehicles. You'll learn how to use engineering methods to make your creations even better. This course will teach you valuable problem-solving skills that will come in handy in future classes and real-life situations. Safety is a top priority, so you'll also be learning how to safely use different tools and materials. You will keep a detailed notebook to track all your engineering ideas and designs. Students will learn Physical Science and Engineering content, as well as Science and Engineering practices.
prerequisites: Grade of 1.5 or higher in Introduction to Chemistry & Physics 9 or Introduction to Physical Science
notes: Note: Recommended for 10th-12th grade; Students will be expected to use tools and materials safely and to keep a detailed Engineering Design notebook.
