description: This Ancient World History course explores the foundation of human cultures through an in-depth study of major civilizations, including Mesopotamia, Ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome, China, and India. We will examine how geography, religion, social structures, economics, and cultural accomplishments shaped these societies and continue to influence the modern world. Each unit will incorporate comparisons to modern society, helping students draw connections between the past and present. By the end of the course, students will gain a deeper understanding of the lasting impact of ancient civilizations on contemporary life.
notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 9

description: This course looks at the history of the United States, starting with the end of the Civil War. Students will compare past events to what is going on in the world today. Students will conduct independent research, and write arguments about the past and the present.
credits_text: 1.0 Social Studies (meets American history and government requirement)
prerequisites: Modern Society, Introduction to Social Studies or Honors Modern Society
notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 10 or 11

description: Migration and immigration have been central in the making of American history and culture. It has changed the social, political, economic, racial, and cultural fabric of America and the world. In this course, students will look at the movement of people in the Americas and coming to the Americas from Columbus and the transatlantic slave trade to the many migrations since. Essential topics, readings, and multimedia provide historical context to current debates over immigration, migration, assimilation, integration, “legal” and “illegal” and citizenship. Students will research various historical push and pull factors in immigration and migration. Students will be able to analyze and articulate current events in immigration and connecting. Students will show their proficiency by being able to compare and contrast, and explain from several points of view, the history of immigration and what it means to be “American”. Students will be asked to connect community, personal, national, and international experiences.
prerequisites: US History (can be taken concurrently)
offering_note: Offered every other year (next offering is 2027/2028)
notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 10 or above; Offered every other year (next offering is 2027/2028)

description: In this course, ideas of Sociology and Psychology will be combined, where students will examine: ways that their brain works, ways that they interact with society, and ways that trauma impacts individuals. By the end of the course, students will be able to “ask good questions” about themselves and the world around them.
prerequisites: US History (can be taken concurrently)
notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 10 or above; There is a significant amount of reading, and the writing of a 5-page paper.

description: Welcome to Modern History Through Film! This course examines American history from the 1940’s to the present through the lens of cinema. Film is not just entertainment—it is also a primary source that reflects the views, values, anxieties, and perspectives of the time in which it was made. Through analyzing films and film clips, we will develop critical thinking skills to understand how history shapes culture and how culture shapes our understanding of history.
prerequisites: US History (can be taken concurrently)
notes: Note: Recommended for Grades 11 and 12; There will be a significant amount of writing, reflection, discussion, and critique of ideas.

description: In this course, students will examine the history, culture, environmental, social, religious, and contemporary aspects of East Asia focusing on Korea, Japan, and China. We will use literature, film, visual arts, and music as historical sources. Students will show proficiency by comparing and contrasting various eras and countries including our own, develop a research topic and questions based on their interests, and share their findings. By the end of the course, students will be able to critically discuss current international relations, human commonalities and differences, and their impact on the student’s own life.
prerequisites: US History (can be taken concurrently)
offering_note: Offered every other year (next offering is 2026-2027)
notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 11 and 12; Offered every other year (next offering is 2026-2027)

course_name: Save Your Money. Know Your Rights.
description: Students will explore personal finance (budgeting etc.), basic economics, and how to participate in government - we will examine questions such as: Why do prices “keep going up?” Where is my money going? What does it mean to be a citizen? What are the responsibilities of a citizen to their government? What about a government’s responsibilities to its citizens? In this class, we explore these questions while asking students “what’s your plan after graduation?”
prerequisites: US History (can be taken concurrently)
fulfills_text: Recommended for Grade 11 and 12; This course meets the Financial Literacy requirement for the Class of 2027 and beyond
notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 11 and 12; This course meets the Financial Literacy requirement for the Class of 2027 and beyond

description: and counselor approval and demonstration of academic readiness In this college-level course, students will be introduced to the systematic and scientific study of the behavior and mental processes of human beings and other animals. Students are exposed to the psychological facts, principles, and phenomena associated with each of the major subfields within psychology. They also learn about the ethics and methods psychologists use in their science and practice. This course contributes to academic distinction in Wellness.
credits_text: 1.0 credit (DE); 1.5 credits (AP, when taken with the lab)
prerequisites: US History; teacher recommendation - attend required teacher meeting to be scheduled in late spring
notes: Note: Recommended for Grade 12; Juniors pursuing early college or advanced learning may request enrollment, pending instructor; Catalog lists both a DE and an AP option

description: This course offers a flexible, student-driven environment where students can learn Social Studies through non-traditional pathways. Specific humanities and social studies standards and proficiencies are mastered through a plan decided collaboratively by the student, counselor, Flexible Pathways Coordinator, and Social Studies teacher. This adaptable model supports a variety of goals, ranging from credit recovery for missed core requirements to enrichment opportunities such as independent passion projects, historical research, capstones, or advanced civic and global studies that extend beyond the standard curriculum. Additionally, Cosmos “U” can provide targeted support for students engaged in career-based internships or online courses. Whether a student needs daily structure to catch up or a flexible schedule to dive deeper into a specific area of historical or social inquiry, Cosmos "U" provides the teacher oversight and resources necessary to succeed.

This course builds on the skills and knowledge gained in middle school art. Students will learn how to use the creative process to create interesting and meaningful compositions. Students will create artworks in drawing, painting, and other media. This class has a strong emphasis on creative problem-solving and meaning making through visual arts. Proficiencies covered: create and respond.

In this course, students will gain the skills to draw realistically from observation as well as develop a personal style and voice in drawing media. Gesture drawing, contouring, perspective, and shading techniques will be explored through still life, portrait, and landscape drawing with a variety of drawing materials. Projects will be enriched with art history, presentation, and critique. Proficiencies covered: create, respond, and connect.
prerequisites: Art I

description: In this course, students will use several different painting techniques and mediums to create meaningful artworks. Acrylics, oils, and watercolors will all be explored to create works from observation, imagination, and photo references. Projects will be enriched with art history, presentation, and reflection. Proficiencies covered: create, respond, and connect.
prerequisites: Art I
offering_note: Offered every other year (next offering is 2027-2028)
notes: Note: Offered every other year (next offering is 2027-2028)

description: In this course, students will use digital photography to create strong compositions with personal meaning. The course includes techniques for taking photos using digital SLR cameras and editing those photos using open-source software. When students leave this course, they will be able to take good, meaningful photos on any device. Proficiencies covered: create, respond, and connect.
prerequisites: Art I
notes: Note: This course requires lots of work done outside of class!

description: In this course, students will explore tools and programs for creating digital artworks. The course includes digital drawing, basic animation, digital photography and editing, and various types of digital design. The work for this course will primarily be done in ProCreate on iPads. Proficiencies covered: create, respond, and connect.
prerequisites: Art I

description: Advanced techniques in drawing and painting will be explored as will alternative media techniques. Students will examine their existing art portfolio and create new artworks in order to create a comprehensive portfolio for college applications. This course can be taken multiple times for credit. Proficiencies covered: create, respond, and connect.
prerequisites: Teacher recommendation (Drawing and Painting suggested)
notes: Note: This course is designed for highly motivated visual arts students.

description: This course explores ceramic hand-building and pottery wheel techniques. In this course students will create both functional and sculptural works. Due to the nature of the course being offered every-other year, if the course requests are greater than the number of seats available, priority will go to 11th and 12th graders. Proficiencies covered: create.
offering_note: Offered every other year (next offering is in 2026-2027)
notes: Note: Offered every other year (next offering is in 2026-2027)

description: In this elective course, students will learn multiple ways of approaching drawing and composition. With a focus on drawing, students will use various sketching techniques and other methods for planning artworks. By the end of the course, students will work to improve their skills in drawing, composition, and creative problem-solving in visual art. Proficiencies covered: create.

This course offers a flexible, student-driven environment where students can learn Art through non-traditional pathways. Specific artistic standards and proficiencies are mastered through a plan decided collaboratively by the student, counselor, Flexible Pathways Coordinator, and Art teacher. This adaptable model supports a variety of goals, ranging from credit recovery for missed core requirements to enrichment opportunities such as independent passion projects, portfolio development, capstones, or advanced studio studies that extend beyond the standard curriculum. Additionally, Cosmos “U” can provide targeted support for students engaged in career-based internships or online courses. Whether a student needs daily structure to catch up or a flexible schedule to dive deeper into a specific medium or creative process, Cosmos "U" provides the teacher oversight and resources necessary to succeed.

This class is for students who are already playing a band instrument at Riverside Middle School and/or may have studied privately, new to the district, or if you're an upper classman who played at some point in your schooling. The class will help you refine your own personal skills, but will also combine those talents creating the new "Cosmos Band”. The class will cover musical fundamentals and explore many styles of music. These students will have performances throughout the school year
prerequisites: Past experience playing a band instrument of at least one year.
notes: Duration: Every other day for the year

description: This class is for anyone who has the desire to sing in small groups and large group settings. Students will learn music and vocal fundamentals while combining their efforts to create a choir. Many styles of music will be explored, including musical theater. These students will have performances throughout the school year TBD.
notes: Duration: Every other day for the year

description: This class is for any student who wishes to test the waters in the world of music. They can explore the possibilities of starting an instrument with the potential of joining one of the performance groups in the future. Students will learn some of the basics of music structure and will be provided opportunities to try varied instruments and vocals to find out if they have the knack and desire to move forward in the music program.

This class is exactly like the title suggests. This is an opportunity to learn more about the history and styles of music in the world around us. You will study the evolution of music from Bach to Rock and how it relates to the evolution of societies around the world. We will study the big names and musical styles to create an informed consumer of the performing arts beyond High School.

An Introduction to Guitar class provides foundational skills for beginners, covering proper posture, tuning, basic chords, and essential strumming patterns for acoustic and electric instruments. Designed for beginner to novice, this course teaches students to read music, tablature, and chord diagrams to play simple songs, enhancing dexterity and confidence.

This course is an introduction to the Spanish language and culture. Students will start to develop the skills of listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students will learn to understand and communicate in the language at a basic level with simple verbal and written responses. Foundational grammar, essential sentence structures, and everyday vocabulary will be taught in this course. Students will also be introduced to customs, traditions and everyday practices of the Spanish-speaking world. By the end of the course students will be able to engage in basic conversations about themselves. A combination of texts and supplementary materials is used.

Students will build upon the basic vocabulary and grammar mastered in Spanish I. Students will expand their listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills. In this course, the difficulty of grammar structures, writing tasks, and reading texts increases. Learning Spanish requires extensive exposure to the target language and getting used to communicating in that language. Students are encouraged to fully immerse themselves in the Spanish classroom. A combination of various texts and supplementary materials is used.
prerequisites: Spanish I

description: In Spanish III, students deepen their proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, and writing acquired in Spanish I and II. This course focuses on more advanced grammar, vocabulary, and sentence structures. Students will engage with authentic texts, explore diverse cultural themes from Spanish-speaking countries, and participate in conversations on a variety of topics. Emphasis is placed on developing fluency and confidence through consistent practice and interaction in Spanish. By the end of the course, students will be prepared to communicate effectively in various contexts and further their language studies. This course is dual enrollment through River Valley Community College.
prerequisites: Spanish II and Teacher Recommendation

description: In this course students will expand their language skills mastered in the previous years. More complex grammatical structures are introduced and vocabulary learned in previous years is expanded and recycled. Students are called upon to speak and write with more complexity and accuracy. During this course students make every attempt to communicate in Spanish with the teacher and peers. A combination of various texts and supplementary materials is used.
prerequisites: Spanish III

description: This course is designed for students who are interested in communicating in a world language at an advanced level. Students will acquire knowledge of thematic vocabulary and more complex grammatical structures. Students are asked to speak and write with more complexity and accuracy. This course will increase students’ ability to read and appreciate literary texts in Spanish. During this course students communicate in Spanish with the teacher and peers. At the completion of the course students are expected to be able to communicate with a native speaker about everyday topics.
prerequisites: Spanish IV

description: In this course, students will work towards progress on their IEP Goals and Objectives. Both instruction and assessment will focus on developing the skills identified within student’s the IEP. Progress will be reported quarterly on the IEP. Instructional topics may include math, reading, writing, social emotional learning and executive function depending on the needs of the individual.
prerequisites: Students MUST be on an IEP as this course is one method for receiving specialized instruction as outlined in the IEP.

description: The Academic Resource Center, also known as ARC, is a classroom in which students in grades 9-12 receive additional resources and study strategies to further their academic potential and success. Weekly mini-lessons are provided to teach and provide practice in organization, study, and literacy strategies such as active reading, using graphic organizers as a pre-writing strategy, etc. The bulk of the time is given to students to work on their academic course work with assistance from the ARC teacher. The mission of ARC is to provide a space where all students feel safe to seek assistance on their learning journey in a welcoming and respectful classroom; it is a place where questions can be asked, concepts revisited and reviewed, and students’ work, with guidance, to reach their academic potential.
This course provides support and preparation for mainstream classes to students in which English is not the primary language spoken in their home.
prerequisites: For students in which English is not the primary language spoken at home.

description: In this course, students will be exposed to a variety of concepts to help them prepare for life after high school. Units may include topics in digital citizenship, media literacy, career exploration, executive functioning skill-building, and more. This course may include in-town field trips to the Department of Labor office and/or local industries.
prerequisites: Aimed at 9th/10th grade students. Strongly recommended prior to completing a Work-Based Learning experience.

description:
In this full-year course, students will learn and gain reading and writing skills in English in a manner designed to address their individual learning needs. This is a modified course that uses a variety of texts to address the PBGRs defined by Springfield High School. By the end of the course, students will develop their reading comprehension and writing skills (including but not limited to grammar, usage, and mechanics). Students will also complete a research project in which they will read for understanding, evaluate sources to determine their reliability, and develop writing pieces requiring them to synthesize information from different sources into a cohesive written report. Skills gained within this course will assist students after graduation in gaining meaningful employment or skills to continue on to post-secondary education. Reading, writing, language, and research proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
Part I will be offered to students in 9th and 10th grade and will focus on building formative and foundational skills. Part II will be offered to 11th and 12th graders and will focus on life skills, which will include, but not be limited to, resume building, reading for understanding, and formal writing.
notes: Open to: All O.D.P. students and others as referred by SHS; Section: English

description:
In this course, students develop foundational algebraic thinking and number sense needed for daily life and future employment. Instruction focuses on understanding numbers, operations, and patterns, with an emphasis on practical application rather than abstract theory. Students will:
• Strengthen basic math facts and operations
• Use calculators appropriately and efficiently
• Work with variables, simple expressions, and equations
• Explore ratios, proportions, and basic graphing
• Apply algebraic reasoning to real-life problem-solving scenarios Instruction is individualized and paced according to student need. Real-world examples and hands-on activities support comprehension and engagement.
notes: Open to: All 9-10 ODP students and others as referred by SHS; Section: Mathematics Course Sequence

description:
This course emphasizes spatial reasoning, measurement, and practical geometry skills used in everyday life and the workplace. Students learn to recognize and apply geometric concepts through hands-on and visual learning experiences. Students will:
• Identify and describe basic geometric shapes and figures
• Develop measurement skills including length, area, volume, and perimeter
• Understand time, scheduling, and elapsed time
• Apply geometry concepts to real-world tasks such as construction, layout, and design
• Use tools and technology, including calculators and measurement instruments Instruction is individualized, with a focus on functional applications that support independence and vocational readiness.
notes: Open to: All 9-10 ODP students and others as referred by SHS; Section: Mathematics Course Sequence

description:
This course builds students’ ability to collect, interpret, and use data to make informed decisions. Emphasis is placed on understanding information commonly encountered in the workplace and daily life. Students will:
• Collect, organize, and interpret data using charts and graphs
• Understand basic probability and risk
• Explore averages, trends, and comparisons
• Apply statistical thinking to real-world scenarios such as surveys, production data, and quality control
• Develop problem-solving and critical thinking skills Project-based learning is a core component of this course, allowing students to apply statistical concepts in meaningful, hands-on ways.
prerequisites: Algebra Foundations or Geometry and Measurement
notes: Open to: All 11-12th ODP students and others as referred by SHS; Section: Mathematics Course Sequence

description:
This course focuses on practical financial skills necessary for independent living and employment. Students apply math skills through real-world financial decision-making and business-based projects. Students will:
• Develop budgeting, saving, and spending skills
• Understand banking, wages, taxes, and payroll concepts
• Explore personal finance topics such as credit, loans, and consumer responsibility
• Apply math skills through business simulations and projects
• Strengthen problem-solving, planning, and organizational skills Project-based learning is emphasized. Students may participate in small business projects (such as a bread, coffee, or popcorn business), allowing them to apply math, teamwork, and workplace skills in authentic settings.
prerequisites: Algebra Foundations or Geometry and Measurement
notes: Open to: All 11-12th ODP students and others as referred by SHS; Section: Mathematics Course Sequence

description:
This course introduces students to basic life science concepts with a focus on health, human body systems, and everyday biological processes. Instruction emphasizes understanding how science connects to personal wellness, caregiving, and workplace expectations. Students will:
• Explore basic human body systems and personal health
• Understand nutrition, hygiene, and disease prevention
• Identify living vs. non-living things
• Learn about plants, animals, and ecosystems
• Develop observation and classification skills Hands-on activities, visual supports, and real-life examples are used to support comprehension and independence.
notes: Open to: All 9-10th ODP students; Section: Science Course Sequence

description:
This course focuses on foundational concepts of physical science that relate directly to everyday life and work environments. Emphasis is placed on safety, cause-and-effect relationships, and practical problem-solving. Students will:
• Identify properties of matter (solids, liquids, gases)
• Explore changes in matter and basic chemical reactions
• Understand forms of energy (heat, light, sound, electricity)
• Learn about forces, motion, and simple machines
• Apply science concepts to workplace and home safety Instruction includes hands-on experiments, demonstrations, and applied learning connected to real-world contexts.
notes: Note: This and the previous foundational course will rotate years; Open to: All 9-10th ODP students; Section: Science Course Sequence

description:
This course helps students understand the relationship between humans and the environment, emphasizing responsibility, conservation, and community awareness. Students explore how environmental decisions impact daily life and the workplace. Students will:
• Learn about natural resources and conservation
• Understand recycling, waste management, and sustainability
• Explore weather, climate, and natural hazards
• Examine human impact on ecosystems
• Apply environmental concepts to school, home, and community settings Project-based learning may include school or community sustainability projects, gardening, or environmental audits.
prerequisites: Either Life Skills & Living Systems OR Matter, Energy & Safety (foundational courses)
notes: Open to: All 11-12th ODP students; Section: Science Course Sequence

description:
This course integrates science concepts with vocational skills and workplace applications. Students apply scientific reasoning to problem-solving, safety procedures, and technology use in employment-related settings. Students will:
• Apply scientific concepts to vocational tasks
• Understand workplace tools, machines, and basic technology
• Practice safety procedures and hazard awareness
• Explore cause-and-effect in real-world systems
• Develop inquiry and problem-solving skills Hands-on projects and simulations allow students to apply science knowledge in authentic vocational and life contexts.
prerequisites: Either Life Skills & Living Systems OR Matter, Energy & Safety (foundational courses)
notes: Note: This course will rotate years with the Environmental course; Open to: All 11-12th ODP students; Section: Science Course Sequence

description: The first year course places an emphasis on transferable skills, how to be a good high school student, and how those same skills will help lead to success in the workplace. Students will examine their interests through a variety of activities and career interest inventories, and will start building goals for themselves as they start to think about life after high school. Sociology, Economics, and Inquiry proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
notes: Open to: 1st year O.D.P. students

description: During the second year of study, students will work on developing pre-employment skills such as understanding help-wanted ads, talking on the phone with an employer, completing different kinds of job applications, completing interest inventories, and building resumes. Students will also do some video job exploration, analyzing work expectations, available jobs they may not have considered, and educational requirements for a variety of rewarding careers. Sociology, Economics, and Inquiry proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
prerequisites: Pre-Vocational I
notes: Open to: 2nd year O.D.P. students

description: The final year of Pre-Voc is designed to prepare students for job placement and life after graduation. Areas of study will include: choosing an occupation, finding a job, keeping a job, and management of work and adult responsibilities, such as accepting constructive criticism and learning appropriate behaviors at the workplace. In addition, they will explore topics related to budgeting, basic credit/debit card skills, accessing community resources, and planning and preparing meals. By the end of the course, students will have an understanding of the components of an independent, adult life. Sociology, Economics, Inquiry, Number and Quantity, and Health proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
prerequisites: Pre-Vocational I and II
notes: Open to: 3rd and 4th year O.D.P. students

description: This is an orientation to shop safety regulations with units on measuring, using basic hand tools, and some power tools, and different building materials. Small projects will be the vehicle for learning individual and group skills. Students will learn about refinishing furniture and how they can flip furniture for personal use or for profit. Students will have a final project, which will require the use of a variety of tools and materials. Engineering, Modeling with Geometry, Create, Perform, Present proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
notes: Open to: Grades 9-12 (preference to grade 9)

description:
This course provides students with individualized, hands-on instruction in practical life skills needed for independent living and successful community participation. Students learn to plan, shop for, and prepare meals, maintain living spaces, manage personal hygiene and health, budget money, and organize recreation and leisure activities. Instruction emphasizes real-world application through classroom projects and community-based experiences such as visits to stores, laundromats, and other local resources, helping students build independence, problem-solving skills, and self-confidence.
ODP Life Management (Independent Living & Community Skills, Grades 9–12)
• Plan, shop for, and prepare meals independently
• Maintain personal living spaces and hygiene routines
• Budget and manage money for daily living needs
• Apply problem-solving and decision-making in community settings
• Organize and participate in recreation, leisure, and wellness activities
• Demonstrate independence, safety, and self-management in daily life
notes: Open to: Grades 9-12

description:
This is a two-part sequence in nutrition, food preparation, consumerism, and food presentation. Students are introduced to the concepts of safety and sanitation; food selection, care, storage, and proper usage; measurements, nutrition, baking basics, and simple food preparation. Health proficiencies are being addressed in this course.
Major Topics or Themes: (additional topics may be covered)
• Kitchen safety and sanitation
• Nutrition
• Reading recipes
• Using standard cooking measurements
• Baking
notes: Open to: All O.D.P. students

description:
On-the-Job Training (OJT) is a community-based learning experience designed to support high school students with disabilities as they develop the skills, confidence, and independence needed for successful employment. Through a combination of classroom instruction and supervised work placements, students gain real-world experience in job settings aligned with their interests, abilities, and long-term goals.
In this course, students learn essential workplace skills such as communication, problem-solving, teamwork, time management, and self-advocacy. Classroom instruction reinforces practical concepts including workplace expectations, safety procedures, professionalism, and career exploration. Instruction also includes foundational banking and financial skills connected to employment, such as understanding paychecks, using bank accounts, managing deposits and withdrawals, tracking earnings, and practicing responsible use of debit cards and other financial tools. Students apply both workplace and financial skills at their job sites with guidance from teachers, job coaches, and employer partners. The OJT program emphasizes individualized, strengths-based instruction with appropriate accommodations and gradual skill development. By the end of the course, students will have built a work portfolio, gained hands-on employment experience, and developed foundational work and money-management skills to support competitive employment or continued career training after high school.
prerequisites: Pre-Voc I and II
notes: Open to: 3rd-year O.D.P. students or 11th-grade status

description:
On-the-Job Training (OJT) is a community-based learning experience designed to support high school students with disabilities as they develop the skills, confidence, and independence needed for successful employment. Through a combination of classroom instruction and supervised work placements, students gain real-world experience in job settings aligned with their interests, abilities, and long-term goals.
In this course, students learn essential workplace skills such as communication, problem-solving, teamwork, time management, and self-advocacy. Classroom instruction reinforces practical concepts including workplace expectations, safety procedures, professionalism, and career exploration. Instruction also includes foundational banking and financial skills connected to employment, such as understanding paychecks, using bank accounts, managing deposits and withdrawals, tracking earnings, and practicing responsible use of debit cards and other financial tools. Students apply both workplace and financial skills at their job sites with guidance from teachers, job coaches, and employer partners. The OJT program emphasizes individualized, strengths-based instruction with appropriate accommodations and gradual skill development. By the end of the course, students will have built a work portfolio, gained hands-on employment experience, and developed foundational work and money-management skills to support competitive employment or continued career training after high school.
prerequisites: Pre-Voc I, II, and III
notes: Open to: 4th year O.D.P. students or 12th grade status

description:
This course focuses on understanding and managing emotions while building the interpersonal skills necessary for healthy relationships in all areas of life: with peers, family, teachers, supervisors, and community members. We will emphasize relationship skill building and maintaining by exploring concepts like empathy, perspective-taking, effective communication, and conflict resolution. The goal is for students to develop a strong sense of self, understand their social impact, and cultivate the skills to form and sustain meaningful, positive connections.
Key Skill Areas: Self-Awareness & Self-Management
• Identifying and labeling personal emotions and triggers.
• Developing appropriate coping and stress-reduction strategies.
• Understanding personal strengths and areas for growth. Social Awareness & Empathy
• Recognizing verbal and non-verbal social cues (tone of voice, body language).
• Taking another person's perspective in different scenarios.
• Showing respect and understanding for diverse backgrounds and viewpoints. Relationship Skills & Communication
• Initiating and maintaining positive conversations.
• Practicing active listening skills.
• Assertively communicating needs and boundaries.
• Offering and appropriately receiving constructive feedback. Responsible Decision-Making & Conflict Resolution
• Identifying problems in relationships and generating solutions.
• Using a step-by-step process to resolve disagreements respectfully.
• Understanding the importance of compromise and when to seek mediation.
notes: Open to: 9-12

description:
This course is designed to equip students with the "brain-based" skills needed to plan, organize, manage time, and successfully complete tasks in school, at home, and in future workplace settings. We will focus on developing the internal tools necessary for self-regulation and independent action. Students will learn practical strategies to improve working memory, task initiation, sustained attention, goal setting, and organizational habits. Mastery of these skills is crucial for transitioning from high school into adult life and employment.
Key Skill Areas: Organization & Planning
• Using planners/digital tools effectively.
• Breaking large tasks (projects, long-term assignments) into manageable steps.
• Organizing physical and digital materials (binder, drive). Time Management & Prioritization
• Estimating the time needed for tasks.
• Setting realistic deadlines and meeting them.
• Distinguishing between 'must do,' 'should do,' and 'can wait. Task Initiation & Sustained Attention
• Overcoming procrastination and starting tasks promptly.
• Minimizing distractions and maintaining focus.
• Developing self-monitoring strategies to check work. Cognitive Flexibility & Goal Setting
• Adjusting plans when faced with unexpected changes or setbacks.
• Using feedback constructively to improve performance.
• Setting and tracking simple, measurable short-term goals (e.g., SMART goals).
notes: Open to: 9-12

description: This is an introductory course that is designed to present students with an awareness of the process of film production by studying curriculum units focused on screenwriting, art direction, cinematography, visual effects, sound and music, and more. Students will view and analyze a variety of films, short subjects, animation, and documentaries. A final project in an area of film production chosen by the student is required.
notes: Open to: Grades 9-12

description: This course will be an in-depth overview of early American history through WWII. Units may include the European exploration (“discovery”) of America, the first European settlements of America, the triangle trade, the 13 original colonies, the American Revolution, the War of 1812. From there the Mexican-American , Civil, Spanish American Wars may be discussed ending with WWI and WWII. History and Civics proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
notes: Open to: Grades 9-12

description: A simple approach to understanding the world of visual arts. Students will be exposed to a broad range of imagery, media, artists, and periods of history. This course illustrates the meaning of art in social and cultural life throughout history. Students will learn about different media and styles. They will have the opportunity to experience hands-on learning by creating a variety of art projects. The goal is for students to become more confident in their visual literacy. Visual and Performing Arts, Respond, Connect Personal, Connect Cultural proficiencies will be addressed in this course.
prerequisites: Based on intensity of need
notes: Open to: Grades 9-12

description:
This course provides explicit, individualized instruction in foundational literacy and communication skills necessary for academic learning, employment, and daily life. Instruction focuses on reading, writing, speaking, and listening through multi-sensory, structured, and functional approaches. Students will develop skills in:
• Letter–sound relationships and word recognition
• Reading comprehension using adapted and high-interest texts

course_name: Introduction to Advanced Manufacturing and Engineering
description: Almost everything we touch, use and even eat on a daily basis is somehow connected to manufacturing. Manufacturing is the foundation for all other industries. Engineering is the application of scientific principles and practices to real world problems, to find solutions. Introduction to Advanced Manufacturing and Engineering provides tools and technologies to make these solutions a reality. You can’t have one without the other. This introductory course will allow students to explore the many types of engineering and manufacturing in a “hands-on” way. Students will design and build robots, program and fly drones, build single-cylinder motors and learn to use parametric modeling software and 3D printers. They will also learn how to use a variety of hand and machine tools to make products out of a variety of materials. This class is for anyone who has wondered how to take an idea from your head and make it a reality.
notes: Instructor: Mr. Gray; Section: RVTC Foundation Courses (open to grades 9-12 for 2026-2027)

Students will explore wildlife and their habitats, develop bird-watching skills for data collection through Project Feederwatch, and gain introductory knowledge in wildlife identification, and habitat management. This course offers an engaging blend of science, nature, and practical application - perfect for students eager to learn by doing.

description: Students enrolled in RVTC programs have the opportunity to take their education beyond the classroom through the Co-op program. Once the classroom teacher feels you’re ready, you can be placed at a worksite related to your technical program. The work experience can be after school or during school as a substitute for part of your technical program. Work-based learning experiences may be paid or unpaid, depending on the placement. Students earn one additional elective credit for every 180 hours of time on the job (maximum of three credits per year). Students are required to document work hours; work hours may be transferable toward completion of Vermont Registered Apprenticeship Programs. Students must remain enrolled in an RVTC program and may not schedule other classes during RVTC program time to be in the Cooperative Education program.

description:
In the Pre Tech program at RVTC, you get to tackle real-world problems and work with tools and materials hands-on. It’s all about building the skills you’ll need for your future career. In the first part of the school year, you’ll explore the different career clusters at RVTC and practice employable skills in each of those areas. The second half of the school year you will choose a career that inspires you and create your own project based on that career.
In Pre Tech, we team up with other RVTC programs to solve technical challenges. We also visit different local employers to help you discover some of the careers that suit you. From childcare to welding, computer disassembly to cooking, video shooting to designing and marketing products - we cover a lot! If you like mixing academic and hands-on learning, or are interested in technical education, or if you’re just trying to figure out your path in life, Pre Tech is the place to be!.
If you learn best by balancing academic and hands-on learning styles, or believe you have a future in technical education, or just want to figure out what to do with your life, then Pre Tech is the place for you!

description:
In your first year of the Business Management and Entrepreneurship program, students delve into the fundamental aspects of business, with a primary emphasis on establishing a robust financial foundation. The opening focus of the year is on Personal Financial Management, where students gain a comprehensive understanding of their individual finances. This knowledge serves as a crucial precursor to handling the financial intricacies of a business.
Transitioning into the second semester, the program’s curriculum strategically pivots toward the dynamic realm of Digital Marketing. Throughout the semester, students gain valuable insights into contemporary marketing methodologies, digital platforms, and emerging trends that are instrumental in crafting effective and impactful marketing campaigns.
Students not only grasp theoretical concepts but also acquire practical experience by actively participating in Campus Connection, the school store. This hands-on involvement allows them to apply the acquired knowledge in a real-world setting, enhancing their skills and preparing them for the dynamic challenges of the business environment.

description:
In Business Management and Entrepreneurship II students delve deeper into the multifaceted world of business operations. The first semester of the course unfolds as an immersive exploration into the realm of Small Business Management. During this phase, students actively engage in a hands-on business simulation, designed to replicate the challenges inherent to starting and sustaining a small business venture.
Transitioning into the second semester the focus shifts to QuickBooks, a preeminent financial accounting software widely embraced across various industries. Through interactive modules, students gain practical experience in utilizing QuickBooks, honing their skills in financial tracking, reporting, and analysis. The emphasis on QuickBooks not only enhances students' proficiency In essence, the Business Management & Entrepreneurship II course transcends traditional learning paradigms, providing students with a holistic and experiential education that prepares them to navigate the complexities of contemporary business environments with confidence and proficiency.

description:
The manufacturing portion of Advanced Manufacturing and Engineering Level I will introduce you to machine tools, measuring instruments, and machining operations, and how they relate to the production of consumer goods. We’ll study the industrial models of both “job shops” and “production plants” and their relationship between engineering, design, production control, and manufacturing. Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM) and robotics will also be covered.
In the engineering portion of Advanced Manufacturing and Engineering I will focus on design communication through the learning of SolidWorks parametric modeling software. It will also address many of the foundational elements and principles of engineering such as force, acceleration, mass, power and trajectory.
The first-year curriculum was designed to be preparing students for the nationally recognized NIMS credentialing exams in seven machining areas. It will also prepare students to take the Certified SolidWorks Associate certification exam. In addition, we encourage students to build youth leadership skills by participating in our local and state chapters of SkillsUSA and competing in skill and leadership events at all levels.
prerequisites: Algebra I or concurrent enrollment
fulfills_text: Embedded credits: 3 elective credits
notes: Scheduled: Full year, 2 hours per day; Open to: Grades 10-12; Section: Technical programs

description:
The strong engineering focus of the first semester of AM&E II is placed on digital electronics and advanced solid modeling (SolidWorks). Students will experience all aspects of digital electronics through hands-on breadboarding and simulation software. Students will build a variety of digital projects and also learn to build and program microcontrollers like Arduino. Advanced robotic programming and construction will also be highlighted in Level II. Engineering Design and Development is the senior capstone of the PLTW curriculum. Students normally dedicate their entire fourth quarter to this independent, industry-driven capstone project and are evaluated by industry professionals upon its completion.
On the manufacturing side of the curriculum, students will become proficient in Mastercam computer aided manufacturing software as well as develop skills in setting up, operating and programming 3,4 and 5 axis CNC machines. Additive manufacturing (3D printing) is also emphasized in the heavily, lab-based curriculum. Several NIMS credentials are available in both CNC Turning and CNC Milling. The use and programming of Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM) and its related software (Verisurf) is also taught in year two. Field trips, job shadows and internships are also an integral part of the year two curriculum.
prerequisites: Grade of 70 or better in Advanced Manufacturing and Engineering I

description: Health Sciences Level One students will study a wide range of subjects. Students examine the history of healthcare, complementary and alternative modalities, and learn medical terminology, the language most speak in healthcare. Lessons will include the body’s systems as students begin learning about the diseases and disorders affecting each system using a hands-on approach. Students will be certified in CPR/First Aid/AED, Blood Borne Pathogens, HIPAA, and Stop the Bleed. One highlight of the year is job shadowing, which allows the students to spend time with employers in the workplace, observing the ins and outs of each potential career pathway. Level one provides opportunity for dual enrollment with River Valley Community College, an option that offers three (3) transferable college credits in Medical Terminology.

description:
This program introduces students to a wide range of forest management practices and the foundational skills needed for careers in natural resources. The curriculum builds proficiency in key areas including dendrology (tree and leaf identification), basic wildlife and fisheries management, tree growth, introductory geology, the water and nutrient cycles, timber harvesting, forest inventory techniques, and map-and-compass navigation (orienteering). Students also receive training in tractor safety and maintenance, chainsaw operation and safety, and preparation for annual FFA competitions.
In addition, students participate in the Northeast Woodland Training Game of Logging certification program, gaining industry-recognized credentials, and take part in field trips that reinforce classroom learning.
Through this program students develop the technical knowledge, professional vocabulary, and practical skills essential for success in natural resource careers.

description:
Level II students will build on the skills developed in Level I while exploring advanced topics such as forest insects and diseases, Wildland fire ecology and management, and enhanced map-and-compass orienteering. They will also create a comprehensive forest management plan that includes both forestry and wildlife management goals. Students will also develop a business plan, deepening their understanding of real-world industry practices.
Students will have opportunities to participate in job shadowing and cooperative work experiences, providing valuable insight into careers in natural resources. Field trips further enrich their learning by exposing them to professional environments and hands-on applications. FFA membership continues in Level II, offering additional opportunities for leadership development and career growth.
prerequisites: Grade of 70 or better in Horticulture and Natural Resources I or written instructor permission

description:
Industrial Trades provides opportunities for students in four different trade areas. All students work with blueprints, learning how to sketch, read, and build from them. We emphasize workplace safety and practical application of skills in Electrical, Plumbing, HVAC and Welding. Welding units include Stick, MIG, TIG, Oxy-Acetylene cutting, Plasma cutting, and fabrication skills. During the Electrical focus, students will design and build a small section of wall to run electrical boxes and light switches. During the Plumbing focus, students will learn how to mock up a basic sink on a pedestal. The HVAC focus will be on learning about constructing sheet metal ducts. They will also learn about CNC plasma and how to fabricate structural and non-structural projects throughout the year.
If you are interested or are considering a career as an electrician, plumber, HVAC technician, welder, general property manager, physical plant manager, contractor, Industrial Trades is the ideal match for you. The class is limited to 16 students to provide plenty of hands-on lab projects and individual instruction to meet the individual needs of the students. At the end of the two-year program, you will have a step-up to start your next step in a career or in pursuing further training in your chosen industry.
prerequisites: Basic Algebra and Geometry Skills
notes: Scheduled: Full Year, 2 hours per day; Open to: Grades 10, 11 and 12 (sophomores require an interview); Section: Technical programs

description:
After successfully completing Industrial Trades I, students will choose either a cooperative work placement or staying in the lab to further their welding skills. Specific learning will explore the details of their chosen field. During the second quarter, students will learn the fine art of interviewing, resume writing, cover letters and job/career searches. During the second semester, students will concentrate in one of the many areas in Industrial Trades. Students are also eligible to enroll in the evening electrical and plumbing-related apprenticeship classes starting their licensing requirements immediately while still in high school, giving them a huge advantage when searching for employment.
Using a hands-on, independent approach to a variety of performance-based projects, they will be prepared for cooperative work placements, apprenticeships, and leadership skills including participation in local, state, and national SkillsUSA activities. Graduates may continue further educational opportunities to obtain industry certifications (such as plumbing and electrical licenses or HVAC and American Welding Society certifications), including two or four-year college programs or apprenticeship training, or they may seek entry-level positions within the trade areas.
prerequisites: Grade of 70 or better in Industrial Trades I or written instructor permission

description: Technology Essentials is a class centered around various software and technical skills needed for basic computer literacy. We begin with Industry-standard programs Adobe Photoshop and Adobe Illustrator to manipulate images and vector graphics. Students can earn college credit through River Valley Community College in New Hampshire and take the Adobe Graphics course in addition to the Web Design course. Students build website pages with HTML and CSS using Adobe Dreamweaver and Notepad, then explore javascript and python programming. This class is creative and engaging and prepares students for graphic design, web design, or programming careers. Microcontrollers like Arduino, Raspberry Pi, Micro:bit and mBots and cyberbots allow students to interact and invent with technology.

description:
Students explore with hands-on learning in the lab to develop an in-depth knowledge of computer components and operating systems. Students learn to build a complete computer system through a combination of a lab classroom and hands-on activities, ordering parts, assembling and configuring a computer, installing software, and troubleshooting both hardware and software problems. They discover best practices in maintenance, safety issues and take full responsibility for maintaining computer equipment in the classroom and lab. The students work primarily on Windows machines and are exposed to Macintosh and Linux systems. Students compete in CyberStart at local, state and national levels. When completing the program, they are prepared for a national certification exam, CompTIA’s IT Fundamentals, CompTIA’s A+ Core 1 & 2, and may earn up to three college credits at the River Valley Community College.
Hands-On is an exciting look into the inner workings of the technology we use every day. It’s a chance to learn how to manage, repair, and even build computers from their separate components. We understand how to fix printers and manage networks, skills needed for businesses everywhere. Not only can students take their CompTIA IT Fundamentals certification exam, opening countless job opportunities, but we can also come to understand the technology seen everywhere in modern life.
prerequisites: Keyboarding skills; Basic computer navigation skills

description: The focus and content of this course, which satisfies the 12th grade English requirement, will shift markedly by semester. In semester 1, emphasis will be placed on personal essays that conform to the prescriptions of the Common Application, although students may tailor their work for alternative purposes. Time will be devoted to developing college-level vocabulary and designing creative projects that employ that vocabulary. College-level research tools will also be introduced. Semester 2 will be more differentiated; students will be able to propose and pursue their own projects, so long as they demonstrate critical reading and writing skills in these pursuits. Conceptually, the course will pose questions about trends in popular culture and our individual responsibilities therein. Throughout the year, we will examine literature and film dealing with this theme.

We will examine filmmaking choices, critical responses, and their social and cultural ramifications. Students will learn to use the extended vocabulary of literary analysis to explore issues such as identity, gender, and conflict and develop essential understandings about fiction, character development, society, and the art of storytelling.

Students will also explore techniques for researching and crafting speeches, as well as receiving constructive feedback to improve their delivery. By the end of the course, students will be prepared to speak with clarity and confidence in a variety of settings, from classroom presentations to future public speaking opportunities.

description: Graphic Design Level III: Designed to teach the students the fundamental operational and mechanical skills necessary for working simultaneously in both Adobe programs, Photoshop and Illustrator. The class is structured to introduce students to the illustrative section of graphic images and to teach the students how to combine the two programs to achieve quality illustrations. The students learn how to develop an eye for design and investigate the essential organizational skills while being trained in both Adobe Programs, Photoshop and Illustrator. Students gain an understanding of the illustrative portion of Graphic Design Program through customary projects grounded in rendering techniques to effectively generate self-portraits, expressive caricatures, and book illustrations and graphic novels.
prerequisites: Successful completion of the prior level
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Arts

description: Graphic Design Level IV: Designed to further a student who is seriously interested in Graphic Design. The student works on independent projects that will further the students technical and visual design skills in both Adobe programs, Photoshop and Illustrator. The class is structured to introduce students to the commercial section of graphic images. The students learn how to develop an eye for design and investigate the essential organizational skills while being trained in-both Adobe Programs, Photoshop and Illustrator. Students gain an understanding of the commercial portion of graphic images through customary projects grounded in package design and other technically complex projects. Students develop package designs for products and learn about the visual and symbolic prerequisites for selling a product.
prerequisites: Successful completion of the prior level
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Arts

description: In Ceramics I, students will explore the creative and technical aspects of clay through handbuilding techniques and ceramic design application. This introductory course provides a foundation in the art of ceramics, encouraging students to experiment with form, texture, and design while developing a deeper understanding of the materials and processes involved in creating pottery and sculptural works. Throughout the semester, students will learn to manipulate clay through methods such as pinch pots, coils, and slabs. Emphasis will be placed on developing fine motor skills, artistic expression, and craftsmanship. Students will also explore various glazing and surface design techniques in order to bring their clay creations to life with color and texture.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Arts

description: Ceramics II, III, and IV is designed for students who have developed a foundational understanding of clay and wish to deepen their skills and explore their artistic voice in a more self-directed environment. Building on techniques learned in Ceramics I, these classes emphasize independent work, creative exploration, and the development of a personal style. Students will be encouraged to push their technical and artistic boundaries through a variety of handbuilding and wheel throwing techniques, with an increased focus on refinement, complexity, and innovation. Throughout these courses, students will have the opportunity to work on individual projects, setting their own goals and exploring ideas that reflect their unique interests and artistic vision. Emphasis will be placed on self-direction, allowing students to take ownership of their creative process while continuing to grow in technical proficiency and confidence. In addition to mastering advanced ceramic techniques, students will engage in critical self-reflection, peer critiques, and group discussions to foster a collaborative environment that supports artistic growth. Success in this course requires students to practice studio habits such as knowledge and care for tools and materials, work completion, time management and contributing to the cleanliness and safety of the studio space.

The course will cover an array of mediums, including printmaking, screenprinting, bookmaking, collage, and experimental assemblage. Students will have the opportunity to combine 2D and 3D elements, pushing the boundaries of traditional art forms. Emphasis will be placed on personal expression and hands-on experimentation, encouraging students to integrate different materials and processes to create unique works of art. By the end of the course, students will have developed a broader understanding of how to merge various techniques into cohesive, innovative pieces . In addition to the exploration of new media, students will engage in critical self-reflection, peer critiques, and group discussions to foster a collaborative environment that supports artistic growth. Success in this course requires students to practice studio habits such as knowledge and care for tools and materials, work completion, time management and contributing to the cleanliness and safety of the studio space.

description: World History 9 is an examination of history from early humans to approximately 1800. It explores the themes of trade, empire building, belief system creation, and expansion. The course's foundation is historical study and therefore dedicates significant time to analysis and evaluation of primary and secondary sources as well as other methodologies of academic history. Students will demonstrate their learning in diverse ways, with a strong foundation in writing and discussion skills.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Global Citizenship

description: 19th and 20th Century World History explores the ideas and events that got the world to where it is today. The course engages in deep dives into topics such as the French and Industrial Revolutions, Imperialism, Nationalism, and modern developments in the 20th century. The course will dedicate significant time to analysis and evaluation of primary and secondary sources as well as other methodologies of academic history. Students will demonstrate their learning in diverse ways, with a strong foundation in writing and discussion skills. The course culminates in a student driven project that focuses on Inquiry, Research & Communication skills.
prerequisites: World History 9
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Global Citizenship

description: Students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes from 1200 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical connections; and utilizing reasoning about comparison, causation, and continuity and change over time. The course provides six themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: humans and the environment, cultural developments and interactions, governance, economic systems, social interactions and organization, and technology and innovation. Students also learn to write intentionally to score on AP specific rubrics and to develop test taking methods of reducing selections for multiple choice. These skills are essential to narrowing the scope of World History knowledge to address pertinent questions and relevant key words in prompts to help higher performance on the exam.
prerequisites: World History 9
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Global Citizenship
notes: Recommended a grade of 85 or higher in World History 9 or Teacher recommendation.

description: US History focuses on in-depth analysis of major themes of the US history era including economic, social and political history, foreign and domestic policy, as well as race, ethnicity, gender and sexuality. The course will primarily take a historical lens, though we will spend significant time exploring civics and geography as well. Woven through it all is the development of inquiry skills; building in all of us the skills and ability to ask questions of the world around us, develop arguments and analyze the arguments of others. The course is designed such that as we progress, more freedom is given to students to develop their own questions, though there may be a guiding topic or purpose.
prerequisites: World History 10 or AP World History
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Global Citizenship

description: In AP U.S. History, students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in nine historical periods from approximately 1491 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical connections; and utilizing reasoning about comparison, causation, and continuity and change. The course also provides eight themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: American and national identity; work, exchange, and technology; geography and the environment; migration and settlement; politics and power; America in the world; American and regional culture; and social structures.
prerequisites: World History 10 or AP World History
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Global Citizenship
notes: Recommended a grade of 85 or higher in AP World History or World History 10 or Teacher recommendation.

description: This course will explore the ideas, theories, and methods of the scientific study of behavior and mental processes. Students will examine the concepts of psychology through reading and discussion and will analyze data from psychological research studies. Students will connect psychological concepts and theories to real-life scenarios and understand and interpret data. Through inquiry and critical thinking students will gain insight and awareness of human development, emotion and motivation, how we acquire knowledge, how our mind perceives and processes the world, and how we are all affected by where and how we live.
prerequisites: World History 10 or AP World History
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Global Citizenship
notes: Recommended a grade of 85 or higher in AP World History or World History 10 or teacher recommendation.

course_name: Current Issues and World Affairs I
description: In this course, we will be exploring the current state of the globe on a variety of flexible topics based on what is presently happening in the nation and world at large. From wars, natural disasters, and social injustices to cultural developments, elections, and technology, the course will discuss which topics are presently developing in our local and global communities. Within the structure of the course, we will focus on several key, reoccurring themes, including political systems in action, international relations and cultures, local and global economies at work, and connecting local and global issues. There will also be a primary focus on how we obtain and utilize a variety of news information. This will involve exploring how to best research and comprehending biases from certain sources and perspectives and how that informs views. To be successful in this course, students will have an interest in discussing and analyzing developments in our modern world while also looking to connect world history and future predictions for how events develop. Our main academic focuses will include discussion, reflection, and research, so students should be ready to work self-sufficiently and consider their personal perspective. This course will be invaluable for anyone looking to discuss and explore what is currently happening as well as knowing how to best obtain and approach information. Students may take CIWA II, III, & IV as the topics discussed change based on student interest and context.
prerequisites: World History 10 or AP World History
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Global Citizenship
