description: In this course, students will explore key economic concepts like GDP, inflation, unemployment, tax policy and economic growth. They'll examine how government policies, such as fiscal and monetary actions, affect national economies and individuals' lives. Through real-world examples and current events, students will develop a deeper understanding of economic systems, global trade, and the role of central banks. This course helps students build critical thinking skills while exploring the major forces shaping today's global economy.
prerequisites: World History 9
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Global Citizenship

description: This course is designed for students to gain a greater understanding of money and its role in their lives and futures. The course will focus on how saving, borrowing, and investing works, the magic of compounding interest, personal finances and the consumer decision-making process. Following that, we will learn about a variety of career fields and individual jobs using widely available databases of employment and salaries, job shadowing assignments, and by hosting regular professional guest speakers. This course is essential for anyone expecting to earn a living in the future.
prerequisites: World History 9
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Global Citizenship

description: In this course, students will study the fundamental principles that govern individual markets, businesses, and consumer behavior. Topics include supply and demand, market structures, pricing strategies, and the government’s role in regulating markets. Students will also explore how factors such as incentives, competition, and resource allocation affect decision-making for consumers and producers. Through real-world examples and case studies, students will develop a deeper understanding of how economic forces shape everyday choices and the functioning of local and global markets.
prerequisites: World History 9
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Global Citizenship

description: State and Local Government introduces the structure, function and procedures for decision making at the national, state and local level with an emphasis on state and local government. This course will cultivate the knowledge, skills and dispositions in students to be engaged community members invested in the common good, community service and the issues in which they are individually invested.
prerequisites: Completion or concurrent enrollment of US History or AP US History
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Global Citizenship

description: This course is to provide students time to build on foundational mathematics skills. Topics include basic operations, fractions, factoring, percentages, solving equations, probability, and measurement. The goal of this course is to create strong mathematical understanding in order to move on to Algebra.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math

description: In Pre-Algebra, students will work to strengthen their mathematical foundations in order to be better prepared for Algebra I. Students will work on number sense, rates and ratios, and integer operations and rational numbers. These units will work to improve arithmetic skills before moving on to graphing proportional relationships, equivalent expressions and equations, and linear relationships. Pre-Algebra spends time on these algebraic skills in order to begin getting students comfortable with the abstraction that is required in Algebra I.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math

description: This course introduces many of the fundamental building blocks of high school mathematics. The topics of study will include the number system, simplifying expressions, solving and manipulating equations, linear equations, systems of linear equations, understanding and building functions, and manipulating polynomials and quadratics. Students will also spend time building connections between algebra topics and data and statistics. Students will learn to visually represent data and analyze their findings. In this course students will learn logical reasoning and problem solving skills that will be applicable in all future math courses.
prerequisites: Successful completion of 8th grade math and/or Pre-Algebra.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math

description: This course introduces the student to the second major field of mathematics. The study of geometric figures and their properties is axiomatically developed using definitions, postulates and theorems. Course content includes the study of geometric relationships in both two and three dimensions and utilizes the coordinate system to relate geometric concepts to the student’s background in algebra.
prerequisites: Algebra 1
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math

description: This is a course designed for students to continue learning concepts from Algebra 1 and to introduce new concepts in Algebra 2. The major subjects covered in this course are Functions, Linear Functions, Quadratic Functions, and various other Functions, including Polynomials. Within each Function, we will cover writing equations, solving equations and graphing. We will learn how to apply different functions to represent different real-world scenarios.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Geometry
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math

description: This course is an extension of Algebra I. The course is designed to give more of an understanding of our number system and the use of axioms in mathematical manipulation. The major subjects covered are quadratics, polynomials, set theory, identities, rational expressions, relations and functions, logarithms, trigonometry, and statistics and probability.
prerequisites: Algebra I and Geometry; Geometry may be taken concurrently
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math

description: This course is intended for those students with a strong aptitude in mathematics or for those who want to prepare for calculus and other advanced math and science courses. The first semester deals with an extension of algebra, polynomial functions, rational functions, exponential functions, and logarithms. The second semester consists of a comprehensive study of trigonometry including analytical trigonometry.
prerequisites: Algebra II and Geometry
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math

description: This course is open to those students with a strong record of mathematics achievement. The course covers a review of coordinate geometry and elementary functions and is then followed by a discussion on limits, a study of the derivative and applications, and the integral and applications. Graphing technology is used to aid learning. Science and business uses of calculus are included.
prerequisites: PreCalculus
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math

description: This is a fast-paced college level course designed to prepare students for the AP Examination in Mathematics, Calculus AB exam. The course provides excellent preparation for college mathematics, and students who do well on the AP Exam can receive up to 4 credits at the college they attend. The course covers functions and graphs, including algebraic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic functions, and the calculation of limits, as well as topics in differential and integral calculus. Science and business uses of calculus are included.
prerequisites: Pre-Calculus or Calculus
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math

description: This half-year course presents an introduction to basic statistical methods that can prepare students to take AP Statistics, if they choose, or for a college level statistics course. The course will cover topics such as distributions and graphical representations and measures of central tendency and variability, normal distribution, scatter plots, experimental design, frequency tables, and probability rules.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Geometry; May be taken with Algebra II
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math
offering_note: Math electives: offering based on demand (per pathways chart, p.25)

description: The purpose of this course is to introduce students to the major concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing, and drawing conclusions from data. Students are exposed to four broad conceptual themes: · Exploring Data: Describing patterns and departures from patterns · Sampling and Experimentation: Planning and conducting a study · Anticipated Patterns: Exploring random phenomena using probability and simulation · Statistical Inference: Estimating population parameters and testing hypotheses AP Students will be expected to take quizzes and tests throughout the courses based on the format of the actual AP stats exam (i.e. multiple choice and long answer problems). You must have a T1-84 series calculator for both Statistics and AP Statistics.
prerequisites: Algebra II OR Foundations of Algebra II and Statistics
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math

description: This one semester course will combine math and psychology to answer the overarching question: How do humans make decisions, and what types of errors take place? Students will simulate real-world game shows, and delve into different types of cognitive biases. Project-based learning will be emphasized throughout the course.
prerequisites: Algebra 1 and Geometry; may be taken with Foundations of Algebra II or Algebra II
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math
offering_note: Math electives: offering based on demand (per pathways chart, p.25)

description: This is a class designed to provide support and instruction to students who are developing their math skills. Students access this course through SHS faculty recommendation. This class can be taken multiple times, for up to 1 total math credit. Additional credits will be awarded as elective credit only.
prerequisites: Students are not able to individually register for this course but will be scheduled for the course based upon teacher recommendation.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Math
notes: Students are not able to individually register; scheduled by teacher recommendation.

description: Concert band is a musical organization, which offers instruction and playing experience for players of woodwind, brass and percussion instruments for grades 9-12. The band represents the school at various concerts and other events annually. The course includes the study of music literature through performance, developing skills in interpretation, phrasing, intonation, balance, together with the understanding of various forms and styles. Students are eligible for participation in auditioning for various festivals including the Northeastern Vermont District Music Festival and Vermont All-State Music Festival. If a student is enrolled in both band and chorus they will receive .5 band credit and .5 chorus credit.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Arts Credit
notes: Credit .5 or 1 as printed.

description: This ensemble is designed for students who enjoy singing and would like to learn more about music and vocal technique. In the course students will perform songs in three- and four-part harmony, learn basic music notation related to interpreting choral music, and develop skits in interpretation, phrasing, intonation, balance and performance. Concert selections will include music from a wide variety of cultural and historical genres. Chorus members are eligible to participate in area music festivals including the Northeastern VT District Music Festival and the Vermont All-State Music Festival. If a student is enrolled in both band and chorus they will receive .5 band credit and .5 chorus credit.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Arts Credit
notes: Credit .5 or 1 as printed.

description: From rock to folk, funk to pop, the guitar is a versatile instrument that lets artists across the world express themselves through music. In this course, we’ll be learning about the fundamental techniques needed to play the guitar as well as some related skills like music theory and songwriting.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Arts Credit

description: Students who participate in the high school musical will engage in a wide variety of skills and activities related to musical theater. Students participating as actors on stage will hone skills relating to acting, dancing, singing, and storytelling in the musical theater style. Students participating on the technical crews will work in a variety of areas, including stage managing, backstage tech crew, lighting and sound design, props, art design, hair and makeup design, photography, and playing in the live pit band. The musical is a great chance for any student to be part of theatrical production and experience the performing arts. This is not a course that students select as part of their course registration process but sign up for separately through the music department. A student may earn up to .5 credits total, each experience is worth .25 credits to meet the district/state distribution requirement for Arts in a manner other than the traditional classroom experience. Students who participate in the musical are eligible for the Alternative Arts credit and the student is responsible for completing the alternative arts form. Not eligible for community service.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Arts Credit; to meet the district/state distribution requirement for Arts in a manner other than the traditional classroom experience (up to .5 credits total)
notes: program; not selected during course registration; signed up for separately through the music department; each experience worth .25 credits; alternative arts form required

description: How do music makers capture their ideas in recorded form for us to enjoy over our speakers or headphones? In this course, students will learn about the basics of music production in this introductory course. Students will listen to and analyze landmark records, learn the basics of how to operate a digital audio workstation (DAW), and try their hand at creating their own original music. This course is open to anyone with a genuine curiosity about the process of creating recorded music. No previous musical experience is required!
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Arts Credit

course_name: Music History - A Study of The Human Affinity For Sound
description: An ancient human hit a hollow log with a stick. One thing led to another, and The Beatles released Abby Road. In this course, students will join Mr. Gagnon on a journey throughout the entirety of human history through the vehicle of music, from the first known musical compositions, to the classical masters, to the birth of hip-hop, to the new music that’s being written and performed today. Students in this course will spend time listening to music, discussing the technical aspects and historical context of important artists, songs, and styles, and doing whatever else Mr. Gagnon thinks would be fun. No previous musical experience is required!
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Arts Credit

description: Students will participate in a variety of games in teams of 3-12 players. Schedules, matchups, Tournaments, playoffs, brackets, and standings can all be used as students work with their team to succeed. Students will gain knowledge of each game including the rules and developing the understanding to referee games. Students that value a team environment will do well in this class. The games might include soccer, basketball, volleyball, wiffleball, flag football, ultimate frisbee, floor hockey, thoukball, handball, and dodgeball.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Physical Education

description: Students will participate individually or with a partner in many activities. Students who can motivate themselves and prefer to play alone will enjoy this class. Students will learn the rules for many games and also participate in some tournaments. Activities are likely based on student interest but could include tennis, pickleball, badminton, spikeball, kanjam, washers, cornhole, bocce, dance, yoga,track and field, orienteering, and outdoor activities.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Physical Education

description: Students that want to make improvements to their physical and mental health will succeed in this class. Utilizing the weight room, the outdoor track, and other PE facilities, students will spend class time learning techniques, designing workout plans, and exercising in a way to meet their goal. Students will work out almost every day with some occasional game time based on the interests of the class.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Physical Education

description: The Stowe School Board approved the earning of up to .5 credits to meet the graduation requirement for physical education, in a manner other than the traditional classroom experience. Students can receive .25 credit per a sports season they participate in. Students can earn up to .5 credit total of ALT PE credit toward graduation. To meet SHS graduation requirements students must have a total of 1 PE credit. The student can earn the remaining PE credit through SHS physical education courses. Students are responsible for completing the Alt PE form. Students are required to take one physical education course (one semester) and earn .5 credit before they can access alternative PE credit. This cannot be used to replace Health Education.
prerequisites: Students must complete the Alt. PE form
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Physical Education; to meet the graduation requirement for physical education, in a manner other than the traditional classroom experience (up to .5 credit)
notes: program; .25 credit per sports season; Alt. PE form required

description: This course's foundation is rooted in the National Health Education Standards. Students will work towards developing skills of effective communication, goal setting, analyzing influences, accessing valid and reliable information, and demonstrating health enhancing practices. Students will aim towards demonstrating proficiency in these health skills through exploration of content themes including mental and emotional health, substance use prevention, human sexuality, violence and injury prevention, and public health. By completion of the course students should demonstrate proficiency for multiple indicators identified by the Vermont Portrait of a Graduate for Health Education: learner agency, global citizenship, academic proficiency, communication, critical thinking and problem solving, and well-being.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Health

description: Culture Through Cuisine class aims to accomplish three main things. The first is teaching students nutrition through cooking healthy meals from scratch. The meals we create come from various cultures throughout the world. The second is to build the skills to make conscious food choices at the individual, societal, and environmental level. The course explores food justice concepts and examines food injustices occurring in our world in order to impact food choices. Finally the course examines personal identity and culture through exploration of the intersectionality of food and culture. Students will examine social determinants of health and how those impact our food choices, as well as work towards developing a personal food identity project. Students will be assessed on their core knowledge of nutrition, the ability to practice safe and healthy practices while cooking and in the kitchen, as well as advocacy.
prerequisites: Health
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: Earth Science is designed as a class to study phenomena at various scales across natural and human systems. During this course students will be expected to develop written communication skills to construct evidence-based arguments. As for analysis students will have to accurately develop models and perform manipulations to models to then explain scientific phenomena. Students will also be working on investigative skills that focus on error analysis centralized around human error while measuring data manually. As for content Earth Science includes understanding the existence of our universe (the Big Bang), Earth’s history and its age, Earth’s systems (plate tectonics, feature formation, weathering, & erosion), the development of weather and climate change, and studying how humans alter the Earth and how to better sustain our resources (human sustainability).
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Science

description: Biology, which students may take after successful completion of 9th grade Earth Science, utilizes investigations and independent research to introduce life science concepts and advance scientific skills. Investigations will emphasize analyzing patterns in data to identify human and systematic error. Students will independently record and manipulate data using digital sensors, tools and software. Data analysis will emphasize the creation and manipulation of models, and applying mathematical and statistical computations to determine accuracy, precision, and significance. Analysis and reasoning of these experiments will be communicated through formal lab reports and in-class tests. Major areas of content will focus on investigating ecological interdependence, modeling the structural and functional relationships of biomolecules and cells, investigating energetic enzymatic systems within organisms, modeling and analyzing genetic inheritance and expression, and finally modeling and analyzing evolutionary pressures and changes.
prerequisites: Earth Science
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Science

description: Chemistry, which students may take after successful completion of 10th grade Biology, uses an understanding of energy and forces at atomic and subatomic scales to understand our world. Investigations will develop students' chemistry-related lab skills and ability to work quantitatively with the precision necessary to be effective chemists. Analysis will build off of 10th grade skills while increasing student’s use of quantitative models and their ability to connect abstract models to fundamental scientific laws and theories. Major topics of study include gas laws, matter and energy, atomic structure, chemical bonding, mathematics of chemistry, and kinetics and equilibrium.
prerequisites: Earth Science and Biology
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Science

description: This course will cover in detail the following topics: graphical analysis, measurement, analytical methods, Newtonian Mechanics (linear motion, work energy, power and momentum), electrostatics, basic DC electric circuits, and magnetism. Students will have the opportunity to use digital sensors (motion sensors, photogate timers, smart pulley timers, force sensors, current, voltage, and resistance sensors) and associated software in order to study the topics mentioned above. The course is organized around experiments, inquiry projects and engineering projects performed in class.
prerequisites: Algebra II, Earth Science, and Biology
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Science

description: Advanced Placement Biology, offered at the high school level, is designed to reflect as closely as possible a freshman-level biology course in college. Students enrolled in this course will be expected to take the AP Examination in mid-May for advanced placement credit in college. Topics to be covered include biochemistry, cellular biology, molecular biology, molecular genetics, Mendelian genetics, evolution, taxonomy, and microbiology, the diverse characteristics of plants and animals and ecology. Laboratories will be an integral part of each of these topics. Students will be expected to do a great deal of independent study. The course will terminate by allowing students several weeks to study and work on a project of their choosing. This class will next be offered in 2027-2028
prerequisites: Biology and Earth Science. Completion or current enrollment in Algebra II. Can be taken concurrently with Chemistry or Physics.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Science
offering_note: This class will next be offered in 2027-2028 (not offered 2026-27)
notes: Recommended a grade of 85 in either Biology or Chemistry

description: This fast-paced course is designed to prepare students for the AP exam in Environmental Science and the potential for college credit. Through this course, students will learn the scientific principles, concepts, and methodologies required to understand the interrelationship of the natural world, to identify and analyze environmental problems both natural and human made, to evaluate the relative risks associated with these problems, and to examine alternative solutions for resolving and/or preventing them. This class will be offered in 2026-2027
prerequisites: Biology and Earth Science. Completion or current enrollment in Algebra II. Can be taken concurrently with Chemistry or Physics.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Science
offering_note: This class will be offered in 2026-2027
notes: Recommended a grade of 85 in Biology or Chemistry

description: Advanced Placement Physics 1, is the equivalent to a first-semester college course in algebra-based physics. The course covers Newtonian mechanics (including rotational dynamics and angular momentum); work, energy, and power; and fluids. The ability to develop and use physics knowledge by applying it to the practice of scientific inquiry and reasoning is at the heart of this physics course. Students will construct knowledge through experimenting, analyzing, making conjectures and arguments, and solving problems in a collaborative setting throughout the course. Students enrolled in this course will be expected to take the AP examination in mid-May for advanced placement credit in college. After the exam, students will have several weeks to work on an engineering design task of their choosing.
prerequisites: Earth Science, Biology, and Algebra II.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Science

description: Food science is focused on scientific phenomena and their chemical interactions. The molecules the course studies are salts, fats, carbohydrates, and proteins. Students will learn about the structure of each molecule, its interactions,why we consume them, and how they can be manipulated to achieve desired culinary outcomes. Students should have strong inquiry skills, ability to conduct experiments, data analysis, modeling, and scientific writing. Students should expect attendance to be important as the class will have frequent labs, with heavy emphasis on methods, data collection, modeling, and conclusions.
prerequisites: Earth Science
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: This class will examine the physiology, anatomy, and biochemistry of the human body, focusing on healthy minds and bodies. The course will be organized around the 11 body systems and their structure and function. Students should be advanced in their inquiry skills, ability to conduct investigations, data analysis, modeling, and scientific writing. Various units will pair body systems together to test how they impact one another like how the use of the muscular system impacts one's cardiovascular endurance. This class will include many self-designed inquiry labs that will require students to use peer-published scientific studies to understand recent discoveries in the field of physiology to help support their own conclusions. A strong science background is encouraged for those who enjoy both content and investigations.
prerequisites: Biology
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Science

description: In this semester long course students will have the opportunity to follow their own interest in learning how things work. Participants will use multiple strategies depending on interest and the object involved including: reading and research, inquiry investigations, organized disassembling of objects, and building of analogs using available materials. Interested in music? Here’s your chance to study the science of instruments. Use sound sensors to measure and visualize sound waves and develop an Inquiry investigation. Try your hand at building your own instruments. Have you wondered how motors and generators work? Take one apart, study electromagnetism and learn to build a simple one of your own. Can you maximize its torque? If you’re curious about an object there are lots to learn. This course is well suited to motivated independent students.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: S.T.E.A.M. It is a semester-long course that exposes students to the many intersections between Science, Technology, Engineering, Art/Design, and Math. During the course of the semester, students explore these fields through hands-on project-based designs, design challenges, engaging text, and other media. This course is designed to introduce students to new tools and materials, and allows for skills acquisition and gain proficiency through practice. Projects range from creating 3D models using SketchUp and TinkerCAD and a 3D printer, to DC electronics circuitry, and soldering. Students should be prepared to be introduced to and use power and hand tools, design objects using both pencil/paper and CAD software, research and then communicate solutions to common problems, and build prototypes of everything from 3D printed game pieces, to small wooden boxes, to working Bluetooth enabled stereo speakers. Other topics include: · Coding/Computer Programming · Arduino Microcontrollers/Physical Computing · Working Machines/Robotics
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Art

description: S.T.E.A.M. II, III, IV are advanced, project-driven courses designed to expand on the skills and concepts introduced in S.T.E.A.M. I. In these semester-long classes, students will deepen their understanding of the intersections between Science, Technology, Engineering, Art/Design, and Math through more complex and interdisciplinary challenges. Building upon prior knowledge, students will engage in collaborative projects that integrate advanced CAD design, robotics, programming, and circuit building. Throughout these courses, students will work on multi-step projects, where they will prototype, test, and refine solutions to real-world problems. They will use cutting-edge tools such as CNC machines, advanced 3D modeling software, and microcontroller platforms (e.g., Raspberry Pi) to create functional, innovative designs. Students will also delve into more advanced coding techniques, utilizing languages such as Python and C++ to control more sophisticated systems.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Fine Art

description: This introductory course teaches the foundations of programming with emphasis on helping students understand basic Javascript logic and syntax. Students will learn basic command structure, input/output function, and simple code-based image generation. By the end of the course, students will be able to independently code their own basic Javascript programs. An interest in coding is recommended but no prior coding knowledge is required.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: This course is a continuation of Introduction to Coding I and builds on learning by adding sophistication to prior learning as well as introducing more advanced Javascript coding concepts/structures. By the end of this course, the goal is each student to recreate a simplified version of one of several well-known video games. The scope of material covered in Coding I & II is equivalent to a semester-long college-level course.
prerequisites: Coding I
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: This course provides students with a hands-on introduction to the exciting field of Robotics. Through a combination of theoretical learning and practical application, students will explore the fundamentals of robotics, including mechanical design, electronics, programming, and problem-solving. Using industry-standard hardware and software, students will work both individually and in teams to design, build, and program their own robots to complete various challenges and tasks. Topics covered will include: 1. Introduction to Robotics: History, applications, and current trends 2. Mechanical Design: Basics of robot chassis, joints, and mechanisms 3. Electronics: Understanding sensors, actuators, and microcontrollers 4. Programming: Introduction to coding languages such as Python and C++ for robot control 5. Sensors and Feedback: Utilizing sensors for navigation, object detection, and feedback control 6. Control Systems: PID control, feedback loops, and tuning 7. Robot Platforms: Exploring different types of robots such as wheeled, legged, and aerial 8. Applications: Real-world examples of robotics in industry, healthcare, and beyond 9. Team Projects: Collaborative design and implementation of robotic systems to solve specific challenges 10. Ethical and Societal Implications: Discussions on the impact of robotics on society, ethics, and responsible innovation
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: French I is an introductory course that emphasizes fundamental understanding of vocabulary, structures, and culture of the francophone world. The course aims to build novice communication skills across the modalities of speaking, writing, reading and listening. The course also includes cultural projects that are designed to build student knowledge of the people and customs of the French-speaking world.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: This course is designed to develop French proficiency in communication at the intermediate level. New verb tenses are introduced along with other grammar concepts aimed at creating sentences that are more complex. Students also continue to explore different aspects of French culture and new vocabulary through the different modalities of speaking, reading, writing and listening.
prerequisites: French I or 8th grade French with teacher recommendation
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: In French III, students expand their capacity to communicate in the French by adding more complex verb tenses and grammar structures to their repertoire. This allows the student to generate more of his/her own meaning in a greater range of contexts. Vocabulary study continues to focus on relevant and authentic situations but also incorporates areas of student interest. In addition to embedding cultural knowledge into communication activities, French III offers stand-alone thematic units on cultural topics of the francophone world. At this level, students also begin to read more passage-length texts than in previous levels.
prerequisites: French II
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: In French IV, students enter the advanced level of French study. This course tackles the more complex verb tenses and grammar structures necessary to comprehend and communicate in more challenging language situations. This course requires students to read and write more substantive pieces in the target language. Classroom conversations are more sustained than in previous levels and require students to discuss topics from class readings. Readings include works of French literature as well as current events and contemporary media articles.
prerequisites: French III
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: French V represents an advanced opportunity for students who desire to increase the authenticity and fluency of their communication. This course offers contemporary materials, activities, and perspectives that prepare students to engage confidently and knowledgeably in francophone regions near and far. In addition to focusing on fluency and contemporary expression, the course also includes reading that is more extensive and writing activities thatResemble the demands of intermediate college-level literature and culture courses. This is a full-immersion class.
prerequisites: French IV
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: This is an introduction to Spanish class. We will use a variety of strategies to provide students with the opportunity to acquire the Spanish language and learn about the culture of Spanish speaking countries. The goal is to understand, speak, read and write at beginner level.
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: Students will continue to develop comprehension skills and acquire high frequency Spanish structures. Throughout the course, we will read short stories and novels that make connections to relevant world events. We will also listen to songs and watch videos on a variety of topics. Discussions in class will be based on the student's interests as well themes that arise from our reading and listening activities.
prerequisites: Spanish I or 8th grade Spanish with teacher recommendation
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: This course is a continuation of Spanish II, where more advanced vocabulary and structures are introduced through discussions, pictures, videos and songs. We will again read short stories and leveled readers to connect to Spanish culture and language.

description: This course will include the study of art/beauty, family and community, global challenges, science and technology, and contemporary life. We will use songs. videos, short texts and books to dive into all those themes while at the same time acquire more Spanish.
prerequisites: Spanish III
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: This course is designed to increase students' communication in the target language both written and spoken. We will continue to explore the themes we started in Spanish IV going deeper in our discussions as students' acquisition of Spanish improves. As in previous classes, we will be watching videos, learning songs, reading short stories and texts as well as books.
prerequisites: Spanish IV
fulfills_text: Credit Type: Elective

description: Independent Study experiences provide students the chance for a highly personalized investigation and analysis of a topic of interest outside of the regular SHS curriculum. Only in exceptional cases will Independent Studies cover the same content/proficiencies as a course already offered in the SHS Program of Studies. However, in these cases, the independent study will act as an extension or “deeper dive” into proficiencies already covered in an SHS course the student has taken previously. All independent study experiences must be advised by a current SHS employed/licensed faculty. Therefore, it is the decision of the faculty member if they will act as an advisor for an independent study. Students planning to apply for an independent study must complete all forms BEFORE the proposed first day of the study. If a student is interested in an independent study option, they will need to meet with their school counselor. All approved and completed Independent Study experiences, supported by a SHS faculty member, will appear on the SHS transcript and the proficiency earned will be factored into the SHS GPA. * Students being tutored outside of school by persons not employed by the district do not earn credit or a grade and therefore, no tutoring experience will appear on the transcript. Students may be paired with a community mentor to act as an additional guide for the independent study.
notes: program; All approved and completed Independent Study experiences, supported by a SHS faculty member, will appear on the SHS transcript

description: The SHINE program offers students differing levels of exposure to the world of work, depending on their interests. Possibilities include: ● Informational interviews with professionals in a career field of interest to the student ● Worksite visits ● Interview skills and practice ● Resume development ● Local employment and Community Service opportunities In addition to the above experiences are open to Juniors and Seniors. The SHINE coordinator also designs and manages formal internships for students. Students will work with the SHINE coordinator on pre-internship activities and preparation, and then be paired with a mentor in the greater Stowe community in the career field of their choice. The student is expected to complete 40 hours of work either remotely or at the internship site (schedule to be determined by the mentor and student, could be school hours, after school, weekends, etc.) Students will be assessed using LSUU Mission Related Goals and specific work site skills. This is a flexible, fantastic opportunity for students to get professional experience and school credit at the same time. Students enrolled in SHINE will not meet as a class, but there will be occasional cohort meetings and regularly scheduled meetings with the SHINE coordinator. Prerequisites: Demonstrate proficiency in Scholarly Habits or by permission of instructor. Semester Course for .5 credit and students may be extended/repeated for other internship opportunities.

Grammar units may be self-paced throughout the semester with vocabulary incorporated into literature units. English 10 is a genre study with an emphasis on the development of themes, literary devices, and literary techniques. Writing skills continue to be an integral part of this course, with both thesis and essay writing, as we develop arguments and literary responses to our reading. Grammar will emphasize sentence construction, and vocabulary will integrate an approach to the SATs. The outline of this course is similar to English 10; however, the chosen texts will be more challenging, and the pace will be faster. Students will be expected to do a fair amount of work outside of class. Due to the nature of proficiency-based learning, students will be expected to work independently and develop positive habits of mind in their approach to their learning.
prerequisites: English 9 and a teacher recommendation. If you are new to the honors program, you must also write a letter (to the English Department) explaining: 1) what skills you have that you think make you eligible for this course and 2) why you want to be enrolled in it.

description: English 11 is a genre study with an emphasis on the development of themes, literary devices, and literary techniques. Writing will pull together prior skills to hone solid text and quote analysis in short and essay responses. Grammar will emphasize sentence construction, and vocabulary will be text-based. Literature options will be a mix of classics and more modern texts. Due to the nature of proficiency-based learning, students will be expected to work independently and develop positive habits of mind in their approach to their learning.

The AP English Literature and Composition course is designed and taught thematically with an emphasis on core readings along with modern and contemporary selections that illuminate and expand upon a variety of themes. AP English Literature and Composition closely follows the requirements described in the AP English Literature and Composition Course and Exam Description (CED), including the fundamentals of literary analysis and introductory college composition. Each week students discuss and engage in a variety of writing activities focusing on argumentation, interpretation, analysis, rhetorical strategies, exposition, structure, and style. Students read and study a variety of American and British novels, plays, poems, and short stories from the 16th century to the present. The course focuses on the experience of literature, the interpretation of literature, the evaluation of literature, and writing to develop stylistic maturity and sophistication. Students practice their writing via numerous timed essays, which may be revised several times, as well as longer essays that require outside research and MLA formatting. Students also practice oral communication skills through presentations, regular classroom discussions, and Socratic seminars.
prerequisites: Prerequisites include English 10 Honors OR teacher recommendation. If you are new to the honors program, you must also write a letter (to the English Department) explaining: 1) what skills you have that you think make you eligible for this course and 2) why you want to be enrolled in it.

description: English 12 is a genre study with an emphasis on the development of themes, literary devices, and literary techniques. Writing will pull together prior skills to hone solid essay responses. Grammar will emphasize focused, individual skills, and vocabulary will be text-based. Literature options will be a mix of classics and more modern texts. Due to the nature of proficiency-based learning, students will be expected to work independently and develop positive habits of mind in their approach to their learning.

This is a dual enrollment class for seniors, which means students will receive both a high school English credit as well as CCV credit, which could also transfer to a specific college or university. This class is writing intensive and will be at a college level. Students will learn strategies for organizing, evaluating, and revising their work. Students will also read a variety of essays and literary texts to examine effective craft and style. A research component will be added to ensure students are familiar with proper steps and formatting for this more complex writing process. This is an opportunity to refine critical reading and writing skills. Students will construct complex essays to enhance their writing skills, and experiment with a greater variety of strategies to interest, inform, and persuade. Outside of class reading and writing is expected
fulfills_text: students will receive both a high school English credit as well as CCV credit
notes: Dual enrollment class for seniors; taught at TVMHS by TVMHS staff (letter, p.2)

description: This will focus on reading books in these popular genres, while emphasizing their literary merit. Common themes across the genres as well as archetypes will be studied. It will be a great chance to explore the common archetypes of characters and plots that are pervasive throughout all literature. Outside of class reading will be expected.
notes: Recommended 9th and/or 10th grade course

description: This is a comparative literature elective – comparing book scenes to their movie version. We will consider literary elements as we read and then see how they are carried out in the movie version. Writing and discussion tasks may ask which version was more effective and why. Be prepared to actively participate in class and maybe even debate with your classmates.
notes: Recommended 9th and/or 10th grade course

description: For those of you who have an interest in WW II or enjoyed reading Night in 10th grade, this course will read some other Holocaust stories and stories about other groups affected by the war. Students will also watch videos and read articles based on war survivors. Outside of class reading will be expected with discussions occurring during class time.
notes: Recommended 11th and/or 12th grade course

description: This will focus on writing short stories, poetry, and even dramas. Students will learn how to take their idea and to turn it into a story. They will unlock their potential as a writer through a workshop format
notes: Recommended 11th and/or 12th grade course

description: This course allows students to read and study short stories and novellas of different literatures. They read such characteristic forms of this genre as the fantastic tale, the literary fairy tale, the classical novella and the mystery tale. Students focus upon such central questions as construction of character, the treatment of space and place, narrative point of view, and symbolism.

This course is designed to prepare students for the SAT’s Verbal section of reading comprehension and language skills. Students will read passages and analyze them for elements of theme, audience, point of view, vocabulary, purpose, and more. In addition, students will look at how language and grammatical structures form cohesive sentences so that students can identify errors in the sentences and passages and be able to correct them. Please note that this course will have a lot of repetition in terms of the types of class activities completed. This course is best suited for juniors but open to sophomores who want a jump start on SAT preparation.
notes: Recommended 10th and/or 11th grade course

description: The class provide students with an opportunity to build on the skills practiced in middle school to a proficient level. Topics include Rational Numbers, Radicals, Linear Equations, Functions, Pythagorean Theorem, Volume, Congruence and Similarity.

The fundamental purpose of this course is to formalize and extend the mathematics that students learned in the middle grades. Because it is built on the middle grades standards, this is a more ambitious version of Algebra I than has generally been offered. The modules deepen and extend understanding of linear and exponential relationships by contrasting them with each other and by applying linear models to data that exhibit a linear trend, and students engage in methods for analyzing, solving, and using quadratic functions. The Mathematical Practice Standards apply throughout each course and, together with the content standards, prescribe that students experience mathematics as a coherent, useful, and logical subject that makes use of their ability to make sense of problem situations.
notes: Recommended 8th grade course; Recommended 8th grade course

description: The fundamental purpose of the course in Geometry is to formalize and extend students’ geometric experiences from the middle grades. Students explore more complex geometric situations and deepen their explanations of geometric relationships, moving towards formal mathematical arguments. Close attention should be paid to the introductory content for the Geometry conceptual category found in the high school CCSS. The Mathematical Practice Standards apply throughout each course and, together with the content standards, prescribe that students experience mathematics as a coherent, useful, and logical subject that makes use of their ability to make sense of problem situations.
prerequisites: Algebra 1

description: Building on their work with linear, quadratic, and exponential functions, students extend their repertoire of functions to include polynomial, rational, and radical functions. Students work closely with the expressions that define the functions and continue to expand and hone their abilities to model situations and to solve equations, including solving quadratic equations over the set of complex numbers and solving exponential equations using the properties of logarithms. The Mathematical Practice Standards apply throughout each course and, together with the content standards, prescribe that students experience mathematics as a coherent, useful, and logical subject that makes use of their ability to make sense of problem situations.
prerequisites: Geometry

description: Extending on their understanding of trigonometry and shapes, students will use a plethora of formulas to solve triangles and prove trigonometric identities. Matrices are studied as tools for performing rotations and reflections of the coordinate plane, as well as for solving systems of linear equations. The year concludes with a capstone module on modeling with probability and statistics. The Mathematical Practice Standards apply throughout each course and, together with the content standards, prescribe that students experience mathematics as a coherent, useful, and logical subject that makes use of their ability to make sense of problem situations.
prerequisites: Algebra 2

description: Consumer Math is designed to teach financial literacy and real-world math applications. It prepares students for financial independence by teaching them how to create budgets, calculate taxes, manage bank accounts, and evaluate costs for housing, vehicles, and insurance. The course focuses on applying arithmetic, percentages, and basic algebra to everyday financial decisions

This course is an introduction to the basic ideas and techniques of probability and statistics. Topics may include numerical and graphical descriptive measures, probability, random variables, the normal distribution, sampling theory, estimation, hypothesis testing, correlation, and regression. The use of technology may be required.
prerequisites: Math & Algebra for College or equivalent skills.
notes: Taught at TVMHS by TVMHS staff (letter, p.2)

description: This course will review the basic concepts of mathematics and practice test-taking skills to help prepare students for the mathematics portion of the SAT. Topics include: Linear Algebra, Rates, Statistics, Probability, Polynomials, Functions, Geometry, Imaginary Numbers, Trigonometry, and test-taking strategies.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Algebra
notes: Recommended 11th grade course

description: Entering freshmen will study aspects of the Earth’s surface and interior which includes plate tectonics, mineral and rock formation, mountain building, volcanic and earthquake activity related to plate movement, formation of glaciers and deserts, and the chronology of geologic history. Students will also investigate topics in oceanography and astronomy which includes ocean currents, the seafloor, biological productivity and life forms, origins of astronomy, the solar system and other galaxies, properties of stars and other celestial bodies, and astronomical measurement. This is a lab and inquiry-based class.
notes: Recommended 9th grade course

description: The Biology course will provide students with an overview of the field of modern biology. The scope of concepts will include: molecular biology, cell structure and function, the flow of energy and matter through life systems, reproduction, heredity, evolution and ecology. This course is designed to assist students in the mastery of basic knowledge that they will need in order to become responsible and productive citizens in the 21st century. Students will be expected to engage productively in group work, hands-on activities, and independent research.

This is an advanced class that covers the content of a college level introductory biology class. Students should be motivated and self-directed. This course will go in much greater depth than Honors Biology, and draw on an understanding of Chemistry to understand cellular processes. We will cover a great deal of content, and do in-depth, independent lab work. Students should be prepared to complete regular independent reading and other homework, at least 2-3 hours per week.
prerequisites: recommended completion of Biology or Honors Biology and Chemistry. Highly motivated students without this background can enroll with permission of instructor

description: In this class we will learn about the anatomy and biochemistry of the human brain. We will learn about the latest research into how the brain functions, different brain disorders and mental illness, the function of different neurotransmitters, and how treatments work. We can explore what happens in altered states of consciousness such as dreaming, hypnosis, meditation and near death experiences. This course will rely mainly on online text and books and there will be opportunity to do in depth research into a topic of your choice.
prerequisites: Biology

description: AP Environmental Science course is designed to engage students with the scientific principles, concepts, and methodologies required to understand the interrelationships within the natural world. The course requires that students identify and analyze natural and human-made environmental problems, evaluate the relative risks associated with these problems, and examine alternative solutions for resolving or preventing them. Environmental science is interdisciplinary, embracing topics from geology, biology, environmental studies, environmental science, chemistry, and geography.
prerequisites: Required Prerequisites: Biology; Recommended Prerequisites: Chemistry or Physical Science

description: In this class, students will learn about the ecology of our local environment. First, we will familiarize ourselves with the trees and other species in our school forest, and then students will conduct field experiments that they design. We will cover the role of different interactions between species, disturbances, and nutrient cycling and soils. We will be spending a significant amount of time outside doing independent research.
prerequisites: Recommended Prerequisites: Earth Science and Biological Science.

description: From fertilization through the first 5 years of life, this class will cover the development of organs, movement, intellect and emotion. We will learn about the stages of development of a fetus and different disorders, types of birth and complications. We will look at the current research on development in the first five years: developing motor skills, morals, and intellectual abilities. We will also compare child rearing techniques around the world. This class will require a fair amount of reading.

Physical Science is a laboratory science course that explores the relationship between matter and energy. Students investigate physical science concepts through an inquiry-based approach. Embedded standards for Inquiry, Technology and Mathematics are taught in the context of the standards for Energy, Matter, Motion and Forces.

course_name: Introduction to Chemistry - CCV Dual Enrollment
description: This course is an introduction to the concepts, principles and applications of chemistry. Includes atomic structure, periodicity, structure of matter, solutions, and an introduction to organic chemistry. Includes lab sessions which illustrate the principles of quantitative interpretation of data. Algebra is strongly recommended. *Students may take this course for non-college credit as well*
notes: Taught at TVMHS by TVMHS staff (letter, p.2)

description: This course will build on the content and depth of knowledge started in Earth/Space Science. It will emphasize current discoveries and the future direction of Space Science and the U.S. / World Space Program.
prerequisites: Recommended previous courses: Earth/ Space Science

description: In this class you get to build things that move. We’ll build simple machines like catapults, musical instruments, rockets, pulleys- anything you want. We can also explore coding to make robots that can do things like play music, make an amusement park ride for a mini person, pick things up and take them places, and more. The focus will be on trying out different designs, experimenting, and then adjusting your designs to get success. We’ll learn why and how these things work too.

In this class you’ll learn all about the chemistry of food. Learn about what happens in baking, marinades, food preservation (canning, pickling and more) and more. We will learn what is happening to the chemicals in the food and try out different recipes. We will also try some more experimental foods and see what some of those ingredients on food labels actually do to texture and flavor. This is a hands-on class and you’ll be expected to participate in labs and experiment with your own ideas.

This class will focus on skills that will help you in the outdoors. It will include identification, collection, and preparation of wild foods, learning how to start a fire and use different cook stoves, knots and setting up tents and tarps for shelter, as well as finding your way with a map and compass. We will also learn about telling the weather and first aid skills. This is a hands-on class: we will be outside a lot and doing a lot. You will need to dress ready to go outside and participate in all the learning activities. Students are graded on participation, persistence, collaboration and completion of task.

World History generally covers topics between the Middle Ages and the 20th Century in a sequential approach. In this introductory class, students learn basic skills for approaching non-narrative text, primary and secondary sources, and develop the academic language necessary to read and write history at the high-school level. Students are encouraged to come in to class with their own ideas of what and how they wish to learn. All special interests, abilities, and curiosities are accommodated and nurtured. Students will be encouraged to develop independence and their own voice.
notes: Recommended 9th grade course

description: This course will provide a survey of all of American history from the Pre-Columbian era to the present. We will focus on how and why North America was settled, the founding of the U.S., the impact of settlement on native populations, and the regional differences that led to the Civil War. The second part of the course will focus on Reconstruction after the Civil War, economic change during the Gilded Age, reforms of the Progressive Era, U.S. involvement in WWI, the Great Depression and U.S. involvement in WWII. The last half of the 20th century will focus on consumer society, nuclear developments, Civil Rights, the Vietnam War, and deregulation of the American economy.
notes: Recommended 10th grade course

description: This course is the upper-level of American Studies. This course will provide a survey of all of American history from the Pre- Columbian era to the present. We will focus on how and why North America was settled, the founding of the U.S., the impact of settlement on native populations, and the regional differences that led to the Civil War. The second part of the course will focus on Reconstruction after the Civil War, economic change during the Gilded Age, reforms of the Progressive Era, U.S. involvement in WWI, the Great Depression and U.S. involvement in WWII. The last half of the 20th century will focus on consumer society, nuclear developments, Civil Rights, the Vietnam War, and deregulation of the American economy.
notes: Recommended 10th grade course

description: In this course we will focus not purely on history, but moreover how the government operates in our country. We will review the constitution and federalism, and will then more deeply consider the legal system and the courts, gun control, mass incarceration, immigration, national security, government spending and budgets, Civil Rights, Affirmative Action, elections, political parties, campaign finance, interest groups, public opinion, and the role of the media. Some projects will involve investigating local political issues, as well as becoming more familiar with national politics, current events and the 2024 presidential election.

AP U.S. Government and Politics is a study of both formal and informal structures of government and the processes of the American political system, with an emphasis on policy-making and implementation. The course examines politically significant concepts used to interpret and analyze specific topics, including: constitutional underpinnings; political beliefs and behaviors; political parties, interest groups, and mass media; civil rights and civil liberties. In addition, this course will focus on how governmental and economic institutions affect public policy at the local, state, national and international levels. This course is designed to prepare students for the AP Exam in May.
prerequisites: American Studies 1 and American Studies 2

description: While not defined by, this course will prepare students for the Advanced Placement United States History exam in May. In keeping with the College Board’s requirements, the course includes a college-level textbook, authentic audio and video recordings, as well as primary sources and secondary sources written by historians and scholars. Students will practice writing coherent arguments, identifying and evaluating diverse historical developments, and analyzing evidence about the past from diverse sources. While developing proficiency in all these sophisticated skills, students will also have multiple opportunities to apply detailed specific knowledge about American Identity, Technology, Patterns of Migration, Domestic and Foreign Politics, Environment and Geography, and American Ideas, Beliefs, and Cultures.

This course provides a basic intro into psychology, the study of behavior and mental processes. We will look at some of the major subdisciplines of psychology including: emotions, motivation, psychological disorders, social identifies, interpersonal interactions, and group and cultural processes. AP students will go further in-depth with topics, preparing for the AP exam in May. Students who are interested in psychology but not interested in an AP version will learn the material and design and conduct their own psychological study as a research project.
notes: AP version available; AP students go further in-depth and prepare for the AP exam

description: This course is the upper-level of World History 9. World History generally covers topics between the Middle Ages and the 20th Century in a sequential approach. In this introductory class, students learn basic skills for approaching non-narrative text, primary and secondary sources, and develop the academic language necessary to read and write history at the high-school level. Students are encouraged to come into class with their own ideas of what and how they wish to learn. All special interests, abilities, and curiosities are accommodated and nurtured. Students will be encouraged to develop independence and their own voice.
notes: Recommended 9th grade course

description: This course will investigate the history of labor in the United States. We will begin with the development of unions with immigrant populations in the late 19th century and understand how individual crafts and skilled vs unskilled labor developed into larger organizations. We will also trace the development of government-managed labor institutions like the National Labor Relations Board and other bureaucracies, the merging of larger unions, how contract negotiations work in practice, and how compromises were reached historically between labor and capital. While this is somewhat historical, we will focus significantly on labor today in the United States to better understand how and why union membership has declined and the social, cultural and economic impacts of this.

In this course, students will learn about the most significant revolutions in modern world history, such as the French Revolution, Haitian Revolution, Industrial Revolution, Bolshevik Revolution, Mexican Revolution and the Chinese Civil War that led to the creation of the People’s Republic of China. What led to these major upheavals and what is their legacy? How did revolutionary ideas spread around the world and what impact did they have on the globe? Students will also have an opportunity to study lesser well-known rebellions and revolutions of their choice that occurred during the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.

This course will focus on the first, second, and third waves of feminism in U.S. History. We will explore how various women’s rights advocates have sought to establish equal rights and legal protection over time and analyze how successful they have been at achieving their goals. In addition, women’s cultural contributions in art, music, and film will be a key component of the class. Students will create projects, write essays, and have opportunities to learn about topics that they are interested in exploring in more depth.
