description: Algebra 1 formalizes and extends the mathematics of equivalence, proportional reasoning and describing data which U-32 students learn in the middle grades and Plane Geometry. Algebra 1 is a required, proficiency-based and project-based course to make necessary progress in the graduation standards U-32 students will attain later in Algebra 2 and can expand in Pre-Calculus & AP Calculus. We’ll start the year by performing one-variable statistical analysis on real world data then continue in sequence with two ‘You-32’ projects that leverage our study of linear programming and two-variable statistics to better understand and make an impact in our local school community. The second half of the year will focus primarily on a study of functions, which include linear, exponential, and quadratic as a meaning of modeling what we notice and wonder. Students will be able to meet graduation requirements at the Developing level or above in MCP 1 and 2 in this course. Students will have second opportunity to score proficient in MCP 4 (Statistics). They need to score proficient twice in MCP 4.
fulfills_text: Students can complete required graduation proficiencies by completing Geometry, Algebra I, and 2 Semesters of Algebra II or equivalent courses.

description: Algebra 2 builds on the skills and concepts learned in Algebra 1 and Geometry. Topics include but are not limited to further study of exponential functions, polynomial functions, and logarithmic functions, transformations, writing arithmetic and geometric sequences with explicit formulas, probability, and linear regression. Abstract mathematical ideas are approached using verbal, pictorial, and concrete presentations. Assessments will include quizzes, projects, and unit tests. Problem solving and critical thinking activities are an integral part of the curriculum. Upon successful completion of Algebra 2, students will be prepared to take either Pre-Calculus, AP Pre-calculus, AP Statistics, or Mathematics Modeling. Students will be able to meet graduation requirements at the Proficient level or above in MCP 1 and 2 in this course. Students will have third opportunity to score proficient in MCP 4 (Statistics). They need to score proficient twice in MCP 4.
prerequisites: Algebra 1
fulfills_text: Students can complete required graduation proficiencies by completing Geometry, Algebra I, and 2 Semesters of Algebra II or equivalent courses.

description: Algebra 2 STEM is a uniquely accelerated, application-focused, and depth-driven version of Algebra 2. Algebra 2 STEM is proficiency-based; however, it provides students many opportunities to strive for advanced levels of understanding and go beyond what is expected for proficiency for graduation. We will start the year in the same place as Algebra 2 with a study of sequences but then pivot to a review and extension of systems through the lens of matrices. After giving the same attention to quadratics and higher order polynomial functions, the second half of the year will focus primarily on an intense study of exponential and trigonometric functions and how we can manipulate, model, and transform them. This full-year course will conclude with a brief journey of Statistics to make inferences about real-world populations. Upon successful completion of Algebra 2 STEM, students will be prepared to take either Pre-Calculus, AP Pre-calculus, AP Statistics, or Mathematics Modeling. Students will be able to meet graduation requirements at the Proficient level or above in MCP 1 and 2 in this course. Students will have third opportunity to score proficient in MCP 4 (Statistics). They need to score proficient twice in MCP 4.
prerequisites: Teacher Recommendation

description: Academic HS Mathematics Support is an academic intervention that supplements core mathematics instruction for students who have skill and/or conceptual gaps that may keep them from mastering essential prerequisite skills. In a small group with a maximum of 5-7 students, students will receive evidence-based, explicit instruction that meets their specific learning needs while working towards proficiency-based graduation requirements. Students could be enrolled for up to a year based on their needs and progress on individualized goals that are set by the teacher and student and are monitored using data. Students may transition out of the class by quarter based on their progress. Students will be recommended for this support based on their performance on state, district and classroom assessments. Only students who are recommended may take this class.
notes: academic intervention

description: The fundamental purpose of the course in Geometry is to formalize and extend students’ geometric experiences from the middle grades. Students explore more complex geometric situations and deepen their explanations of geometric relationships, moving toward formal mathematical arguments. The Mathematical Practice Standards apply throughout this course and, together with the content standard (MCP4.1 Understand geometric concepts and constructions, prove theorems, and apply appropriate results to solve problems), prescribe that student experience mathematics as a coherent, useful, and logical subject that makes use of their ability to make sense of problem situations. The geometry course will also explore probability, including independent and conditional probability, interpreting data, and compound events. Major emphasis will be on congruence, similarity, right triangles, trigonometry, proofs, expressing geometric properties with equations, and modeling with geometry. Students will be able to meet graduation requirements at the Proficient level or above in MCP 3 in this course. Students will have first opportunity to score proficient in MCP 4 (Statistics). They need to score proficient twice in MCP 4.
fulfills_text: Students can complete required graduation proficiencies by completing Geometry, Algebra I, and 2 Semesters of Algebra II or equivalent courses.

description: Pre-Calculus is the culmination of Algebra and trigonometric skills acquired from all previous courses. Students will work with families of functions including polynomial, exponential, logarithmic, rational, and trigonometric functions. Students will analyze these functions in four ways: numerically, algebraically, graphically, and contextually. Pre-calculus will prepare students for Calculus at either the high school or college level.
prerequisites: All math graduation requirements met and teacher recommendation

description: AP Pre-calculus prepares students for other college-level mathematics and science courses. Students explore everyday situations and phenomena using mathematical tools and lenses. Students will learn content and skills common to college pre-calculus courses that are foundational for careers in mathematics, physics, biology, health science, social science, and data science. Students study each function type through their graphical, numerical, verbal, and analytical representations and their applications in a variety of contexts. Assessments will include homework, quizzes and tests. Students will be encouraged to take the AP test. See page AP section for additional information.

description: This course is intended for those students who want a calculus course before entering college. description: AP Chemistry is designed to be taken by students after the successful completion of a first-year course in high school chemistry and concurrently with high school physics. It is aimed at students who want to obtain a deeper understanding of the concepts introduced in first year chemistry. The focus will be on mastering the types of skills generally covered in a first-year college chemistry course. Chemistry is the study of matter and its changes. No matter what your future plans, an understanding of the nature and behavior of the atoms and molecules that make up the world is essential to success in every field of endeavor. Special emphasis will be placed on titration math, electrochemistry, and reaction rates and mechanisms. This course also includes an extensive laboratory component focused on developing inquiry skills, emphasizing experimental design and data analysis. This is a course that is designed to prepare students for the AP exam in early May. Taking the AP exam is strongly encouraged, but is not a requirement. The standards addressed are the same as those in first year chemistry, but at much greater depth than for a high school course.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Advanced Chemistry, and recommendation of the chemistry instructor (or permission of the instructor). As strong math skills are also a necessity, it is recommended that students either have completed, or be concurrently enrolled in, Pre-calculus or its equivalent

description: In this course students will explore many of the essential physics principals present in the world around them. Emphasis is placed on understanding the important concepts and being able to apply them to explain and make predictions about a wide range of “real world” situations. Mathematical analysis is an important component of Physics, but it is limited to the use of Algebra II level skills and concepts. In this course, students develop scientific inquiry, critical thinking, and communication skills through lab investigations and lab reports. Through homework assignments, they build reasoning and problem-solving skills. Topics covered will include: kinematics, Newton’s laws, energy transfers, momentum, circular motion, wave motion, electrostatics, electrical circuits and magnetism. This course closely follows the College Board’s Advanced Placement (AP) Physics 1 course, and students are highly encouraged to sign up to take the AP Physics 1 exam in May.
prerequisites: Recommendation of current science teacher. Successful completion of Algebra 1 and Geometry, and concurrent enrollment in either Algebra II or Pre-Calculus
notes: Listed under catalog heading 'SCIENCE – 11th and 12th GRADE PROGRAM'

description: AP Physics 2 is a full-year course that is the equivalent of a second-semester introductory college course in algebra-based physics. The course is designed to build on the conceptual understanding usually attained in an introductory course in physics and should be taken as a second-year course after students have had either AP Physics 1 or a similar introductory course. AP Students cultivate their understanding of physics through inquiry-based investigations as they explore these topics: fluids; thermodynamics; electrical force, field, and potential; electric circuits; magnetism and electromagnetic induction; geometric and physical optics; and quantum, atomic, and nuclear physics. This course will help students develop a deep understanding of the foundational principles that shape classical mechanics and modern physics. By confronting complex physical situations or scenarios, the course is designed to enable students to develop the ability to reason about physical phenomena using important science practices, such as explaining relationships, applying and justifying the use of mathematical routines, designing experiments, analyzing data, and making connections across multiple topics within the course.
prerequisites: Successful completion of AP Physics 1 (or equivalent), and concurrent enrollment in Pre-Calculus
notes: Listed under catalog heading 'SCIENCE – 11th and 12th GRADE PROGRAM'

description: AP biology differs from other high school courses in the range and detail of topics covered. It is designed for students who are highly self-motivated and have a keen interest in learning about the nature of life. Students must have a strong work ethic and should demonstrate the ability to balance a heavy academic course load. Curricular content includes biochemistry, cell biology, cellular processes, cellular energetics and regulation, heredity, molecular genetics, evolutionary biology, and ecology. This course also includes an extensive laboratory component focused on developing specific science practices, including experimental design and data analysis. AP Biology covers much of what is offered in most college introductory biology courses, and therefore maintains stringent academic guidelines.
notes: Recommended course sequence to prepare for exam: Successful completion of Biology and Advanced Chemistry, demonstrating Proficient to Advanced in both courses. This course has a summer assignment. Students enrolled in this course are expected to take the Biology AP Exam | Listed under catalog heading 'SCIENCE – 11th and 12th GRADE PROGRAM'

description: This course provides students with an opportunity to learn about what plants need in order to grow successfully, basic horticulture practices, and the concept of sustainability. Semester one focuses on the elements and processes that are needed for plants to grow successfully. In addition to learning about what plants need, students conduct and analyze soil tests in the greenhouse and the garden, and plant and maintain garden beds. Students will apply their knowledge of photosynthesis by conducting an investigation that looks at the impact on plant growth of different variables related to photosynthesis. Semester two focuses on units that include learning about our current food system and the impacts of climate change, as well as plant interactions and pest management. Students will undertake an engineering design project related to improving food production. Students also learn about aspects of garden design and planning, and will be involved in planning, preparing, and planting in the greenhouse and the school garden.
prerequisites: Completion of Biology
notes: Students can take either Fall or Spring semester, or both | Listed under catalog heading 'SCIENCE – 11th and 12th GRADE PROGRAM'

description: This course is designed for the hands-on learner who has a strong work ethic, likes to be outside and get dirty and has a desire to work cooperatively with their peers. Students will be outside for much of the semester. The relationship between Vermont plants, wildlife and environment will be studied. Specific topics covered will be organism life cycles and behavior, ecosystem energy flow, population dynamics, forest succession, forest and wildlife management, and the forestry industry. Students will gain an appreciation for their surrounding forest through field study. Additionally, Vermont scientists and foresters will be invited to speak on recent studies and practices.
prerequisites: Completion of Biology
notes: Listed under catalog heading 'SCIENCE – 11th and 12th GRADE PROGRAM'

description: Anatomy and Physiology is an advanced-level elective for students who are interested in pursuing a variety of medical fields. This course will provide students with an opportunity to experience a high-level science course with expectations similar to those that will be seen in college. Students should be prepared to work collaboratively and independently to complete labs and dissections, study and memorize complex medical terminology, and explain the relationship between the structure and function of our amazing body systems. Topics will be tailored to individual classes around student interest. Semester 1 (A&P Fall) will focus on units such as the integumentary system, skeletal system, muscular system, nervous system, human senses, and/or endocrine system. The first semester will end with a bioengineering project that will encompass skills and information gained during the semester. Semester 2 (A&P Spring) will focus on units such as blood, cardiovascular system, lymphatic and immune system, respiratory system, digestive system, and/or excretory system. The second semester will also end with a bioengineering project that will encompass skills and information gained during the semester.
prerequisites: Completion of Biology and Chemistry or concurrently enrolled in Chemistry
notes: Students can take either Fall or Spring semester, or both | Listed under catalog heading 'SCIENCE – 11th and 12th GRADE PROGRAM'

description: In this course, students will develop an understanding of important physics and engineering principles through hands-on investigations, with an emphasis on practical applications in real-life situations. Students will work in teams to problem solve different physics and engineering challenges while gaining an understanding of the related concepts. Examples of the types of challenges students might work to solve could include: determining how airbags help save lives, designing and building a bridge that can hold the greatest amount of weight, or creating the most efficient wind turbine.

description: Forensic Science is a course that is designed for students that prefer a hands-on approach and like to get up out of their seats and try to figure it all out. Forensic Science focuses on the scientific practices and includes collecting crime scene evidence, analyzing data, and making claims about crime scene cases. Students will learn to collect and analyze evidence that could include soil, documents, DNA, blood, toxicology, entomology, fingerprints, hair, fibers, etc. Students will work on making claims about crime scenes using both collected evidence and background research to support their thinking. At the beginning of the course, students will have options for some units to choose which types of evidence they are most interested in learning about.
notes: Listed under catalog heading 'SCIENCE – 11th and 12th GRADE PROGRAM'

description: The first semester traces the rise of modern America from the Civil War through the turn of the 20th century, the changes and challenges wrought by explosive industrialization, urbanization, and immigration. In the second quarter, the focus is economic, examining the boom of the 1920’s and the subsequent bust of the Great Depression. In the second semester, students examine the rise of America as a global superpower over the course of the twentieth century and examine the historical challenges and responses of U.S. foreign policy. Students will research and debate current challenges for the U.S. in the world. The last quarter examines popular culture of modern America and its insights into cultural change. Students will examine the evolution of music, television, movies, news media, sports, fashion, and art through original projects

description: This course is a rigorous, fast-paced survey of American History. Students read a textbook over the course of the year and work to develop skills as historians and writers, interpreting primary documents and making historical arguments. Writing is a major focus throughout the year. In addition to regular in-class analyses of primary documents, students will research and write an essay in each semester: a work of local history in the first semester and a family history in the second. In May, students take the Advanced Placement test in U.S. History, which includes challenging on-demand essays. Some preparation for the test takes place in class but after school study groups meet regularly in the second semester. This class is a great introduction to U.S. History and regularly engages students in challenging discussion, but it is also a serious academic commitment. There is a significant summer reading assignment (six chapters from the text, with a test on the first day of class), and a chapter of the text is due almost every week in the school year. Students should talk with their Social Studies teacher if they are unsure about taking this course.

The Transition Academy of U-32 is a specialized program for students receiving services through an Individual Education Plan (IEP). Eligible students require additional skill and knowledge acquisition beyond required high school credits. Programs are individualized and vary depending on student capabilities, needs, and interests. The Transition Academy provides academic, independent living, and employment skill training both on campus and within the local community. Student curriculum is based on needs determined through skill inventories and family input. Academics include practical applications of math, literacy, communication, and technology. Independent living skills covered in this class include public safety, meal management, health and hygiene, and personal management. Employment opportunities focus on student areas of interest that foster transferable skills applicable across job settings. The Transition Academy collaborates with outside agencies to strengthen student opportunities and provide continued support beyond U-32. Enrollment in the Transition Academy is evaluated annually by the IEP Team. Maximum duration of the program lasts until the day prior to the student’s 22nd Birthday, as per Vermont Special Education Regulation 2360.2.

description: The Vermont Virtual Learning Cooperative connects students with Vermont schools. Their goal is to overcome the three most common barriers that prevent students from taking the courses they want or need in schools. These barriers are the availability of courses, accessibility to courses, and the flexibility of your education. For example, are you interested in taking a course that is not available at your school? VTVLC finds the course you want to take from another Vermont school that offers that course online. Is there a course that you want to take at your school that you cannot access because you are required to take a different class during the same schedule time? VTVLC works with your school to give you access to the courses you want during a time that works for you by offering the course online. All courses offered by VTVLC online are accessible from anywhere, anytime. Whether you learn best at 1 am or 1 pm, at school, at home, or online, where your courses are only a click away.

description: Driver Education equips students with the skills and knowledge needed to drive safely and responsibly. This course addresses essential questions such as how driving decisions impact personal and community wellness, how to prevent accidents, and how self-awareness affects driving behavior. Key Focus Areas: ●Developing safe driving habits and decision-making skills to reduce accident risks. ●Addressing critical issues like DUI, distractions, and sleep deprivation. ●Preparing students for the Vermont Driver’s Exam through classroom and behind-the-wheel instruction. Course Requirements: ●Classroom Instruction: 30 hours ●Behind-the-Wheel Instruction: 6 hours with a licensed instructor and 40 hours supervised driving with an adult. Outcomes: ●Students who meet academic and driving standards will earn a certificate to test for their license. Those who do not complete requirements may retake the course or arrange additional practice time. ●Parental involvement and supervised practice are strongly encouraged to ensure student success and safety on the road.

description: STRIVE is available by recommendation for students in grades 9-12. The foundation of this course is to reflect and build on students’ knowledge and understanding of the guideline “I challenge myself”, and understand through self-challenge that I can grow as a learner. Students are taught learning strategies, which will help them become more active, independent learners. STRIVE is designed to investigate, identify and further understand oneself as a learner in all environments. In addition to learning strategies, students have opportunities to work on goals in basic academic skills. These are different for every student, depending on needs, and might include reading comprehension, math computation, or writing. Students have opportunities to apply learning strategies and academic skills while receiving support with coursework or while preparing for tests.

description: Skills in Literature is a highly individualized course designed to develop your basic literacy skills through the exploration of various types and samples of literature from around the world. The course offers a chance for you to work closely with a teacher in a smaller group setting, helping you identify and reach your writing and reading goals.

In this course, you will examine a wide variety of literature and non-fiction texts, with emphasis on building reading and writing skills essential for high school success. You will be introduced to the close reading of texts and develop an understanding of writing as a process. Writing instruction focuses on clarity, development of ideas, and literary techniques, as well as on sentence crafting and parts of speech.

You’ll examine important ideas such as tolerance, rebellion, individualism, and community by reading and discussing novels, short stories, plays, essays, and political documents. In American Literature, you’ll create personal written responses to literary and informational texts using pre-writing, outlining, drafting, revising, proofreading, and presenting texts as part of a literate community.

Recommended for students interested in the history of literature, in college-level reading skills, and in discussion of important ideas.

You will respond to visual texts through writing and storyboarding, as well as creating visual texts. Recommended for students interested in study of film and other media.

Formal and informal writing assignments help you refine your personal writing process and create texts of your own, including dramatic performances, film storyboards, analytical essays, and various creative writing pieces. This course includes the study of novels, plays, poetry, short stories, essays, drama, film, and television. Recommended for all students.

description: In this interdisciplinary honors course you will address some of the core questions of human existence: What is the purpose of life? How should I live? What should I value? How should I relate to others and to the world? How do I know what is true, what is good, what is beautiful? Students explore these questions by examining the art, literature, and philosophy of diverse cultures throughout history. The focus is on the relationships between self, society, and subject matter. The purpose is not to teach specific answers, but to help you develop, clarify, and enrich your own belief systems and to deepen your understanding of yourself. The course concludes with student presentations of extended personal research essays to a panel of community members. Recommended for students interested in engaging deeply with important ideas and personal beliefs.
prerequisites: 9th Grade English & American Literature

Recommended for students who are well organized and highly motivated to study language, rhetoric, and non-fiction writing in depth.
prerequisites: English teacher signature on course selection sheet. Successful completion of summer reading assignments and acceptable performance on the assessment of summer reading assignments.

description: In this course students challenge themselves physically and mentally in an atmosphere that is safe, supportive, and fun. The program is designed to build confidence, self-esteem, trust, cooperation, and communication skills. Activities may include, but are not limited to, noncompetitive games, group problem solving initiatives, trust activities, knot tying, belaying techniques, as well as low and high ropes course challenges.
notes: Recommended for 9th graders (will be preselected for 9th grade students)

description: This class is a skills based learning environment focusing on varying dimensions of wellness. Some examples of skills practiced include, but are not limited to, analyzing influences, advocacy, decision making and accessing valid and reliable information. The class covers topics including mental health/mental illness, nutrition, substance abuse prevention, sexuality and more through projects, guest speakers and small and large group discussions.
notes: Recommended for 9th graders (will be preselected for 9th grade students)

description: For those students who have encountered wellness and/or fitness challenges, this class is designed for you. Healthy Living & Fitness allows students to design and carry out their own personal wellness plan. Each student develops lifelong wellness skills and habits by practicing new learning in the areas of nutrition, cooking, stress management, and physical fitness. Students have help figuring out the best and easiest ways to develop core strength, tone muscles, eat nutritionally, and generally achieve physical and mental fitness.

Personal Fitness introduces students to the benefits of lifelong fitness by teaching them how to assess their fitness levels, write a personal fitness plan, and monitor and adjust the plan accordingly. Students learn proper technique and safety concerns of all weight room equipment. They are introduced to basic anatomy, the components of fitness and exercise, goal setting, and circuit training as well as examining recent trends in personal fitness.

This class combines a mixture of traditional team sports, individual sports, and lifetime leisure activities. Students demonstrate knowledge of rules and skills required to play a variety of sports. Sportsmanship, team play and fitness are incorporated into each unit. The goal is for students to learn the fundamentals skills needed for enjoyment and active participation in lifetime activities.

This class will build on the skills that students learned in PE1, and new sports and activities will be offered. Students will continue to demonstrate knowledge of rules and skills required to play while learning advanced strategies and tactics. Students will take ownership of the class through running tournaments and self-refereeing, taking responsibility for calling their own fouls and resolving disputes. Students may be required to run warm-ups or drills for teammates demonstrating knowledge acquired during prior Physical Education courses.

Skills in Math is a class that helps students feel more confident and get better at math. In this class, students practice important basics like addition, subtraction, fractions, and geometry, which help them in other math classes. Students also learn everyday math skills they can use in real life, like math for shopping, measuring, or budgeting. The class includes activities, step-by-step practice, and real-life examples, and students get the support they need to learn at their own speed. The goal of the course is to help students grow, understand math better, and feel ready for future math classes. The student must be recommended by a teacher for this course.

Bridge to Math 1 is a preparatory course designed to support students as they build the skills and confidence needed for success in Math 1. Students engage in problem-solving activities that emphasize making sense of algebraic relationships, working with numbers and quantities, and representing ideas using tables, graphs, and equations. Students also strengthen collaboration, communication, and critical thinking skills as they explain their ideas and learn from others. Students will practice the following skills: algebraic expressions, integers, equations and functions, decimals, fractions, exponents, ratios, proportions, percents, area, and graphing.

Math 1 is a foundational high school course in which students develop algebraic reasoning while making connections across geometry, and statistics. Students work through rich problem-solving tasks that ask them to represent relationships using graphs, tables, equations, and words. Through exploration and discussion, students analyze patterns, compare solution strategies, and justify their thinking using mathematical language. The course emphasizes modeling real-world situations and interpreting data to make sense of quantitative information. Students regularly collaborate with peers, communicate their ideas clearly, and reflect on their problem-solving processes. Math 1 builds the skills and habits of mind needed for continued success in higher-level mathematics. Units of study include the following: Sequences, Linear & Exponential Functions, Equations, Inequalities & Systems, Geometric Transformations & Symmetry, and Modeling Data.

Math 2 builds on the concepts and problem-solving strategies developed in Math 1 as students deepen their understanding of algebra and geometry. Students explore relationships of quadratics, absolute value, piecewise functions and use multiple representations including graphs, tables, diagrams, and equations, to analyze and solve problems. Through investigations involving geometric reasoning, students examine similarity, right triangles, and spatial relationships to make sense of mathematical structure. The course emphasizes reasoning, justification, and strategic thinking as students tackle increasingly complex tasks. Students collaborate regularly, communicate their ideas clearly, and compare solution methods. Math 2 supports continued growth in mathematical confidence and prepares students for more advanced coursework.
prerequisites: Math 1

description: Geometry is a course where students analyze figures using diagrams, coordinate representations, and algebraic reasoning to solve meaningful problems. Through exploration and visual modeling, students examine similarity, congruence, and the properties of polygons and circles. The course emphasizes explaining and justifying reasoning, making connections between algebra and geometry, and applying ideas to real-world situations. Students collaborate, test conjectures, and refine their thinking through discussion and problem solving. Geometry develops spatial reasoning and logical thinking skills that support continued success in mathematics.
prerequisites: Math 1

description: Problem Solving is a course that helps students strengthen and apply mathematical skills across a range of content areas through rich, non-routine problems. Students engage in challenging tasks that require them to analyze situations, choose appropriate strategies, and reflect on the effectiveness of their approaches. The course emphasizes critical thinking, persistence, and making sense of unfamiliar problems rather than memorizing procedures. Students also practice test-taking strategies and learn how to approach SAT and ACT–style questions with confidence and efficiency. Through discussion and reflection, students refine their reasoning and communication skills. This course is recommended for juniors or seniors preparing for SAT or ACT assessments.
prerequisites: Math 2

description: Math 3 builds on the mathematical reasoning and problem-solving strategies developed in Math 1 and Math 2 as students engage with more complex and connected ideas. Students explore relationships between functions, analyze patterns, and use algebraic, geometric, and trigonometric reasoning to model and solve problems. Through investigations and real-world applications, students make connections across representations such as graphs, equations, diagrams, and data. The course emphasizes explaining thinking, justifying solutions, and evaluating the reasonableness of results. Students collaborate regularly and communicate their ideas clearly as they tackle challenging tasks. Math 3 prepares students for advanced mathematical study by strengthening both conceptual understanding and strategic problem solving. Units of study in Math 3 include the following: Inverse Functions, Logarithms, Polynomials, Modeling with Geometry, and Trigonometry.
prerequisites: Math 2

description: Advanced Mathematical Topics is an exploratory course in which students investigate a variety of advanced mathematical ideas through problem solving, modeling, and analysis. Students work with abstract and applied concepts to analyze patterns, represent relationships, and solve complex problems using multiple representations. The course encourages curiosity, persistence, and creative thinking as students explore less traditional areas of mathematics and make connections across topics. Technology, including graphing calculators, is used to visualize relationships and support mathematical reasoning. Students regularly explain their thinking, compare strategies, and refine their understanding through discussion and reflection. Advanced Mathematical Topics will examine the following math topics including: Combinatorics & Probability, Sequences & Series, Conics, and Polar Coordinates & Complex #’s. This course is appropriate for students who have completed Math 3 or higher-level math and are interested in deepening their mathematical experience.
prerequisites: Math 3

description: Pre-Calculus examines all math topics at a deeper level with a strong emphasis on using real-world Pre-Calculus is a course in which students deepen and connect their understanding of algebraic and trigonometric ideas in preparation for advanced mathematics. Students analyze functions, explore relationships between multiple representations, and use mathematical models to investigate real-world situations. Through problem solving and guided exploration, students strengthen their ability to reason abstractly, make connections across topics, and explain their thinking clearly. Technology, including graphing calculators, is used to visualize behavior of functions and support analysis. The course emphasizes persistence, strategic thinking, and collaboration as students tackle increasingly complex problems. The topics included in this course are linear relations and functions, systems of linear equations and inequalities, polynomial and rational functions, trigonometric functions, identities and equations, exponential and logarithmic functions. *Pre-Calculus prepares students for college-level mathematics and may be taken as a dual enrollment course through the Community College of Vermont if enrollment criteria are met.
prerequisites: Math 3
notes: Footnote *: may be taken as a dual enrollment course through the Community College of Vermont if enrollment criteria are met

description: Statistics is a course for students interested in understanding how data is collected, analyzed, and used to draw meaningful conclusions. Students analyze real-world data and situations, and interpret results using numerical, graphical, and written representations. Students will design a semester-long investigative project based on the core concepts of the course. The course emphasizes statistical reasoning, critical reading, and clear written communication as students evaluate claims and justify conclusions with evidence. Students regularly use technology, including graphing calculators, to model data and support analysis. Through discussion and reflection, students build skills that are valuable in research-based fields and everyday decision making. *This course prepares students for college-level statistics and may be taken as a dual enrollment course through the Community College of Vermont if enrollment criteria are met.
prerequisites: Math 2
notes: Footnote *: may be taken as a dual enrollment course through the Community College of Vermont if enrollment criteria are met

description: Calculus is a one-semester course taught in conjunction with AP Calculus, covering the first-semester topics in the sequence. Students explore limits, continuity, and the concepts of derivatives, derivatives of functions, real-world applications of derivatives, and integrals. Technology, including graphing calculators, is used to visualize and deepen understanding. The course emphasizes explaining reasoning, justifying solutions, and connecting ideas across mathematical topics.
prerequisites: Pre-Calculus

description: AP Calculus 1 (AB) is a college-level course designed for students ready to explore the fundamental ideas of calculus in depth. Students investigate limits, continuity, derivatives, and integrals through problem solving, and real-world applications. They learn to analyze functions, solve complex problems, and interpret results while justifying their reasoning using mathematical language. Students also develop strategies for approaching challenging tasks independently and collaboratively. AP Calculus 1 (AB) prepares students for success in AP exams and for future studies in science, mathematics, engineering, and other advanced fields.
prerequisites: Pre-Calculus and Summer assignments are required.

description: This course will focus on drama as a unique form of creative expression. A workshop approach will be used to increase students’ comfort with playwriting and acting. Students will work on their acting through established plays, acting games, and their own writing.

Students experience the process of learning a wide variety of band literature in varying musical styles. The ensemble performs in several concerts and parades. Students experience the process of improving technique, rhythm reading and sight reading in order to become more independent. Students have the opportunity to receive critical feedback on their individual performance as well as critique and reflect on their personal and their ensemble’s process and growth. Students are expected to participate in all performances which often occur in the evenings or on weekends.
prerequisites: Minimum two years of band experience or permission of the director.
notes: Offered During Compass

description: Students experience the process of learning a wide variety of choral literature in varying musical styles and languages including sacred and seasonal music. The ensemble performs in several concerts. Students experience the process of improving vocal technique, rhythm reading and sight singing in order to become more independent. Students receive critical feedback on their individual performance and critique and reflect on their personal and their ensemble’s process and growth. Students are expected to participate in all performances which often occur in the evenings or on weekends.
notes: Offered During Compass

description: This class provides introductory guitar lessons to students in a group setting. No prior experience is needed. Students experience the process of learning to tune guitar strings, change guitar strings and the fundamentals of guitar technique in order to perform during the semester. Students follow a guitar method book with different styles of music and accompaniment patterns. VUHS guitars are available for use, but students are encouraged to bring their own.

Students learn secondary instruments while continuing to experience growth on their primary instruments. They compose and arrange music designed to be played by small ensembles. Students experience the process of working toward a performance and reflect on their process and personal growth.
prerequisites: High School Symphonic Band

description: This course is designed to give students an understanding of the history of modern music and the ability to listen to music in an active and professional way. This course is designed for all students, including those who have little to no previous music experience. Music is presented with a historical perspective and emphasizes prominent composers, musical periods and styles. Students will get to learn about the origins of our current music, the development of electronic music and everything in between.

Students will learn the basics of how music really works and will be provided with the tools to write their own music. Students will study chords, melody, harmony, rhythm, counterpoint and part writing to understand, analyze and compose written music. In addition, students will get practice in ear training to better understand the music they listen to and recognize what is happening in both modern songs and classical compositions.

This class is designed to provide introductory piano lessons to students in a group setting. No prior experience is needed. Students experience the process of learning the fundamentals of piano technique in order to perform during the semester. They have the opportunity to create a short composition and reflect on their growth during the semester.
This class is a continuation of Piano Class I. Students further refine their piano technique and create a more advanced composition.
prerequisites: Piano Class I

description: This class is an exploration into production and creation of popular music through the medium of modern “rock” band for students in grades 9-12. Students will be provided with the opportunity to learn and grow in basic knowledge of guitar, keyboard, bass, drum set, vocals, and creation of music through a “rock” combo. This course is designed so that any level of student can be a part of the ensemble and directed towards growth on each of the instruments. (Students wishing to play instruments not listed above are still welcome to join.)

This course is designed for students who wish to improve their vocal technique and solo voice. They explore aspects of good posture, diction, breathing, and tone as well as study solo repertoire in classical, pop, and musical theater styles. Students have in-class coaching and performance opportunities and study sight-singing.
prerequisites: One year of Concert Choir or teacher permission

description: This class provides an introduction to music from around the world through drumming. Students will have the opportunity to play with the Vergennes African Drum Ensemble and learn the fundamentals of drumming on a number of different percussion instruments. Students will also learn the basics of reading music and the historical context for the music we perform.

course_name: Introduction to Life and Physical Science
description: This is a standards-based course focusing on creating scientifically literate students. Students will learn about topics in both physical and life science, basic laboratory skills, and other skills necessary to be successful in the science classroom. Topics range from the origin of our universe to cellular energetics. Ultimately students will gain a better understanding of the science they experience in their everyday lives and to help inform their future course selections. The majority of class assignments can be completed during class. Generally, outside work will only be required when students do not use class time effectively. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered include Systems, Energy, and Matter.
notes: Foundational course that supports access to future coursework, recommended for 9th graders (will be preselected for 9th grade students)

course_name: Biology: Anatomy and Physiology (formerly Human Biology)
description: This science course starts with cell structures and functions. Students will build microscope skills in order to identify cells and organelles. We will study each body system and focus on how healthy systems maintain homeostasis, while disruptions in homeostasis cause illness. Within each unit students will have freedom to explore diseases, build models, and practice lab techniques. Life is going to throw students “curveballs”; they or someone they love has been diagnosed with a disease and now students must learn about it and make a plan for supporting this person. This class requires use of class time and some time at home to finish assignments. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered include Systems, and Structure and Function.
prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

description: This course will explore ecosystems, including photosynthetic producers, food webs, invasive species, ecosystem dynamics, and biomes. Students will delve into key characteristics of living things, as well as specific traits of the diverse animal groups through reading, exploring local natural resources, and hands-on simulations. There are several choice-based projects for students to learn about topics of interest to them. This course emphasizes class work rather than homework, but work will need to be finished at home if class time isn’t used effectively. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered include Change Over Time, Stewardship, Energy, and Systems.
prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

description: This new course will offer students an opportunity to explore how DNA works. We will explore the fundamental principles of how inherited traits are passed down (genetics) and how these traits change over time in populations (evolution), as well as how scientists can manipulate DNA to alter both genetics and the course of natural selection. Key topics include the structure and function of DNA, protein synthesis, inheritance patterns, genetic variation, natural selection, and how these mechanisms drive speciation and other evolutionary processes. This course will require students to spend some time outside of class to finish assignments. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered include Systems, Structure and Function, and Change over Time.
prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

description: This course provides students with the opportunity to explore the important systems and processes that shape our planet, influence our lives, and inform environmental decision making. Major content knowledge will center around understanding the atmosphere, hydrosphere, and lithosphere as systems. Application of that content knowledge will be integrated into experiences with environmental stewardship. These experiences will include outside projects working with local invasive species, restoration ecology, and environmental testing. Workload emphasizes completion during class by fully engaged students and may involve finishing classwork, making outdoor observations, and collecting samples as homework. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered will include Systems and Patterns, and Stewardship.
prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

description: This class will cover topics in physics with an emphasis on establishing a strong conceptual understanding of content and basic math foundation. Application of content is embedded in connections made through hands-on experiences related to daily life and careers. Main topics will include motion, force, energy, waves, and electricity. Workload emphasizes completion during class by fully engaged students and will involve finishing as homework. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered will be Change Over Time, Matter and Energy, and Systems and Patterns.
prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

description: This class will introduce students to the fundamental content and skills related to the field of chemistry by emphasizing the establishment of a strong conceptual understanding and basic math foundations. Application of content is embedded in connections made through hands-on experiences related to daily life and careers. Main topics will include properties of matter and its behavior during changes. Workload emphasizes completion during class by fully engaged students and will involve finishing as homework. The VUHS Science Proficiency covered is Matter and Energy.
prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science

description: This laboratory science course is designed as a foundation for students interested in the future study of chemistry, a STEM profession, or medical profession. The first half of the course focuses on concepts concerning the classification of matter, atomic structure, and chemical bonding. The second half investigates increasingly specific conceptual and mathematical aspects of chemical behavior and chemical reactions. Laboratory work is an integral and frequent part of the course where students gain laboratory skills while experiencing hands-on connections to content. Routine homework will be expected as preparation for and extension of the classroom experience. The VUHS Science Proficiency covered is Matter and Energy.
prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science and successful completion of Math 2

description: This laboratory science course is intended for students that have a strong interest and aptitude for future study and/or application of science in STEM fields. The scope of topics will be those of a traditional physics course focusing on mechanics, waves, optics, electricity, and magnetism. An emphasis is placed on developing critical thinking and problem-solving skills through the application of mathematical and conceptual understanding of content. Labs and projects are inquiry based and allow students to discover fundamental relationships that govern the world around them. Routine homework will be expected as preparation for and extension of the classroom experience. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered will be Change Over Time, Matter and Energy, and Systems and Patterns.
prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science and successful completion of Math 3, or concurrent enrollment in Math 3 with a math teacher recommendation

description: This is a college-level laboratory course based on the Advanced Placement Biology curriculum. The course covers a wide variety of biology topics in great detail and thus will make demands of even the most dedicated students. Topics range from biochemistry, cells and genetics in the first semester, to evolution and ecology in the second semester. Summer work is meant to review basic chemistry content and give students a better understanding of the work level before the add/drop period. In addition to reading a college-level text, students will demonstrate understanding through a variety of written assignments, perform inquiry-based laboratory experiments, and prepare to take the AP test in May. Students should expect to commit a significant amount of time to this course’s workload. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered include Structure and Function, Systems, Energy, Matter, Change Over Time, and Stewardship.
prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science and either Wildlife Ecology; Introduction to Anatomy and Physiology; Genetics, Evolution, and Biotechnology; or Chemistry. Ms. Thompson’s signature on the course selection sheet is required. Summer assignments required.

description: This is a laboratory course based on the College Board AP Physics 1 curriculum. To be successful in this course, students must understand basic principles of physics, and demonstrate knowledge using critical thinking and reasoning skills. Key components of demonstration will be the ability to express thoughts mathematically, and conceptually through written language and calculation. Students need to be academically motivated, have a strong foundation in math, and have an interest in developing problem-solving skills. The course covers the full breadth of classical physics topics found in a first semester introductory algebra/trig-based college physics course. Consequently, students should expect to devote a significant amount of time studying material beyond the designated class time. VUHS Science Proficiencies covered will be Change Over Time, Matter and Energy, and Systems and Patterns.
prerequisites: Introduction to Life and Physical Science and successful completion of, or concurrent enrollment in, Pre-Calculus. Mr. Francis’ signature is required on the course selection sheet. Summer assignments required.

description: The human world around us is constantly changing. In World Geography and Cultures we are going to investigate the factors that have influenced change throughout the course of human history. We are going to begin our studies by being able to identify countries from many different continents, investigating world religions, and learning about how beliefs and values shape cultures. We will study concepts such as culture, civilizations, philosophy, nationalism, imperialism, and genocide. As we look at all of these larger pieces of the puzzle of world history we will look at how groups of people and individuals make change. Throughout this course, we will work on our analytical skills, by learning how to gather reliable sources, find accurate pieces of evidence and make solid claims. These skills will allow us to understand our world better and allow us to go out and become better world citizens.
notes: Foundational course that supports access to future coursework, recommended for 9th graders (will be preselected for 9th grade students)

description: Students focus on the major forces that contributed to the shaping and emergence of modern America and make connections to their own lives at the local, state, national and international levels. Students use historical inquiry methods to conduct research. They will understand the value of consulting both primary and secondary sources to help them gain an understanding of the history of the United States. Students use current technology to conduct and present their research.
fulfills_text: required for graduation (US History requirement)
notes: Recommended for 10th grade

description: In this century, it is critically important to not only be a citizen of one’s own nation, but to see the world as a global community. In this course students explore how the American identity and experience has been shaped—and will continue to be shaped—by a diverse array of cultural influences and traditions. Students compare and contrast social and political movements while investigating contemporary issues. Students look at how these issues impact local, state, national and global policies and laws. This class includes critical analysis of public issues and allows students to participate in research, discussion, debate and real-world experiences supporting the curriculum.
prerequisites: U.S. History
fulfills_text: required for graduation (Civics requirement)

description: This class provides students with the opportunity to better understand the world. Students will stay up to date on current issues via class discussion, research, and presentations. They will learn critical thinking skills, how to evaluate media bias, and how to discuss difficult topics respectfully. Students will be challenged to strengthen their opinions with evidence and explore multiple perspectives on a variety of issues.

This course introduces the scientific study of the human mind and behavior. Understanding the hidden drivers of human nature, from how we learn to how we handle stress, allows us to navigate our lives and relationships with greater empathy and insight. We will explore three major units: positive psychology, memory/learning, and social influence. You will participate in “psych-labs” to test theories of perception and analyze case studies of famous experiments. By the end of the term, you will be able to identify cognitive biases and interpret scientific research. Expect a mix of collaborative projects and multiple-choice assessments. While there is no heavy nightly racing, you will engage in daily experiments, film analysis, and classroom discussions. Some project work may require time outside of class. This is for anyone curious about people or considering careers in counseling, marketing, or healthcare. No prior science background is required. Just an open mind and a willingness to look at the world through a different lens.

Vermont History will provide students with learning opportunities to analyze and discuss the impact of major forces that contributed to the shaping of Vermont from the early geological era to the present. We will use primary and secondary sources to learn about our local community and the history of Vermont. Students will conduct research about local, historical topics and present their findings by writing small papers, and making maps and timelines. This course will help students understand how geography and historical impacts have impacted the state they now live in.

AP Government and Politics offers students an in-depth exploration of the American political system, emphasizing the foundations, institutions, policies, and processes that shape the U.S. government. This course covers the Constitution, federalism, civil liberties, political ideologies, interest groups, political parties, and the roles of the three branches of government. Students will analyze how citizens engage with the government through voting, activism, and public opinion. The course also highlights the impact of media and political behavior on policy-making. Through critical reading, discussion, and writing, students develop the skills needed to evaluate government actions and political developments. By preparing for the AP exam, students gain a comprehensive understanding of the political landscape, fostering informed citizenship and encouraging active participation in democratic processes.
prerequisites: Requires Social Studies teacher signature on course request sheet.
fulfills_text: Successful completion of this course fulfills the Modern Citizenship requirement

description: This course addresses the belief that now is the time for students to discover if any aspects of Engineering or Architecture could be part of their future. It presents the idea that know-how is not necessarily an intuitive ability. Students can begin to develop an operational knowledge of Engineering and Architecture by applying themselves to a disciplined course syllabus. While learning 3D software will expand students’ capacity to professionally present work, they must also bring a free expression of imagination and creativity to fully realize the opportunity this curriculum presents. Those who discover an interest in these fields are encouraged to enroll in the PHCC Engineering & Architecture Design Program during grades 11 or 12.

This course expands upon the concept that Engineering and Architecture precepts are a conveyable body of knowledge. Those who wish to further develop their understanding from CAD I will complete relevant assignments focusing on innovative design and systems analysis incorporating science, technology, engineering & math. This curriculum requires each student to propose, complete and present several Product Design Innovations. Students can continue to pursue their interest in these fields by enrolling in the Engineering & Architecture Design program at PAHCC.

This course is designed for students who have completed CAD I and CAD II and wish to progress and practice their skills on individual, self-directed projects. Students will further explore the advanced tools in the Key Creator, Chief Architect, and 3D printing software. Students may also choose to explore and learn introductory skills in other CAD software such as SketchUp, Revit, and AutoCAD360. Students must have excellent foundational CAD skills, and be self-motivated to create an individual path to progress their learning.

Equip yourself with the essential tools to thrive in a digital world. This course focuses on mastering everyday apps like the Google Suite while navigating the complexities of ethical AI use. Students gain troubleshooting skills to fix common tech issues and explore digital literacy. Additionally, students have the opportunity to apply design skills to create tangible products using tools like vinyl cutters and a glowforge lasercutter. Students leave with a versatile toolkit of practical digital skills for future success.

This course introduces the fundamentals of logic and design using LEGO Spike Prime kits. Students combine hands-on building with computer science, constructing mechanical attachments with LEGO Technic pieces to solve specific puzzles. You will explore modern problem-solving techniques, including an introduction to AI-assisted coding, to program robots to operate autonomously. The focus is on critical thinking, troubleshooting, and teamwork. This is a beginner-level course designed to build a foundation in computational thinking through trial and error.

Ever thought of starting your own business or being involved in the management of a small business? In this course students choose a reasonable business concept and write a real business plan detailing what it would look like to put their ideas into action. The business plan must clearly explain how the business will operate, the target market, and the financial situation. Students consider what technology can make this task easier or the final product better. The class visits with local business owners during the course. Students should be able to impress an admissions counselor, a potential employer, or even a lender with their completed business plan.
fulfills_text: This course is eligible to earn .5 Technology credit and .5 elective credit, or 1.0 elective credit. Please consult your school counselor for details.

description: In this course, students explore and complete various activities, challenges and projects based on STEM (Science Technology Engineering Math). STEM proficient students are able to answer complex questions and develop solutions for challenges and real-world problems while applying the rigor and relevance of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics content. The challenges are “hands-on” activities intended to develop and reinforce critical thinking and problem-solving skills.

Art Essentials is an introductory art course for students to learn the basics of two dimensional art. It is a prerequisite for every other high school art offering. In Art Essentials students will explore and experiment with a variety of artistic media and techniques as they study the elements of art (line, shape, value, space, texture, color and form). Each unit of study will focus on a different element of art through a variety of formative assignments with a final summative project highlighting students’ knowledge/skill in that element in a finished work of art for display. The majority of work will be done in class, but there will be biweekly sketchbook formative assignments for students to work on independently outside of class. All students who wish to take visual art should take Art Essentials as a starting point.

and dive deeper into painting. In this course students will expand on their basic drawing skills learned in Art Essentials. Students will improve their skills in observational drawing, shading, painting, color theory, and composition through still life drawing and portrait painting from a combination of life and photographs. Students will work with a variety of drawing and painting media, including but not limited to graphite, charcoal, colored pencils, and acrylic paint. The majority of work will be done in class, but there will be biweekly sketchbook formative assignments for students to work on independently outside of class.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Essentials
notes: Intermediate Drawing & Painting is an opportunity for students to push their technical drawing skills

description: Advanced Painting & Color Theory is designed for students looking to challenge themselves in painting and gain a more intimate knowledge and understanding of color. In this course students will learn advanced acrylic painting techniques. The majority of work will be done in class.
prerequisites: Successful completion of Art Essentials and Intermediate Drawing & Painting

description: This course offers students an excellent opportunity to grow as an artist while developing within a medium that increases technical proficiency. In this course students will explore forms of artistic digital media including digital illustration and stop motion animation on iPads. Class time will be spent learning the basics of digital illustration with Procreate, working on various assignments and learning how to incorporate layers, levels, and other editing tools into a wide variety of images and themes. Students will be introduced to the iMovie program while creating animated short videos.
prerequisites: Art Essentials

description: In this course, students will expand on the skills learned in Digital Media. Students will extend their learning in digital illustration, graphic design, and animation using a variety of creative programs to create more advanced and in depth, independent artistic projects. The majority of the work will be done in class once students have designed independent projects to work on and complete during the semester. This course is for students who have taken Digital Media and are looking for a new creative challenge
prerequisites: Digital Media

description: In this course students will create multiple types of additive sculpture with a variety of materials. They will explore 3-D design and learn how to build sculptures of humans, animals, buildings, and more. The work will all be done in class through design creation, review with the teacher through conversation, and the final build of the sculpture. This class is for students who have taken Art Essentials and would like to expand their artistic knowledge in 3-dimensional design.
prerequisites: Art Essentials

description: In this course students will have the opportunity to extend their learning from Sculpture . Each project will build off of the skills they gained in Sculpture and challenge them to build new skills. description: Dual Enrollment allows eligible students to earn both high school and college credit through approved college courses. Dual enrollment is one of several ways students may access college-level learning while enrolled at VUHS and is subject to a required planning and approval process. Students must have completed their sophomore year and receive prior approval from the School Counseling Office before enrolling in a dual enrollment course, whether using a state funded voucher or paying independently. Approval is based on readiness for college level coursework, progress toward graduation requirements, and the student’s overall academic plan. Dual enrollment is not automatic and cannot be arranged independently. Approved dual enrollment courses become part of both the VUHS high school transcript and the college transcript. Dual enrollment plans must be reflected in the student’s Personalized Learning Plan (PLP) as part of the graduation planning process. VUHS students most commonly participate in dual enrollment through the following Vermont institutions: ●University of Vermont ●Vermont State University ●Community College of Vermont ●Norwich University ●Saint Michael’s College ●Champlain College Availability, timelines, and course options vary by institution and by year. Students interested in dual enrollment should meet with their school counselor early in the planning process to review eligibility, required steps, and approved course options.

description: Vermont’s Early College Program is a full-year alternative to a student’s senior year of high school. Through this program, students complete their senior year of high school while earning some or all of their first year of college credits at the same time. College tuition is covered by the state of Vermont. Some Early College programs offer on-campus housing. Families and students are responsible for costs not covered by the state, including housing (if applicable), transportation, textbooks, and meals. Early College programs are available through the Community College of Vermont, Norwich University, and Vermont State University. Early College participation requires planning and school approval. Interested students should connect with their school counselor for guidance, eligibility review, and support with the application process.

description: Eligible seniors may apply to take a Middlebury College course at no cost. Enrollment is limited, and the timing of a Middlebury course may impact a student’s Vergennes Union High School schedule. To qualify, students must be prepared for college-level work, have successfully completed the highest-level coursework available at VUHS in the subject area they wish to study, and meet additional Middlebury College requirements. A three- or four-credit Middlebury College course counts as one credit toward high school graduation. Students do not earn college credit from Middlebury College, and the course does not transfer to other colleges or universities. Students interested in this option must meet with their school counselor for information about eligibility, additional requirements, and the application process. Applications are submitted in the spring of junior year for semester one courses and in December of senior year for semester two courses.

description: The Walden Year is an outdoor education program offered through The Willowell Foundation. Launched in fall 2024, the program acknowledges the history of The Walden Project, an outdoor learning program previously offered through Vergennes Union High School, and operates as a distinct and separate program. The Walden Year provides an interdisciplinary, immersive learning experience with a focus on environmental studies, writing, and philosophy. Inspired by Henry David Thoreau’s time at Walden Pond, the program emphasizes learning through sustained engagement with the natural world and supports student-centered, inquiry-based learning connected to individual interests and reflection. Doing so will prompt a meeting with a school counselor to determine whether this flexible pathway aligns with graduation requirements, learning goals, and individual needs. description: Student enrollment in Driver’s Education is limited to 20 students per class, and selection will be prioritized by student’s date of birth. A student must have a valid Vermont Learner’s permit on the first day of class. A proficiency grade will be issued for driver’s education. This course consists of five parts: ● Classroom component (at least 30 hours) which may be conducted in-person or remotely. ● Behind the wheel component (at least 6 hours), The B-T-W and observation time is done in the Driver education vehicle. ● Observation component (at least 6 hours) ● Parent/Guardian component (practice driving time). Parent component is 40 hours of supervised practice driving time of which 25 hours is during student enrollment in the Driver Education Course. ● Social Responsibility component (student’s attitudes and behaviors). Students are expected to follow appropriate GRCSU Health and Safety Guidelines, demonstrate self-respect to themselves and others, think before they act, accept responsibility for their actions, participate in group discussions and follow the rules in the school setting and outside on the road. If minimum attendance requirements are not met, the student will be dropped from the course. How is a student assessed? (Learning Target/Course Assessments) ● In the classroom phase, the student must score at least proficient on each unit discussed, and score at least 80 on the final exam. ● Students must show they are responsible citizens with socially responsible attitudes and behaviors. Attitudes and behaviors will have a bearing on whether students will receive a Driver Education Completion Certificate. ● In the driving phase, the student will have a driving route to practice various techniques and skills. ● Students will be given a mock final road test for their final drive. They must score at least 80% proficiency on the Driver Education Final Road Test. ● Parents will be required to attend a parent meeting or schedule an initial check-in meeting with the instructor. What will Driver Education students learn? (Enduring Understanding/Indicators) The classroom has nine units of knowledge and understanding. It includes but is not limited to the following: Getting ready to drive, understanding driver vehicle readiness, laws of the road, basic driving, maneuvers (parallel park, VT Turnaround, and hill start), managing risks, time and space, rural and city driving, interstate driving, impaired driving, distracted driving, use of the safety systems, physics and car crashes, biology and car crashes, adverse conditions, environmental issues, insurance, basic car and tire maintenance, and trip planning.

description: This course is the second half of Drivers Ed. The students will have an opportunity to see different college and career paths, and talk to speakers to gain a better understanding as to how they can take their education and transition into a career opportunity. Students will also take a look at goal-setting and the decision making process in order to better understand how decisions we make today can affect our futures. description: This course, designed in collaboration with Vermont State College System (VSCS), Vermont Agency of Education (AOE) and Vermont Student Assistance Corporation (VSAC), is a pilot course that is designed to ensure that seniors, who have studied math through Algebra II, are ready for college-level math after high school. This class will revisit essential concepts and skills from Numbers and Operations, Algebra, Functions, Geometry and Data and Statistics. Using hands-on problem-solving tasks, EMC2 will strengthen your foundational math skills, your critical-thinking skills, and give you a chance to show what you know through alternate assessment methods. This course emphasizes understanding of math concepts and not memorizing algorithms. You will engage in real-world applications and problem-solving tasks that require you to work with others and communicate your thinking process. Successful students will learn the math skills necessary to succeed in college and careers. The Vermont State College System (VSCS) has agreed that successful completion of this course will qualify students to enroll in credit bearing college math at any VSCS school without the need for remediation. description: The focus is on learning to construct and defend compelling arguments. Students will engage in civil discourse as they investigate rhetoric and its impact on culture through analysis of notable fiction and nonfiction texts, from pamphlets to speeches to personal essays. Through this analysis, students learn how speakers and writers persuade an audience to adopt their point of view. Students continue to develop more precise writing skills and write literary analysis, arguments, and narrative pieces, focusing on the skills of topic development, organization, diction/syntax, and the use of textual evidence. Grammar is reviewed through writing to emphasize the finer points of mechanics and word choice, and vocabulary is drawn from both the readings and from other sources. Students prepare for and participate effectively in a range of conversations to express their ideas and learn from/build on the ideas of others.
notes: Objective: To introduce the theory and practice of rhetoric, the art of persuasive writing and speech, and the value of informed citizenship.

Reading and writing activities in the course also deepen students’ knowledge and control of formal conventions of written language (Ex: vocabulary, diction, syntax, spelling, punctuation, paragraphing, genre). Course readings facilitate informed citizenship and thus increase students’ capacity to enter into consequential conversations after evaluating sources from all sides of a meaningful issue. Students will build awareness of a writer’s purposes, audience expectations, and subjects, as well as the way conventions and the resources of language contribute to effectiveness in writing.
